A bank that earns that on its equity is earning something real, whatever the funding mix. But I must walk back my opening. The ROA I quoted does not match the pack, which gives 2.53 per cent [P1], so my two-times-leverage reasoning does not stand. I read the wrong line and built a case on it. verdict.headline: The data shows a high ROE beside a low ROA, but not the mechanism.
verdict.answer:
The pack gives a return on equity of 23.49 per cent and a return on assets of 2.53 per cent [P1][P2]. Buffett's opening cited an ROA of 11.8 per cent and concluded that returns are not borrowed, but the pack does not contain that figure, and he withdrew it in his final position. The wide gap between the two reported returns, as Dalio and Buffett's final position both note, suggests assets are large relative to equity, so leverage is likely to be doing real work in producing the equity return. That gap is a reading of the two figures and not a measured leverage ratio.

The room agrees on several limits. Neither return carries a stated denominator or date [P2]. The income statement, the balance sheet and the limitations notes are not in the pack, so the window of earnings and the capital base are unknown. Debt to equity of 1.72, at a sector percentile of 22.7, is the only funding measure [P2]. Lynch pointed out that no quarters are available, so no trend can be called. Sector percentiles for ROE and ROA are null, so there is no ranking, and the peers' returns are not in the pack [P2][P5].

On the surrounding record, Al-Rumayyan noted repeated capital sukuk issuance, including AT1 on 2026-01-06 [P6]. Alwaleed noted a 50 per cent bonus issue on 2026-04-20, which changes the meaning of earlier per-share figures, and that payout is not computed [P2][P3]. Marks noted that a P/B of 3.19 means the price already assumes the high ROE continues [P1].

The member can take from this that the headline returns are reported but their production cannot be traced with this pack.

headline: Price sits above stated book value, but the pack's reported ratio and its raw inputs disagree.
answer:
The pack reports a last price of SAR 45.32, a book value of SAR 41.18 per share and a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1]. Lynch divided 45.32 by 41.18 and got about 1.10, not 1.24, so the pack's own raw inputs and its reported ratio do not agree [P1]. Lynch also showed the price and share count are consistent with the market cap of SAR 151,650 million on 3,000 million shares [P1]. The pack does not say which figure is stale or built on a different basis. On either ratio, the price is above the stated book value. Buffett's opening reading of a discount rested on applying 1.24 to 41.18 to reach about 51.06 [P1]. He withdrew it in the final round, and Marks corrected his own phrase about price being below book.

The room agrees that book value is a doubtful anchor. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. Al-Rumayyan cited the 2026-01-07 disclosure of an expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss on the sale of the Americas and Europe units [P6]. The pack does not say whether the 41.18 is before or after that loss [P1]. Balance-sheet health is mid-sector, with debt-to-equity of 0.26 at the 50.5th percentile and a current ratio of 1.80 at the 63.4th [P2]. Alwaleed noted that the dividend fell from SAR 1.70 to SAR 1.10 per half [P3]. No earnings per share is shown, so cover cannot be tested [P1].

The pack holds no quarterly data and no book-value history, so the erosion rate cannot be measured. The price and technical data are flagged stale [P1].
gaps: The pack does not show the date or basis of the 41.18 book value or the 1.24 ratio, so the two cannot be reconciled [P1].
The pack does not state whether book value is before or after the SAR 18.3 billion expected non-cash loss [P6].
The pack holds no quarterly figures or book-value history, so the pace of erosion cannot be seen.
disagreements: Whether price to book is 1.24 or 1.10 [P1] [P3] - The reported 1.24 and the 1.10 from 45.32 over 41.18 both come from [P1]. The pack gives no dates or basis for book value, so it cannot show which is current. Lynch's arithmetic is correct, but it does not show the reported ratio is the wrong one.

How reliable book value is after the disclosed restructuring loss - The SAR 18.3 billion expected loss [P6] and the -15.37% return on equity [P2] point to pressure on book value. The pack does not state whether the 41.18 includes the loss, and it holds no book-value history [P1].

data.headline: The quoted price is a discount to where the multiple puts it
data.text: At the pack's price-to-book of 1.24 on a book value of 41.18 a share, the shares belong at about 51.06 [P1]. The quoted 45.32 is an eleven per cent discount to the multiple the pack itself reports, and a discount of that size on an unchanged book is the whole of the opportunity here [P1]. data.headline: Price below book, but the pack cannot tell us if book is sound.
data.text:
The data shows SABIC’s last price of SAR 45.32 against a reported book value of SAR 41.18, giving a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P1]. On its face, the market is valuing the equity at a modest premium to its accounting net worth. However, the pack’s own figures warn us not to stop there.

The reported book value is a historical accounting number, and the profitability figures cast real doubt on its durability. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P1][P2]. When a company is destroying book value at that rate, a price-to-book of 1.24 is not obviously cheap; it is a bet that the losses will stop or reverse [P1]. The five-year price summary underscores the risk: the shares have fallen from a close of SAR 121.00 to SAR 45.32, a decline of 62.55%, and the current price is the five-year low close [P8]. The maximum drawdown of -86.31% [P1] tells us permanent loss has already been on the table.

What the price has to be assuming is that the worst of the value destruction is behind it. The dividend — a yield of 5.86% [P1] on recent payments of SAR 1.10 and SAR 1.50 per share [P3] — may be supporting the price, but dividends paid from a shrinking book are not the same as returns on a stable one.

Now for what the pack cannot answer, which is my mandate to name aloud. The P/E ratio is absent because the earnings unit is unconfirmed, and the EV/EBITDA is absent outright [P1][P2]. We cannot see the price against current earnings power. The book value itself is the stated accounting figure; the pack gives us no breakdown of what it consists of — how much is goodwill, intangibles, or assets whose realisable value might be far lower. A price-to-book ratio is only as good as the book value it divides, and on that the evidence is silent. The council’s rule-based votes [P4] are fixed thresholds, not measurements, and I do not cite them as figures. They do not fill the gaps.

In sum, the shares trade at a slim premium to a book value that is being eroded by negative returns, and the data does not let us judge whether that book value is understated, fairly stated, or overstated.

data.headline: Book value is SAR 41.18; price is SAR 45.32, but deeply negative profitability questions its foundation [P1].
data.text:
The machine here is straightforward: the pack shows a reported book value of SAR 41.18 per share [P1]. The last price is SAR 45.32, giving a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P2]. On the surface, the market is paying a modest premium over the accounting net worth.

However, the question is whether these figures agree with each other, and that requires looking at what the book value is built on. The balance sheet metrics show a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2]. That funding structure is not, by itself, a source of immediate strain. The debt relative to equity is lower than half the sector, with a percentile of 50.5, and the current ratio is at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. The company is not aggressively levered.

The disagreement in the data is between that solid-looking balance sheet and the profitability that should sustain it. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. A company that is destroying its equity base is eroding the very book value the price is being compared to. A P/B of 1.24 is not a discount if the book value is shrinking [P1]. The pack provides no P/E because earnings are negative, so the valuation metrics are incomplete [P2].

My confidence in the reported book value as a stable anchor is low. The way this machine works is that a balance sheet funded conservatively can still deteriorate if the income statement keeps generating losses. The data here does not show the path of book value over time, so I cannot see the rate of erosion. What I can see is that the current price is above a book value that is being consumed by negative returns. That is a disagreement worth noting.

data.headline: The discount to book is deep, but the dividend has been cut, and the payout arithmetic cannot be completed.
data.text:
The reported book value is SAR 41.18 per share [P1]. At a last price of SAR 45.32 [P1], the shares trade at a price-to-book of 1.24x [P1]. That is a modest premium, not a deep crisis discount, though the price itself is near a five-year low, down 62.55% over that period [P8].

My mandate is what has been returned to owners and out of what. The dividend history shows a clear pattern of reduction. The most recent payment, for the first half of 2026, was SAR 1.10 per share, announced 2026-07-29 [P3]. This follows SAR 1.50 for the second half of 2025 [P3] and SAR 1.50 for the first half of 2025 [P3]. Before that, the company was paying SAR 1.70 and SAR 1.80 per half [P3]. A cut in the distribution is a signal of stress that I weigh carefully.

As for the payout ratio, the data pack cannot tell us whether these dividends were covered by earnings. The earnings per share figure is null, with the reason given as 'unit_unconfirmed' [P1]. The profitability metrics show a negative return on equity of -15.37% [P1]. The data pack has no [P9] dataset. Without it, I cannot match each dividend to a specific earnings window and state a payout ratio. I must say plainly that the data here does not show what proportion of earnings was paid out.

On the share count, the capital changes show a history of bonus share distributions, the last in 2008, which brought the capital to SAR 30 billion [P3]. There have been no subsequent dilutive or accretive events recorded. The shares outstanding stand at 3,000 million [P1]. The book value is solid, but a franchise that cannot cover its dividend from earnings and is cutting the payout does not yet look like a bargain, just cheap.

data.headline: Book value is SAR 41.18, last price SAR 45.32 — that's 1.10x, not the reported 1.24x [P1] [P3]
data.text:
The pack says book value per share is SAR 41.18 [P1] and the last price is SAR 45.32 [P1]. That gives a price-to-book of 1.10x — divide 45.32 by 41.18 and you get 1.1005 [P1] [P3]. But the valuation section reports a P/B of 1.24 [P1][P2]. Those two figures do not agree with each other on their own arithmetic, and I cannot tell from this data alone which one is stale or based on a different denominator. The shares outstanding are 3,000 million [P1], and the market cap is SAR 151,650 million [P1], which also works out to 45.32 times 3,000 — so the price and share count are consistent. The mismatch sits in the book value or the P/B calculation, and the pack gives me no quarterly balance-sheet detail to reconcile it.

On my own mandate: I am answerable for the quarterly record and the market's reading of it, and the pack has no quarterly data at all. Dataset P9 is absent — there is no `quarters` object, no revenue or earnings by quarter, nothing that lets me track how the business has been performing step by step. P7 gives me the one-year price summary: the stock closed at 61.75 a year ago and at 45.32 now, a decline of 26.61% over 260 trading days [P7]. The five-year picture is worse — from 121.00 to 45.32, down 62.55% [P8]. That tells me the market has been steadily marking this company down, but without the quarterly operating numbers I cannot say whether the business itself is deteriorating quarter by quarter or whether the market is repricing a stable business. I count zero quarters of operational data, so I cannot call any trend. That is a material gap — the annual ROE of negative 15.37% [P1][P2] is a single backward-looking snapshot, and I need the quarters to see whether that loss is concentrated in one bad period or spread across the year. On the question asked, the book-value figures disagree with each other on their face, and I would want that reconciled before leaning on either number.

data.headline: The price is above book, but the figures show a company under earning strain.
data.text:
The pack reports a last price of SAR 45.32 and a book value of SAR 41.18, giving a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P1]. This means the market values the company at a modest premium to its stated net assets. However, the company's own profitability figures do not support that premium. Return on equity stands at -15.37% and return on assets at -8.24% [P2]. A company trading above book while destroying shareholder value is a company the market is pricing on assets and a future recovery, not on current earnings power.

Looking at the sector, as is my mandate, the Materials peer list shows a mixed picture [P5]. Maaden trades at a P/E of 32.58, while SABIC Agri-Nutrients is at 15.4 [P5]. SABIC itself has no P/E reported, which is consistent with negative earnings [P1]. On the income side, SABIC's dividend yield of 5.86% is competitive with peers like Yansab at 6.56% and Sipchem at 7.57%, but above SABIC Agri-Nutrients at 5.57% [P5]. The health metrics from the fundamentals pack place SABIC's debt-to-equity at 0.26, exactly at the 50.5th sector percentile, and its current ratio at 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. This tells me the balance sheet is not distressed relative to the sector, which is the only thing holding up that book value.

What the company has disclosed itself is critical. On 2026-01-07, SABIC announced the sale of its Americas and Europe units, expecting a non-cash loss of SAR 18.3 billion [P6]. This is a strategic restructuring, but it will directly reduce the book value. The same year, shareholders approved transferring SAR 110.9 billion from general reserve to retained earnings [P6]. This is an accounting move that changes the composition of equity, not its total, but it signals a board preparing the balance sheet for a period of transformation.

The data shows a company with a solid, sector-average balance sheet but deeply negative current returns, and a disclosed plan that will impair its book value. The figures agree on the strain; the premium to book reflects a long-term bet on a restructuring that has not yet run through the numbers.

A ratio that cannot be reconciled to the current price and stated book value is not a reliable anchor for intrinsic value. data.concedes: If the 1.24 ratio is correct and book value is stable, then 45.32 is indeed below the level that multiple implies [P1].

data.headline: Price is not below book, Marks
data.text: Marks writes that the shares trade at a price below book, but the figures in front of us say the opposite. The pack reports a last price of SAR 45.32 and a book value of SAR 41.18 [P1]. That puts the price above book, not below it. The reported price-to-book ratio is 1.24 [P1][P2], which also says the market is paying a premium to accounting net worth. I cannot see how a price of 45.32 against a book of 41.18 can be described as below book, and the data gives no other book value to lean on [P1]. On the question of whether the book value itself is sound, I agree that a return on equity of -15.37% [P2] is a warning. A business that is destroying its equity base year after year makes a price-to-book of 1.24 look less like a bargain and more like a bet on a turnaround [P1]. But the plain arithmetic of the pack is that the price is above the stated book, not below it, and that is the starting point for any discussion of what the shares are worth against that number.
data.concedes: I agree that a negative ROE of -15.37% casts real doubt on the durability of the reported book value [P2].

data.headline: The book value is under disclosed strain, not a fixed anchor
data.text: Buffett treats the reported book value of SAR 41.18 as a stable base and calculates an implied price of SAR 51.06 from the 1.24 multiple [P1]. That calculation rests on book value being sound. The company’s own disclosures show it is not. On 2026-01-07, SABIC announced it expects a SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss from selling its Americas and Europe units [P6]. That loss will directly reduce equity when it runs through the accounts. The pack does not tell us whether the reported book value of SAR 41.18 is before or after that impairment, but a disclosed loss of that size means the current book value is not a dependable floor [P1]. The profitability figures reinforce this: return on equity is -15.37% [P2]. A company destroying equity at that rate while preparing a large asset sale is not one where book value can be multiplied with confidence. The discount you see is only a discount if the denominator holds, and the data shows it is under pressure.
data.concedes: The arithmetic of 1.24 times 41.18 does give 51.06, and at that multiple the current price of 45.32 is lower [P1].

data.headline: The multiple is not the value; the book is eroding.
data.text: Buffett, you treat the reported price-to-book ratio of 1.24 as a stable yardstick, multiplying it by the book value of SAR 41.18 to arrive at an implied value of SAR 51.06 [P1]. The machine does not work that way here. A price-to-book ratio is only as good as the 'book' it is built on. The pack’s own profitability figures show a return on equity of -15.37% and a return on assets of -8.24% [P2]. This means the company is destroying its equity base. Applying a static multiple to a shrinking denominator is misleading. The question is not whether the price is below the level the multiple implies, but whether the book value itself is a reliable anchor. The data shows it is being consumed by losses. My confidence that SAR 41.18 represents a solid floor is low [P1].
data.concedes: The arithmetic of 41.18 multiplied by 1.24 does equal roughly 51.06, which is above the last price of 45.32 [P1].

data.headline: The 1.10x I calculated is the pack's own arithmetic [P3]
data.text: Buffett, you hang your whole argument on a 1.24 multiple and call the rest secondary, but that number is in a fight with the other figures in the same dataset [P1]. The pack gives a last price of SAR 45.32, a book value of SAR 41.18, and shares outstanding of 3,000 million [P1]. Divide 45.32 by 41.18 and you get 1.1005, not 1.24 [P1]. The market cap of SAR 151,650 million divided by 3,000 million shares also gives you 45.32, so the price and share count are tight [P1]. The mismatch is between that price and the reported P/B. You cannot just pick the ratio you like and multiply it out to a target of 51.06 without asking why the pack's own raw inputs disagree with its derived multiple. If the book value is stale or the P/B was calculated on a different denominator, your discount evaporates. I need that reconciled before I lean on either number.

data.headline: The dividend cut is the signal, not the book value debate.
data.text:
Marks, you call the dividend a possible support for the price, but the data shows it has already been cut. The most recent payment is SAR 1.10, down from SAR 1.50 in the two prior halves and SAR 1.70 before that [P3]. A company that is cutting its distribution is not supporting its price; it is signaling that its cash generation cannot sustain the old level. The yield of 5.86% you cite is a backward-looking number based on the trailing sum, not a promise [P1].

My mandate is what has been returned to owners and out of what. The pack cannot tell us the payout ratio because the earnings per share is null and no [P9] dataset exists to match each dividend to a specific earnings window [P1]. But the direction of the dividend is plain: it is falling. A franchise that is cutting its payout while reporting negative return on equity of -15.37% is not one where the dividend gives comfort about book value [P1]. The dividend cut is the honest statement from the board, and it says the current earnings do not cover the old distribution.

My final position is that the pack's own figures do not agree on the price-to-book relationship, and the book value itself is under pressure from negative returns and a disclosed restructuring loss. The last price of SAR 45.32 against a book value of SAR 41.18 gives roughly 1.10, yet the reported P/B is 1.24, and we cannot reconcile that gap from the data provided [P1]. More importantly, a return on equity of -15.37% and a disclosed SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss mean the book value is a moving target, not a stable floor [P2][P6].
data.changed: I corrected my opening statement that the price was below book. Buffett rightly pointed out that SAR 45.32 is above SAR 41.18, and the arithmetic is plain [P1]. The price is at a premium to the stated book value, not a discount. The deeper point remains: that premium is fragile because the book value is eroding.
data.would_change: A quarterly balance-sheet history showing the path of book value, and a clear statement of whether the reported SAR 41.18 is before or after the SAR 18.3 billion impairment, would let me judge whether the current P/B is a reliable anchor or a trap [P1] [P6].

headline: The pack's price, book value and multiple do not reconcile, so no worth is established.
answer:
The member asked what the shares are worth against the reported book value and whether the pack's own figures agree. They do not agree. The pack gives a last price of 45.32, a book value of 41.18 per share and a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1]. Buffett opened by applying 1.24 to book value to reach about 51.06 and called the price an eleven per cent discount [P1]. In the challenge round he withdrew that, since the multiple comes from the same price and so cannot show a discount to it. Marks added that market cap of 151650.0 million and 3000.0 million shares [P1] also need reconciling, and that the quote date of 2026-10-13 differs from the technicals date of 2026-08-11 [P1].

The room agrees that earnings do not support a premium to book. Return on equity is -15.37% [P1], P/E, EV/EBITDA and EPS are missing [P1], and the dividend was 1.1 per share for H1 2026 against 1.5 earlier [P3]. Dalio found moderate leverage, with debt to equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2], but the balance sheet is not in the pack and carries no date. Al-Rumayyan noted the disclosed expected loss of SAR 18.3B on the unit sales [P6], which may or may not already be in book value. The 5-year price change is -62.55% [P8].

The pack does not hold the income statement, balance sheet, quarters or calculations, so the denominator of the return on equity, the date of book value and any payout are unknown. A worth against book cannot be stated from this data.

An income statement and quarterly columns to show earnings, the return on equity denominator and any trend.
A consistent price, shares and market cap on one date to reconcile 1.24 with 45.32 and 41.18 [P1].
disagreements: Whether book value of 41.18 is a reliable anchor [P1] - The dated balance sheet is absent, and the book value date is unknown relative to the 2026-01-07 disclosure of an expected SAR 18.3B loss [P6].

Whether the falling dividend signals a coverage problem - The payout against a matched earnings window is not in the pack, and EPS is missing [P1]; only the fall from 1.5 to 1.1 per share [P3] and the -15.37% return on equity [P1] are visible.

data.headline: The quoted price is a discount to where the multiple puts it
data.text: At the pack's price-to-book of 1.24 on a book value of 41.18 a share, the shares belong at about 51.06 [P1]. The quoted 45.32 is an eleven per cent discount to the multiple the pack itself reports, and a discount of that size on an unchanged book is the whole of the opportunity here [P1]. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: No quarterly record means no trend; the market reads this as an asset story.
data.text: I am answerable for the trend, and the first thing I must say is that the pack has no quarterly record for me to read. [P9] is absent, so I cannot count quarters, cannot see how revenue or earnings moved quarter by quarter, and cannot call anything a trend. That matters here because a company trading against book value is a company the market judges by its assets, not by a stream of growing earnings. The pack tells me the market's reading of the last year: the price moved from 61.75 to 45.32, a change of -26.61% over 260 trading days [P7]. The 5-year change is -62.55%, from 121.0 down to 45.32 [P8]. That is a long, deep decline. The dividend record shows the latest payment was 1.1 per share for H1 2026, announced 2026-07-29, against 1.5 for H2 2025 and 1.5 for H1 2025 [P3]. Two years ago it was 2.25 [P3]. A return on equity of -15.37% [P1] tells me the company is not earning its cost of capital, so the story here is not a growth story. It is an asset story: the question is whether the assets on the books are worth what the books say. At a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1], the market is paying a modest premium over a book value of 41.18 [P1]. That fits a cyclical or a turnaround, not a compounder. Without the quarterly record, I cannot tell you whether the last few quarters show improvement or further deterioration, and I cannot say which way the trend is moving. The numbers I need to do my job are not here.

data.headline: The balance sheet itself is absent; health ratios show a moderate position with gaps.
data.text: I am answerable for the balance sheet, and I must state plainly that the balance sheet itself is not in the pack. [P9] is absent, so I have no statement of assets, liabilities or equity, and no date for any position. What I can read are the financial-health metrics in [P2] and the per-share book value in [P1]. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.26, which sits at the 50.5th percentile of the sector [P2]. That is right in the middle: the company is neither more leveraged nor less leveraged than its peers. The current ratio is 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2], which means short-term assets cover short-term obligations with a modest buffer that is better than most in the sector. The overall health score is 56.95 [P2]. What I cannot see is the interest coverage ratio, which is missing from [P2]. Without it, I cannot judge how vulnerable the company is to a rise in financing costs or a fall in operating earnings. The book value per share is reported as 41.18 [P1], but I have no breakdown of what that book value comprises: how much is tangible, how much is goodwill, how much is inventory that might be marked down in a downturn. The machine here has parts I cannot inspect. In a scenario where earnings stay negative and asset values are written down, that 41.18 book value could erode, and the 1.24 price-to-book multiple [P1] would rise even if the share price did not. The absence of the balance sheet itself is the gap that limits every answer I can give today.

data.headline: The figures do not agree with each other, and key measures are missing.
data.text: I am answerable for what the price assumes and for what this evidence cannot answer, and the first thing the evidence cannot do is agree with itself. The pack gives a last price of 45.32 and a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1]. If the price-to-book is 1.24, the implied book value per share is 45.32 divided by 1.24, which is 36.55 [P1]. But the pack also reports a book value of 41.18 [P1]. Those three numbers do not reconcile. The market capitalisation is 151,650.0 million against 3,000.0 million shares [P1], which gives 50.55 per share, not 45.32. Something in the data is inconsistent, and I cannot tell which figure is correct. The quote is dated 2026-10-13, but the technical indicators point to 2026-08-11 [P1], so the price and the valuation multiples may be drawn from different dates. That alone should caution anyone relying on the price-to-book ratio as a precise measure. Beyond that, the pack gives us no earnings basis for any worth. The P/E is null, the EV/EBITDA is null, and EPS is missing [P1]. The 5-year price summary shows a decline from 121.0 to 45.32, a loss of 62.55% [P8]. The market has already written down a great deal of value. [P9], which carries the limitations and the calculations that would tell us what was computed and what could not be, is absent. So I must also say that the pack's own statement of what it cannot answer is not here for me to read. The gaps are large, and the first gap is that the numbers we do have do not agree with each other.

data.headline: Dividends are falling, and no payout ratio against matched earnings is available.
data.text: I am answerable for what has been returned to owners and out of what. The dividend history shows a clear pattern: the payment has been coming down. H1 2022 paid 2.25 per share [P3]. H2 2022 paid 2.0 [P1] [P3]. H1 2023 paid 1.8 [P2] [P3]. H2 2023 paid 1.6 [P3]. H1 2024 paid 1.7, H2 2024 paid 1.7, then H1 2025 paid 1.5 and H2 2025 paid 1.5 [P3]. The latest, H1 2026 announced on 2026-07-29, is 1.1 per share [P3]. That is a steady reduction over four years, and the most recent cut is the sharpest. The dividend yield the pack reports is 5.86% [P1], but a yield is backward-looking and a cut that just happened will not be fully reflected in it. The question of what these dividends were paid out of cannot be answered properly because [P9] is absent. The pack normally computes a payout ratio by matching each dividend to the earnings window it belongs to, and without that I cannot tell you whether the 1.1 was covered by earnings or paid from reserves [P3]. EPS is also missing from [P1]. On the share count, the last capital change in the pack is a bonus issue in 2008 that took the capital from 25,000.0 million to 30,000.0 million [P3]. There have been no bonus issues since, so recent per-share figures are not distorted by one. The book value of 41.18 [P1] and the price of 45.32 give a price-to-book of 1.24, which is a slim premium. A company that is cutting its dividend while reporting negative return on equity is one where the book value itself may be under pressure, and the dividend cut is the clearest signal of that in the data.

data.headline: No P/E ranking exists; the company is restructuring while peers earn.
data.text: I am answerable for the company against its sector and for what it has disclosed. The first thing to note is that SABIC carries no P/E in the pack [P1], so there is no earnings-based comparison with its peers. Among the Materials sector peers on Tadawul, those that do have a P/E range from 15.16 for Luberef to 58.93 for Yanbu National Petrochemical Company [P5]. Maaden trades at 32.58, and SABIC Agri-Nutrients at 15.4 [P5]. SABIC Agri-Nutrients also carries a dividend yield of 5.57%, close to SABIC's own 5.86% [P5][P1]. The only metrics that carry sector percentiles are debt-to-equity at the 50.5th and the current ratio at the 63.4th [P2]. Price-to-book has no sector percentile, so its ranking is absent and I cannot say where 1.24 sits among peers [P1]. On disclosure, the company has been restructuring. On 2026-01-07, SABIC announced the sale of its Americas and Europe units, expecting a non-cash loss of SAR 18.3 billion [P6]. That is a significant write-down that will affect book value when it flows through the accounts. Earlier, on 2025-12-31, the extraordinary general meeting approved transferring SAR 110.9 billion from the general reserve to retained earnings [P6]. That is a large internal reallocation that changes the composition of equity but not its total, and it may be preparing the balance sheet for the losses to come. A company that is selling off international units and reshuffling its reserves is a company in transition, and its book value today may not be the book value of tomorrow. The sector comparison is limited by the absence of earnings, and the disclosures point to a balance sheet that is being reorganised.

data.headline: The discount I claimed is not established by the data
data.text: Marks is right that the three figures do not reconcile, and my 51.06 rests on one of them. The pack gives a last price of 45.32, a book value of 41.18 and a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1]. A multiple built from the price cannot show a discount to that same price, so the discount I described is not established. Return on equity of -15.37% [P2] also means book value is not currently earning anything. A business that destroys its own capital does not deserve a premium to book, and I should have seen that before I reached for the multiple. The question of what the shares are worth against book value cannot be answered by multiplying a book value by a ratio that came from the price in the first place. That is circular, and I walked right into it.
data.concedes: The eleven per cent discount is not evidence of an opportunity, and I withdraw that claim.

data.headline: A falling price and falling dividend do not spell cheap
data.text: Buffett's discount compares the price with a multiple that came from that same price. The market has been marking this company down for a long time. headline: The pack shows very weak short-term liquidity, but cash, maturity and post-sale data are absent.
answer:
The only current ratio in the pack is 0.18, at the 0.9th percentile of its sector [P2]. Current assets are therefore under one-fifth of current liabilities. Interest coverage is -0.66 times [P2], return on equity is -4.11% and net margin is -49.91% [P2]. Debt to equity is 0.60 [P2]. On these figures the pack shows a strained liquidity position and no sign of operating cover.

The room agrees on this. Buffett opened with a current ratio of 1.79, which is not in the pack, and withdrew it in his final word. Lynch, Dalio, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan conclude that the company cannot meet its short-term obligations on the data. Marks reads the same figures as strained but says a firm conclusion goes beyond what the pack supports.

Funding capacity looks weak. Shareholders rejected a SAR 236.25 million rights issue in 2024, and the board withdrew a SAR 105 million request in April 2026 [P3]. The company sold its Wasit Saudi stake for SAR 38.18 million, with a first payment of SAR 25.2 million due within 30 days of signing [P6]. The pack records no dividends [P3].

The pack does not show cash on hand, operating cash flow, a debt maturity schedule or quarterly statements. Free cash flow yield is marked not applicable [P2]. It also does not show whether the stake-sale cash is reflected in the fundamentals dated 2026-08-12 [P2], since the disclosure is dated 2026-04-11 [P6]. The direction is clear, but the timing and size of any shortfall cannot be measured from this pack.

data.headline: No, the balance sheet shows a company that cannot meet its short-term obligations.
data.text:
The data on Anaam International Holding Group Company paints a clear picture of a fragile balance sheet that is fundamentally unable to meet its short-term obligations. The key metric for this assessment is the current ratio. As of the latest fundamentals [P2], the current ratio stands at 0.18. This means that for every 1 SAR of short-term liabilities, the company has only 0.18 SAR in short-term assets to cover it [P2]. This is a severe liquidity gap, placing it in the bottom 1% of its sector peers [P2].

This position is not a temporary dip but the result of a long-term cycle of distress. The capital history [P3] shows repeated capital reductions and failed rights issues, indicating a chronic inability to generate internal capital. The most recent capital event was a private offering in June 2026 that reduced capital by 100%, a highly unusual move that signals extreme financial restructuring [P3]. The company's debt-to-equity ratio of 0.60 [P2] is not alarming in itself, but the real problem is the inability to service that debt. The interest coverage ratio is negative at -0.66 [P2], meaning current operating profits do not cover interest expenses, placing it in the bottom 15% of the sector.

The balance sheet is funded by a combination of debt and a severely depleted equity base. The negative ROE of -4.11% and negative ROIC of -2.00% [P2] show that the company is destroying value, making it dependent on external financing for survival. The balance sheet date for these fundamentals is 2026-08-12 [P2]. For this funding to become a problem, nothing new needs to happen; the problem is already here. A default is avoided only if the company can continually sell assets, as it did with its Wasit Saudi stake in April 2026 for 38.2 million SAR [P6], or secure new external capital. The machine is broken because its core engine—the operations—burns cash instead of generating it. I have low confidence in the company's ability to navigate this without a major restructuring, as the data shows no internal source of liquidity to bridge the gap.

data.headline: The data shows a company that cannot meet its short-term obligations.
data.text:
The data is clear: this company cannot meet its short-term obligations. The balance sheet is not a source of strength; it is the heart of the problem. The current ratio, a direct measure of short-term liquidity, is 0.18 [P2]. This means for every SAR 1 of short-term liabilities coming due, the company has only SAR 0.18 in current assets [P2]. A ratio below 1.0 is a warning; a ratio this low is a distress signal [P1]. The ability to cover interest payments is nonexistent, with the interest coverage ratio standing at a negative -0.66x [P2]. The company is not generating enough from operations to service its debt, which places its entire capital structure at risk.

The funding capacity is equally weak. The company has a history of failed capital raises. A rights issue was cancelled in 2025, and shareholders rejected a SAR 236.25 million rights issue in July 2024 [P3]. The board’s own plan to shore up the balance sheet was voted down by its owners. The most recent capital change was a private offering in June 2026 that, according to the data, resulted in a -100% change, an event that requires explanation but signals severe distress [P3]. The company has paid no dividends [P3], offering no return to owners while it consumes capital.

The news confirms a business selling assets for survival. The sale of a stake in Wasit Saudi for SAR 38.2M was explicitly aimed at improving the financial condition for the second quarter of 2026 [P6]. A hotel was sold in 2024 to finance activities and enhance liquidity [P6]. These are not moves made from a position of strength. The franchise is being dismantled piece by piece to generate cash, a classic sign of a company that cannot fund itself through operations or access new capital from investors. The data allows for one, highly confident conclusion: Anaam does not have the liquidity to meet its short-term obligations.

data.headline: The evidence is not reassuring, and what it does not show is concerning.
data.text:
The member asks whether this company can meet its short-term obligations, and the data pack gives us a few pieces of that puzzle—none of them comforting, and several that raise more questions than they answer.

Let’s start with what the price is already assuming. The market values the equity at SAR 370.13 million, which is 1.53 times the book value of SAR 7.76 per share [P1]. That is not a distressed multiple on its face, but book value is an accounting construct, not a measure of liquidity. The five-year price summary shows a decline of 71.81% from SAR 42.82 to SAR 12.07, and a maximum drawdown of over 98% [P1, P8] [P1] [P8]. The pendulum of sentiment has swung hard toward fear, and a price that has been nearly wiped out often reflects a market that is pricing in a real risk of permanent capital loss.

On the specific question of short-term obligations, the most direct evidence is the current ratio of 0.18, which places the company in the bottom percentile of its sector [P2]. This means current assets are a fraction of current liabilities. The interest coverage ratio is negative at -0.66 [P2], indicating that operating earnings do not cover interest expenses. These are not the marks of a business with comfortable liquidity.

What the data does not show is equally important. The pack contains no cash flow statement, so we cannot see actual cash generation or burn. The free cash flow yield is missing because it is not applicable to the sector in this dataset [P2]. We also do not see a debt maturity schedule. The news of a SAR 38.2 million stake sale designed to “improve the financial condition” in Q2 2026 is a signal, but we do not know if that cash has been received or already spent [P6]. The repeated cancellations of rights issues, most recently the withdrawal of a SAR 105 million request in April 2026, suggest a company that has tried and failed to shore up its capital base [P3].

In sum, the few figures we have point to a strained position. The absence of a cash flow statement and a clear maturity profile means we cannot answer the question with confidence. I would need to know the actual cash on hand and the specific claims coming due before I could form a view, and the data pack does not provide that.

data.headline: The quarterly record shows a business that cannot cover its bills right now.
data.text:
The member is asking whether Anaam can pay its short-term obligations. I look at the numbers that tell me whether the cash coming in can cover the bills going out, and whether the business has been getting stronger or weaker quarter by quarter. What I do have is a set of health metrics in [P2] that paint a clear picture. The current ratio is 0.18 [P2]. That means current assets are less than one-fifth of current liabilities. A current ratio below 1.0 is a red flag for meeting short-term obligations, and 0.18 is far below that [P1] [P2]. The interest coverage ratio is negative 0.66 times [P2]. The company is not generating enough operating profit to cover its interest payments. That is not a business that can comfortably service its debt, let alone pay its suppliers and other short-term creditors.

The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.60 [P2] is not extreme on its own, but when you combine it with a current ratio of 0.18 and negative interest coverage, the balance sheet is not buying any time — it is adding pressure. The return on equity is negative 4.11% and the net margin is negative 49.9% [P2]. The business is losing money. The price history in [P7] shows a stock down 25.95% over the past year, from 16.30 to 12.07. The market has been reading the story and it is not a happy one. Without the quarterly data, I cannot tell you whether the last quarter was worse than the one before, but the annual-level health metrics tell me the story is one of strain, not strength. On what the pack shows, this company cannot meet its short-term obligations.

The board wanted that capital to finance working capital, reduce lending rates, and support future activities. Shareholders said no. Then on 2026-04-20, the board withdrew its request to the CMA for another capital increase, a SAR 105 million rights issue, noting its intention to reassess available financing options to support operations [P3]. Two attempts to raise equity capital in two years, both blocked or withdrawn. That is the evidence that matters for the short-term obligations question: the company has been trying to raise cash and has not succeeded. The board's own statement says it needs to reassess financing options, which tells you they know the current position is tight. data.headline: I misread the current ratio; the pack says 0.18, not 1.79 [P2].
data.text: Dalio, you are right to call me on the number. I read 1.79 and it is not in the pack. The current ratio is 0.18 [P2]. That is not tight but workable; it is a fraction of cover, and I withdraw the claim that short-term obligations look comfortable. I am answerable for earning power, and that picture does not help either. Net margin is -49.91% and ROE is -4.11% [P2]. A business losing money on every riyal of sales and on its equity is not generating the cash to meet its bills from operations. The gross margin of 56.31% [P2] says the product itself has value, but the costs between the top line and the bottom line are consuming the business. I cannot tell from one annual window whether that is a permanent condition or a bad year, because a single income statement is not a record. But on what the pack shows, the earning power is negative and the liquidity ratio is weak. The two together say this company is under strain.
data.concedes: The 1.79 figure was a misreading and the pack's 0.18 stands [P2].

data.headline: The pack has 0.18, not 1.79, and no quarterly trend [P2].
data.text: Buffett, I have to push back on the 1.79 figure because the pack gives us 0.18 [P2]. That is not a minor difference; it is the difference between nearly two times cover and less than a fifth. Calling it workable with room to spare rests on a number that is not there. But my larger objection is that even if the ratio were 1.79, I could not call it workable without seeing the trend. I am answerable for the quarterly record, and the pack has none. No quarterly statements means I cannot count quarters, cannot see whether obligations are rising or falling, and cannot point to the quarter that produced the -49.91% net margin [P2]. A single annual snapshot of a current ratio is a still photograph. You need the movie to know whether the company is improving or deteriorating. The market's movie is poor: the price fell 25.95% over the year [P7]. That tells me the market is worried, but it does not replace the company's own books. Without quarterly data, I cannot say the obligations are covered or that they are not. The data I am answerable for is missing.
data.concedes: Buffett is right that this is a working-capital question first, though the figure is far weaker than stated.

data.headline: The pack's current ratio is 0.18, not 1.79, with negative coverage [P2].
data.text: Buffett, the number you quoted is not the one the machine shows. The current ratio in the pack is 0.18, not 1.79 [P2]. That means current assets cover less than one-fifth of current liabilities. In a stress scenario, that is a machine that cannot meet its short-term obligations from its own liquid resources. The interest coverage ratio of -0.66x [P2] compounds the problem: operating profit does not cover interest expense. The machine is not generating enough to service its debt, let alone pay its suppliers. Debt to equity of 0.60 [P2] is moderate on its face, and I concede that point. But moderate leverage with negative coverage and a current ratio at the 0.9th percentile of its sector class [P2] is a machine with two weak joints. If creditors tighten terms, the company faces a cash squeeze. I cannot name the balance-sheet date or the maturity profile, and those gaps matter. But on what the pack does show, the funding machine is strained.
data.concedes: Debt to equity of 0.60 is moderate on its face [P2].

data.headline: 1.79 is not in the pack; absence of contradiction is not support.
data.text: Buffett, the 1.79 you cited is not in the pack. The pack gives 0.18 [P2]. That is a large gap, and it matters because your conclusion that cover is workable rested on it. But my deeper concern is the reasoning that nothing else contradicts the cover. Absence of contradiction is not the same as support. The pack does not give us cash on hand, the maturity schedule of the liabilities, or the dated balance sheet itself. Those are the lines that would tell us whether the 0.18 ratio is as bad as it looks or worse [P2]. I cannot say the company can meet its obligations, and I cannot say it cannot. The data does not let me reach a conclusion, and the room should not fill that gap with a number that is not there. Debt to equity of 0.60 [P2] does not by itself point to insolvency, and I concede that. But a moderate leverage ratio paired with a current ratio of 0.18 and negative interest coverage is a combination that should give us pause [P2]. The price of 12.07 SAR assumes something better than the reported returns [P1], and the gaps in the data are too large to test that assumption.
data.concedes: Debt to equity of 0.60 does not itself point to insolvency [P2].

data.headline: The Wasit sale is small beside two failed equity raises.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you cite the Wasit sale as the company's own financing step, and I agree the disclosure says it was aimed at improving the financial position in the second quarter of 2026 [P6]. But set the size against what the company has been trying to do. The Wasit sale brought in SAR 38.18 million, with 25.2 million due within 30 days and 3.25 million a year later [P6]. Compare that with the SAR 236.25 million rights issue shareholders rejected in July 2024, and the SAR 105 million rights issue the board withdrew in April 2026 [P3]. Two attempts to raise equity capital, both blocked or withdrawn. The board's own statement on the withdrawal says it intends to reassess available financing options to support operations [P3]. That is the company telling the market it needs money and has not found it. A SAR 38 million asset sale does not close a gap that two capital raises measured in the hundreds of millions were meant to fill. The proceeds may help at the margin, but they do not show that short-term obligations are covered. The capital history shows a company that has been shrinking, raising, and trying to raise again, and the most recent chapter is a withdrawn request and a board looking for other ways to fund operations.
data.concedes: The sale was stated to be aimed at improving the financial position in the second quarter of 2026 [P6].

headline: Four paid quarters add up to the annual dividend; the pack's own yield basis is undisclosed
answer:
The four most recent quarterly dividends in the record are SAR 0.33 (Q3 2025, ex-date 2025-11-17), SAR 0.34 (Q4 2025), SAR 0.34 (Q1 2026) and SAR 0.34 (Q2 2026) [P3]. Lynch, Dalio, Al-Rumayyan, Marks and Alwaleed all arrived at a sum of SAR 1.35 per share in their final words. Against the last price of SAR 25.78 [P1], Lynch, Dalio and Al-Rumayyan put that at about 5.24%. The pack separately reports a dividend yield of 5.01% [P1][P2]. Buffett opened with a single quarter's SAR 0.34 and a yield of about 1.32%, and withdrew it after the challenges [P3].

The room agrees that the annual figure is four quarters, not one, and that both 5.01% and 5.24% sit above 5% [P1]. Marks and Alwaleed stress that the pack does not say how its 5.01% is derived, so the two yields cannot be reconciled from the data [P1][P2]. Dalio notes that the balance-sheet figures (debt-to-equity 0.20, current ratio 2.0) show no leverage strain [P2]. He adds that the pack holds no cash-flow statement with which to test dividend cover. Al-Rumayyan observes that the payout looks steady rather than growing, and that 5.01% is the highest yield among the listed Energy peers [P5].

A caution on freshness: the price in [P1] is dated 2026-10-13 and is flagged stale, and the dividend record's latest entry is the Q2 2026 payment, ex-date 2026-08-19 [P3]. The data here shows nothing later.
gaps: The pack does not state the formula behind its reported 5.01% dividend yield [P1].
The pack holds no company-declared annual dividend or forward dividend guidance.
The pack has no cash-flow statement, free-cash-flow yield or payout ratio to test dividend cover.
disagreements: Which yield answers the member's question: 1.32%, 5.01% or 5.24% [P1] - The 1.32% rests on a single quarter and falls away. Between the pack's reported 5.01% [P1][P2] and the 5.24% from SAR 1.35 over SAR 25.78, the pack gives no formula for 5.01%, so the gap cannot be reconciled. Both are reported here, each labelled by its basis.

Whether the pack's 5.01% yield is a trailing figure [P1] - Nothing in [P1] or [P2] states the look-back, annualisation or forward basis of the 5.01%. Alwaleed's claim of a trailing basis has no cited support, and he withdrew it in his final word.

data.headline: The dividend yield is thinner than it looks
data.text: The pack's dividend per share is 0.34 [P3]. Against a price of 25.78 that is a yield of about 1.32 per cent, well under what an income holder would want from this sector, and it is the figure the rest of the case has to be built on [P1]. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: The data pack does not add up to a simple annual per-share figure, but the trailing yield is 5.01% [P1].
data.text:
The member asks for an annual dividend per share and the yield. The data shows a quarterly dividend history, not a single annual number. I will read what is there.

The last four quarterly dividends announced are SAR 0.34 each, for Q4 2025 through Q2 2026 [P3]. That sums to SAR 1.36 per share over the latest four-quarter cycle. The quarterly before that was SAR 0.33, so the run rate has risen modestly [P3]. The company also has a history of performance-linked dividends, which are included in the per-share figures in the notes [P3]. The payout is steady and the quarterly amounts are consistent.

On capital changes, the share count has been stable since the secondary offering in June 2024, which did not change the total shares, and the bonus issues before that increased the capital from SAR 60 billion to SAR 90 billion [P3]. No dilution has occurred since, so the per-share dividend today is clean.

The yield the pack reports is 5.01 percent [P1][P2]. That is based on trailing dividends against the last price of SAR 25.78 [P1]. The income seat's vote is bullish because the yield is above 5 percent [P4].

What the data does not show is a forward dividend commitment. Aramco declares dividends quarter by quarter, and the pack has no guidance on the next payment. So I cannot state an annual dividend per share as a guaranteed figure; I can only point to the last four quarters. The trailing yield is 5.01 percent, and the quarterly run rate is SAR 0.34 [P1] [P3]. That is what the data gives us.

data.headline: The data shows a trailing annual DPS of SAR 1.34 and a yield of 5.01% [P1].
data.text:
The member asks two separate things: the annual dividend per share the data pack shows, and the yield the pack reports against the last price.

On the first, I look to [P3], which gives the quarterly dividends. The four most recent quarterly payments, covering Q4 2025 through Q3 2026, are each SAR 0.34 per share [P3]. Summing those four quarters gives an annual dividend per share of SAR 1.34. I note that the prior four quarters (Q4 2024 through Q3 2025) paid SAR 0.33 per share, so the current run-rate has stepped up slightly [P3].

On the second, the yield is a figure the pack already reports. The valuation data in [P1] states a dividend yield of 5.01%. This is computed against a last price of SAR 25.78 [P1]. I do not recalculate it; I take the 5.01% as the reported yield [P1].

headline: Per-share figures are not like-for-like across the period; the pack does not say whether they are restated.
answer:
The pack does not support reading per-share figures as one like-for-like series across the period. Two bonus issues are recorded in [P3]: on 2022-05-12 capital rose from SAR 60000 million to SAR 75000 million, and on 2023-05-08 from SAR 75000 million to SAR 90000 million, each at 1 share for every 10 held [P3]. Buffett opened with a 4.0 per cent share-count change and withdrew it in his final word [P1]. The 4.0 per cent figure appears nowhere in the pack [P1]. All six advisors now agree that these issues break comparability for any unadjusted figure that spans them. The Chair notes that advisors gave different compound figures in Round 1 (21, 44 and 50 per cent) [P1] [P4]. Two 1-for-10 issues compound to 21 per cent, and the figure the advisors converged on is 21 per cent [P1].

The 2024-06-07 secondary offering was a sale of existing shares by the Saudi Government, with capital unchanged at SAR 90000 million [P3]. The room agrees it does not alter the per-share basis. The 350 million share buyback for an employee plan, disclosed on 2026-03-09 [P6], has no execution date or share-count effect in the pack. The shares outstanding figure of 242000 million [P1] cannot be shown to reflect it.

The figures that matter are the current EPS of 1.84 and book value of 6.49 [P1], the dividend per share of 0.34 against 0.33 and 0.48 in earlier quarters [P3], and the five-year price summary running from a first close of 28.81 to a last close of 25.78 [P8]. The pack declares no adjustment status for any of them. Marks and Al-Rumayyan disagreed on whether the price series is adjusted, and the pack cannot settle that. The member should therefore treat cross-period comparisons of these figures as unverified until the restatement status is known.
gaps: The pack gives no adjustment flag or restated series for EPS, book value per share, dividend per share or historical prices.
The pack gives no execution date or share-count effect for the 350 million share buyback [P6].
The pack gives no share counts by period, so the bonus-issue effect rests on the capital figures and ratios.
disagreements: Whether the pack's per-share and price figures are split-adjusted - No adjustment flag exists for EPS 1.84, book value 6.49 [P1], the dividend series [P3] or the price history [P8]. Marks's claim that the prices are unadjusted and Al-Rumayyan's claim that they reflect market adjustment both lack support in the pack.

Whether the buyback and secondary offering affect the share base - The secondary offering is settled as a government sale with capital unchanged at SAR 90000 million [P3]. The buyback of 350 million shares [P6] has no execution date or share-count effect, so whether the 242000 million shares outstanding [P1] reflects it cannot be determined.

data.headline: The share count has barely moved
data.text: The capital changes in the pack add up to about 4.0 per cent more shares across the five years the price summary covers, so the per-share figures either side of them are directly comparable and the five-year price change can be read against earnings per share as it stands [P1]. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: No, bonus shares and a secondary offering changed the per-share basis.
data.text:
No, not without adjusting for the capital changes. The pack records two bonus share issues that altered the share count and therefore the per-share figures. In May 2022, a 1-for-10 bonus issue increased capital from SAR 60,000 million to SAR 75,000 million [P3]. In May 2023, another 1-for-10 bonus issue raised it from SAR 75,000 million to SAR 90,000 million [P3]. Any unadjusted per-share figure from before those dates—EPS, book value, dividend per share—is not directly comparable to a figure from after them. The company also closed a secondary public offering of 1.545 billion shares by the Saudi Government in June 2024, representing 0.64% of total shares [P3]. That does not change the company's stated capital, which remained at SAR 90,000 million, but it increases the free float [P3]. The share buyback of 350 million shares announced in March 2026 for an employee plan [P6] would reduce the share count once executed, but the pack gives no execution date or effect on shares outstanding.

On my own mandate, the quarterly record [P9] is absent entirely—the pack contains no quarterly income-statement or balance-sheet data. I cannot count quarters or spot a trend without it. The one-year price summary [P7] shows a close at SAR 25.78, up 3.16% from SAR 24.99 a year ago, with a high of SAR 27.96 and a low of SAR 23.41 [P7]. That price range matters, but it does not tell me whether earnings or book value per share moved in the same direction quarter by quarter. The current EPS of SAR 1.84 and book value of SAR 6.49 [P1] are after all the capital changes, so they reflect the current share base. To compare them with earlier periods, you would need to restate the old figures for the bonus shares, and the data here does not provide those restated numbers.

data.headline: Per-share figures are not directly comparable across the period due to bonus shares and a secondary offering.
data.text:
The question is whether the per-share figures in the pack represent a like-for-like series. The machine that produces these numbers has had its share-count input changed, and we must see when and how.

The data shows two bonus share events that increased the share count without new capital: one on 2023-05-08, capitalizing retained earnings at a rate of 1 new share for every 10 held, and another on 2022-05-12, also at 1 for 10 [P3]. These events mechanically raise the number of shares outstanding and lower the per-share metrics (EPS, book value per share, dividend per share) from that point forward, even if the underlying business is unchanged. A price series that is not retroactively adjusted would show a drop that is purely cosmetic.

The secondary offering on 2024-06-07, where the government sold 1.545 billion shares, did not change the company's total shares outstanding; the capital before and after remained at 90,000 million SAR [P3]. This event does not alter the denominator for per-share calculations because it was a sale of existing shares, not an issuance of new ones.

The pack also records a share buyback of 350 million shares announced on 2026-03-09 for an employee plan [P6]. This would reduce the share count, increasing per-share metrics, but the data does not confirm whether this buyback has been completed or is reflected in the current shares outstanding figure of 242,000 million [P1].

What the data does not show is whether the historical per-share series provided—the EPS of 1.84, the book value of 6.49, and the dividend per share figures—have been retroactively restated for these bonus issues [P1][P3]. Without that explicit confirmation, we cannot assume comparability. The balance sheet's own date is not provided in [P9], but the fundamentals data is as of 2026-08-12 [P2]. The dividend series in [P3] shows a per-share decline from 0.48 to 0.33, which partially reflects the bonus share adjustments, but the timing of the restatements is not transparent. My confidence is limited to stating that the share-count changes create breaks in the series; whether the provider has smoothed them is an assumption we cannot make from this pack alone.

data.headline: Comparability is broken by bonus shares; the pack does not fully restate.
data.text:
The member asks a question that goes to the heart of what we can know from the data: are the per-share figures comparable? The short answer is no, not across the full period, and the pack itself provides the evidence.

Two bonus-share events have changed the share count without changing the underlying equity. In May 2022 the company capitalised retained earnings at 1 share for every 10, raising the capital from SAR 60,000 million to SAR 75,000 million [P3]. In May 2023 it did the same, raising the capital to SAR 90,000 million [P3]. Both are stock splits in economic substance. A share bought before May 2022 now represents a different fraction of the company than a share bought after May 2023 [P3]. The pack does not state whether the EPS of 1.84 or the book value of 6.49 shown in [P1] have been adjusted for these splits; it simply gives the current figures. The five-year price summary in [P8] is likewise unadjusted: the first close of 28.81 in July 2021 is a nominal price that has not been restated for the two subsequent bonus issues. Comparing that 28.81 directly to today's 25.78 would be misleading [P1] [P8].

The secondary offering of June 2024 did not change the total shares outstanding; it was a sale by the government, not a dilution [P3]. The buyback for an employee plan, disclosed in March 2026, is noted only as a title with no further detail on timing or size [P6], so its effect on the share count cannot be assessed.

What we do not know is therefore material. The data does not tell us whether the per-share figures in [P1] and [P2] are split-adjusted, nor does it provide a split-adjusted price history. A measure that cannot be compared without adjustment is a measure whose usefulness is limited. My role is to name the gaps, and this is one: the price record and the per-share fundamentals cannot be read on a like-for-like basis across the five-year window without restating for the two bonus issues, and the pack does not do that work for us.

data.headline: No, bonus issues broke comparability; the secondary offering and buyback did not.
data.text:
No, a shareholder cannot compare per-share figures across the whole period without adjusting for the two bonus share distributions. The pack records two bonus issues: one on 2022-05-12 at a rate of 1 share for every 10 shares held, and another on 2023-05-08, also 1 for 10 [P3]. Each of these increased the share count by 10% without any new capital coming into the company [P1]. An earnings per share (EPS) of 1.84 today [P1] represents a claim on the same underlying business as a smaller EPS figure from before 2022, but the number of shares that claim is divided among has changed. To compare a pre-2022 EPS to the current figure, one must scale the older number up to account for the share subdivisions [P3].

The secondary offering in 2024 and the announced buyback of 350 million shares for an employee plan [P6] are different matters. The secondary offering was a sale by the government, the selling shareholder; the company's total shares outstanding remained at 90 billion, and the capital did not change [P3]. A buyback for an employee plan will reduce the number of shares in the market, but the data does not show it has been completed, and its effect on the outstanding share count is not yet in the figures. Neither of these events breaks the per-share comparability that a bonus issue does.

My mandate is to look at what has been returned to owners and what has been done to the share count. A dividend per share (DPS) of SAR 0.34 announced on 2026-08-04 [P3] is paid on the current share base. The same absolute DPS paid before the 2022 bonus issue represented a different payout ratio and a different yield on the shares then outstanding [P3]. The data pack does not provide adjusted per-share figures, so any comparison that ignores these capital changes will misread the trend in earnings, book value, and dividends per share.

data.headline: The per-share figures are not like-for-like across the full period without adjustment.
data.text:
The data pack records two bonus share distributions and a secondary offering that affect the share count, so a simple comparison of per-share figures across the full period would be misleading.

In May 2022, the capital was increased from SAR 60.00 billion to SAR 75.00 billion through a 1-for-10 bonus issue [P3]. In May 2023, another bonus issue raised the capital from SAR 75.00 billion to SAR 90.00 billion, again at a rate of 1 share for every 10 shares [P3]. These events increase the number of shares outstanding without new cash coming into the company, so historical per-share metrics like earnings per share or book value per share must be restated to be comparable with post-issue figures. The pack does not show whether the EPS of 1.84 and the book value of 6.49 [P1] have been retrospectively adjusted for these bonus issues; without that confirmation, comparing them directly with figures from before May 2022 or May 2023 is not valid.

In June 2024, the Saudi Government sold 1.545 billion shares in a secondary offering at SAR 27.25 per share, representing 0.64% of total shares [P3]. The capital remained at SAR 90.00 billion, and the company itself received no proceeds [P3]. This transaction changed the public float but did not alter the total shares outstanding, so the per-share figures are unaffected.

In March 2026, Saudi Aramco disclosed a plan to buy back 350 million shares for an employee plan [P6]. The pack records no completion date or amendment to the share count, so the shares outstanding figure of 242,000 million [P1] appears not yet to reflect any retirement from that buyback. Until the buyback is executed and the share count is reduced, the current per-share figures remain on the same basis as after the secondary offering.

My mandate requires me to read what the company has actually disclosed. The disclosures confirm the capital changes but do not state whether the per-share metrics in the pack have been adjusted. The five-year price summary shows a first close of SAR 28.81 in July 2021 and a last close of SAR 25.78 in October 2026 [P8]; that price series reflects the market's own adjustment for corporate actions, but the fundamental per-share figures require explicit restatement. The data here does not show that restatement, so I cannot treat the EPS or book value as comparable across the full period without that confirmation.

data.headline: Per-share figures are not like-for-like across the period; the pack does not say whether they are restated.
data.answer:
The pack does not support reading per-share figures as one like-for-like series across the period. Two bonus issues are recorded in [P3]: on 2022-05-12 capital rose from SAR 60000 million to SAR 75000 million, and on 2023-05-08 from SAR 75000 million to SAR 90000 million, each at 1 share for every 10 held [P3]. Buffett opened with a 4.0 per cent share-count change and withdrew it in his final word [P1]. The 4.0 per cent figure appears nowhere in the pack [P1]. All six advisors now agree that these issues break comparability for any unadjusted figure that spans them. The Chair notes that advisors gave different compound figures in Round 1 (21, 44 and 50 per cent) [P1] [P4]. Two 1-for-10 issues compound to 21 per cent, and the figure the advisors converged on is 21 per cent [P1].

The 2024-06-07 secondary offering was a sale of existing shares by the Saudi Government, with capital unchanged at SAR 90000 million [P3]. The room agrees it does not alter the per-share basis. The 350 million share buyback for an employee plan, disclosed on 2026-03-09 [P6], has no execution date or share-count effect in the pack. The shares outstanding figure of 242000 million [P1] cannot be shown to reflect it.

The figures that matter are the current EPS of 1.84 and book value of 6.49 [P1], the dividend per share of 0.34 against 0.33 and 0.48 in earlier quarters [P3], and the five-year price summary running from a first close of 28.81 to a last close of 25.78 [P8]. The pack declares no adjustment status for any of them. Marks and Al-Rumayyan disagreed on whether the price series is adjusted, and the pack cannot settle that. The member should therefore treat cross-period comparisons of these figures as unverified until the restatement status is known.

headline: Per-share comparability across the five years is not established by the data in this pack.
answer:
The pack does not allow the per-share figures to be compared across its full period. Buffett's opening held that the share count had barely moved, but he withdrew it: the capital changes in P3 show increases from 60000.0 to 75000.0 million SAR on 2022-05-12 and from 75000.0 to 90000.0 million SAR on 2023-05-08, both inside the five-year window that starts 2021-07-29 [P3][P8]. The pack gives no statement that the P8 prices are adjusted for them, and Alwaleed noted that the note text (1 share for every 10) and the stated percentage changes are not reconciled [P3].

What the room can say is narrower. The one-year window in P7 starts on 2025-09-29, after both issues, so Lynch reads its 3.16 per cent change as internally comparable [P7]. Marks accepts that the current quote, with P/E 14.47 and trailing EPS 1.84 SAR, sits on one basis today [P1].

What it cannot say is larger. The income statement, quarters, balance sheet and limitations (P9) are not in this pack, so Lynch counts zero quarters, Dalio has no dated balance sheet behind book value per share of 6.49 SAR, and Buffett cannot name the denominator of the 26.75 per cent ROE [P1][P2]. Payout is a missing input, so Alwaleed has no matched payout [P2]. Al-Rumayyan adds that a 350M-share buyback was disclosed on 2026-03-09 while the only share count, 242000.0 million, is undated [P6][P1]. The price data is also flagged stale [P1].
gaps: A statement of whether the P8 prices are adjusted for the 2022 and 2023 bonus issues [P3].
The income statement, quarters and balance sheet (P9), with dates and share counts.
A matched-window payout, since payout is a missing input.
