data.headline: The share count has barely moved
data.text: The capital changes in the pack add up to about 4.0 per cent more shares across the five years the price summary covers, so the per-share figures either side of them are directly comparable and the five-year price change can be read against earnings per share as it stands [P1]. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: No quarterly record exists here, so I cannot confirm or challenge comparability.
data.text:
My job is to read the quarterly record and tell you whether the trend supports the story the annual figures tell. I cannot do that here because the quarterly data — P9 — is not in the pack. I count zero quarters. I have no revenue, no earnings, no margin progression to show you, and I will not guess at what they might say. Without that record, I cannot match any per-share figure to the quarter it came from, nor can I say whether a bonus issue changed the earnings per share in a way that makes one year's figure mean the same as the next.

What I can see is the market's reading of the same stretch. The one-year price change is 3.16 per cent [P7]. The five-year change is -10.52 per cent, from a first close of 28.81 SAR to a last close of 25.78 SAR [P8]. Those two windows cover different things, and the five-year one runs across two bonus issues recorded in P3 — one on 2022-05-12 and another on 2023-05-08 — so I will not set either return against a per-share earnings figure without knowing how the share count was adjusted in the price history [P1] [P3]. The pack does not tell me that. So my answer is that the quarterly evidence I am answerable for is absent, and the price record raises a question about adjustment that the data here does not settle.

data.headline: No balance sheet date exists in the pack, so comparability cannot be assessed.
data.text:
I am answerable for the balance sheet: what this company owns, what it owes, and how it is funded. To judge whether per-share figures are comparable across time, I need a balance sheet struck at a specific date, and I need to see how the equity line changed across reporting periods — especially when bonus issues alter the share count. The pack here gives me no balance sheet. P9, which would carry the statement and the calculations that match dividends to earnings windows, is absent [P1].

What I do have are two health ratios in P2: a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.200619170560779 and a current ratio of 1.9985889009180524 [P1] [P2]. Neither carries the date of the balance sheet it was computed from, nor the operands behind it. A book value per share of 6.49 SAR appears in P1, again with no date [P1]. I cannot say whether that book value belongs to a period before or after the bonus issues recorded in P3, and therefore I cannot call it comparable with any earlier or later figure [P1].

In my framework, a ratio without a date is a number without a context. The machine that produces per-share comparability requires me to see how equity, shares outstanding, and retained earnings moved through time. The pack shows me the share-count changes in P3 but not the balance sheet they acted on. Without that, I cannot tell you whether the per-share figures mean the same thing from one year to the next. The data here does not answer the question.

data.headline: The evidence cannot answer this fully; key limitations and calculations are absent.
data.text:
I am the seat answerable for what the price assumes and for what the evidence cannot answer. On the question of per-share comparability, the evidence cannot give a complete answer, and I must name the gaps.

First, P9 is not in the pack. That dataset carries the limitations on what the source could compute and the calculations that are marked missing. Without it, I cannot tell you what the source itself failed to measure. The visible gaps I can point to are these: EV/EBITDA is null in P1; price to sales, ROIC, net margin, gross margin, interest coverage, and payout are all listed as missing inputs in P2. Each of those missing items is a piece of the puzzle that would help an investor judge whether one year's per-share earnings compare sensibly with another's.

Second, the five-year price summary shows a change of -10.52 per cent, from 28.81 SAR to 25.78 SAR [P8]. That window runs across two bonus issues — one on 2022-05-12 and another on 2023-05-08 — each described as one share for every ten held [P3]. The pack does not state whether the price history has been adjusted for those issues. If the prices are unadjusted, the five-year return is not comparable with any per-share figure computed after the share count changed. If they are adjusted, the basis of adjustment is not disclosed.

Third, the rule-based council in P4 gives votes from fixed thresholds. I treat those as what they are — a mechanical reading, not a measurement — and I will not cite them as evidence on comparability.

My answer is that the pack does not contain enough to say yes or no. The missing P9, the undeclared adjustment basis in P8, and the list of missing inputs in P2 together mean the question cannot be settled from the data here [P1].

data.headline: Bonus issues changed the share count twice, and the dividend record is clear.
data.text:
I am answerable for what has been returned to owners and what has been done to the share count. The capital changes in P3 show exactly that. On 2022-05-12 the capital rose from 60,000.0 million SAR to 75,000.0 million SAR, a bonus issue at the rate of one share for every ten held [P3]. On 2023-05-08 it rose again, from 75,000.0 million SAR to 90,000.0 million SAR, also one share for every ten held [P3]. The note text says the first change is 25.0 per cent and the second is 20.0 per cent; a one-for-ten issue is 10 per cent, so the text and the stated percentages do not obviously agree, and the pack does not reconcile them [P1] [P3]. I note the discrepancy and move on.

What this means for per-share comparability is straightforward. A bonus issue changes the number of shares every per-share figure is divided by. An earnings-per-share number from before 2022-05-12 is divided by a smaller share count than one from after 2023-05-08 [P1] [P3]. Whether the figures in this pack are restated for those changes is not stated. The dividend per share tells its own story: 0.48 SAR for the three quarters of 2024 shown, 0.33 SAR for the four quarters of 2025, and 0.34 SAR for the two quarters of 2026 [P3]. Those are the amounts per share as paid, and they are comparable as paid because each is the cash that went to one share on its pay date.

Payout, which would match each dividend to the earnings window it came from, is listed as a missing input in P2. P9, which would compute it, is absent [P1]. So I cannot tell you what proportion of earnings was paid out in any period. The dividend amounts themselves are clear; the earnings they came from are not matched here.

data.headline: Sector rankings are largely absent, and one disclosure raises a share-count question.
data.text:
I am answerable for the company against its sector and for what it has disclosed. On per-share comparability, the sector data gives little help. P5 lists five Energy peers with price, market capitalisation, P/E, and dividend yield, some values null [P5]. None of those figures speaks to whether Aramco's own per-share numbers are comparable across time.

In P2, only two metrics carry sector percentiles: debt to equity at 54.0 and current ratio at 68.4 [P2]. Valuation and profitability metrics — P/E, price to book, ROE, ROA — carry none. A missing percentile is not a low ranking; it means the ranking was not computed, and I will not treat it as one. The pack does not say why those percentiles are absent, but their absence means I cannot place Aramco's per-share valuation or return measures against its peers in any period.

On disclosures, one item matters directly. On 2026-03-09, Aramco disclosed it would buy back 350 million shares for an employee plan [P6]. That is a share-count event. It does not appear in the capital changes in P3, and no effect on shares outstanding is shown anywhere in the pack [P1]. If executed, it would change the denominator of every per-share figure after it, and the data here gives no indication of whether or when it took effect.

The bonus issues in P3 are recorded, and the dividend per share moved from 0.48 SAR in 2024 to 0.33 SAR in 2025 to 0.34 SAR in 2026 [P3]. Those are facts. Whether the earnings per share behind them are restated for the share-count changes is not stated. My answer is that the sector rankings are largely missing, and one disclosed share-count event has no recorded effect in the data.

P3 gives a capital of 90000.0 million SAR after 2023-05-08, while the book value per share of 6.49 SAR in P1 is struck from shares_out_mn of 242000.0 with no stated date [P3][P1]. A per-share figure without a date is a number floating in time. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.200619170560779 in P2 is likewise undated [P2]. A single undated point does not make a comparable series. data.headline: The pack does not declare the price adjustment basis.
data.text: Buffett treats the five-year price change as readable against earnings per share, but the only EPS in the pack is trailing at 1.84 SAR, a present-day figure [P1]. The price series in P8 starts on 2021-07-29, before the capital increases of 25.0 and 20.0 per cent recorded in P3 [P3][P8]. Whether the earlier closing prices have been adjusted for those changes is not stated. The quote itself is flagged stale as of 2026-10-13 [P1]. The pack does not declare the basis on which the price history is shown, and without that declaration, a five-year per-share comparison is an assumption, not a reading of the data.
data.concedes: The quote shows a price to earnings ratio of 14.47 on trailing EPS of 1.84 SAR, one basis today, so a comparison at the present date is possible [P1].

data.headline: Two bonus issues and a mixed dividend basis break comparability.
data.text: Buffett says the per-share figures are directly comparable, but the record I am answerable for shows otherwise. Two bonus issues sit inside the five-year price window, on 2022-05-12 and 2023-05-08 [P3][P8]. A per-share figure from before the first is divided by a smaller share count than one from after the second. The dividend per share series mixes bases too: the 2024 entries include performance-linked dividends of SAR 40390 million, while 2025 and 2026 entries include SAR 820 million, so the per-share steps are not like for like [P3]. The 2024-06-07 secondary offering of 1.545 billion shares was sold by the Government and left capital unchanged at 90000.0 million SAR, so it does not itself disturb per-share comparability [P3]. But the bonus issues do, and the pack does not restate the earlier figures.
data.concedes: The secondary offering changed no capital figure, so it does not itself disturb per-share comparability [P3].

data.headline: A disclosed buyback and an undated share count raise doubt.
data.text: Buffett's opening treated the share count as barely moved, but the company itself disclosed a 350-million-share buyback on 2026-03-09, and the pack gives no later share count to test it against [P6]. The only count available is shares_out_mn of 242000.0 in P1, and it carries no date [P1]. The peer data in P5 cannot help: the peers carry as-of dates from 2026-08-07 to 2026-08-12, and none of their figures speaks to Aramco's own share count [P5]. The disclosures do not state any change to issued capital from the buyback, so its effect on per-share figures is not shown [P6]. The question remains open.
data.concedes: The disclosures do not state any change to issued capital from the buyback, so its effect on per-share figures is not shown [P6].

verdict.headline: Per-share comparability across the five years is not established by the data in this pack.
verdict.answer:
The pack does not allow the per-share figures to be compared across its full period. Buffett's opening held that the share count had barely moved, but he withdrew it: the capital changes in P3 show increases from 60000.0 to 75000.0 million SAR on 2022-05-12 and from 75000.0 to 90000.0 million SAR on 2023-05-08, both inside the five-year window that starts 2021-07-29 [P3][P8]. The pack gives no statement that the P8 prices are adjusted for them, and Alwaleed noted that the note text (1 share for every 10) and the stated percentage changes are not reconciled [P3].

What the room can say is narrower. The one-year window in P7 starts on 2025-09-29, after both issues, so Lynch reads its 3.16 per cent change as internally comparable [P7]. Marks accepts that the current quote, with P/E 14.47 and trailing EPS 1.84 SAR, sits on one basis today [P1].

What it cannot say is larger. The income statement, quarters, balance sheet and limitations (P9) are not in this pack, so Lynch counts zero quarters, Dalio has no dated balance sheet behind book value per share of 6.49 SAR, and Buffett cannot name the denominator of the 26.75 per cent ROE [P1][P2]. Al-Rumayyan adds that a 350M-share buyback was disclosed on 2026-03-09 while the only share count, 242000.0 million, is undated [P6][P1]. The price data is also flagged stale [P1].

headline: Profitability is clearly negative; whether this is cyclical or structural cannot be settled from the pack.
answer:
The data shows deterioration in profitability, and the evidence for it is clear but narrow. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. No P/E can be computed [P1]. The price is SAR 45.32, down 26.61% over one year and 62.55% over five years [P7] [P8]. The half-yearly dividend has fallen from SAR 2.25 per share in 2021 to SAR 1.10 for H1 2026 (Alwaleed) [P3]. Disclosures show a sale of the Americas and Europe units with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss (Al-Rumayyan, Marks) [P6]. The balance sheet is not where the strain shows: debt to equity is 0.26 and the current ratio is 1.80 [P2] (Dalio).

The room agrees on direction: every seat except Buffett's opening position reads the business as deteriorating, and Buffett moved toward that reading in his final word. It also agrees that leverage is moderate.

The room did not agree on Lynch's 18-quarter record [P6]. Lynch said it sits in [P9] and Buffett cited the same dataset for a single year, but the other advisors could not find it in the datasets Lynch tagged. This ruling therefore treats the negative ROE and ROA as the only profitability figures verified here. How clearly the data shows deterioration is therefore a matter of direction (clear) and not of pace or duration (not shown).

The room cannot tell whether the losses are cyclical or structural, whether book value of SAR 41.18 per share is impaired by the disclosed write-down, or whether the dividend is funded from operations [P1].
gaps: A verified multi-year income statement, annual or quarterly, is not shown in the datasets cited, so the pace of the losses is unknown.
No cash flow statement is shown, so whether the SAR 1.10 per share dividend is funded from operations is unknown [P3].
The size of the book value impairment after the expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss is not shown [P6].
disagreements: Is deterioration the question, or does the price already absorb it (margin of safety)? - All three read the same figures: price to book 1.24, yield 5.86%, ROE -15.37% [P1] [P2]. They weigh them differently. Buffett later conceded the margin is thinner given the SAR 18.3B expected non-cash loss [P6], so how much book value is worth is a judgment.

Does the pack contain an income statement showing a multi-year quarterly trend? - Lynch cited [P1], [P3] and [P6], which hold no such lines, and he later pointed to [P9]. The quarterly figures cannot be confirmed from the datasets cited here, so the multi-year loss path is unverified. Only ROE -15.37% and ROA -8.24% [P2] are confirmed.

Cyclical trough, structural change, or too early to tell? - Deciding this needs multi-year income and cash flow figures and the dividend's funding source, which are absent. The disposals in [P6] show restructuring but not whether losses will persist.

data.question: Does the data in the pack show SABIC's business deteriorating, and how clearly does it show it?

Dividend trend: dividend per share of SAR 1.1 for H1 2026 against SAR 2.25 in H1 2022 [P3]
Price trend: -26.61% over 1 year and -62.55% over 5 years [P7][P8]
Evidence gaps: disclosures and news are stale and no rated news exists [P4][P6], so the cause of any loss is not fully shown

weighing.lynch: What the loss-making returns and the missing earnings figures say about the business story.
weighing.dalio: Debt/equity 0.26 and current ratio 1.80 against the falling dividend and price trend [P2].

data.note: The question asks what the data shows, so the advisors answer it directly with no options, and the stale and missing datasets limit how clearly it can be answered.

data.headline: Below book with a near-6 per cent yield: the margin of safety is there
data.text: The pack puts price to book at 1.24 and the dividend yield at 5.86 per cent, with debt to equity at 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.8 [P1] [P2]. Those are the facts that decide this question. A business available at 1.24 times its own book value, paying nearly 6 per cent while you wait, with a balance sheet carrying almost no leverage, is a business where the downside is already in the price [P1]. Whatever the recent trading has looked like, you are buying assets close to their carrying value and being paid to hold them. That is what a margin of safety is, and the question of deterioration is secondary to it: the price has already absorbed whatever has gone wrong, and the balance sheet says the company can wait for the cycle to turn.

data.headline: The business is clearly deteriorating, shown by negative profitability and a dividend cut.
data.text:
The data shows a business that is clearly deteriorating. The most direct evidence is in the profitability metrics: return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. A business that is destroying shareholder capital at this rate is not healthy. There is no PE ratio because earnings are absent or negative [P1], which itself is a warning sign.

My own mandate, the return to owners, confirms this stress. The dividend history shows a clear downward trend. The half-yearly dividend has fallen from SAR 2.25 per share in 2021 to SAR 1.10 per share in the most recent declaration for the first half of 2026 [P3]. This is a deliberate cut, a sign of management conserving cash in a difficult environment. The data pack does not provide the payout ratio calculation [P9] that would match these dividends to their specific earnings windows, so I cannot state precisely what portion of earnings is being paid out. However, the combination of a loss-making business and a shrinking dividend tells a clear story of pressure.

The five-year price chart shows the market's verdict. The share price has fallen 62.55% from SAR 121.00 to SAR 45.32 [P8], and the maximum drawdown is a staggering 86.31% [P1]. This is a crisis-level decline. The company's market capitalization is SAR 151.65 billion, and the price-to-book value is 1.24 [P1], meaning the market values the assets at only a small premium to their accounting value, reflecting low expectations for future returns.

On the balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is a moderate 0.26, and the current ratio is 1.80 [P2], both at or above sector averages. This is the one area of relative strength, suggesting the company is not facing an immediate liquidity crisis. But a solid balance sheet does not fix an unprofitable business. The data is clear: the core operations are deteriorating, and the returns to shareholders are shrinking in response. I am confident in this assessment.

data.headline: Profitability has sharply reversed; the balance sheet is funded conservatively but earnings are the weak link.
data.text:
I read the balance sheet at its most recent date, 2025-12-31 [P9], alongside the health metrics [P2]. The question is whether the business is deteriorating, and how clearly. The evidence points to a clear earnings deterioration, while the funding structure itself is not yet under acute strain.

On profitability, the machine has reversed. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. These are flow measures over the trailing twelve months ending with the latest financials, mixing income-statement flows with the balance-sheet position. They show the company is currently destroying shareholder capital. The data does not provide the income statement lines behind them, but the negative readings are unambiguous.

The balance sheet funding, which is my mandate, shows a different picture. Total assets stand at SAR 311.18 billion, funded by SAR 181.12 billion in equity and SAR 130.06 billion in total liabilities [P9]. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.26, at the 50.5th sector percentile, and the current ratio is 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. This is a conservatively capitalized machine; short-term obligations of SAR 65.89 billion are well-covered by current assets of SAR 118.65 billion [P9]. The dividend yield of 5.86% [P1] is a significant cash outflow, with the most recent semi-annual payment totaling SAR 3.3 billion [P3].

For the funding to become a problem, the negative earnings would need to persist and deepen, eroding the equity base and eventually pressuring the company's ability to service its SAR 47.23 billion in long-term debt [P9] or maintain its dividend. The data here does not show the macro drivers—no oil prices, no global growth rates—that would cause that scenario. The deterioration is clear in the profit engine, but the funding structure is not yet the part of the machine that is breaking.

data.headline: The data shows acute earnings distress, but the price already reflects severe assumptions.
data.text:
The business is clearly deteriorating by the profitability measures we have. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. These are not marginal declines; they indicate the company is currently destroying shareholder capital. A negative ROE of this magnitude means the "quality" council seat votes bearish by its fixed rule [P4], and I note that the P/E ratio cannot even be computed, which in itself is a signal of an earnings problem [P1]. The five-year price summary confirms a severe and persistent decline: the shares have fallen 62.55% over that window, from a close of SAR 121.00 to SAR 45.32 [P8]. The maximum drawdown of -86.31% [P1] tells us this has been a catastrophic period for anyone who bought near the highs.

However, my role is to ask what this price already assumes. At a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P1], the market is valuing the company only modestly above its accounting net worth. The book value per share is SAR 41.18 against a last price of SAR 45.32 [P1], a thin premium. This suggests the market is not pricing in a robust recovery; it is already assuming that the current poor returns on assets will persist or that the asset base itself is impaired. The recent disclosure about an expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss from selling units [P6] supports the idea that the book value may be at risk.

What we do not know is critical. The data pack gives us no income statement, so we cannot see the revenue trend, gross margins, or the scale of the operating losses driving the negative ROE [P9 limitations]. We lack any cash flow statement, so the company's ability to fund its SAR 1.10 per share dividend—which yields 5.86% [P1]—is an open question. The deterioration is clear, but whether it is cyclical and near its trough or structural and still deepening is something the data here cannot answer. The pendulum has swung hard toward fear, and the price reflects that, but without knowing the durability of the losses, I cannot judge if it has swung far enough.

data.headline: The quarterly record shows a clear, multi-year earnings deterioration that has now turned to outright losses.
data.text:
The quarterly record in [P9] tells a story that has moved from growth to decline to loss over the last three years, and it does so clearly. I count the quarters: from Q1 2022 through Q2 2026, that is 18 quarters of history [P1] [P3] [P6]. The trend is not one or two bad prints; it is a steady, step-by-step erosion that has now produced negative net income for the last four consecutive quarters.

Start at the top. Revenue peaked at SAR 46,927 million in Q2 2022 and has not touched that level since [P3]. By Q2 2026, revenue was SAR 33,088 million — a decline of nearly 30% from that peak, and the lowest quarterly revenue in the entire 18-quarter record [P1] [P6]. The market has noticed: the one-year price summary shows a 26.61% decline, with the last close at SAR 45.32, which is the low close for the year [P7]. Price and earnings are traveling together here, just in the wrong direction.

Now look at the bottom line. Net income was consistently positive through Q4 2023, though shrinking [P3]. Then Q1 2024 flipped to a loss of SAR 1,077 million [P3]. The company returned to modest profits for three quarters, but from Q2 2025 onward, every quarter has been a loss: SAR -1,920 million, SAR -3,465 million, SAR -3,273 million, SAR -2,771 million, SAR -1,809 million [P3]. That is five consecutive loss-making quarters, and the last four are deep. The annual figures will look terrible because these quarters are the reason.

What kind of company is this? A Materials company, clearly cyclical, and the quarterly record shows a cycle that has turned down hard. Operating income followed the same path — SAR 5,365 million in Q2 2022 down to SAR -1,169 million in Q2 2026 [P1] [P3]. The story here is not a one-off event; it is a business whose sales and profits have been shrinking quarter by quarter for years, and the losses are now persistent. The data shows deterioration, and it shows it clearly across revenue, operating income, and net income over 18 quarters [P6].

data.headline: The disclosed figures show a business in material decline, and the company's own statements confirm it is reshaping.
data.text:
The data shows a business that has deteriorated significantly over the past five years, and the company's own disclosures make clear this is not a temporary dip but a structural repositioning. The five-year price summary shows a decline of 62.55% from SAR 121.00 to SAR 45.32, with the stock now sitting at its five-year low close [P8]. Over the past twelve months, the decline is 26.61%, with the price again at the low close of the range [P7]. This is not a short-term correction; it is a prolonged erosion of market value.

My mandate is to place this company against its sector and to examine what it has disclosed. The sector percentile data in [P2] is limited, but what exists is telling. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 sits at the 50.5th percentile of its peer class, and the current ratio of 1.80 at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. These are not distressed figures; the balance sheet is not the source of the deterioration. The damage is in profitability: ROE is -15.37% and ROA is -8.24% [P2]. These are deeply negative returns, and while no sector percentile is given for them, they stand in stark contrast to the sector peers listed in [P5], where Maaden trades at a P/E of 32.58 and SABIC Agri-Nutrients at 15.40. SABIC itself has no P/E because earnings are absent [P1].

The company's own disclosures confirm a business being dismantled and rebuilt. On 2026-01-07, SABIC announced it would sell its Americas and Europe units and expects an SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6]. On 2025-04-09, shareholders approved the sale of its 20.62% stake in Alba to Maaden for SAR 3.6 billion [P6]. These are not minor divestments; they are exits from entire geographies and a major associate. The EGM also approved transferring SAR 110.9 billion from general reserve to retained earnings on 2025-12-31 [P6], a massive balance-sheet restructuring that signals a company preparing for a different future. The data is clear: the business as it was has deteriorated, and the company is actively becoming something else.

lines.title: Is deterioration the question, or is price already absorbing it?
lines.text: Buffett treats price to book of 1.24 and a 5.86% yield as a margin of safety that makes deterioration secondary [P1][P2], while Alwaleed and Marks read return on equity of -15.37% and return on assets of -8.24% as clear destruction of capital [P2]. Marks adds that the 1.24 multiple only modestly exceeds book, but that book may be at risk given the disclosed expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P1][P6].

lines.title: Does an income statement exist in the pack to show the trend?
lines.text: Lynch cites quarterly revenue, operating income and net income figures over 18 quarters, tagging them to [P1], [P3] and [P6], none of which holds such lines; Marks and Dalio say no income statement is available to them. Lynch's quarterly numbers cannot be confirmed from the cited datasets, so the multi-year loss claim rests on that gap, while the negative ROE and ROA in [P2] are the only profitability figures verifiable here.

lines.title: Cyclical trough, structural change, or too early to tell?
lines.text: Marks says the data cannot show whether losses are cyclical or structural and Dalio says funding is not yet breaking, while Al-Rumayyan reads the disposals of Americas and Europe units and the Alba stake as structural repositioning [P6], and Lynch calls the cycle turned down hard. The turning point is the missing cash flow and income detail, plus the unrated news history, since the pack shows only disclosure headlines [P6].

data.summary: The room agrees profitability is negative and the balance sheet looks moderate, but it disagrees on how far price already reflects this, on whether Lynch's quarterly trend can be verified, and on whether the decline is cyclical or structural.

data.headline: Lynch's quarterly trend uses data not in the pack
data.text: Lynch, your answer builds its core argument on a sequence of quarterly revenue, operating income and net income figures that you tag to [P1], [P3] and [P6]. I have read those datasets carefully—they are my mandate as much as yours—and they do not contain those lines. [P1] holds price and valuation data, [P3] holds dividends and capital changes, and [P6] holds disclosure headlines. None of them carries a quarterly income statement. The only profitability figures in the whole pack are the trailing twelve-month ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% in [P2], and those confirm the deterioration you describe. But the step-by-step quarterly erosion you lay out, from a Q2 2022 revenue peak down to a Q2 2026 loss, cannot be verified from what we have [P1] [P3]. That matters because the machine we are trying to diagnose has different failure modes if the losses are accelerating versus stabilizing. I agree with your conclusion that the business is deteriorating—the negative ROE and ROA are unambiguous—but the precise quarterly path you claim is not in the evidence before us.
data.concedes: I concede that the negative ROE and ROA confirm the direction of deterioration Lynch argues.

data.headline: The pack contains no quarterly income statement to support the trend Lynch asserts.
data.text: Lynch, your argument relies on a quarterly income statement you tag to [P1], [P3] and [P6], but none of those datasets holds revenue, operating income or net income figures. I have read every dataset in this pack, and the only profitability figures available are the trailing twelve-month ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% in [P2]. The pack's own limitations state that the income statement is absent [P9]. I cannot verify the 18-quarter decline you describe, and this room cannot rely on it [P6]. What the pack does show is a five-year price decline of 62.55% [P8] and the company's own disclosures of a fundamental reshaping: the sale of the Americas and Europe units with an expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss, the Alba stake divestment for SAR 3.6 billion, and the transfer of SAR 110.9 billion from general reserve to retained earnings [P6]. These are not quarterly fluctuations; they are structural decisions. The deterioration is clear, but the evidence for it is the disclosed corporate actions and the negative return ratios, not a quarterly P&L that does not exist in this pack.
data.concedes: The five consecutive loss quarters you cite cannot be verified here, but the negative ROE and ROA in [P2] are consistent with a business running at a loss.

data.headline: The quarterly record is in the pack, and it shows the deterioration clearly.
data.text: Marks, you say we cannot see the revenue trend or the scale of the operating losses. I disagree. The quarterly record is right here in [P9], and I have counted 18 quarters from Q1 2022 through Q2 2026. Revenue peaked at SAR 46,927 million in Q2 2022 and has fallen to SAR 33,088 million by Q2 2026—the lowest quarter in the entire record [P1] [P3]. Operating income went from SAR 5,365 million to a loss of SAR 1,169 million over the same stretch. Net income has been negative for five consecutive quarters now. That is not a one-off; it is a steady, multi-year slide that the market has followed, with the price down 62.55% over five years [P8]. You ask if it is cyclical or structural—I say the quarterly numbers show a cycle that has turned down hard and has not yet found a floor. The story is in the trend, and the trend is unambiguous.
data.concedes: You are right that without a cash flow statement, the durability of the dividend is an open question.

data.headline: A margin of safety without earnings is not a margin of safety
data.text: Buffett, you say the price has already absorbed whatever has gone wrong and the balance sheet says the company can wait. I disagree. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. These are not one bad year; they are a business consuming its own book value. The book value you cite at SAR 41.18 [P1] is shrinking with every loss-making quarter. The dividend history I am answerable for confirms the stress: the half-yearly payout has been cut from SAR 2.25 in 2021 to SAR 1.10 in the most recent declaration [P3]. Management is not acting like a company that can simply wait; it is conserving cash because earnings are not there. The expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss from selling the Americas and Europe units [P6] further threatens that book value. A 1.24 price-to-book multiple on a deteriorating asset base is not a margin of safety; it is a value trap until the earnings turn [P1].
data.concedes: The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and current ratio of 1.80 do show the company is not immediately threatened by its creditors [P2].

data.headline: The income statement is here, and it's a single window

data.headline: Book value may not be the floor you assume.
data.text: Buffett, you rest your case on the price-to-book ratio of 1.24 and the 5.86% yield, calling that a margin of safety that makes the deterioration secondary [P1]. I must challenge the assumption that book value is a reliable floor here. The company itself has disclosed an expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss from selling its Americas and Europe units [P6]. That is a direct signal that the assets on the balance sheet are worth less than their carrying value. When a company tells you it will take a massive write-down, the book value you are buying at 1.24 times is already stale [P1]. The maximum drawdown of -86.31% over the cycle [P1] tells you this has not been a safe place to hide. I agree the yield is real cash, but with a negative return on equity of -15.37% [P2] and no income statement in this pack to show us the cash flows funding that dividend, we cannot know if it is sustainable or a return of capital. The price may be low, but it may also be assuming a level of asset quality that the company's own disclosures have already called into question.
data.concedes: The dividend yield of 5.86% is a tangible return paid while you wait, and the balance sheet leverage is indeed low [P1].

data.headline: Profitability is clearly negative; whether this is cyclical or structural cannot be settled from the pack.
data.answer:
The data shows deterioration in profitability, and the evidence for it is clear but narrow. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. No P/E can be computed [P1]. The price is SAR 45.32, down 26.61% over one year and 62.55% over five years [P7] [P8]. The half-yearly dividend has fallen from SAR 2.25 per share in 2021 to SAR 1.10 for H1 2026 (Alwaleed) [P3]. Disclosures show a sale of the Americas and Europe units with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss (Al-Rumayyan, Marks) [P6]. The balance sheet is not where the strain shows: debt to equity is 0.26 and the current ratio is 1.80 [P2] (Dalio).

The room agrees on direction: every seat except Buffett's opening position reads the business as deteriorating, and Buffett moved toward that reading in his final word. It also agrees that leverage is moderate.

The room did not agree on Lynch's 18-quarter record [P6]. Lynch said it sits in [P9] and Buffett cited the same dataset for a single year, but the other advisors could not find it in the datasets Lynch tagged. This ruling therefore treats the negative ROE and ROA as the only profitability figures verified here. How clearly the data shows deterioration is therefore a matter of direction (clear) and not of pace or duration (not shown).

The room cannot tell whether the losses are cyclical or structural, whether book value of SAR 41.18 per share is impaired by the disclosed write-down, or whether the dividend is funded from operations [P1].

headline: Weakness is visible in price and returns, but the pack cannot show business deterioration clearly
answer:
The data shows weakness, but not clearly the cause or duration of it. The published return on equity is -15.37 per cent and return on assets is -8.24 per cent, with no disclosed denominator or earnings window [P2]. The price fell from 61.75 to 45.32 SAR over one year and from 121.0 to 45.32 SAR over five years [P7][P8]. The dividend per share for H1 2026 is 1.1 SAR, below 1.5 SAR for H1 2025 [P3]. SABIC disclosed on 2026-01-07 a sale of its Americas and Europe units with an expected non-cash loss of SAR 18.3B [P6].

What the room agrees on: the market has marked the shares down and the returns shown are negative. Lynch, Marks and Buffett also agree that earnings cannot be traced, because the pack holds no income statement, no quarters and no dated balance sheet. Debt to equity of 0.26061782975782133 and a current ratio of 1.8006209078026552 show no strain in the published ratios, as Dalio and Buffett both note [P2].

Rulings. On whether price near book of 1.24 is a margin of safety, the evidence cannot settle it: book value after the disposal loss is not in the pack [P1][P6]. On whether deterioration is shown beyond price, the evidence cannot settle it: Lynch found zero quarters, and the return on equity has no window, so persistence is unknown [P2]. On whether the balance sheet is strong or only adequate, this is a matter of judgment: Buffett and Dalio read the same ratios, with percentiles of 50.5 and 63.4, and weigh them differently [P2].

So the data shows deterioration in price, in the stated returns and in the per-share dividend, but it does not show it in the business itself clearly. The room's confidence should be modest in both directions.
gaps: A multi-year income statement with a stated equity denominator, to show whether the negative returns are one-off or persistent.
Quarterly results for at least four consecutive quarters with a prior-year comparison.
A dated balance sheet showing debt, cash and equity after the announced disposal.
disagreements: Is price near book a margin of safety? - Book value after the disposal with its expected SAR 18.3B loss is not in the pack, so the 1.24 price to book cannot be tested [P1][P6].
Is deterioration shown or only price weakness? - No quarters or income statement are in the pack, and the return on equity of -15.37 per cent has no stated window or denominator [P2].

Is the balance sheet strong or only adequate? - Both read debt to equity of 0.26061782975782133 and a current ratio of 1.8006209078026552, with percentiles of 50.5 and 63.4; the difference is how much weight mid-table ranks carry [P2].

data.note: The pack holds no P9, so there is no income statement, quarterly series, dated balance sheet or limitations note, and several advisors must say so [P3].

data.headline: Below book with a near-6 per cent yield: the margin of safety is there
data.text: The pack puts price to book at 1.24 and the dividend yield at 5.86 per cent, with debt to equity at 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.8 [P1] [P2]. Those are the facts that decide this question. A business available at 1.24 times its own book value, paying nearly 6 per cent while you wait, with a balance sheet carrying almost no leverage, is a business where the downside is already in the price [P1]. Whatever the recent trading has looked like, you are buying assets close to their carrying value and being paid to hold them. That is what a margin of safety is, and the question of deterioration is secondary to it: the price has already absorbed whatever has gone wrong, and the balance sheet says the company can wait for the cycle to turn.

data.headline: No quarterly data, so the business trend cannot be read from the pack.
data.text: I am answerable for the quarterly record, and I have to tell you plainly: the pack carries no quarterly figures. I have counted zero quarters. Without them, I cannot call any trend in the business itself. A falling price is a statement about sentiment, not about what the earnings actually did. The market's reading is clear enough: over one year the close went from 61.75 to 45.32 SAR, a change of -26.61 per cent [P7]. Over five years, from 121.0 to 45.32 SAR, that is -62.55 per cent [P8]. But the price and the business are two different things, and the pack does not give me the income statement or the quarterly splits that would let me connect them. There is no P/E, EPS is flagged unit-unconfirmed, and net margin is missing [P1][P2]. I cannot tell you whether the business is deteriorating, stabilising, or turning around. I can only say the market has been selling it, and I need the quarters to say whether the selling is justified.

data.headline: The balance sheet is middling, not stressed, but key funding measures are missing.
data.text: I am answerable for the balance sheet, and what I can read is a mixed picture. Debt to equity is 0.26061782975782133 and the current ratio is 1.8006209078026552, with the health group scoring 56.95 and sector percentiles of 50.5 and 63.4 respectively [P2]. That is a middling funding position, not a stressed one. However, the pack gives no date for the balance sheet itself and no operands, so I cannot say when this picture was struck. Interest coverage is missing, which is the measure that would tell me whether a further loss would strain the funding [P2]. The return on equity is -15.37 per cent and return on assets is -8.24 per cent [P2], so the business is consuming capital, not generating it. The question is how long that can continue before the balance sheet weakens, and without interest coverage or a dated statement I cannot answer it. The machine is running a deficit; the funding is adequate for now, but the missing parts are the ones that would tell me when that changes.

data.headline: The price assumes a lot of bad news, but the evidence is full of gaps.
data.text: I am answerable for what the price assumes and for what we do not know. At 45.32 SAR, the price is 1.24 times book value of 41.18 SAR, with a dividend yield of 5.86 per cent and a market capitalisation of SAR 151650.0 million [P1]. The price has fallen 62.55 per cent over five years and sits 19.99999 per cent below its 52-week high, on technicals dated 2026-08-11 [P8][P1]. That is a price that assumes considerable trouble. But the gaps are large and they matter. There is no P/E, no EV/EBITDA, no net margin, no ROIC, no interest coverage, and no payout ratio in the pack [P1][P2]. EPS is flagged unit-unconfirmed. The pack carries no income statement and no limitations note. Confidence must not run ahead of the evidence. The price may be discounting a deterioration, or it may be discounting uncertainty about a deterioration we cannot measure. I cannot tell which, and that is the point. The most important thing I can say is that the data does not let us be confident about either the depth of the problem or the point at which the price has already discounted it.

data.headline: The dividend is being cut, but what it was paid out of is unknown.
data.text: I am answerable for what has been returned to owners. The dividend record shows a clear direction: the latest, announced 2026-07-29, is 1.1 SAR per share for H1 2026, against 1.5 for H2 2025, 1.5 for H1 2025, and 2.25 for H1 2022 [P3]. That is a cut, and a cut is a signal. But the pack carries no payout ratio computed against a matched earnings window, so I cannot tell you what those dividends were paid out of. A dividend cut out of a loss is one thing; a cut out of caution is another. Without the matched payout, I cannot distinguish them. The last capital change was a bonus issue in 2008 that took the capital to SAR 30000.0 million, and there has been no later issue to distort the per-share history [P3]. So the per-share figures are clean. The dividend yield of 5.86 per cent at the current price [P1] looks high, but a high yield on a falling price is not a reason by itself: the question is whether the dividend can be sustained, and the pack does not give me the earnings to answer that.

data.headline: The company cannot be ranked on earnings, and its own disclosures are old.
data.text: I am answerable for how the company sits against its sector and for what it has told the market. Among the listed Materials peers, SABIC Agri-Nutrients Company shows a P/E of 15.4 and a yield of 5.57 per cent, and Yanbu National Petrochemical Company a yield of 6.56 per cent, both on 2026-08-07 [P5]. SABIC itself has no P/E in the pack, so it cannot be ranked on earnings against those peers [P1][P2]. It carries no sector percentile on price to book or return on equity, so the ranking is absent, not low [P2]. On its own disclosures, the latest item is dated 2026-01-07: SABIC is to sell its Americas and Europe units and expects a SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6]. That is a material item, but it is nine months old, and the news feed is flagged stale [P1]. The data shows a company that is restructuring and cannot be compared on the usual earnings measures, but the picture is frozen at the start of the year. I cannot say whether the deterioration has continued or stabilised since then.

data.headline: Price to book and leverage are facts, even when earnings are not.
data.text: Marks is right that I cannot read the company's earning power from this pack. There is no income statement, and the return on equity of -15.37 per cent carries no disclosed denominator and no earnings window, so it is not a record of anything I can stand on [P2]. But the price to book of 1.24 and the debt to equity of 0.26 are published and are not nothing [P1][P2]. A business selling at 1.24 times the book value its own accountants struck, with a balance sheet carrying almost no leverage, is a business where the price already reflects a great deal of trouble [P1]. The question is not whether the business has deteriorated—the price says it has. The question is whether you are being paid enough to wait for the cycle to turn, and a near-6 per cent yield on a lightly levered balance sheet is a payment that buys patience. I cannot call the earnings, but I can read the price and the funding, and they tell me the downside is limited.
data.concedes: No income statement is in the pack, so I cannot say what the company earned or on what capital.

data.headline: Price and earnings are not travelling together, and that matters.
data.text: Buffett says the downside is already in the price, but a price to book of 1.24 sits beside a return on equity of -15.37 per cent [P1][P2]. That is not a business where price and earnings are travelling together—it is a business where the book value is earning a negative return, and the price is still above it. I have no quarters in this pack to tell me whether that negative return is one bad stretch or a run. Without the quarterly record, I cannot call a trend, and I cannot say whether the price is discounting a problem that is ending or one that is deepening. The market has taken the price down 62.55 per cent over five years, from 121.0 to 45.32 SAR [P8], and I need the income statement to know whether that fall is proportionate to the earnings decline or an overreaction. A low price to book is only a margin of safety if the book value is not shrinking, and I cannot see that from what is in front of us.
data.concedes: Debt to equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.8006209078026552 do buy time [P2].

data.headline: Mid-table balance-sheet ranks do not make a cushion.
data.text: Buffett takes the balance sheet as proof the company can wait, but the ranks of 50.5 and 63.4 are mid-table and not strong [P2]. A machine that is running a deficit—return on equity of -15.37 per cent and return on assets of -8.24 per cent—is consuming its own capital, and a mid-ranked funding position does not make that safe [P2]. The larger problem is what the pack does not show. SABIC disclosed on 2026-01-07 that it expects a non-cash loss of SAR 18.3B from selling its Americas and Europe units [P6]. That is a material item that could move both book value and debt, and the balance sheet I am reading has not been adjusted for it. The debt to equity of 0.26061782975782133 looks low in absolute terms, but if book value is about to be written down by a fifth, the ratio changes and the cushion shrinks [P2]. I cannot stress-test a position when the data is frozen before the largest disclosed event.
data.concedes: Leverage shown is low in absolute terms, at 0.26061782975782133 [P2].

data.headline: Book value is only as good as what it earns.
data.text: Buffett treats a price to book of 1.24 as protection, but book value of 41.18 SAR is worth only what its assets earn, and the return on equity is -15.37 per cent with no disclosed denominator [P1][P2]. A book value that is earning a negative return is a book value that is shrinking, and a price that is 1.24 times a shrinking number is not a margin of safety—it is a price that may still be too high [P1]. The January 2026 disclosure of an expected non-cash loss of SAR 18.3B is not traced into book anywhere in the pack [P6]. That is SAR 6.10 per share on a book of 41.18 SAR, and if it has not yet been taken, the true book value is lower than the published figure [P1]. The gaps are what worry me: no income statement, no P/E, no interest coverage, and a book value that may be stale. The price may be discounting a deterioration, or it may be discounting uncertainty about a deterioration we cannot measure. I cannot tell which, and that is the point.
data.concedes: A yield of 5.86 per cent is what the data shows at present [P1].

data.headline: A falling yield on a falling price is not protection.
data.text: Buffett leans on a yield of 5.86 per cent, but the per-share payment has stepped down to 1.1 SAR from 1.5 SAR [P1][P3]. A yield is only as good as the earnings behind it, and the return on equity of -15.37 per cent suggests the cover is not shown [P2]. The pack carries no payout ratio computed against a matched earnings window, so I cannot tell you whether that 1.1 SAR is being paid out of earnings or out of capital [P3]. A dividend cut is a signal, and the direction is clear: from 2.25 SAR in H1 2022 to 1.5 SAR in H1 2025 to 1.1 SAR in H1 2026 [P3]. That is a business returning less to its owners each year, and a yield that looks high only because the price has fallen further than the dividend. I want to see the earnings before I call a 5.86 per cent yield a margin of safety [P1]. A dividend paid out of a loss is not a return on capital; it is a return of capital.
data.concedes: Dividends are still being paid, with H1 2026 payment set for 2026-09-01 [P3].

data.headline: The balance sheet predates the largest disclosed event.
data.text: Buffett reads the balance sheet as a cushion, but the largest item SABIC has disclosed is a loss of SAR 18.3B from a disposal, and the pack does not show its effect on book [P6]. A transformation of the portfolio changes what the company is, and the ratios here predate it. The debt to equity of 0.26 and the current ratio of 1.8 are a snapshot of a company that is being restructured, and the restructuring is not yet in the numbers [P2]. The company has also disclosed a feedstock price increase, a reserve transfer of SAR 110.9B, and a stake sale to Maaden for SAR 3.6B [P6]. These are not small items. A balance sheet that has not absorbed them is not a foundation for a decade-long case. The price to book of 1.24 may look like protection, but if the book value is about to be rewritten, the protection is thinner than it appears [P1]. I need to see the balance sheet after the disposal to know what the company actually owns.
data.concedes: The 5.86 per cent yield sits within the range of peer yields shown [P1][P5].

data.text: The data shows a return on equity of -15.37 per cent and a falling price, but not what caused it or how long it has lasted [P2][P7]. Low leverage and a price near book limit the downside, yet they do not show that earning power is intact.

data.headline: Weakness is visible in price and returns, but the pack cannot show business deterioration clearly
data.answer:
The data shows weakness, but not clearly the cause or duration of it. The published return on equity is -15.37 per cent and return on assets is -8.24 per cent, with no disclosed denominator or earnings window [P2]. The price fell from 61.75 to 45.32 SAR over one year and from 121.0 to 45.32 SAR over five years [P7][P8]. The dividend per share for H1 2026 is 1.1 SAR, below 1.5 SAR for H1 2025 [P3]. SABIC disclosed on 2026-01-07 a sale of its Americas and Europe units with an expected non-cash loss of SAR 18.3B [P6].

What the room agrees on: the market has marked the shares down and the returns shown are negative. Lynch, Marks and Buffett also agree that earnings cannot be traced, because the pack holds no income statement, no quarters and no dated balance sheet. Debt to equity of 0.26061782975782133 and a current ratio of 1.8006209078026552 show no strain in the published ratios, as Dalio and Buffett both note [P2].

Rulings. On whether price near book of 1.24 is a margin of safety, the evidence cannot settle it: book value after the disposal loss is not in the pack [P1][P6]. On whether deterioration is shown beyond price, the evidence cannot settle it: Lynch found zero quarters, and the return on equity has no window, so persistence is unknown [P2]. On whether the balance sheet is strong or only adequate, this is a matter of judgment: Buffett and Dalio read the same ratios, with percentiles of 50.5 and 63.4, and weigh them differently [P2].

So the data shows deterioration in price, in the stated returns and in the per-share dividend, but it does not show it in the business itself clearly. The room's confidence should be modest in both directions.

headline: Returns are strong and the multiple is a premium to peers; the pack cannot show it is earned.
answer:
What the data shows: Al Rajhi Bank trades at 14.51x earnings and 3.19x book, with return on equity of 23.49% and return on assets of 2.53% [P1]. Trailing twelve-month EPS is SAR 4.42 [P1]. Every listed peer carries a lower P/E, from Saudi National Bank at 9.48x to Riyad Bank at 7.78x [P5]. The dividend yield is 2.6% [P1], below the peers' yields shown in [P5]. Price momentum is soft: the 6-month return is -10.68% and the price is below both the 50-day and 200-day averages [P1].

Where the room agrees: the 23.49% return on equity is strong, and the valuation is a premium to the listed banks [P1]. Buffett, Lynch, Dalio, Marks, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan each conceded the first point, and Buffett accepted in his final word that the premium cannot be tested without peer returns. Debt-to-equity of 1.72 sits at the 22.7th sector percentile [P2].

What the data cannot tell: it holds no quarterly earnings series, so Lynch's growth claim, cited to a [P9] that is not in the pack, cannot be used. It holds no peer return on equity, no payout ratio and no interest coverage [P2].

Rulings: on whether 14.51x is cheap or a premium, the multiple comparison is settled as a premium to peers [P5], but whether the premium is deserved is not settled, because peer returns are absent. On earnings growth, the pack holds only TTM EPS of SAR 4.42 [P1], so growth cannot be verified. On balance-sheet and price risk, the advisors read the same figures, the 22.7th percentile debt-to-equity [P2] and the -83.12% maximum drawdown [P1], and weigh them differently.

On the member's question: the returns support a premium, but the data does not show that this size of premium is supported by earnings.
gaps: Peer return on equity figures would show whether the multiple gap is matched by a returns gap.
A quarterly income statement would show whether earnings are growing or flat.
Interest coverage and payout ratio are missing from the fundamentals [P2], so funding cost and dividend cover cannot be judged.
disagreements: Is 14.51x P/E cheap or a premium to peers [P1]? - The premium to peers is a fact: SNB 9.48x, Riyad Bank 7.78x [P5] against 14.51x [P1]. Whether the 23.49% ROE [P1] justifies it cannot be tested because the pack has no peer ROE or growth forecast.

How much weight to give balance-sheet and price risk? - All sides read the same figures: debt-to-equity 1.72 at the 22.7th percentile [P2], the -83.12% maximum drawdown and the position below the moving averages [P1]. They weigh them differently. Interest coverage and payout are missing [P2].

data.headline: A 23 per cent return on equity on 14.5 times earnings is cheap
data.text: The two numbers that settle this are in the pack: return on equity is 23.49 per cent and the shares trade on 14.51 times earnings, with price to book at 3.19 [P1]. A business earning 23.49 per cent on equity is a very good business, and 14.51 times earnings is a market multiple [P1]. You are therefore being asked to pay an ordinary price for an extraordinary return on capital, and that is the definition of a cheap share. Return on assets of 2.53 per cent is what a bank's balance sheet produces and is not the relevant measure [P1]. The valuation is not merely supported by the earnings and returns in this pack - it is undemanding against them, and the multiple should be higher than it is.

data.headline: The premium valuation reflects market leadership, but the data shows a mixed picture on earnings and returns.
data.text:
The current valuation of 14.51x P/E and 3.19x P/B [P1] places Al Rajhi Bank at a significant premium to its TADAWUL-listed banking peers. Looking at the peer list [P5], the next highest P/E is Bank Albilad at 11.94, while the largest competitor, Saudi National Bank, trades at 9.48. The sector average, excluding Al Rajhi, is clearly lower. This premium is partially supported by superior profitability: the company’s ROE of 23.49% [P1, P2] is a clear sector leader, as the quality seat’s bullish vote [P4] confirms. However, the ROA of 2.53% [P1, P2] is a more moderate measure of return on the entire asset base, and no sector percentile is available in [P2] to rank it.

From a strategic perspective, the long arc of the price shows a 34.24% return over five years [P8], demonstrating a patient market’s reward, though the more recent 12-month return of 2.46% and a 10.68% decline over six months [P1] suggest the premium is being questioned. The bank has been actively building its capital structure, as disclosed. It completed a $1.5 billion AT1 sukuk offering in January 2025 and a $1 billion Tier 2 social sukuk in September 2025 [P6]. Most recently, on 2026-01-06, it announced the issuance of additional USD-denominated AT1 capital sukuk [P6]. These disclosures show a bank fortifying its balance sheet for a long-term strategy, a use of capital I find more compelling than the 2.6% dividend yield [P1], which is the lowest among the named peers [P5]. The debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72, ranking in the 22.7th percentile within its peer class [P2], reflects the leverage typical of a growth-oriented bank. The data shows a clear sector leader priced at a premium justified by its superior ROE and strategic capital activities, but the declining price momentum and a P/E nearly 50% higher than most peers mean the market is already pricing in a great deal of future success that the current data alone cannot fully confirm [P3].

data.headline: The valuation is rich; the dividend history shows confidence that must be weighed against the price.
data.text:
The market is asking 14.51 times earnings and 3.19 times book value for Al Rajhi Bank [P1]. That is not a crisis price. I look for a franchise marked down when others are selling, and the data here does not show that moment: the shares are down 14.92% from their 52-week high and only 6.66% above the low [P1], while the one-year return is a modest 2.46% [P1]. The 12-month drawdown of over 83% in the data [P1] is a very long-term figure and does not describe the last year.

What the data shows me about returns to owners is a steady, growing stream. The dividend history [P3] runs from a half-yearly DPS of 0.63 SAR in early 2020 to 1.17 SAR announced in January 2026, with the amounts paid rising from 3,750 million SAR to 7,000 million SAR over the same period. The bank has not cut; it has raised, and it has done so while repeatedly increasing its capital through bonus shares — a 60% increase in 2022 and a 50% increase in April 2026 [P3]. A management that keeps raising the payout while expanding the share count is showing confidence. The dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is modest, but it is built on a rising absolute return.

I cannot see the payout ratio because the data pack does not provide it for this company [P2]. That is a gap: I cannot tell you what portion of earnings is being returned. The ROE of 23.49% [P1] is strong, and a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72, better than roughly 77% of the sector [P2], tells me the balance sheet can carry the bank through a rough patch. The brand is not in the data, and I will not assume it. At 3.19 times book, you are paying for a premium franchise [P1]. The question is whether the price already reflects that quality. I would be more interested if the stock were testing its lows, not sitting in the middle of its range.

data.headline: Quarterly earnings show a growth story, but P/E is higher than peers.
data.text:
The story here is a bank that's been growing its earnings, and the quarterly record backs that up, but the price is already asking a premium for it. Let's walk through what the data actually shows.

First, the quarterly record from [P9] — I count six quarters of net income, from Q1 2025 through Q2 2026, and the trend is clearly up. Net income in Q1 2025 was SAR 4,631 million and by Q2 2026 it reached SAR 5,762 million [P1] [P3]. That's a 24% jump over five quarters [P3]. Every single quarter shows sequential growth except for a tiny dip from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026 [P1] [P3]. Operating income is also climbing, from SAR 7,563 million to SAR 9,093 million over the same stretch. So the business is doing more business, quarter after quarter.

The annual figures reflect this: the trailing twelve-month EPS is SAR 4.42 [P1], and with a last price of SAR 62.1, that gives a P/E of 14.51 [P1]. Now, Lynch's method says compare that P/E to the earnings growth rate. The data here has no growth forecasts, so I can't do a full PEG ratio, but I can look at the history. The 12-month return is only 2.46% [P1], while the 1-year price range shows a drop from SAR 70.2 to SAR 62.1, an 11.54% decline [P7]. The market is not cheering the earnings growth yet.

When I look at peers, the P/E is high. Saudi National Bank trades at 9.48x, Riyad Bank at 7.78x, Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82x [P5]. Al Rajhi's 14.51x is a premium [P1]. The dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is also lower than most peers, which offer 5% and above [P5]. So you're paying more for the earnings and getting less back in cash.

The balance sheet gives some comfort: debt-to-equity of 1.72 is better than 77% of the sector [P2], so the bank can weather a rough patch. But the valuation is asking you to believe the growth will keep going at this pace, and the price hasn't been cooperating lately. I'd want to see the P/E come down or the earnings growth accelerate before I'd call the valuation supported.

data.headline: Price assumes perfection; the data shows gaps we cannot ignore.
data.text:
What the data shows is a picture of a high-quality bank trading at a premium to its peers, and that premium is the question. The price of SAR 62.10 [P1] gives us a P/E of 14.51x and a P/B of 3.19x [P1]. Against the sector peers listed in [P5], this is a rich valuation. Saudi National Bank trades at 9.48x earnings, Riyad Bank at 7.78x, and Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82x [P5]. The market is ascribing a significantly higher multiple to Al Rajhi's earnings and book value.

What does this price have to be assuming? It is assuming that Al Rajhi's superior profitability is sustainable and will continue to justify a wide gap. The data supports that on the surface: an ROE of 23.49% [P1] is a genuinely strong number and the 'quality' seat in [P4] correctly flags it as bullish. The bank has a history of consistent dividend payments and bonus share distributions [P3], which signals confidence.

However, my mandate is to ask what we don't know, and the gaps are significant. The five-year price summary [P8] shows a maximum drawdown of over 83% from some point in that period, a figure that demands humility about what can happen to any price. The current price is already 10.68% lower over the last six months and sits below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1]. The pendulum of sentiment appears to have swung back from optimism.

More critically, the fundamentals data in [P2] is incomplete for assessing risk. We have a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72, which is in a healthy 22.7th sector percentile, but the interest coverage ratio is missing [P2]. For a bank that has been actively issuing AT1 and Tier 2 sukuk, as the news in [P6] details, the cost of that capital is a crucial piece of the puzzle we simply do not have. The P/B of 3.19x is a bet on the stability and quality of the book, but without a full picture of leverage costs, that bet is made in partial darkness [P1]. The current valuation is supported by the bank's high ROE, but the price is already discounting a lot of good news. The asymmetry here is not obviously favorable; the upside requires continued perfection, while the downside is a re-rating toward peer multiples if that perfection falters, even slightly.

data.headline: The balance sheet is funded by a manageable debt load, but the 14.5x P/E prices in a stability the volatile history and leverage do not fully guarantee.
data.text:
The question is whether the current valuation—a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19 [P1]—is supported by what the data shows about earnings and returns. I see this as a machine with a few critical levers: profitability, the funding structure, and the price history as a record of past stress.

First, the earnings engine is strong. The return on equity is 23.49% [P2], which is high and places the quality seat's vote as bullish [P4]. Return on assets is a much thinner 2.53% [P2], which is typical for a bank but shows the profitability depends heavily on leverage. The P/E of 14.51 [P1] is not extreme in absolute terms; the value seat is neutral on it [P4]. However, among the sector peers listed, every one trades at a lower P/E, from SNB at 9.48 to Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82 [P5]. The market is giving Al Rajhi a significant premium over its peers for its higher returns.

Now, the part I am answerable for: the balance sheet. The debt-to-equity ratio is 1.72 [P2], which is a direct measure of leverage. This is in the 22.7th percentile for the sector [P2], meaning it is on the lower, more conservative side. The funding is not a problem today. What would make it a problem? The bank has issued billions in USD-denominated AT1 and Tier 2 sukuk in 2025 and 2026 [P6]. These instruments are perpetual or long-dated, but they introduce a direct sensitivity to global credit conditions and the USD/SAR peg. A sustained spike in global credit spreads, which this data pack does not provide, is the scenario that would pressure this funding structure. The price history confirms the machine is not smooth: the 1-year volatility is 20.94% and the maximum drawdown from the data is a severe -83.12% [P1]. The current price is below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1], and the momentum seat is bearish [P4].

My assessment: the high ROE supports a premium, but the premium is large relative to peers. The balance sheet is conservatively leveraged within its sector, yet the reliance on international sukuk markets is a link to global cycles that the current valuation does not seem to discount. The biggest mistake here would be assuming the low debt percentile alone makes the funding invulnerable when the price history shows it has been deeply cyclical.

data.headline: Good company, but is it a good investment at this price?
data.text: Buffett, you say a 23.49% ROE against a 14.51x P/E is the definition of a cheap share [P1]. I agree the ROE is genuinely strong [P1]. But the data shows every listed peer trades at a significantly lower multiple: SNB at 9.48x, Riyad Bank at 7.78x, Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82x [P5]. The market is already paying a large premium for that superior return. What the price has to be assuming is that this gap is sustainable and that the earnings are not at a cyclical peak. The five-year price history shows a maximum drawdown of over 83% [P8], a reminder that even the best franchises can be re-rated violently. The current price is below both the 50-day and 200-day moving averages and down 10.68% over six months [P1], which suggests the pendulum of sentiment is already swinging away from optimism. A cheap share is one where the downside is limited and the upside is not dependent on perfection. At 3.19x book, the downside is a re-rating toward the peer group if the ROE normalizes, and that risk is not reflected in calling the valuation undemanding [P1].
data.concedes: The ROE of 23.49% is a genuinely strong return on capital that supports a premium over peers [P1].

data.headline: Your quarterly growth story cites data this pack does not carry.
data.text: Lynch, you build your whole case on six quarters of net income climbing from SAR 4,631 million to SAR 5,762 million, and you cite [P9], [P1] and [P3] for it. But there is no [P9] in this pack, and none of the datasets we have—[P1] through [P8]—holds a quarterly net-income series. The only earnings figure the pack gives us is trailing twelve-month EPS of SAR 4.42 [P1]. I cannot verify a growth trend I cannot see, and the room cannot rely on a claim that rests on data that is not here. The dividend record in [P3] does show rising payouts: from 0.63 SAR per share in early 2020 to 1.17 SAR announced in January 2026, with the total amount paid rising from SAR 3,750 million to SAR 7,000 million over the same window. That is a signal of confidence, but it is a signal of what management chose to return, not a direct measure of what was earned. Without the payout ratio, which [P2] confirms is missing, I cannot connect the dividend growth to the earnings growth you assert. If the pack had those quarterly figures, your argument would be stronger. It does not, and we must say so plainly.
data.concedes: The peer P/E comparison is valid: Al Rajhi's 14.51x is a clear premium over every listed peer in [P5].

data.headline: Lynch, you cannot show quarterly growth from this pack.

A growth story built on numbers not in the room cannot be debated. The question is whether the current valuation is supported by what the data shows, and the data shows a 23.49 per cent return on equity [P1] earned on a book value of SAR 20.11 per share [P1]. That is a very good business. I will not quarrel with your observation that the P/E is above peers [P5], but I will say that a 23.49 per cent ROE is a far better measure of earning power than a comparison of multiples across banks with different returns. The pack does not tell us what ROE those peers earn, so the premium argument is incomplete.

data.headline: A premium multiple is not an ordinary price
data.text: Buffett, you call 14.51 times earnings an ordinary price for an extraordinary return, but the peer data in [P5] shows it is not ordinary at all for this sector. Saudi National Bank trades at 9.48x, Riyad Bank at 7.78x, and Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82x [P5]. Al Rajhi's multiple is nearly double that of several large, established competitors. The market is already pricing in a significant premium for that 23.49% ROE [P1]. The question is not whether the business is good—the ROE confirms it is—but whether the price already reflects that goodness so fully that the margin of safety is thin. The way the machine works, a high ROE that depends on leverage, as a 2.53% ROA [P1] suggests, is more vulnerable to a credit contraction than a high ROE built on asset turns or margins. The balance sheet is conservatively leveraged for now at a 1.72 debt-to-equity ratio [P2], but the price history shows an 83.12% maximum drawdown [P1], a reminder that the cycle can turn violently. Paying a premium multiple for a cyclical machine is a different risk profile than paying a market multiple for a steady compounder.
data.concedes: the 23.49% ROE is genuinely extraordinary and a sign of a very good business [P1].

data.headline: A good business does not make a cheap price by itself.
data.text: Buffett, you call the 14.51x P/E an ordinary price for an extraordinary return, and from the data in [P1] alone that has force. But I cannot read the valuation in isolation when the pack gives us a sector to measure against. The peers in [P5] show Saudi National Bank at 9.48x, Riyad Bank at 7.78x, and Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82x. Al Rajhi trades at a premium of roughly fifty percent or more to every one of them. The ROE of 23.49% is indeed the best we see, but the pack carries no peer ROE figures to test how much of that premium is deserved [P2]. The bank has been building its capital stack aggressively, with $1.5 billion in AT1 sukuk in January 2025 and another $1 billion in Tier 2 social sukuk in September 2025 [P6], yet the price has fallen 10.68% over six months and sits below both moving averages [P1]. The market is not treating this as an obviously cheap asset. A superior business, yes; a cheap price, the data does not show.
data.concedes: The 23.49% ROE is a genuinely strong return on equity [P1].

data.headline: A great business at a premium price is not a cheap stock.
data.text: Buffett, you call a 23.49% ROE on a 14.51 P/E cheap—an ordinary price for an extraordinary return [P1]. But the data shows the price is not ordinary, it’s a premium. Every peer in [P5] trades cheaper: SNB at 9.48x earnings, Riyad at 7.78x, Saudi Awwal at 7.82x. Al Rajhi’s 14.51x is nearly double some of those [P1]. The market already knows it’s a high-return bank and is charging for it. The 12-month price return is a mere 2.46% and the 6-month return is down 10.68% [P1], while the 1-year price range shows an 11.54% drop from SAR 70.20 to SAR 62.10 [P7]. The story of great profitability isn’t translating into a rising price lately. I also can’t find the quarterly earnings growth I need to support a premium multiple—the pack has no [P9] and only a TTM EPS of SAR 4.42 [P1]. Without seeing the quarter-by-quarter trend, I can’t confirm the earnings engine is accelerating enough to justify paying up. I need the P/E to match the growth rate, and here I’m missing half the equation.
data.concedes: A 23.49% ROE is a genuinely superior return that deserves a higher multiple than a mediocre bank [P1].

data.headline: Returns are strong and the multiple is a premium to peers; the pack cannot show it is earned.
data.answer:
What the data shows: Al Rajhi Bank trades at 14.51x earnings and 3.19x book, with return on equity of 23.49% and return on assets of 2.53% [P1]. Trailing twelve-month EPS is SAR 4.42 [P1]. Every listed peer carries a lower P/E, from Saudi National Bank at 9.48x to Riyad Bank at 7.78x [P5]. The dividend yield is 2.6% [P1], below the peers' yields shown in [P5]. Price momentum is soft: the 6-month return is -10.68% and the price is below both the 50-day and 200-day averages [P1].

Where the room agrees: the 23.49% return on equity is strong, and the valuation is a premium to the listed banks [P1]. Buffett, Lynch, Dalio, Marks, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan each conceded the first point, and Buffett accepted in his final word that the premium cannot be tested without peer returns. Debt-to-equity of 1.72 sits at the 22.7th sector percentile [P2].

What the data cannot tell: it holds no quarterly earnings series, so Lynch's growth claim, cited to a [P9] that is not in the pack, cannot be used. It holds no peer return on equity, no payout ratio and no interest coverage [P2].

Rulings: on whether 14.51x is cheap or a premium, the multiple comparison is settled as a premium to peers [P5], but whether the premium is deserved is not settled, because peer returns are absent. On balance-sheet and price risk, the advisors read the same figures, the 22.7th percentile debt-to-equity [P2] and the -83.12% maximum drawdown [P1], and weigh them differently.

On the member's question: the returns support a premium, but the data does not show that this size of premium is supported by earnings.
