headline: Returns look strong, but the earnings record behind them is not in the data
answer:
The data shows a stated return on equity of 23.49 per cent, a price to earnings of 14.51 and a price to book of 3.19, with earnings per share over the trailing twelve months of 4.42 SAR [P1]. Buffett reads that as an undemanding price for a high return. The room agrees the return is strong on its face.

The room also agrees on what is missing. P9 is not in the pack, so there is no income statement, no quarterly record, no balance sheet and no computed payout. Lynch could count no quarters, so no earnings trend can be set against the multiple. Dalio could read only one health metric, debt to equity of 1.7165 with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. Marks notes that return on equity carries no disclosed denominator, and that enterprise value to EBITDA, price to sales, net margin and payout are not available [P2].

Al-Rumayyan shows the bank's price to earnings of 14.51 sits above all eight bank peers, whose multiples run from 7.78 to 11.94, and its yield of 2.6 per cent is below theirs, which run from 3.1 to 6.02 per cent [P5]. The pack carries no peer returns on equity, so the premium cannot be matched to a return advantage. Alwaleed adds that a 50 per cent bonus issue took effect on 2026-04-20 [P3], so older per-share figures sit on a different share count. Price data is also stale, with the quote dated 2026-10-13 and the technicals 2026-08-11 [P1].

So the valuation is consistent with the stated return, but the pack cannot show that the return is durable, how it is funded or how it compares with peers.
gaps: The income statement over several periods, which would show whether the return on equity is durable.
The equity denominator behind the published return on equity.
Quarterly earnings with a comparison year, which would show the trend.
disagreements: Is 14.51 times earnings cheap against the stated return on equity [P1]? - The decision turns on peer returns on equity, which the pack does not contain. It shows peer multiples of 7.78 to 11.94 [P5] against 14.51 [P1], but without peer returns the premium cannot be called earned or unearned.

Can the stated return be trusted without the statements? - The 23.49 per cent return on equity is published [P1], but P9, its denominator and the funding detail are absent, and the debt to equity of 1.7165 [P2] has no stated operands. The figure that would decide this is not in the pack.

Does the 2.6 per cent yield and the bonus issue weaken support for the valuation [P1]? - Both read the same figures: the 2.6 per cent yield [P1] and the 2026-04-20 bonus issue [P3]. Alwaleed weights returns paid to owners and Buffett weights return on capital, which is a difference in weighting and not a difference of fact.

data.note: The question asks whether the data supports the valuation, not what to do, so it is framed as a choice between readings of the data.

data.headline: A 23 per cent return on equity on 14.5 times earnings is cheap
data.text: The two numbers that settle this are in the pack: return on equity is 23.49 per cent and the shares trade on 14.51 times earnings, with price to book at 3.19 [P1]. A business earning 23.49 per cent on equity is a very good business, and 14.51 times earnings is a market multiple [P1]. You are therefore being asked to pay an ordinary price for an extraordinary return on capital, and that is the definition of a cheap share. Return on assets of 2.53 per cent is what a bank's balance sheet produces and is not the relevant measure [P1]. The valuation is not merely supported by the earnings and returns in this pack - it is undemanding against them, and the multiple should be higher than it is.

data.headline: Quarterly record absent; earnings growth cannot be checked against the multiple.
data.text:
My job here is to read the quarterly trend, and I cannot do it. The pack I was given holds P7 and P9. P9, with the quarterly income statements, is not here [P3]. I have no quarter to count, no sequence to read, no way to say whether earnings are accelerating, flattening or turning down. One number — trailing twelve-month earnings per share of 4.42 SAR [P1] — tells me where the bus is, not whether it is speeding up or slowing down. Without a growth rate I cannot test a price-to-earnings multiple of 14.51 [P1] against the pace of earnings, which is the first thing I would do with any company. The story is not checkable.

What I can see is the market's own reading of the last year. The one-year price summary runs from 2025-09-29 to 2026-10-13: first close 70.2 SAR, last close 62.1 SAR, a change of -11.54 per cent [P7]. That is the market marking down the multiple even as the trailing earnings figure sits at 4.42 SAR [P1]. The price is telling us something the quarterly record might explain, but that record is absent. I lean to B because the return on equity of 23.49 per cent [P1] looks strong on its face, but the earnings history and trend needed to confirm the multiple are simply not shown.

data.headline: Balance sheet absent; leverage behind the 23.49% ROE cannot be measured [P1].
data.text:
I am answerable for the balance sheet, and P9 — which holds the statements, the funding mix and the leverage calculations — is not in this pack. I cannot give you a position date, a deposit-to-loan ratio, a measure of wholesale funding dependence, or any of the other levers that tell me how a bank's machine is built. The one health metric shown is a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.7165, with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. That is a rank, not a judgment, and it tells me this bank carries less debt relative to equity than most of its peers in the sector class it was ranked in. But the pack does not say which operands sit behind that ratio, whether it mixes a stock and a flow from different dates, or what is in the numerator.

The return on equity of 23.49 per cent [P1] is the headline that catches every eye. In banking, a high return on equity can come from a wide lending spread, from fee income, or from leverage. Without the balance sheet I cannot tell you which one is driving it. A machine that produces 23.49 per cent with low leverage is one thing; the same return with high leverage is another, because the second one breaks faster when funding tightens [P1]. The data cannot answer that question. I lean to B: the returns look strong, but the record behind them — the balance sheet that funds them — is not shown.

data.headline: Price assumes ROE persists; material gaps limit what we know.
data.text:
The price of 62.1 SAR [P1] implies 14.51 times trailing earnings and 3.19 times book value [P1]. A price-to-book of 3.19 on a bank is a statement: the market believes the 23.49 per cent return on equity [P1] is durable and perhaps growing. The five-year price summary shows a close of 62.1 SAR against a high close of 76.52 SAR and a first close five years ago of 46.26 SAR [P8]. The share has given back a good deal of its peak, and the one-year return is -11.54 per cent [P7]. The price is not demanding the best-case outcome, but it is still demanding a lot.

What we do not know is material. P9, with its limitations and its income statement, is absent from this pack [P3]. I cannot see the denominator behind the return on equity, the revenue line, or the cost structure. Enterprise value to EBITDA is null, and price to sales, net margin and payout are all missing inputs [P2]. These are not gaps at the margin; they are the core of the income statement. The price data itself is stale, with the quote dated 2026-10-13 and the technicals dated 2026-08-11 [P1]. The rule-based council's votes [P4] are fixed thresholds, not measurements, and I will not cite them as figures. I lean to B: the multiple runs ahead of the evidence we actually have, and the gaps are too wide to call it supported.

data.headline: Dividends shown, but what they were paid out of is absent.
data.text:
I am answerable for what was returned to owners and out of what. P3 shows a dividend history: 1.17 SAR per share for the second half of 2025, ex-dividend 2026-04-20, totalling 7,000 million SAR, and 0.50 SAR per share for the first half of 2025 [P3]. The yield is 2.6 per cent [P1]. Those are the cheques written. What I cannot tell you is what they were written against, because P9, which matches each payout to its earnings window, is not in this pack [P3]. I will not assemble a payout ratio from a dividend list; counting a dividend that falls outside the window is how a payout reads as four-fifths when it is really something else.

There is one thing the data does show clearly: a 50 per cent bonus issue on 2026-04-20 raised the capital from 40,000 million SAR to 60,000 million SAR, one new share for every two held [P3]. Every per-share figure before that date — earnings, book value, dividends — was struck on a different share count. The earnings per share of 4.42 SAR [P1] is a trailing figure and may already reflect the new count, but the data does not state that plainly. The bonus issue is a return of capital in another form, and it tells you management had confidence to distribute shares rather than cash. But confidence is not a payout ratio. I lean to B: the dividends are shown, but the earnings record they were paid from is not.

data.headline: Premium to every peer on P/E; sector rankings and earnings disclosures absent.
data.text:
Against the eight bank peers in P5, dated 2026-08-07, Al Rajhi Bank trades at a price-to-earnings of 14.51 [P1] while every one of them ranges from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5]. That is a premium to the entire peer set. Its dividend yield of 2.6 per cent [P1] sits below every peer, which range from 3.1 to 6.02 per cent [P5]. The market is paying more for each riyal of earnings and accepting less in cash return. That is a judgment about quality and growth, and it may be right, but the data does not show the earnings trend that would confirm it.

P2 gives no sector percentile for price-to-earnings or return on equity, so there is no ranking there. That is not a low ranking; it is an absent one. The disclosures in P6 are capital instruments: an AT1 sukuk offering announced on 2026-01-06, a 1 billion USD Tier 2 social sukuk completed on 2025-09-09, and earlier sukuk issuances [P6]. These tell me the bank is active in managing its capital structure and has access to international markets. The one news item, dated 2026-08-02, concerns Saudization memoranda of understanding [P6]. None of this is about earnings, and none of it bridges the gap between a 14.51 multiple and a peer set trading at 7.78 to 11.94 [P1] [P5]. I lean to B: the premium is clear, but the earnings record and peer returns needed to support it are not shown.

data.headline: The stated return still outweighs the missing denominator.
data.text: Marks, you are right that the pack does not disclose the denominator behind the 23.49 per cent return on equity [P1]. But the figure is published, and it sits alongside a book value of 20.11 SAR per share [P1]. Earnings per share of 4.42 SAR and a price of 62.1 SAR [P1] fit the price-to-earnings of 14.51. A business earning 23.49 per cent on its stated equity, offered at 14.51 times those earnings, is cheap on its face [P1]. Nothing in this pack contradicts that return. I concede that one window of figures from an absent income statement is not a record of durability. But the question is whether the valuation is supported by what the data shows, and what it shows is a high return on a stated book value at an ordinary multiple.
data.concedes: The income statement is absent, so one window of figures is not proof of durability.

data.headline: A multiple without growth is just a number.
data.text: Buffett, you call 14.51 times earnings undemanding, but a multiple is only cheap against the growth rate, and the pack gives me no earnings growth and no quarters to count [P1]. I cannot check the story. The six-month price return is -10.68 per cent [P1], so the market is not paying up on a visible trend — it is marking the share down even as the trailing earnings per share sits at 4.42 SAR [P1]. That is the market telling us something the quarterly record might explain, but that record is absent. A high return on equity of 23.49 per cent [P1] is a strong headline, and I concede that. But a multiple without a growth rate is like a speed without a direction, and I cannot call the valuation supported when the trend is invisible.
data.concedes: The stated return on equity of 23.49 per cent is high [P1].

data.headline: Funding is the machine behind the return.
data.text: Buffett, you treat the return on equity as the whole case, but a return of 23.49 per cent [P1] says nothing about how it is funded. Return on assets is 2.53 per cent [P1], and the debt-to-equity ratio is 1.7165 with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. A bank that earns 23.49 per cent on equity with a debt-to-equity ratio ranked in the low twenties among its peers is a different machine from one earning the same return with higher leverage [P1]. I concede that return on assets is the less relevant measure for a bank, as you say. data.concedes: Return on assets is the less relevant measure for a bank, as Buffett says.

data.headline: The price assumes durability the pack cannot demonstrate.

headline: Trailing earnings appear to cover the dividend and leverage is low, but cash flow and interest cover are unshown.
answer:
The pack shows trailing EPS of SAR 1.84 [P1]. The latest four declared dividends are SAR 0.34, 0.34, 0.34 and 0.33 per share [P3]. The room agrees that earnings exceed the dividend: Dalio puts the payout at about 73% on a SAR 1.35 sum [P1][P3]. The balance sheet supports this, with debt to equity of 0.20 and a current ratio near 2.0 [P2]. Return on equity is 26.75% and the yield is 5.01% [P1]. Alwaleed adds that the capital record shows bonus shares funded from retained earnings and no dilution [P3].

The pack does not publish a payout ratio, free cash flow yield or interest coverage; each is marked missing or not applicable [P2]. Marks is therefore right that coverage is derived rather than stated. Dalio and Al-Rumayyan add that the company issued bonds and sukuk, so debt service is the unmeasured stress point [P6]. The pack contains no quarterly EPS and no forward commodity data, so it cannot show how far earnings could fall before the payout is strained.

On the evidence, the dividend looks covered by trailing earnings and supported by a low-leverage balance sheet. Whether it is funded from operating cash rather than borrowing cannot be shown from this data. This describes the data and is not advice.

data.headline: The dividend is covered by earnings; its safety depends on debt-service capacity the data here does not show.
data.text:
The question is whether the earnings machine generates enough to sustain the dividend, and what would break that link. I start with what the data shows. Earnings per share over the last twelve months are SAR 1.84 [P1]. The dividend per share over the same period, summing the last four quarterly payments, totals SAR 1.35 (0.34 + 0.34 + 0.34 + 0.33) [P3]. The payout from earnings is therefore about 73%. That is a comfortable coverage ratio. The return on equity of 26.75% [P1][P2] shows the underlying business is highly profitable on the equity base, which supports the dividend capacity.

Now I look at the balance sheet to see what would have to happen for the funding to become a problem. The position I am answerable for is struck at the date of the last fundamentals update, 2026-08-12 [P2]. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.20 [P2]. This is low leverage; the machine is funded overwhelmingly by equity, not debt. The current ratio is 2.00 [P2], meaning liquid assets are twice short-term obligations. That provides a buffer for the dividend if earnings dip briefly.

What the data does not show is the interest-coverage ratio [P2]. That is a critical missing piece. Without it, I cannot see how many times operating earnings cover the interest bill on the bonds and sukuk the company has been issuing [P6]. If earnings fell, the first stress point would be debt service, not the dividend. A scenario where the dividend is cut would likely require a sustained drop in earnings large enough that management chooses to preserve cash for debt payments and the large capital programs, such as the Jafurah gas project [P6]. The data here contains no oil prices or macro forecasts, so I cannot assign a probability to that earnings drop. My confidence in the dividend's safety is therefore limited to saying the current earnings cover it well, the balance sheet is not heavily indebted, and the main risk I cannot measure is how far earnings could fall before debt service is threatened.

The previous three quarters were also SAR 0.34, and before that we saw a steady SAR 0.33 for four quarters [P3]. This is a company that has raised its regular dividend. Now, the critical question: is it covered? The trailing twelve-month earnings per share are SAR 1.84 [P1]. Four quarterly payments of SAR 0.34 total SAR 1.36 [P3]. That is a payout ratio of roughly 74%. The earnings cover the dividend with a comfortable margin. The company is not stretching to pay it. The return on equity of 26.75% tells you the earnings themselves are generated from a highly profitable base [P2].

The balance sheet also speaks to safety. A debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 is low, and a current ratio near 2.0 shows ample liquidity [P2]. This company does not need to borrow to pay its owners.

We must also look at the share count. The capital has been stable since the last bonus issue in 2023, which increased shares by 20% [P3]. That bonus was funded from retained earnings—a signal of confidence, not dilution. The secondary offering in 2024 was a sale by the government, not the company; it did not change the share count or the capital [P3]. The per-share figures we use today are clean.

What the data does not show me is the exact payout ratio computed against a matched earnings window for the most recent dividend. The pack does not provide a [P9] dataset with that calculation. What the company has disclosed reinforces this picture of stability, not fragility. data.headline: Coverage is not computable from this data, but the record shows a consistent, growing dividend.
data.text:
The member's question is the right one, but the data pack does not let me answer it directly. To judge whether a dividend is covered, I need a payout ratio — dividends per share divided by earnings per share — or at least the total dividends paid against net income. Neither figure is present. [P1] gives us an EPS of 1.84 and a dividend yield of 5.01%, and from the quote of 25.78 I can see that the implied annual dividend is roughly 1.29 per share [P1]. That looks comfortably below the 1.84 in earnings [P1]. But the dividend record in [P3] tells a more granular story. The last four quarterly dividends total 1.35 per share, which is 0.34 for each of the last three quarters and 0.33 for the quarter before that [P3]. That brings the trailing payout to about 73% of the 1.84 in TTM earnings — a figure the data does not state and that I note only as a rough inference, not as a computed fact [P1].

What the data does show is a dividend that has been paid without interruption across every quarter in the record. The base dividend has been stable, and performance-linked dividends have been added in several periods, as the notes in [P3] describe. The company has also grown its capital through bonus shares, which tells me retained earnings have been substantial enough to capitalise. On the balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 is low [P2], and the current ratio of nearly 2.0 suggests ample liquidity to meet near-term obligations. These are signs of a strong financial position, not signs of a dividend under stress.

What I do not know is just as important. The pack provides no free cash flow yield, no interest coverage ratio, and no payout ratio — each of them is marked as missing or not applicable in [P2]. Without free cash flow, I cannot see whether the dividend is funded from operations or from debt. Without those figures, any statement about coverage is an assumption, not an observation. The price, at 14.5 times earnings [P1], is not demanding, but that tells me about valuation, not about dividend safety. On the evidence available, the dividend looks well-supported by a strong balance sheet and a consistent record, but the data does not permit a conclusive answer on coverage.

data.headline: A 26.75 per cent return on equity and almost no debt: the dividend is safe [P1]
data.text: Safety here is a question about the business, and the business answers it. Return on equity is 26.75 per cent and return on assets 15.86 per cent, debt to equity is 0.20 and the current ratio is 2.0 [P1] [P2]. A company earning those returns with that little borrowing does not cut its dividend. The yield of 5.01 per cent is therefore about as secure as a yield gets in this market, and the arithmetic of what share of earnings is being paid out is a second-order detail beside the quality of the earnings themselves [P1]. Profitability of that order and a balance sheet of that strength are what make a distribution safe, and both are published in the pack rather than derived from it.

data.headline: I cannot check coverage quarter by quarter because the quarterly record is absent.
data.text:
The question is whether the dividend is covered by earnings, and for me that means counting the quarters. I need to see each quarter's earnings laid out next to each quarter's dividend, so I can tell whether the money that went out the door came in the same door. The pack has a dividend history in [P3] and a trailing earnings-per-share figure of 1.84 SAR with a price-to-earnings of 14.47 in [P1], but it has no quarterly income statements. Zero quarters to count. I cannot call a trend, I cannot say whether a particular quarter strained the payout, and I cannot tell you whether the 0.34 SAR per share paid for Q2 2026 was comfortably earned or not [P1] [P3].

The market's own reading of the stretch is mixed. Over one year the price moved 3.16 per cent from 24.99 to 25.78 SAR, with an average volume of 11.3 million shares over 260 trading days [P7]. Over five years the picture is different: the price fell 10.52 per cent from 28.81 to 25.78, with a high close of 38.64 and a low of 23.13, across 1,300 trading days and an average volume of 12.3 million [P8]. That tells me the market has not been steadily rewarding the dividend story.

What kind of company is this? A 6.4 trillion SAR market capitalisation, a 5.01 per cent yield, a 26.75 per cent return on equity, a 15.86 per cent return on assets [P1] [P2]. That is a large steady company, not a fast grower. For that kind, the dividend is the story. But the story is only as good as the quarterly record that supports it, and that record is not here. I like the yield, I like the returns, but I cannot do my homework without the quarters. The data does not answer the member's question.

data.headline: The balance sheet itself is absent, so I read only ratios that do not show what strains funding.
data.text:
The member asks about coverage and safety, and for me safety is a balance-sheet question: what does this company own, what does it owe, and what scenario would make that funding a problem? The balance sheet itself, with its date and its line items, is not in this pack. I have only the ratios that were computed from it.

Debt to equity is 0.2006, at a sector percentile of 54.0 [P2]. The current ratio is 1.9986, at a sector percentile of 68.4 [P1] [P2]. The composite health score is 61.2 [P2]. Those numbers say leverage is moderate and short-term liquidity is comfortable relative to the sector. But a ratio is only a summary: without the operands I cannot see whether the debt is short-term or long-term, fixed or floating, secured or unsecured, or what currency it is in. I cannot see what assets stand behind the current ratio, or whether they are cash, receivables, or inventory that might not be liquid in a stress scenario.

Interest coverage is missing because the inputs were not available, and free cash flow yield is not applicable to the sector [P2]. Those are two of the most important measures for the question at hand. Interest coverage would tell me how many times earnings cover the interest bill, which is the first thing that goes wrong when funding strains. Free cash flow would tell me whether the dividend is being paid out of cash the business actually generates after it maintains itself. Both are absent.

The scenarios I would normally build—a sustained drop in oil prices, a credit crunch under the peg, a forced reduction in government spending—require data on revenues, costs, and the maturity profile of the debt, none of which the pack provides. The ratios I have do not say what would have to happen for the funding to become a problem, because I cannot see the funding itself. The data here does not answer the safety question.

data.headline: The price assumes a safe dividend, but the data to check coverage is absent.
data.text:
At 25.78 SAR, dated 2026-10-13 and flagged stale, the market prices Saudi Aramco at 14.47 times trailing earnings of 1.84 SAR per share, with a dividend yield of 5.01 per cent [P1]. A five per cent yield in a world where many large companies pay less tells me the market is not treating this dividend as a sure thing. The five-year price change is minus 10.52 per cent, and the maximum drawdown over that period is minus 40.14 per cent [P8] [P1]. A stock that has fallen forty per cent from its high is one the market has already questioned.

The more important thing is what we do not know. Payout ratio is missing for lack of inputs [P2]. That is the single most direct measure of dividend coverage, and it is not here. Interest coverage is also missing, and net margin is missing. Free cash flow yield is not applicable to the sector [P2]. Every one of those gaps sits between us and an answer to the member's question. We cannot see the income statement, we cannot see the cash flow statement, and the pack's limitations section—which I am answerable for reading—would normally tell us why, but the pack here carries no such statement.

The dividend history in [P3] shows payments of 0.34 SAR per share for the three most recent quarters, up from 0.33 for the four before that, and 0.48 in 2024 when large performance-linked amounts were included. That pattern suggests the board has confidence. But a board's confidence is not the same as coverage. A company can pay a dividend from borrowing, from asset sales, or from past retained earnings, and none of those would show up in the yield alone.

What the price assumes is that the 5.01 per cent yield is sustainable [P1]. What the data can show is that the assumptions cannot be checked. The gaps are not small; they are the gaps that matter. The room's confidence must not run ahead of its evidence, and on coverage the evidence is simply not here.

data.headline: The dividend was paid, but the pack does not show what it was paid out of.
data.text:
I am answerable for what was returned to owners and out of what. The pack shows the first half clearly: the dividend was paid, quarter after quarter. The most recent is 0.34 SAR per share for Q2 2026, announced 2026-08-04, totalling 82,060 million SAR [P3]. Before that, 0.34 for Q1 2026 and Q4 2025, then 0.33 for the four quarters from Q3 2025 back to Q4 2024, and 0.48 in 2024 when performance-linked dividends ran at 40,390 million SAR or more each quarter [P3]. The base dividend has been steady; the performance-linked portion has come down sharply from 2024 to 2025 and 2026 [P1] [P3].

The second half—what it was paid out of—is not in the pack. The payout ratio against a matched earnings window is missing for lack of inputs [P2]. I will not assemble one myself from the dividend list, because a dividend that falls outside the earnings window gives a wrong reading, and the pack's own payout calculation, which matches by date, could not be completed. Without it, I cannot tell you whether the 0.34 SAR was a comfortable distribution or a stretch [P3].

The share count matters here. Bonus issues in May 2022 at a rate of one for ten and May 2023 at one for ten increased the capital from 60,000 million to 75,000 million and then to 90,000 million SAR [P3]. Every per-share figure before those dates is on a different base. A 0.48 SAR dividend in 2024 was paid on 242,000 million shares [P1]; a dividend of the same amount per share before the bonus issues represented a smaller total payout. The secondary offering in June 2024 did not change the capital [P3].

A 5.01 per cent yield on a 25.78 SAR price [P1] is attractive. The company has never cut the base dividend in the record shown. But coverage is a number, not a pattern, and that number is absent. I can say the dividend was paid; I cannot say it was earned.

data.headline: The yield leads the sector, but coverage is not shown and the comparison is thin.
data.text:
I look at this company against its sector, and the sector comparison on dividends is sparse. Against the exchange's Energy peer list, Saudi Aramco's 5.01 per cent yield [P1] compares with 3.22 per cent for The National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia and 2.48 per cent for ADES Holding Company. Petro Rabigh, Arabian Drilling Company, and Saudi Arabian Refineries Company show no dividend yield at all [P5]. Aramco leads the peers that pay, but those peers are far smaller: the largest, The National Shipping Company, has a market capitalisation of 27,907 million SAR against Aramco's 6,413,000 million [P5] [P1]. The comparison says little about coverage because the businesses are not comparable in scale or in kind.

No sector percentile exists for dividend yield or payout ratio in [P2]. The health metrics that do carry percentiles—debt to equity at 54.0 and current ratio at 68.4, with a composite health score of 61.2—are middling within the sector, but they speak to the balance sheet, not to the earnings that fund the dividend [P2].

The company's own disclosures are more instructive. A 4 billion dollar bond issuance was completed on 2026-02-02 across four tranches, with maturities out to 30 years and coupons from 4 to 6 per cent [P6]. A 3 billion dollar sukuk was completed on 2025-09-17 with five- and ten-year tranches [P6]. These are large, long-dated, dollar-denominated obligations. They tell me the company can access global debt markets at reasonable rates, which supports liquidity. They also tell me the company is borrowing while paying a dividend, which is a choice worth noting for a long-horizon investor: cash paid out is cash not retained for the next decade.

The member asks about coverage, and the data to answer that—the payout ratio, the free cash flow, the earnings matched to the dividend window—is not in the pack. The yield is high, the peers are few, and the disclosures show a company that can raise capital. But coverage itself is not shown.

data.headline: Quality is not coverage, and I should have said so.
data.text: Marks is right that I stated safety without a payout figure. The published return on equity of 26.75 per cent carries no stated denominator or date [P2], and no income statement is in this pack to show a multi-year record. One return is not a record, so my word safe is a reading of quality, not a measure of coverage. A business that earns high returns on little debt is one I would expect to cover its dividend, but expectation is not the same as proof. The member asked a direct question about coverage, and the direct answer is a payout ratio matched to an earnings window. That ratio is missing [P2]. I cannot fill that gap with a return on equity, however strong.
data.concedes: The payout against earnings is not second-order; it is the direct answer and the pack does not hold it.

data.headline: Two ratios are not a quarterly record.
data.text: Buffett calls the dividend about as secure as a yield gets, but that rests on two ratios and no quarters. Without quarterly earnings I cannot say whether the 0.34 SAR per share declared for Q2 2026 [P3] was earned in that quarter. A strong ratio does not replace the homework. I need to see each quarter's earnings next to each quarter's dividend, and the pack gives me zero quarters to count. The trailing earnings per share of 1.84 SAR and the price to earnings of 14.47 [P1] are at least consistent with profitable operation, but they are a single trailing number, not a record I can trace through the dividend dates. A 5.01 per cent yield on a 25.78 SAR price [P1] looks attractive, but I cannot call it covered without the quarters.
data.concedes: The trailing earnings per share of 1.84 SAR and the price to earnings of 14.47 [P1] are at least consistent with profitable operation.

data.headline: Adequate leverage is not proof of safety.
data.text: Buffett treats 0.20 debt to equity as proof the dividend is safe [P2]. A 54.0 percentile on that measure and a health score of 61.2 [P2] describe an adequate position, not an exceptional one. The measure linking debt to the dividend, interest coverage, is absent [P2]. Without it, I cannot see how many times earnings cover the interest bill, which is the first thing that strains when funding tightens. Low borrowing and a current ratio near 2.0 [P2] are real cushions against a short earnings dip, but a cushion is not a guarantee. The balance sheet itself is not in the pack, so I cannot see the maturity profile, the currency mix, or whether the debt is fixed or floating. Safety is a stress-test, and the inputs for that test are not here.
data.concedes: Low borrowing and a current ratio near 2.0 [P2] are real cushions against a short earnings dip.

data.headline: Coverage is the question, not quality.
data.text: Buffett calls the payout arithmetic second-order, which inverts the question. The member asked about coverage, and the one figure that answers it, payout, is withheld as missing inputs [P2]. Quality ratios say the business earns well, not that this dividend is covered. A 26.75 per cent return on equity [P2] is a real sign of profitability, and I concede that. But profitability and coverage are not the same thing. A company can earn a high return on its equity and still pay a dividend it cannot sustain from current earnings, especially when the return figure carries no stated denominator or date. The gaps in this pack—payout, interest coverage, net margin, free cash flow—are the gaps that sit between us and an answer. The room must not fill them with a quality reading.
data.concedes: A 26.75 per cent return on equity [P2] is a real sign of profitability.

data.headline: The dividend was already cut in this record.
data.text: Buffett says the dividend does not get cut, yet the history shows a fall from 0.48 per share in 2024 to 0.33 in the 2025 payments [P3]. That drop was mostly the performance-linked part, which was 40,390 million SAR in one 2024 quarter and 820 million SAR afterwards [P3]. A reduction has already happened in this record. The base dividend has held, but the total distribution to owners fell sharply, and that is a cut in the money that reached shareholders. The three latest payments of 0.34 per share [P3] are steady and slightly higher, which suggests the board has stabilised the payout at a new level. But a cut is a cut, and the record shows one. Coverage cannot be assessed without the payout ratio, which is missing [P2], but the direction of the total distribution is in the data.
data.concedes: The three latest payments of 0.34 per share [P3] are steady and slightly higher.

data.headline: The yield is unranked, and the company is borrowing.
data.text: Buffett calls the yield about as secure as any in this market, but the pack ranks it against nothing: yield carries no sector percentile [P2]. The disclosures show the company raised debt in 2025 and 2026 [P6], which sits oddly beside a claim of almost no borrowing without a dated balance sheet. A 4 billion dollar bond issuance across four tranches and a 3 billion dollar sukuk [P6] are not trivial. The debt to equity of 0.2006 [P2] is low in absolute terms, and I concede that. But borrowing while paying a dividend is a choice: cash that goes to bondholders and shareholders is cash not retained for the next decade. For a long-horizon investor, that choice matters. The yield may be secure today, but the data to prove coverage is absent, and the debt programme says the company is funding itself from multiple sources.
data.concedes: The debt to equity of 0.2006 [P2] is low in absolute terms.

data.text: A 26.75 per cent return on equity and 0.20 debt to equity describe a business that should cover its distribution, but they do not prove it does [P2]. I withdraw the claim that the dividend does not get cut, because the pack shows no matched payout and no earnings record. The returns and low borrowing are consistent with a sturdy business, but coverage cannot be confirmed from this pack.
data.changed: I withdraw the claim that the dividend does not get cut, because the pack shows no matched payout and no earnings record.
data.would_change: An income statement over several years with a stated equity denominator and a matched-window payout would settle it.

data.text: I cannot say whether the quarterly record supports the dividend, since none is in the pack. The price shows no collapse over a year but a lower level than five years ago [P7] [P8]. Without quarters to count, I cannot call a trend or match a dividend to the earnings of the same period.
data.would_change: Quarterly net income for at least four quarters, with a comparison year, would let me call a direction.

data.text: The ratios show moderate leverage at a 54.0 percentile and adequate liquidity at a 68.4 percentile, but a scenario of lower earnings against steady payouts cannot be built from lines that are not here [P2]. The mistake that would hurt most is taking ratios as coverage. Interest coverage and the balance sheet itself are absent, and without them safety is unmeasurable.
data.would_change: A dated balance sheet with cash, debt and operating cash flow lines, plus interest coverage, would let me test scenarios.

data.text: The price at 25.78 SAR assumes the 5.01 per cent yield continues, but the pack cannot show that earnings cover it [P1]. Confidence should stop at what the ratios show: a 26.75 per cent return on equity is a real sign of profitability, but it is not coverage [P2]. Payout, interest coverage, and the income statement are missing, and those are the gaps that matter.
data.would_change: A matched-window payout and a dated income statement would let me say what the yield assumes.

data.text: The base dividend has been steady at 0.33 to 0.34 per share since the performance-linked part shrank from the 2024 level of 0.48 [P3]. But the earnings behind it are not shown, and the payout ratio is missing [P2]. Coverage is unmeasured here, however regular the payments.

data.text: Peers are too small and too few to rank the yield, and the disclosures say nothing about dividend policy [P5] [P6]. Past bond issues are evidence about past moments, not a forecast. The yield leads the sector on the data shown, but leadership without a ranking is only a list.

verdict.headline: Strong returns and low leverage are shown, but dividend coverage itself is not measured
verdict.answer: The pack does not contain a payout against matched earnings, so coverage is not shown. Payout is withheld for missing inputs, as are interest coverage and net margin [P2]. What it does show is a profitable, lightly borrowed company: return on equity of 26.75 per cent, return on assets of 15.86 per cent, debt to equity of 0.2006 and a current ratio of 1.9986 [P2]. Trailing earnings per share are 1.84 SAR against a latest quarterly dividend of 0.34 SAR per share [P1] [P3]. Buffett opened by calling the dividend safe on those returns, then withdrew that certainty after Marks pointed out that no payout figure or earnings record is held and that the return carries no stated denominator [P2]. Alwaleed showed that the per-share dividend was 0.48 in 2024 and 0.33 in the 2025 payments, mostly through the performance-linked part, and has been 0.34 for the three latest payments [P3]. Lynch found no quarterly record, so no trend can be called. Dalio notes the ratios are undated and the operands are not shown. Al-Rumayyan notes that the peers are much smaller and that bond issues were completed on 2026-02-02 and 2025-09-17 [P5] [P6]. The room agrees that the business looks profitable and the recent payments steady. It cannot say how much of earnings the dividend takes, or how it would hold if earnings fell.

headline: The pack shows one high return on equity reading, not evidence that it lasts.
answer:
The pack gives a single return on equity figure for Jarir: 67.25% [P1][P2]. Return on assets is 25.88% [P2] and debt-to-equity is 0.0 [P2]. Dalio and Marks both noted that this means the return is not produced by borrowing. No dataset holds a multi-year or quarterly ROE series, ROIC or net margin; ROIC and net margin are marked missing_inputs [P2]. Lynch pointed out that the quarterly dataset he is answerable for, [P9], is not in the pack.

The room agrees on this. Buffett opened by reading the figure as a visible moat. In his final word he accepted that one trailing window is not a record. All six advisors ended by saying the pack shows strength, not durability.

Supporting context exists but does not close the gap. Alwaleed cited quarterly dividends of SAR 0.15 to SAR 0.28 per share over two years [P3], though the payout ratio is missing [P2]. Al-Rumayyan and Lynch cited 2026 showroom openings [P6]. The disclosures say their financial impact would begin in Q1 2026, and the pack does not show the return on that capital [P6]. Al-Rumayyan also noted the market capitalisation of SAR 20,532 million against peers [P5].

Marks and Al-Rumayyan read the five-year price change of -13.87% [P8] and the P/E of 18.43 [P1] as the market doubting persistence. Neither figure measures ROE persistence, so this is an inference rather than a finding.

The answer to the member: the data does not show that 67.25% is durable [P1]. It shows one strong reading on a debt-free balance sheet. The pack also flags its price, technical and news data as stale, which limits how current the context is [P1].
gaps: The pack has no multi-year or quarterly ROE history to show whether 67.25% is a peak, a trough or a steady state [P1].
ROIC and net margin are missing_inputs [P2], so the drivers of the return cannot be checked.
The payout ratio and free cash flow yield are unavailable [P2], so the cushion behind the dividend cannot be seen.
disagreements: Whether price history shows the market doubts the return is durable - The five-year change of -13.87% [P8] and P/E of 18.43 [P1] are in the pack. Neither is tied to ROE history, so they cannot show what the market believes about persistence. An ROE series alongside the price record would be needed.

Whether dividends, a debt-free balance sheet and expansion support durability - All four read the same figures: dividends of SAR 0.15 to SAR 0.28 per share [P3], debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2] and showroom disclosures [P6]. They agree these are supportive but not proof. How much weight they carry is a matter of judgment, since the payout ratio and the return on new capital are absent.

data.headline: A 67 per cent return on equity is a moat you can see in the numbers
data.text: Return on equity of 67.25 per cent is not a number an ordinary retailer produces [P1]. It is earned on a book value of about 4.8 a share, so this is a substantial business earning extraordinary returns on real capital, and that is what a durable competitive advantage looks like in the figures. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: The data shows a high current ROE but lacks the multi-year history to prove durability.
data.text:
The data pack shows a return on equity of 67.25% for Jarir [P1], a figure that is also confirmed in the fundamentals dataset [P2]. This is an exceptionally high snapshot of profitability. However, the question asks about durability, and on that point the data in the pack is largely silent. We are given a single reading, not a time series. There are no historical ROE figures for the last five or ten years to show if this level has been consistently sustained or if it represents a recent peak. The long-term price summary shows the stock is down 13.87% over five years [P8], which, while not a direct measure of ROE, suggests the market has not compounded value at this rate over that period. Without a decade of return data, I cannot conclude from this pack that the 67.25% is durable [P1].

Looking at the company against its sector, my mandate, we see that Jarir is the dominant player by market capitalization at SAR 20,532 million, far exceeding peers like Aldrees (SAR 11,970 million) and United Electronics (SAR 5,432 million) [P5]. Its P/E of 18.43 is lower than most peers that have a positive earnings multiple, such as Al-Saif Stores (37.3) and SACO (41.45), but higher than United Electronics (10.43) [P5]. This scale and relative valuation suggest a leadership position, but do not speak to the persistence of its returns.

Regarding disclosures, the company has been actively investing in expansion. In 2026 alone, it disclosed new showroom openings in Madinah (SAR 21 million), Al Baha (SAR 29 million), and a replacement showroom in Kuwait (SAR 15 million) [P6]. These are clear signals from management that they see opportunities to deploy capital for growth, a necessary condition for sustaining high returns. However, the financial impact of these investments is only expected to begin appearing from Q1 2026 [P6], so the current data does not show the returns on this new capital. The company's balance sheet, with a debt-to-equity ratio of zero and a sector percentile of 89.7 [P2], provides a strong capacity to fund this expansion without strain, which is a supportive factor for future durability, but not proof of it.

data.headline: A single 67.25% ROE reading is a snapshot, not proof of durability [P1].
data.text:
The data provides a single reading of return on equity at 67.25% [P1][P2]. To assess durability, I need to see how this machine has operated over a full cycle. The pack shows no historical ROE series, no trend, and no breakdown of the drivers—profit margins, asset turnover, and leverage—that build this number. Without that, I cannot see whether this is a peak, a trough, or a steady state.

My mandate is the balance sheet, and here the data tells a clear story about the funding structure. As of the latest fundamentals dated 2026-08-12 [P2], the company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2]. This means the balance sheet is funded entirely by equity and operational liabilities, not by financial debt. This is a structurally robust position. The current ratio is 1.37 [P2], indicating short-term assets cover short-term liabilities, though the percentile of 45.0 within its sector [P2] shows this is not exceptional.

The primary scenario where this funding becomes a problem is not a credit crunch, since there is no debt to refinance. The risk is operational. If the business generates negative free cash flow, the company would need to draw on its cash or liquidate current assets to cover its liabilities. The data does not provide a free cash flow yield [P2] or a detailed cash flow statement, so I cannot stress-test this. The durability of a 67.25% ROE on an unlevered balance sheet is a question of whether the earnings power that drives it is stable [P1]. The balance sheet itself is not the source of fragility here; the fragility, if any, lies in the income statement's cyclicality, which the data does not let me measure.

data.headline: One quarter's ROE is a snapshot, not a story of durability.
data.text:
The pack gives me one reading for return on equity: 67.25% [P1, P2] [P1]. That is a single number, a snapshot. I cannot tell from one photograph whether the runner is sprinting or jogging. Durability is a movie, and I need more frames.

My job in this room is to look at what the business has been doing quarter by quarter. The datasets I am answerable for are [P7] and [P9]. [P7] shows me the market's reading over one and five years, but it does not break down earnings. The crucial dataset for the member's question is [P9], which should hold the quarterly financials. However, the data pack I have in front of me contains no [P9]. There is no quarterly record of revenue, earnings, or ROE to examine. I cannot count the quarters of high returns, I cannot see if the trend is steady, improving, or starting to fade, and I cannot name the quarter that drove the annual figure.

What I can see from other parts of the pack is that Jarir has been actively opening new showrooms with significant investments—SAR 29 million in Al Baha, SAR 21 million in Madinah, SAR 15 million in Kuwait [P6]. This is a company in expansion mode, and a high ROE is exactly what you would expect from a retailer that can open new stores with high returns on the capital it puts in. That is a good story, but the numbers to prove that these returns are durable are simply not in this pack. The single ROE figure is the whole history I have. I need to see that 67.25% held up over many quarters, through different economic weather, before I can call it durable [P1]. Right now, the data does not show it.

data.headline: A single reading of 67.25% ROE shows strength, not durability [P1].
data.text:
The pack gives us one figure for return on equity: 67.25% [P1]. That is a high number, and it tells me the company earned significant profits against its equity base over the period that figure was measured. But the question is about durability, and on that point the data in front of us offers only a single snapshot. A photograph of a sprinter mid-stride does not tell you if he can run a marathon. We see one measurement point, and there are no historical ROE figures in the pack to compare it to [P2]. Therefore, the data does not show that this return is durable; it only shows it was high at the time of the last calculation.

My mandate is to look at what has been returned to owners and out of what, and the dividend history does offer a longer lens. Over the last eight quarters, the company has paid a steady stream of dividends: SAR 0.15 to SAR 0.28 per share each quarter [P3]. The most recent four payments total SAR 0.95 per share. This consistent cash return to shareholders, without a cut, is a tangible sign of confidence from the boardroom. It suggests management sees sustained earnings power, not a one-time windfall. The share count has also been stable at 1,200 million since the last bonus issue in 2018, meaning this per-share payout has not been diluted [P3]. However, the pack does not provide the payout ratio [P2], which would show us precisely what portion of earnings is being distributed. Without that, we cannot see the margin of safety within the dividend.

So, the data shows a company with a very high current ROE and a pattern of steady, undiminished dividends. This is a picture of strength. But to call it durable, I would need to see that ROE sustained across different economic cycles. That history is not in this pack. I like what I see, but I do not mistake a strong quarter for a permanent condition.

data.headline: The data shows one high ROE reading; durability is not in the data.
data.text:
The question is whether a return on equity of 67.25% is durable, and the data here simply cannot answer that [P1]. What the pack gives us is a single, point-in-time figure [P1]. That 67.25% is an impressive number, far above the rule-based quality seat's 20% bullish threshold, but it is a snapshot, not a trend [P1] [P3]. Durability requires a history of returns that shows this level can be sustained, and that history is absent from these datasets.

This is exactly the kind of gap my mandate requires me to name. The pack's fundamentals section [P2] confirms the ROE value but provides no sector percentile and no time series. We cannot see whether 67.25% is a peak, a trough, or a steady state for Jarir [P1]. The five-year price summary [P8] shows a closing price that has fallen 13.87% from 20.12 to 17.33 over that period, which suggests the market has not been pricing in a permanently high and stable return on capital. If the market believed this ROE was durable and would grow, the price would likely reflect a different history.

Furthermore, several metrics that could help assess the quality and sustainability of those returns are missing. The pack cannot compute ROIC or net margin, both marked as 'missing_inputs' [P2]. Without ROIC, we cannot compare the return on equity to the return on all invested capital, a crucial check on whether high leverage is flattering the ROE. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0 [P2], which tells us this high ROE is not driven by debt, but that only deepens the mystery of what the missing pieces would show.

My role is to ask what the price is assuming. A 67.25% ROE is so far above any cost of capital that the current P/E of 18.43 [P1] implies the market does not believe this is the permanent state of affairs. If it did, the multiple would be far higher. The data shows a single, excellent result. It does not show it can be repeated. That is the critical difference, and the pack leaves us in the dark on it.

data.headline: One ROE reading is not a moat
data.text: Buffett, you call the 67.25% ROE a moat visible in the numbers and treat everything else as secondary [P1]. But the pack shows a single reading, not a decade of them. I agree the figure is exceptional, but durability is a pattern over time, and that pattern is absent. My mandate requires me to look at the company against its sector. Jarir’s market capitalisation of SAR 20,532 million dwarfs its peers, and its P/E of 18.43 sits below Al-Saif Stores at 37.3 and SACO at 41.45 [P5]. This leadership is a better starting point for a long-horizon case than one ROE reading. The five-year price change of -13.87% also gives me pause: if the market believed this return was permanent, the price would likely reflect a different history [P8]. The company’s disclosures show management is investing for growth, with three new showrooms opened in 2026 alone [P6]. That is what a durable franchise should do, but the data does not yet show the returns on that capital. A single snapshot, however brilliant, is not the same as proof of permanence.
data.concedes: The 67.25% ROE is an exceptional figure that signals a strong competitive position [P1].

A debt-free company can still have volatile profits. The durability of a 67.25% return is a question of whether the earnings engine that produces it is stable, and the pack is silent on that [P1]. data.headline: A single ROE is not a moat; the price says so.
data.text: Buffett, you call the 67.25% ROE a visible moat and everything else secondary [P1]. I disagree. A moat implies durability, and a single reading cannot prove that [P1]. It is a multiple that, in my view, prices in significant uncertainty about the sustainability of that 67.25% [P1]. data.headline: One number is a snapshot, not a franchise
data.text:
Buffett, you call a 67.25% ROE a visible moat and treat everything else as secondary [P1]. I disagree. A single reading of return on equity shows strength at a point in time, not durability. A brand and a leading position are assets I value highly, but we need evidence they can sustain returns through cycles, and that evidence is absent here. The pack holds no historical ROE series, no ROIC, and no net margin [P2]. We are all looking at the same photograph; you are calling it a movie.

My mandate shows a board that has paid steady, undiminished dividends—SAR 0.15 to SAR 0.28 per share each quarter over the last two years [P3]. That is a tangible sign of confidence, and I like it. But even that consistent payout is not proof that 67.25% is the permanent earnings power [P1]. Without a payout ratio [P2], I cannot see the cushion. A high number, even an extraordinary one, is not the same as a durable one. The data does not let us tell the difference.
data.concedes: A 67.25% ROE is an extraordinary number that signals a strong competitive position at the time it was measured [P1].

data.headline: A single window is not a record, but it is not nothing either.
data.text: Lynch, you say one quarter’s ROE is a snapshot, not a story, and you are right that the pack gives us no [P9] to count the quarters. But you also say the single ROE figure is the whole history you have, and that understates what is in front of us. The income statement in [P9] is missing, yes, but [P2] gives a published ROE of 67.25% and a published ROA of 25.88% [P2]. A business that earns 67 cents on a dollar of equity and 26 cents on a dollar of assets over a full year, with zero debt [P2], is not a sprinter caught mid‑stride. It is a business that has just run a mile in three minutes. That one mile does not prove it can run a marathon, but it tells you something about the runner that an ordinary retailer cannot match.
data.concedes: I concede that without a multi‑year record we cannot prove durability; a single twelve‑month window is only the first chapter.

headline: The pack shows one high return, not a multi-year record of durability.
answer:
The data shows a published return on equity of 67.25 per cent and a return on assets of 25.88 per cent [P1]. It does not show that these returns are durable. The multi-year income statements and balance sheet (P9) that would show the earnings window, the denominator and the trend are not in this pack, so Buffett's earning-power test, Lynch's quarterly count and Dalio's dated balance sheet could not be run. The published return on equity states no denominator and carries no sector percentile [P2].

What the pack does show is consistent with a strong business but proves nothing about persistence. Debt to equity is 0.0 [P2], so leverage does not explain the return (Dalio). Dividends have been paid in every quarter listed, the latest being 0.2 per share announced 2026-08-10 [P3] (Alwaleed). Disclosures from 2026-01-26 and 2026-04-08 describe showroom openings [P6] (Al-Rumayyan). The room agrees that leverage is not the source of the return and that a single ratio is not a record. Buffett corrected his book value figure to the pack's 1.41 and withdrew the claim that the return alone proves a moat [P1].

Rulings: the book value dispute is settled by the pack. Whether the return is durable cannot be settled from this evidence. Whether dividends and expansion corroborate durability is a difference of weighting, since both sides read the same figures.

data.headline: A 67 per cent return on equity is a moat you can see in the numbers
data.text: Return on equity of 67.25 per cent is not a number an ordinary retailer produces [P1]. It is earned on a book value of about 4.8 a share, so this is a substantial business earning extraordinary returns on real capital, and that is what a durable competitive advantage looks like in the figures. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: Without quarterly earnings the trend is invisible; the price suggests a recent improvement.
data.text: I am answerable for the quarterly record, and the P9 quarters are not in this pack. Without those columns I cannot count a single quarter, so I cannot call a trend or say which way earnings are moving. What the pack does give is the market's reading of the same stretch. Over the year to 2026-10-13 the close rose 24.95 per cent from 13.87 to 17.33 [P7]. That is a strong twelve months. Over five years the change is -13.87 per cent [P8]. A strong year after a flat-to-weak five is not the same as steady earnings. The return on equity figure I see is 67.25 per cent [P1]. That is a single number with no quarterly build-up shown. I cannot say whether it is a one-off or the latest in a run. The market's twelve-month return of 33.78 per cent [P1] suggests it has been pricing in something good, but I need the quarterly sales and earnings to know if the business itself is actually growing into that price. One good year of price gains after a five-year loss does not by itself prove durability. I would want to see at least four to six quarters of steady or rising earnings before I used the word durable. The data here does not give me that.

data.headline: The balance sheet is absent; little debt means little visible strain, but I cannot see the funding.
data.text: I am answerable for the balance sheet, and the P9 balance sheet with its dated position is not in this pack. I cannot give the date of the position I am reading, and I cannot name the lines in the statements that would break under strain. The health metrics available are debt to equity of 0.0, at the 89.7 percentile of the sector, and a current ratio of 1.37 at the 45.0 percentile [P2]. A current ratio mixes a stock and a flow with no stated date here, so I cannot pass it off as a single moment. Zero debt means the funding strain from creditors is low on the face of it. That is one part of the machine working smoothly. But I cannot see what funds the assets: is it retained earnings, payables, or something else? The machine that produces a 67.25 per cent return on equity [P1] is opaque without the balance sheet. A high return on equity can be durable if it is funded by genuine competitive advantage and not by leverage. With no debt, leverage is not the driver here. But I cannot see the equity base itself, the asset composition, or the cash conversion. The scenario I cannot rule out is that the return on equity is high because the equity base is thin relative to the earnings, and that a single bad year could wipe out a large part of it. The data does not let me test that.

data.headline: The price assumes a lot; the pack has large gaps and the return on equity cannot be ranked.
data.text: The price as of 2026-10-13 is 17.33, and that quote is flagged stale [P1]. At that price the market is paying 12.28 times book value and 18.43 times earnings [P1]. Those multiples assume the return on equity will remain high. The question is what the evidence can and cannot support. The gaps are large. P9 with its limitations and calculations is not in this pack, so I cannot read the notes that tell us what the data cannot answer. Return on invested capital and net margin are missing inputs [P2]. Enterprise value to EBITDA is not available [P1]. The 67.25 per cent return on equity carries no sector percentile, so it cannot be ranked against peers [P2]. I do not know the denominator behind it, nor over what period it was struck. A number without its construction is a headline, not a measurement. The five-year price summary shows a high close of 21.66 and a low of 12.06, with the last close at 17.33 [P8]. That is a wide range, and the maximum drawdown of -65.72 per cent [P1] says this share has fallen hard before. A durable return on equity should show up in a share price that compounds, not one that gives back two-thirds of its value. The data here does not let me conclude durability. It lets me say the price is assuming it, and the evidence to check that assumption is largely absent.

data.headline: The dividend record shows rising payments, but the earnings that funded them are not shown.
data.text: I am answerable for what has been returned to owners and out of what. The matched-window payout from P9 is not in this pack, so I will not assemble one from the list and risk counting a dividend outside its window. What was paid is visible. The latest dividend is 0.2 per share announced 2026-08-10, after 0.21 announced 2026-05-11 and 0.26 announced 2026-03-31 [P3]. The same quarter a year earlier, announced 2025-08-06, was 0.16 [P3]. That is a rise from 0.16 to 0.2 in the comparable quarter [P3]. Looking back further, the Q4 2024 dividend was 0.23 announced 2025-03-24, and the Q4 2025 dividend was 0.26 announced 2026-03-31 [P3]. The payments have been rising. A company that raises its dividend across several quarters is showing confidence. The last capital change is a bonus issue on 2018-10-28 that took capital from 900.0 to 1200.0 million, a 33.33 per cent increase [P3]. Older per-share figures were restated by it. Which earnings funded these payments is not shown because the matched payout window is not in the pack. A dividend can be durable if it is paid from steady earnings. It can be fragile if it is paid from a one-off gain or from a shrinking equity base. The data does not tell me which is the case here. I see rising payments and a long history of quarterly dividends. That is a positive sign, but it is not proof of durable returns on equity.

data.headline: Against the sector Jarir is mid-pack on price; the return on equity ranking is absent.
data.text: I am answerable for the company against its sector and for what it has disclosed. Against the peer list, Aldrees trades at a price to earnings of 26.07 and United Electronics at 10.43, against Jarir's 18.43 [P5][P1]. Dividend yields run from 1.67 per cent for Aldrees to 7.65 per cent for United Electronics, against Jarir's 5.16 per cent [P5][P1]. Jarir sits in the middle of its peer group on these measures. The return on equity of 67.25 per cent carries no sector percentile [P2]. That means the ranking is absent, not low. I cannot say whether 67.25 per cent is exceptional for this sector or merely good, because the data does not rank it [P1]. The company's own disclosures are about expansion. On 2026-01-26 it opened a SAR 21 million showroom in Madinah [P6]. On 2026-04-08 it opened a SAR 15 million showroom in Kuwait [P6]. These are company disclosures about physical openings, not about the durability of returns. A company that is opening new locations is investing for growth. Whether those investments will earn returns as high as the existing business is a question the data does not answer. The news item from 2026-07-15 reports Gulf sales up 29 per cent and operations unaffected by shipping disruptions [P6]. That is a positive signal about the top line, but it is a news report, not a company disclosure, and it says nothing about return on equity. The sector context shows a company that is neither the most expensive nor the cheapest, paying a mid-range dividend, and expanding its footprint. The durability of its returns on equity is not something the sector data or the disclosures settle.

verdict.headline: The pack shows one high return, not a multi-year record of durability.
verdict.answer:
The data shows a published return on equity of 67.25 per cent and a return on assets of 25.88 per cent [P1]. It does not show that these returns are durable. The multi-year income statements and balance sheet (P9) that would show the earnings window, the denominator and the trend are not in this pack, so Buffett's earning-power test, Lynch's quarterly count and Dalio's dated balance sheet could not be run. The published return on equity states no denominator and carries no sector percentile [P2].

What the pack does show is consistent with a strong business but proves nothing about persistence. Debt to equity is 0.0 [P2], so leverage does not explain the return (Dalio). Dividends have been paid in every quarter listed, the latest being 0.2 per share announced 2026-08-10 [P3] (Alwaleed). Disclosures from 2026-01-26 and 2026-04-08 describe showroom openings [P6] (Al-Rumayyan). Against this, book value is 1.41 per share and price to book is 12.28 [P1], so the equity base is small relative to the price. Price change is 24.95 per cent over one year but -13.87 per cent over five [P7][P8], and the maximum drawdown is -65.72 per cent [P1] (Lynch, Marks). The quote is flagged stale [P1].

The room agrees that leverage is not the source of the return and that a single ratio is not a record. Buffett corrected his book value figure to the pack's 1.41 and withdrew the claim that the return alone proves a moat.

Rulings: the book value dispute is settled by the pack. Whether the return is durable cannot be settled from this evidence. Whether dividends and expansion corroborate durability is a difference of weighting, since both sides read the same figures.

headline: Valuation is full and the trend is strong; they conflict less than framed, but earnings and cash flow are unverified.
answer:
The pack shows a share at SAR 17.33 with a P/E of 18.43 and a price-to-book of 12.28 [P1]. The value seat votes bearish because the P/E is above its 16x neutral threshold [P4]. The trend is positive: a 12-month return of 33.78%, a price above both the 50-day and 200-day averages, and a bullish MACD [P1]. Over five years the price is down 13.87%, from 20.12 to 17.33 [P8], and the maximum drawdown is -65.72% [P1].

The room agrees on the balance sheet: debt-to-equity is 0.0 and the current ratio is 1.37 [P2]. It also agrees that ROE of 67.25% and a 5.16% dividend yield are strong [P1], and that the free cash flow yield is missing [P2]. Buffett and Dalio both note that a 67.25% ROE earned on unleveraged equity makes an 18.43 P/E less demanding [P1]. Alwaleed points to SAR 0.95 per share paid over the last four quarters without a cut [P3]. Al-Rumayyan adds that Jarir is the largest peer by market capitalisation, at SAR 20,532 million [P5].

How far the two signals conflict depends on whether recent earnings growth justifies the multiple. Lynch cites quarterly revenue and net income growth from a dataset labelled P9, which is not in this pack, so those figures cannot be verified here [P7]. The data does show that valuation and trend measure different things: one says the price is not cheap, the other says it has risen. They are not strictly contradictory, because the trend can continue alongside a full multiple. Whether the multiple is earned is the open question. The pack cannot show whether the ROE and yield are backed by cash generation, since free cash flow yield, EV/EBITDA and payout ratio are unavailable [P2]. Several price and news inputs are also flagged stale [P1].
gaps: Free cash flow yield and payout ratio are missing, so ROE and dividends cannot be tied to cash generation [P2].
The quarterly revenue and net income record Lynch cites is not in the pack, so earnings growth cannot be checked against the P/E.
Price, technical and news data are flagged stale, so the latest trend reading may not be current [P1].
disagreements: Is the 18.43 P/E demanding or reasonable [P1]? - The deciding figure is earnings growth. Lynch's quarterly record (P9) is not in the pack, so the growth rate cannot be checked against the P/E of 18.43 [P1]. The value seat's bearish vote is a fixed 16x rule [P4], not a test of growth.

Do valuation and trend truly conflict, or is the rise a recovery? - Both sides read the same figures: 33.78% over 12 months [P1] and -13.87% over five years [P8]. Each period is a fact; whether the recent move is a continuing trend or a recovery of lost ground is a weighing of those periods, not a missing number.

How much weight can the missing cash-flow data bear? - Free cash flow yield, EV/EBITDA and payout ratio are absent [P2]. The unbroken dividend record [P3] shows payments were made, not that operating cash covers them, so the durability question cannot be closed from this pack.
