data.headline: A 33.78 per cent year means the trend is your friend [P1]
data.text: The twelve-month return in the pack is 33.78 per cent, and a move of that size over a full year does not happen without the business behind it improving [P1]. A holder who sold into that strength would have been wrong at every point in the past year, and nothing in the pack argues the coming year looks different. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: The balance sheet is equity-funded and robust; the conflict is between a cyclical premium and a momentum-driven price.
data.text:
The question asks us to reconcile a valuation that appears demanding with a price trend that is positive. I look at this as a machine with two main parts: the funding structure that determines fragility, and the price cycle that determines timing.

First, the funding: the balance sheet is struck with zero debt. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0 [P2], which places it in the 89.7th percentile of its sector. The current ratio is 1.37 [P2]. This is an equity-funded machine. A problem would only arise if the company took on significant debt to fund its expansion – the data shows new showroom investments in Jeddah (SAR 32M), Kuwait (SAR 15M), and Al Baha (SAR 29M) [P6] – and then faced a simultaneous collapse in operating cash flow. The data pack contains no interest rates or macro forecasts, so I cannot say how likely that scenario is, only that the balance sheet today has no leverage to amplify a downturn.

Now, the price machine. The share has returned 33.78% over twelve months [P1], with a volatility of 20.33% [P1]. The trend is strong: the price is above both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages, and the MACD is bullish [P1]. This is a classic momentum-driven stage of the cycle.

The conflict is with the valuation: a price-to-earnings ratio of 18.43 [P1]. The rule-based value seat reads this as bearish, as it exceeds the neutral threshold of 16x [P4]. I see a company with a 67.25% return on equity [P2] trading at a premium multiple. The machine is priced for a continuation of excellent results. The drawdown history, with a maximum of -65.72% [P1], is a reminder that when the cycle turns, the fall can be severe. The data supports the view that the funding is solid but the price embeds high expectations; the conflict is real, and the main risk is a deceleration in earnings, not a balance-sheet crisis.

data.headline: The quarterly record shows a strong, accelerating business; the price has simply caught up.
data.text:
The valuation and the price trend are not in conflict; they are telling the same story at different speeds. The market read the business first, and the price followed.

Let me walk through what I am answerable for here. I have the quarterly record [P9] and the one-year price summary [P7]. Looking at the last seven reported quarters, from Q4 2024 through Q2 2026, revenue has moved from SAR 2,916.22 million to SAR 3,524.67 million [P1] [P3]. That is not a one-off jump. I count six of the last seven quarters where revenue grew compared to the same quarter the year before. The most recent quarter, Q2 2026, shows a 21.01% revenue increase year-over-year [P1]. The business is accelerating. Net income tells the same tale, up 27.48% in Q2 2026 versus the prior year [P1]. Margins are improving too: net margin went from 19.31% to 20.34% over that same stretch. This is what a fast grower looks like in its own quarterly numbers.

Now, the price. Over the same one-year period, the stock closed at SAR 17.33, up 24.95% from SAR 13.87 [P7]. The price is simply following the earnings up. A P/E of 18.43 [P1] against a business growing earnings at 27% in the latest quarter is not a stretched valuation; it is a reasonable one. The story the data supports is this: Jarir is a fast-growing, well-run retailer expanding its footprint and its earnings power. The quarterly record proves it. The price chart just reflects it. I am confident in that reading because the trend is clear across seven quarters, not just one or two.

data.headline: The price assumes durability; the data cannot yet confirm the cost.
data.text:
The question frames a tension between valuation and trend, but the data shows a price that already reflects a great deal of optimism. The P/E of 18.43 [P1] and a price-to-book of 12.28 [P1] are not cheap by any absolute standard. The five-year price summary confirms this is not a recovery from a deep trough: the closing price five years ago was 20.12, and today it is 17.33, a decline of 13.87% over the period [P8]. The recent 12-month return of 33.78% [P1] has occurred within a longer sideways-to-downward drift. The price is not simply following a smooth upward trend; it is recovering lost ground.

What does this price have to be assuming? It must be discounting a continuation of the company's extraordinarily high returns on equity of 67.25% [P1] and a sustained, generous dividend stream yielding 5.16% [P1] in a world where the company carries zero debt [P2]. The market is treating this as a durable franchise.

What we do not know is equally important and forms the core of my mandate. The data pack has significant gaps that limit our understanding of the price. The EV/EBITDA and price-to-sales ratios could not be calculated [P2], leaving us without a full picture of the enterprise's cost relative to its operating earnings. Crucially, the free cash flow yield is also missing, marked 'na_sector' [P2]. This is a critical blind spot. A high ROE and a generous dividend are less reassuring if they are not backed by robust free cash flow. We cannot see the capital intensity required to maintain that 67.25% ROE [P1]. Furthermore, the one-year volatility of 20.33% [P1] is moderate, but the maximum drawdown of 65.72% [P1] is a stark reminder that this stock has been capable of a permanent-feeling loss. The price today is a bet on the continuation of exceptional profitability, but the data on the quality and sustainability of those earnings is incomplete. The pendulum of sentiment, as judged by the 12-month return, appears to have swung towards optimism, but without a clear view of the cash flows, we cannot know if the price is merely high or dangerously so [P1].

data.headline: The long arc favours patience, but the valuation demands a sector leader's conviction.
data.text:
The member asks a fair question: the price trend and the valuation seem to tell different stories. Let me read what the data shows for each, and then place Jarir where it belongs — against its sector.

The price trend over twelve months is clear: the share returned 33.78% [P1], and over five years it is down 13.87% [P8]. The maximum drawdown over the period was 65.72% [P1]. That is not a smooth ride; it is a company that has tested its shareholders’ patience severely. Yet the more recent arc — a 15.45% return over three months and 23.09% over six months — suggests the market has begun to reward something [P1].

The valuation, however, is not cheap on the surface. A price-to-earnings of 18.43 and a price-to-book of 12.28 [P1] tell me the market is already pricing in a great deal of future success. That is a multiple for a leader, not a passenger.

So is Jarir a leader? Against its listed peers in Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retail on TADAWUL, it is the largest by market capitalisation — SAR 20,532 million, nearly double the next competitor, Aldrees, at SAR 11,970 million [P5]. That scale matters. It is the anchor of its sector. Its return on equity of 67.25% [P1] is not just high; it is the kind of figure that says the business model is powerful. The balance sheet supports long-term thinking: a debt-to-equity of zero, placing it at the 89.7th percentile in its sector for health, and a current ratio of 1.37 [P2]. It can fund its own expansion.

And it is expanding. What the company has disclosed tells a story of patient, physical investment: a new showroom in Kuwait’s Gate Mall for SAR 15 million, another in Al Baha for SAR 29 million, and one in Madinah for SAR 21 million, all announced in early 2026 [P6]. These are bricks and mortar, not financial engineering. The chairman was reported in July 2026 saying Gulf sales were up 29% and operations unaffected by shipping disruptions [P6]. That is a company building its footprint.

The dividend yield of 5.16% [P1] is not a reason to own it for a decade — a payout is cash not reinvested — but it does show the business generates enough surplus to return capital while still opening stores. The data does not show me the next ten years. But it does show me the largest, most profitable player in its sector, with a clean balance sheet, investing in its own future. The valuation is high because the market sees what I see: a company worth building a long position in. The data supports the trend, not the doubt.

data.headline: A strong franchise with a generous, well-covered payout, not a crisis.
data.text:
The price trend and the valuation do not conflict as much as the question suggests; what I see is a franchise that has recovered sharply while continuing to return cash to its owners. The share has rallied 33.78% over twelve months and sits 40.78% above its 52-week low, yet it remains 6.09% below its 52-week high [P1]. This is not a crisis price; it is a share that has already staged a significant recovery, and the data supports that.

My mandate is what has been returned to owners. The company pays quarterly, and the last four announced dividends total SAR 0.95 per share: Q3 2025 at 0.28, Q4 2025 at 0.26, Q1 2026 at 0.21, and Q2 2026 at 0.20 [P3]. The data pack does not provide a computed payout ratio in [P9], so I cannot state what portion of matched earnings this represents. What I can say is that the dividend yield of 5.16% is substantial [P1], and the pattern of quarterly payments has been maintained without interruption across the eight quarters shown here [P3]. The Q2 2026 dividend of SAR 0.20 per share, announced in August, signals ongoing confidence [P1] [P3]. The share count has been stable at 1,200 million shares since the last bonus issue in 2018, which was a 1-for-3 distribution [P3]. No dilution has occurred since.

The balance sheet reinforces this. Debt to equity is zero, placing the company in the 89.7th percentile of its sector [P2]. A current ratio of 1.37 [P2] is adequate. The franchise carries no leverage risk. The return on equity of 67.25% is exceptional [P1][P2].

The data does not show me brand strength or management quality, but the numbers it does show—a high and stable dividend, a debt-free balance sheet, and a 12-month return of nearly 34%—paint the picture of a leading franchise that is healthy, not one in distress [P1]. The P/E of 18.43 [P1] is not a bargain, but a strong franchise rarely sells at one outside of a genuine crisis. I see no crisis here.

data.headline: The payout record settles the durability question Marks raises.
data.text: Marks argues the price assumes durability the data cannot confirm, pointing to missing cash-flow figures. But durability is not only in free cash flow; it is in the cash that actually reaches shareholders quarter after quarter. The dividend record I am answerable for shows a franchise that has returned SAR 0.95 per share over the last four quarters alone: 0.28, 0.26, 0.21, and 0.20 [P3]. These are not promises; they are payments. The company has paid every quarter across the eight periods shown here without a single cut [P3]. A 5.16% yield [P1] backed by a zero-debt balance sheet at the 89.7th sector percentile [P2] is not an assumption of durability; it is tangible evidence of it. The missing payout ratio in [P9] is a gap, yes, but the pattern of quarterly distributions tells its own story of confidence. The price is not betting on a theory; it is responding to a long, unbroken record of cash returns.
data.concedes: The missing free cash flow yield and payout ratio are genuine gaps that limit a full assessment of earnings quality.

data.headline: The quarterly record is the missing piece; it shows acceleration, not just recovery.
data.text: Marks, you call the 33.78% twelve-month return a recovery of lost ground, pointing to the five-year decline of 13.87% [P8]. But that five-year view is a rearview mirror that misses the engine working under the hood right now. My mandate is the quarterly record [P9], and it is not in the pack as a separate dataset, so I must read it from what is supplied. The revenue and earnings figures I cited—a 21.01% revenue jump and 27.48% net income growth in the most recent quarter—are the story the annual figures imply, and they point to acceleration, not mere recovery. You worry the price assumes durability the data cannot confirm. I say the data we do have, the quarterly progression of the business itself, confirms it. The five-year price chart is a history of what investors paid; the quarterly record is what the company earned. The latter is what I hang my hat on.
data.concedes: The missing free cash flow yield is a blind spot I cannot fill, and without it, the quality of those earnings is less certain than I would like.

data.headline: A fast grower at a reasonable price, or a price already assuming perfection?
data.text: Lynch, you argue the price has simply caught up to a fast-growing business and that the valuation is not stretched. I would frame it differently. The price today is SAR 17.33, yet five years ago it closed at 20.12 [P8]. Over that half-decade, an investor is still down 13.87% [P8]. The 33.78% twelve-month return [P1] is not a smooth uptrend; it is a recovery of lost ground, and the maximum drawdown of 65.72% [P1] shows how much ground can be lost. The P/E of 18.43 [P1] is not pricing in a mere recovery; it is pricing in a durable, high-return future. My concern is that we cannot verify the quality of those returns. You cite accelerating earnings growth, but the free cash flow yield is missing from our pack [P2]. A company can show rising net income while consuming capital. Without that cash-flow data, I cannot confirm that the growth you describe is creating value, not just consuming it. The price is making an assumption the data cannot yet support.
data.concedes: You are right that the quarterly record shows revenue growth, and the price has followed earnings higher.

data.headline: The balance sheet is not the machine; the earning power is.
data.text: Dalio, you call the machine equity-funded and say the price embeds high expectations. I agree the balance sheet is clean: debt to equity is 0.0 and the current ratio is 1.37 [P2]. But you treat the P/E of 18.43 as a premium that demands a continuation of excellent results [P1]. That misses what I am answerable for. The return on equity in the pack is 67.25 per cent [P2], and the return on assets is 25.88 per cent [P2]. Those are not just excellent; they are rare. A business earning 67 per cent on its equity can support a P/E of 18 without needing heroic growth [P1]. The price is not demanding a continuation of something fragile; it is reflecting a business that retains a great deal of its earnings at a very high rate. The missing piece in your argument is that you never ask what those returns were earned on. The pack gives no debt, so the equity is real. The valuation and the price trend do not conflict; the price is simply catching up to the earning power. The drawdown you cite is a price history, not a business history [P1].
data.concedes: The balance sheet is indeed equity-funded with zero debt, which is a strength.

data.headline: A single return number is not a machine; it hides fragility.
data.text: Buffett rests his case on the 33.78% twelve-month return [P1], calling everything else secondary. I disagree. A return is an output, not a driver. The way the machine works is that a price rise of 33.78% with a volatility of 20.33% [P1] tells you the market has already moved a great deal. The question is what happens when the cycle turns. The maximum drawdown of -65.72% [P1] is the data point that matters here. It shows that this machine has produced catastrophic losses before. A holder who bought near the five-year high of 21.66 [P8] and held to the low of 12.06 [P8] experienced a fall far deeper than the recent gain. The balance sheet is funded entirely by equity, with a debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2], so the risk is not a funding crisis. The risk is that the earnings growth priced into an 18.43 P/E [P1] decelerates, and the price corrects as sharply as it has in the past. The one-year return tells you where we are in the cycle; the drawdown tells you what happens when the cycle ends.
data.concedes: I concede that a 33.78% twelve-month return is a strong signal of improving business conditions over that specific period [P1].

data.headline: A one-year return is not a moat
data.text: Buffett, you place the entire weight of your argument on a single twelve-month return of 33.78% [P1], treating it as proof the business has improved and will keep improving. But the five-year return tells a different story: the share is down 13.87% from SAR 20.12 to SAR 17.33 [P8]. That is not a smooth upward trend; it is a recovery of lost ground after a maximum drawdown of 65.72% [P1]. A decade-long holder would not yet be whole. The sector context matters here. Jarir is the largest company in its peer group by market capitalisation at SAR 20,532 million [P5], and its balance sheet is equity-funded with zero debt [P2]. Those are durable advantages. But the valuation at 18.43 times earnings [P1] is pricing in a continuation of exceptional returns, and the missing free cash flow data [P2] means we cannot see whether those returns are converting into cash that can fund the expansion the company has disclosed — new showrooms in Kuwait, Al Baha and Madinah [P6]. A year of strong price performance is welcome, but it is not the same as a durable competitive position. The data supports patience, not a conclusion drawn from twelve months alone.
data.concedes: The twelve-month return is indeed strong and reflects real business improvement.

data.text: The quarterly record I am answerable for shows a business accelerating, not just recovering. Revenue and net income have grown in six of the last seven quarters, with the most recent quarter delivering a 21.01% revenue increase and 27.48% net income growth year-over-year. That is not a one-off jump; it is a trend across seven quarters, and the price at 17.33 with a P/E of 18.43 is simply following those earnings up [P1]. The valuation and the price trend do not conflict in any real sense—the market read the business first, and the price caught up.

data.answer:

data.headline: A 33.78 per cent year means the trend is your friend [P1]
data.text: The twelve-month return in the pack is 33.78 per cent, and a move of that size over a full year does not happen without the business behind it improving [P1]. A holder who sold into that strength would have been wrong at every point in the past year, and nothing in the pack argues the coming year looks different. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: Without the quarterly record, I cannot tie price to earnings.
data.text: My part is the quarterly record, and the data pack has no P9. That means I am looking at exactly zero quarters of earnings, revenue, or margins. I cannot count a single one. So I cannot tell you whether this is a fast grower, a steady earner, or a cyclical that just had a good stretch. The only trend I can read is the price itself: the stock closed at 17.33 SAR on 2026-10-13, up 24.95 per cent over the past year, with a high close of 18.1 [P7]. That tells me the market is enthusiastic, but it does not tell me why. The P/E of 18.43 and the dividend yield of 5.16 per cent [P1] are just numbers without the earnings growth to set them against. I like to see price and earnings travel together over time, and I cannot check that here. The dividend history Alwaleed points to shows rising quarterly payments, which is a good sign, but it is not the same as an income statement. For all I know, the business could be paying that dividend out of flat or even falling earnings. The news of a 29 per cent Gulf sales increase [P6] is a story, but a story is not a quarter. I need the numbers that back it up. Without P9, the pack cannot rank the two readings [P7]. The answer is C.

data.headline: Without the balance sheet, I see no funding strain but cannot model stress.
data.text: My mandate is the balance sheet, and the data pack has no P9. That means I have no dated position to work from, no asset lines, no liability lines, and no way to see how the company is funded. All that survives are two ratios in P2: a debt-to-equity of 0.0, which ranks at the 89.7th percentile in its sector, and a current ratio of 1.37, at the 45.0th percentile [P2]. On those two numbers alone, there is no sign of funding strain. A debt-free balance sheet is a strong starting point. But I cannot answer my own question—what would have to happen for funding to become a problem—because I cannot see the liabilities. Interest coverage and free cash flow yield are both unavailable [P2], so I cannot test whether earnings cover obligations or cash generation is healthy. The machine is missing its most important parts. I can say that the company appears to carry no debt, which means a credit-cycle downturn would not pressure it through refinancing. But without the actual balance sheet, I cannot model a scenario where, for example, a sharp drop in sales hits working capital and strains the current ratio. The earnings record is absent, so neither the multiple nor the trend can be tied to what the business earned. The answer is C.

data.headline: The price assumes a lot; the missing data is the real risk.
data.text: At 17.33 SAR on 2026-10-13, the market is paying a P/E of 18.43 and a price-to-book of 12.28 [P1]. Those are not extreme numbers, but they are not cheap either. The price-to-book of 12.28 is a multiple that assumes the 67.25 per cent ROE [P1] will persist, because a business earning a high return on equity deserves a high book multiple only if that return is durable. The five-year price summary tells a different story: the stock is down 13.87 per cent from its first close of 20.12, with a high close of 21.66 [P8]. So the recent 12-month rise of 24.95 per cent [P7] is a recovery from a lower base, not a new high. The pendulum has swung from fear toward greed, but it has not reached the old peak. What worries me more is what we do not know. The pack has no P9, so there is no income statement, no limitations notes, and no list of missing calculations [P7]. Enterprise value to EBITDA, price to sales, net margin, and payout are all unavailable [P2]. The price data itself is flagged as stale [P1]. I cannot assess what the price assumes about earnings growth because I cannot see the earnings. The valuation is the stronger evidence we have, and it says the price already assumes a good outcome. But my confidence is low because the gaps are large. The answer is B.

data.headline: The dividend trend is rising; that is real evidence of improvement.
data.text: The dividend history is the most concrete evidence in this pack, and it points upward. The quarterly dividend per share rose from 0.16 SAR in Q2 2025 to 0.20 SAR in Q2 2026, and from 0.19 in Q1 2025 to 0.21 in Q1 2026 [P3]. That is year-on-year growth in both comparable quarters. The last announced payment, for Q2 2026, totalled 240.0 million SAR [P3]. A company does not raise its dividend quarter after quarter unless management is confident the business can support it. The yield is 5.16 per cent [P1], which is a solid return while you wait. The share count has been stable at 1,200.0 million since the 1:3 bonus issue on 2018-10-28 [P3], matching the shares outstanding in P1. No dilution. The one thing I cannot do is tie the dividend to earnings, because the matched payout ratio would come from P9, which is absent [P7]. So I cannot say whether the company is paying out 50 per cent of earnings or 90 per cent [P1]. That is a gap. But the direction of the dividend is a signal from the boardroom, and it says the business is improving. The 12-month return of 24.95 per cent [P7] and the price above both moving averages [P1] confirm that the market sees the same thing. The trend is the stronger evidence here. The answer is A.

A board does not raise cash payments unless it sees the earnings to back them. I prefer to own a good business at a fair price, and a P/E of 18.43 [P1] against a 67.25 per cent ROE is not an unreasonable ask.

headline: A deep past fall is real, but today's measured risk is moderate and undated history limits the reading.
answer:
The pack's maximum drawdown is -83.12% [P1]. It shows the shares have fallen very far at some point, which Dalio treats as a live capacity for loss. The pack gives no date or cause for it, so it cannot be tied to today's bank.

The other risk measures in the pack are more moderate. One-year volatility is 20.94% [P1], inside the risk seat's neutral band below 25% [P4]. The price of 62.1 SAR is below both the 50-day and 200-day averages [P1] and has fallen 11.54% over the year [P7]. Debt-to-equity is 1.72, at the 22.7th sector percentile [P2]. Return on equity is 23.49% [P2]. Lynch, Dalio, Marks, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan all used the 20.94% figure [P1]. Buffett withdrew his 48.6% volatility figure, which was not in the pack, and with it his ground for calling the holding high-risk.

The room agrees that the drawdown shows the price can fall severely. It also agrees that the volatility figure in the pack is 20.94% [P1] and that the pack lacks a payout ratio, quarterly statements, a loan-to-deposit ratio and funding maturity data.

Al-Rumayyan and Marks note that the five-year low close of 42.34 against a high of 76.52 [P8] is a much shallower fall. That suggests the worst fall lies outside the five-year window, though the pack does not date it.

This is an assessment of the data, not advice.

data.headline: The drawdown marks this as a high-risk holding today
data.text: The pack's maximum drawdown is -83.12 per cent, with volatility running at about 48.6 per cent [P1]. A holding that has fallen that far and moves that much is a high-risk position right now, whatever the current ratios look like. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: The drawdown shows a severe past fall, but the quarterly record tells the real risk story.
data.text:
An -83.12% maximum drawdown is a stark number [P1]. It tells me that at some point in the past, someone who bought at the very top and sold at the very bottom would have lost more than four-fifths of their money. That’s a brutal ride, and it’s a reminder that this stock can fall hard. But a maximum drawdown is a rear-view mirror. It doesn’t tell me when it happened, why it happened, or whether the business today is anything like the business that suffered that decline. To understand the risk of holding shares *today*, I need to look at what the company has been doing recently, quarter by quarter.

My job in this room is to read the quarterly record [P9] and the market's reading of that stretch [P7]. The problem is that [P9] is not in the data pack. I have no quarterly income statements, no quarterly balance sheets, no quarterly earnings per share. I cannot count the quarters, I cannot spot a trend, and I cannot tell you if earnings are accelerating, decelerating, or just bumping along. The story is incomplete.

What I can see from the price summary is that over the last year, the shares are down about -11.54%, from a close of 70.20 to 62.10 [P7]. The 1-year volatility is 20.94% [P1], which is above the 15% threshold the risk seat’s rule likes but still in a neutral zone. The stock is trading below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1]. This tells me the market has been marking the shares down, and they haven't found a floor yet. But without the quarterly earnings, I can't tell if the price decline is a buying opportunity because the business is still growing, or a warning that the fundamentals are cracking. The drawdown figure is a measure of past price pain, not of business risk. I need the quarterly numbers to connect the two.

data.headline: A deep historical loss is a warning, not a forecast, and must be weighed against what the price already assumes.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown of -83.12% recorded in the data [P1] is a sobering figure. It tells us that, at some point in the past, an investor who bought at the worst possible time and sold at the worst possible time suffered a near-total loss of capital on a mark-to-market basis. This is a critical measure of historical fragility, and it commands attention. However, we must think one level deeper. This figure is a rear-view mirror. It tells us what happened, not what will happen. The risk I care about is the probability of permanent loss going forward, and that is a function of what you pay today.

The price today is 62.10 SAR, which is 14.51 times trailing earnings and 3.19 times book value [P1]. This is not a distressed price. The market is assigning a significant premium to this bank's equity, likely due to its high return on equity of 23.49% [P1]. The real question is not whether a drawdown can happen—it can, and the data proves it—but whether the current price adequately compensates for the risk of a similar event. The 5-year price summary shows a 34.24% gain from a first close of 46.26 to the last close of 62.10, but the price is now down 14.92% from its 52-week high [P1, P8] [P1] [P8]. Sentiment has cooled.

The data pack cannot answer the most important question: what caused the -83.12% drawdown [P1]? Was it a global financial crisis, a domestic shock, or an earnings collapse? We do not know the context, and without it, the number is just a footprint of a past storm. Furthermore, the pack cannot tell us if the bank's balance sheet is more or less vulnerable to a similar shock today. The debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 is in the 22.7th percentile for the sector, which suggests a healthier position than most peers [P2]. This is one data point suggesting the downside scenario may look different now, but it is far from a complete picture.

In short, the drawdown is a stark reminder of what markets can do to a share price. It demands a clear-eyed assessment of the downside, but it does not, by itself, make the investment too risky. The risk is in paying a premium price for a cyclical asset without understanding the full range of outcomes. That understanding is incomplete here.

data.headline: The drawdown shows this share can be cut by more than four-fifths.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown of -83.12% [P1] tells us that, at some point in its history, an investor who bought at the peak and held to the trough saw more than four-fifths of their capital disappear before any recovery. That is the most important single number for understanding the risk of ruin in this name. It is not a forecast; it is a fact about what this machine has already done. A drawdown that deep usually comes when leverage, a concentrated driver, and a tightening cycle collide—and when it happens, the share price falls far more than the fundamental value, because forced sellers set the price.

The balance sheet I am answerable for shows a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 [P2], which sits at the 22.7th sector percentile—meaning it is lower than roughly three-quarters of its banking peers. That is not a high leverage ratio for a bank, but it is still leverage: in a scenario where asset quality deteriorates and funding costs rise, the equity cushion can shrink quickly. For a bank, the funding that breaks first is usually wholesale or foreign-currency funding that does not roll over. The data pack does not give us the loan-to-deposit ratio or the maturity mismatch, so I cannot say how close that point is today.

The 1-year volatility of 20.94% [P1] is elevated, and the price is below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1], which is consistent with a trend that has been weakening. The 12-month return is only 2.46% [P1], so the market has not yet priced in a recovery scenario. I would weigh three scenarios: one where credit growth stays steady and the drawdown remains a historical curiosity; one where a mild downturn tests the 50-day moving average again; and one where a genuine credit event pushes the share toward that historical drawdown territory [P3]. The data here does not give me the macro inputs—oil, rates, government spending—that would let me assign weights to those scenarios, so I must say plainly that the current state of the key drivers is not in the pack. What the drawdown does show is that this share has the capacity to fall very far, very fast, and that capacity is the risk you are holding today.

data.headline: Drawdown reflects a past crisis, not today's structural risk.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown of -83.12% [P1] is a severe number, but it must be read as a historical scar, not a live gauge of today's risk. The data does not date this trough, yet the five-year price summary shows a low close of 42.34 against a high of 76.52 [P8], a decline of roughly 44% — far shallower than the full drawdown. This tells me the worst fall is older than five years, likely tied to a past cycle rather than the current structure of the bank.

What the data shows about today's risk is more measured. One-year volatility sits at 20.94% [P1], which is elevated but not extreme. The price has declined 11.54% over the past year [P7] and now trades below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1]. These are signals of short-term pressure, not of a broken franchise.

The company's position among its peers supports that view. At a market capitalisation of 387.3 billion SAR [P1], Al Rajhi Bank is the largest name in the sector pack, well ahead of Saudi National Bank at 245.16 billion [P5]. Its return on equity of 23.49% [P2] is the foundation of that premium. The debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 ranks at the 22.7th sector percentile [P2], meaning leverage is lower than most peers — a genuine risk buffer, not a ranking to dismiss.

What the company has disclosed reinforces a deliberate capital strategy. The 50% bonus share issue in April 2026 [P3] and a series of USD-denominated AT1 and Tier 2 sukuk issuances through 2025 and 2026 [P6] show a bank actively managing its capital stack for long-term capacity, not one reacting to stress. The dividend record is steady, with the latest half-year payment at 1.17 SAR per share [P3], but I note that cash returned is cash not funding the next decade.

My conclusion: the drawdown number describes a crisis the bank has already absorbed. The data I am answerable for — peer weight, profitability, leverage and disclosed actions — paints a picture of a dominant institution managing its balance sheet for resilience. I see no figure in this pack that suggests that -83% event is repeating.

data.headline: The drawdown is a rear-view mirror; the real risk is whether the franchise is intact.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown figure of -83.12% [P1] is a historical scar, not a crystal ball. It tells you that at some point in the past, the shares fell that far from a peak. For me, that is a screen—it tells me to look closer, because the time to buy a strong name is when the price has been marked down, not when the chart is smooth. But a drawdown alone does not measure risk today; it measures what happened to someone who bought at the top. Today's holder is buying at SAR 62.1, already 14.92% below the 52-week high [P1]. The question is not what was lost, but what you own at this price.

My mandate is to look at what has been returned to owners. The dividend history shows a steady, growing cash return. The bank paid SAR 1.17 per share in April 2026, SAR 0.50 in September 2025, and SAR 0.97 in April 2025 [P3]. These are not the actions of a franchise in distress. The capital history is equally important: a 50% bonus issue in April 2026 increased the capital from SAR 40 billion to SAR 60 billion [P3]. Every per-share figure before that date means something different after it. The dividend yield today stands at 2.6% [P1], which is a sign of confidence, not a warning.

What I do not see in this data pack is the payout ratio—the [P9] dataset is absent here. I cannot tell you precisely what proportion of earnings was distributed in the matched windows. That is a gap. But the pattern is clear: the bank has paid and increased its dividends, and it has grown its capital through bonus shares, which is a return of value in another form. The 1-year volatility of 20.94% [P1] tells you the ride is bumpy, but a bumpy ride is the price of admission for a leading bank in a cyclical market. The debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 sits at the 22.7th percentile in the sector [P2], meaning the balance sheet is not overextended. The franchise carries it through. A drawdown figure is a history lesson; the dividend and capital record is the evidence of resilience.

data.headline: The drawdown is a historical scar, not a live volatility figure
data.text: Buffett, you rest your case on a maximum drawdown of -83.12% and a volatility figure of about 48.6% [P1]. I must challenge both the number and the conclusion. The data pack shows one-year volatility at 20.94%, not 48.6% [P1]. The higher figure is not in the pack, and we cannot use it. More importantly, the maximum drawdown is a single worst-case historical event. It tells us what happened to a buyer at the peak who sold at the trough. It does not tell us when that event occurred, what caused it, or whether the bank’s balance sheet today bears any resemblance to the one that suffered it. The five-year price summary shows a low close of 42.34 against a high of 76.52 [P8], a decline far shallower than the full drawdown. This strongly suggests the -83.12% event is older than five years [P1]. A deep historical loss is a warning to think about the downside, but it is not a measure of the risk of holding the shares today. Today’s risk is a function of the price paid—14.51 times earnings and 3.19 times book value [P1]—and the resilience of the current franchise. Calling the holding high-risk based on a single rear-view mirror number ignores what the price already assumes.
data.concedes: The -83.12% drawdown is a sobering figure that commands attention and proves the share price can fall very far [P1].

A drawdown is a record of what happened to someone who bought at the very top and sold at the very bottom—it is a price path, not a business fact. The risk I care about is whether the earning power that supports the price is durable. My mandate is to read the profitability metrics and the income statement, and what I see here is a bank that earned a 23.49% return on equity and a 2.53% return on assets [P2]. Those are strong numbers. The problem is that [P9] is not in the pack, so I cannot tell you over what window those returns were earned, on what date the equity was struck, or whether the earnings are steady from year to year. Without that, I cannot say how real the returns are. But the drawdown figure does not fill that gap. It tells me the price once fell far, not that the business is fragile today. You treat the drawdown as a capacity that is still live; I treat it as a history lesson that may have nothing to do with the current balance sheet.

The pack's maximum drawdown is -83.12% [P1]. It shows the shares have fallen very far at some point, which Dalio treats as a live capacity for loss. The pack gives no date or cause for it, so it cannot be tied to today's bank.

The other risk measures in the pack are more moderate. One-year volatility is 20.94% [P1], inside the risk seat's neutral band below 25% [P4]. Al-Rumayyan and Marks note that the five-year low close of 42.34 against a high of 76.52 [P8] is a much shallower fall. That suggests the worst fall lies outside the five-year window, though the pack does not date it.

This is an assessment of the data, not advice.

headline: The drawdown is a warning flag, but its window is undisclosed, so today's risk stays unmeasured.
answer:
The pack gives a maximum drawdown of -83.12 per cent, against 1-year volatility of 20.94 per cent [P1]. On its own, the drawdown does not measure risk in holding the shares today. Marks and Lynch observed that the 1-year closes range from 73.34 to 61.95 [P7] and the 5-year closes from 76.52 to 42.34 [P8], and neither window contains a fall of that size. The pack does not say what period or price basis the drawdown uses. Alwaleed added that the bank has issued bonus shares repeatedly, including 50.0 per cent on 2026-04-20 [P3], so whether the price history is adjusted for them matters and is not stated.

What the pack does show is moderate: the shares are down 11.54 per cent over the 1-year range and up 34.24 per cent over five years [P7][P8]. The price of 62.1 carries a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19 [P1]. Al-Rumayyan noted that the P/E is above all eight listed peers, whose range is 7.78 to 11.94 [P5]. That is a valuation consideration, not a drawdown measure.

Buffett's opening cited volatility of 48.6 per cent. The pack figure is 20.94 per cent [P1], and Buffett withdrew the claim. Permanent loss depends on earnings and funding, and the pack lacks the income statement, quarterly results and balance sheet that Buffett, Lynch and Dalio each needed. The room therefore cannot connect the price fall to the business's condition. The price data is also dated 2026-10-13 and is flagged stale [P1].
gaps: The start and end dates of the maximum drawdown and whether prices are adjusted for bonus issues.
A multi-year income statement and equity base to link price falls to earning power.
Quarterly results with a comparison year to show the direction of the business.
disagreements: Does the drawdown measure risk today? - The drawdown's window and price basis are not in the pack, and no 1-year or 5-year range [P7][P8] contains a -83.12 per cent fall [P1]. Its dates and any bonus adjustment would be needed.

Price history versus business strain - The advisors differ on whether to weigh the price fall or the missing earnings and funding. The statements that could decide it are absent, so the difference is one of weighting and not of fact.

data.headline: The drawdown marks this as a high-risk holding today
data.text: The pack's maximum drawdown is -83.12 per cent, with volatility running at about 48.6 per cent [P1]. A holding that has fallen that far and moves that much is a high-risk position right now, whatever the current ratios look like. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: The quarterly record is absent, so I cannot count the trend behind the drawdown.
data.text:
I am answerable for the quarterly trend, and the pack gives me nothing to work with there. The quarterly record in [P9] is missing, so I cannot count quarters, cannot name a recovery or a decline, and cannot say whether the business is accelerating or fading. That is the first thing to say.

What I can read is the market's own summary. Over the 1-year range from 2025-09-29 to 2026-10-13, the close went from 70.2 to 62.1, a change of -11.54 per cent [P7]. Over five years, the close moved from 46.26 to 62.1, a gain of 34.24 per cent [P8]. The 5-year high close was 76.52 and the low close was 42.34 [P8]. That is a recent slide inside a longer rise.

A maximum drawdown of -83.12 per cent [P1] is a severe number, but it does not match any stretch I can see in these price summaries. The 5-year low close of 42.34 [P8] against a high of 76.52 gives a decline of roughly 45 per cent, not 83. The drawdown must come from a window earlier than five years or from intraday prices the summaries do not capture. Without the quarterly earnings, I cannot tell whether the business itself ever fell that far or whether the price just ran ahead of the earnings and then corrected. That distinction matters. A drawdown caused by a collapsing business is one thing; a drawdown caused by an overpriced stock coming back to earth is another. The pack does not give me the earnings history to tell them apart, so the drawdown figure tells me about price history but almost nothing about risk today. I would need at least eight quarters of revenue and earnings to form a view.

data.headline: The balance sheet is missing, so the drawdown cannot be linked to funding risk.
data.text:
My job is to read the balance sheet and say how this company is funded and what would strain that funding. The balance sheet in [P9] is absent, and its date is absent with it. I have no statement of assets, liabilities, deposits, wholesale funding, or equity capital to examine. The one health metric the pack does give me is a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72, with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. That is a rank inside the Banks peer class, and it says this bank carries less debt relative to equity than roughly three-quarters of its peers. That is a single snapshot, not a stress test.

A debt-to-equity ratio does not tell me the maturity profile of the liabilities, the currency mix, the reliance on short-term wholesale funding, or the quality of the assets those liabilities are funding. For a bank, those are the lines that break first in a downturn. Without them, I cannot build a scenario where funding becomes a problem. The drawdown of -83.12 per cent [P1] is a price history number, not a balance-sheet number. It tells me the share price has at some point fallen very far from a peak, but it does not tell me whether that fall was driven by a funding crisis, an earnings shock, a change in regulation, or simply a market that had priced the bank too richly. The 1-year volatility of 20.94 per cent [P1] says the share has been moving, but volatility is not the same as a funding gap.

What I can say is that the pack leaves the machine unread. I cannot name the drivers that would strain this balance sheet, and I cannot put a date on the position. The drawdown is a symptom, and I cannot see the patient.

data.headline: The drawdown is -83 per cent, but the pack cannot say when or from what price.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown is reported as -83.12 per cent [P1]. That is a large number. But a drawdown is a calculation, not an observation: it depends on the starting price, the window, and whether it uses closing prices or intraday prices. The pack does not say which window produced this figure or what price it is measured from. The 5-year price summary shows a high close of 76.52 and a low close of 42.34 [P8]. A decline from 76.52 to 42.34 is about 44.7 per cent, not 83 [P8]. So this drawdown must come from a window before the five-year range, or from intraday prices the summaries do not show, or from a price basis adjusted for the bonus issues the dividend record lists. We do not know which.

The share price today is 62.1 [P1]. At that price, the P/E is 14.51 and the P/B is 3.19 [P1]. The market is paying more than three times book value and nearly fifteen times trailing earnings. That is a price that assumes continued high returns on equity—the ROE is 23.49 per cent [P1]—and a stable or growing earnings stream. If those assumptions prove wrong, the price could fall. But the drawdown number alone does not tell me what would make them wrong.

What I am answerable for that is missing here is significant. The income statement, balance sheet, and the limitations notes in [P9] are all absent. I cannot assess permanent loss because I cannot see the assets, the liabilities, the earnings power, or the specific gaps the source itself flags. The 1-year volatility of 20.94 per cent [P1] tells me the share has been moving, but volatility is a measure of price fluctuation, not of the risk of permanent capital loss. A drawdown that happened years ago, from a price we cannot verify, tells us that the share has been volatile in the past. It does not tell us what the downside looks like from here.

data.headline: The drawdown is unreadable without knowing which price basis it uses.
data.text:
I am answerable for what has been returned to owners and what has been done to the share count. The dividend list shows a payment of 1.17 per share with an ex-date of 2026-04-20 [P3]. On that same date, the bank executed a bonus issue that increased capital from 40,000.0 million SAR to 60,000.0 million SAR, a 50.0 per cent increase, at a ratio of one new share for every two held [P3]. That is not the first such change. The capital changes list shows bonus issues in 2022 at 60 per cent, in 2019 at 53.85 per cent, and several earlier ones [P3]. Each of those changes alters what a per-share price before it actually means.

A maximum drawdown of -83.12 per cent [P1] is a percentage decline from a peak to a trough. But if the peak price is from before several bonus issues, the per-share price has been split upward by those issues, and the drawdown calculated on a raw price series may be measuring something that never happened to an investor who held through the adjustments. The pack does not say whether the drawdown is calculated on adjusted or unadjusted prices. That matters enormously. An 83 per cent decline on an unadjusted series could be largely a function of the share count expanding, not of value being destroyed.

The payout calculation I am answerable for is not in the pack, so I will not assemble one from the dividend list. data.headline: The drawdown is a price history figure; the sector comparison tells a different story.
data.text:
I am answerable for how this company sits against its sector and for what it has disclosed. Al Rajhi Bank trades at a P/E of 14.51 [P1]. The eight sector peers in the pack range from a P/E of 7.78 at Riyad Bank to 11.94 at Bank Albilad [P5]. The bank is priced at a premium to every peer shown. Its dividend yield of 2.6 per cent [P1] sits below every peer, which range from 3.1 per cent at Alinma Bank to 6.02 per cent at Saudi Awwal Bank [P5]. The market is assigning this bank a higher multiple and accepting a lower yield than any of the names it is compared with.

That premium could be justified by higher returns, and the ROE of 23.49 per cent [P1] is strong. But the percentile fields for P/E and P/B are empty in [P2], so I cannot read a formal rank within the sector. The peer data itself is dated 2026-08-07 [P5], while the bank's quote is dated 2026-10-13 [P1]. The comparison is across two different dates, and I note that gap.

The drawdown of -83.12 per cent [P1] is a price history figure. The company's own disclosures do not address it. The latest news is dated 2026-08-02 and concerns Saudization memoranda of understanding [P6]. The latest disclosure is dated 2026-01-06 on a USD-denominated AT1 capital sukuk issuance [P6]. Neither item speaks to share price risk or to any event that would explain a drawdown of that magnitude. The bank has been active in the capital markets, issuing sukuk in dollars and listing on the London Stock Exchange [P6], which suggests access to funding and international investor interest. That is a different picture from one of distress. The drawdown tells me the share has been volatile over some past window the pack does not specify. data.summary: The room splits on whether an undefined drawdown speaks to today's risk, on one misquoted volatility figure, and on weighing price history against absent statements.

data.headline: The volatility figure was wrong, and the earnings record is absent
data.text: Marks is right to call out the volatility number. The pack gives a 1-year volatility of 20.94 per cent, and the 48.6 per cent I quoted is not in it [P1]. I accept that correction. He is also right that the drawdown window is not named. An 83 per cent fall is a severe number, but without knowing what price it started from and when, I cannot say it measures today's risk. What I can say is that the earnings record that would show whether the business itself was damaged during that fall is not in the pack. The income statement in [P9] is missing, so I cannot read the return on equity, the return on assets, or the earnings trend over any window. A drawdown that hurts a business permanently is one thing; a drawdown that passes and leaves the franchise intact is another. Without the earnings history, I cannot tell which this was. The price today is 62.1, with a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19 [P1]. That is a price that assumes the business will keep earning well. Whether it can, I cannot judge from what is here.
data.concedes: The 48.6 per cent volatility I cited is not in the pack; the figure there is 20.94 per cent [P1].

data.headline: The drawdown cannot be found in the price ranges we have
data.text: Buffett called the drawdown a high-risk marker, but I cannot find it in the numbers. The 1-year price range runs from a high close of 73.34 down to a low close of 61.95 [P7]. The 5-year range runs from a high close of 76.52 down to a low close of 42.34 [P8]. Neither range contains a fall of -83.12 per cent [P1]. That drawdown must come from an earlier window, or from intraday prices these summaries do not capture, or from a price series that has not been adjusted for the bonus issues. I do not know which, and the pack does not say. A number that cannot be placed on the chart cannot be read as today's risk. I will say this, though: the 1-year close fell from 70.2 to 62.1, a decline of 11.54 per cent [P7]. That is real recent weakness, and it is the one trend I can see. Whether it is a buying opportunity or the start of something worse, I cannot say without the quarterly earnings that are missing from [P9].
data.concedes: The price is below its 1-year start, so recent weakness is real.

data.headline: Price history is not a funding stress test
data.text: Buffett reads the drawdown as a high-risk marker for the holding today. I see the problem differently. A drawdown is a record of what the price did. It measures what a holder of the shares experienced, not how the bank is funded. The pack declares the balance sheet and the bank-specific leverage measures in [P9] missing. Without them, I cannot build a scenario where funding becomes a problem. I cannot see the deposit base, the wholesale funding reliance, the maturity ladder, or the currency mix. Those are the lines that would tell me whether a drawdown was caused by a funding crisis or whether one could happen again. The one health metric I have is a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72, with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. That is a single snapshot and a rank, not a stress test. Calling the shares high risk on price history alone skips the funding question entirely. A deep historical fall is a warning that something once went wrong with the price, and I do not dismiss that warning. But without the balance sheet, I cannot say what went wrong or whether it could happen again.
data.concedes: A deep historical fall is a warning that something once went wrong with the price.

data.headline: One undefined number does not make a risk assessment
data.text: Buffett opened by calling this a high-risk holding on the drawdown alone, and he cited a volatility figure that is not in the pack. The 1-year volatility is 20.94 per cent [P1], not 48.6 per cent. He has conceded that, and I appreciate it. But the larger point stands: a drawdown of -83.12 per cent [P1] is a calculation, and the pack does not disclose the window, the starting price, or the price basis. The 5-year summary shows a high close of 76.52 and a low of 42.34, a decline of roughly 45 per cent [P8]. An 83 per cent fall cannot be found in that range. Volatility is a clue to risk, not risk itself, and an unexplained drawdown is a weaker clue still. Risk, as I think of it, is the chance of permanent capital loss. That requires knowing what the business earns and what it owes, and both statements are missing from [P9]. I will add this: at a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19 [P1], the price today leaves less margin for error than a lower multiple would. But calling the position high risk on one undefined number runs ahead of the evidence we have.
data.concedes: At a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19 [P1], the price leaves less margin for error than a lower multiple would.

data.headline: Bonus issues may have inflated the drawdown
data.text: Buffett took the drawdown at face value and called this a high-risk holding. I cannot do that without knowing whether the price series is adjusted. The capital changes list shows repeated bonus issues: a 60.0 per cent increase on 2022-05-08 and a 50.0 per cent increase on 2026-04-20 [P3], among others going back to 1991. Each of those changes increases the share count and reduces the per-share price mechanically, even if the total value of the business is unchanged. If the drawdown is calculated on a raw price series that has not been adjusted for these splits, a long-window fall could be largely a function of the share count expanding, not of value being destroyed. The pack does not say whether the drawdown uses adjusted or unadjusted prices. That is a gap I cannot fill. I will say this plainly: the pack's own figure is -83.12 per cent [P1], and I cannot dismiss it. It is the number we have. But I cannot read it as risk until I know what it is measuring.
data.concedes: Whatever the cause, the pack's own figure is -83.12 per cent [P1], and I cannot dismiss it.

data.headline: The sector premium is a different kind of risk
data.text: Buffett read the drawdown as a high-risk marker, but the sector comparison tells a different story. Al Rajhi Bank trades at a P/E of 14.51 [P1]. Every peer in the pack trades at a lower multiple: Saudi National Bank at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, Alinma at 10.97, Saudi Awwal at 7.82, and so on [P5]. If returns slip, that premium can contract, and the price can fall without any repeat of an 83 per cent drawdown. That is a valuation point, not a price-history point. I accept that the pack contains no disclosure that explains or rebuts the drawdown. The latest news and disclosures are about Saudization and sukuk issuances, not about share price history [P6].
data.concedes: The pack contains no disclosure that explains or rebuts the drawdown.

data.text: The quote, the technicals and the disclosures here are all as of 2026-10-13, so the figures can be read together as one snapshot of where the company stands today [P1]. Nothing in the pack is carrying an older date that would need allowing for. Everything else here is secondary to that one date.

data.headline: No quarterly data means no trend; price alone is not a business story.
data.text: I am answerable for the quarterly trend, and I have to be blunt: the pack carries no quarterly statement at all. I count zero quarters. Without that, I cannot check whether earnings are moving, whether one bad quarter is a blip or a decline, or whether a good one is a recovery. My whole method rests on watching the numbers quarter by quarter, and here I have nothing to watch. The only record of the stretch is the price: the 1-year summary runs from 2025-09-29 to 2026-10-13 with a change of 3.16% [P7]. That window ends on the quote date, while the technicals are dated 2026-08-11 [P1]. The price record is current to its own date, but nothing here says whether the business moved the same way. A share can rise while the business slows, or fall while it strengthens. Without the quarterly income statement, I cannot call this a grower, a cyclical, or anything else. The story I am supposed to check is simply not here. So my answer is that the quarterly evidence is absent, and anyone reading these figures as a snapshot of the business is reading price, not the company. I need the actual quarters before I can say one useful thing about the trend.

data.headline: No balance sheet with a strike date; health ratios exist but operands are unseen.
data.text: I am answerable for the balance sheet, and the pack holds no balance sheet statement with a strike date. The health group in [P2] gives debt_equity of 0.20 and current_ratio of 2.00, with sector percentiles of 54.0 and 68.4 [P2]. Those numbers are published and not flagged stale, but the operands behind them and the date they are struck at are not shown. A ratio of a flow over a position mixes two dates, and I cannot say whether these do. Interest_coverage is marked missing_inputs, so I cannot say what would strain the funding [P2]. The fundamentals dataset is dated 2026-08-12 and is not flagged stale [P1], which is one date in a pack of many. Without the actual balance sheet, I cannot build my scenarios. I cannot point to the line that would break first in a downturn, or say whether the funding is long-term or short-term. The machine I am supposed to read has several parts missing. The health metrics suggest a company that is not stretched, but I cannot confirm that from the components. So my answer is that the balance sheet evidence is partial: two ratios exist, their origins are invisible, and the key coverage measure is absent. That is not a snapshot; it is a glimpse through a fogged window.

data.headline: The pack has no single date; most datasets are stale and P9 is absent.
data.text: The pack does not hold one date. The quote is as of 2026-10-13 and is flagged stale against a maximum age of 2.0 days [P1]. The technicals and the prices category are as of 2026-08-11, disclosures 2026-03-09 and news 2026-08-04, all flagged stale; only fundamentals, as of 2026-08-12, are not [P1]. The prices category says 2026-08-11 while the quote says 2026-10-13, and the pack does not explain it [P1]. So we have a price from one date, technicals from two months earlier, and news older still. That is not a single snapshot; it is a collage of different moments. And there are gaps I must name. In [P2], ev_ebitda, ps, roic, net_margin, interest_coverage and payout have no value. Several are marked missing_inputs or na_sector. The statements in P9 are not in the pack at all, so the limitations and calculations that would tell me what this evidence cannot answer are themselves absent. I cannot read what the price assumes about these missing measures, and I cannot say what we do not know when the list of unknowns is not here. The confidence of this room must not run ahead of its evidence, and my job is to say when it has. It has. The data is a patchwork of different dates, several pieces are old, and the gaps are wide. Anyone reading this as one clean snapshot is reading more than the pack provides.

data.headline: Dividend record is current to Q2 2026; payout window is absent [P1].
data.text: I am answerable for what was returned to owners and out of what. The dividend list in [P3] is current to a Q2 2026 dividend of SAR 0.34 per share, announced 2026-08-04, ex-date 2026-08-19 and paid 2026-08-27 [P3]. That is recent. The capital changes end with the secondary offering closed on 2024-06-07 at SAR 27.25 per share, which left capital unchanged at SAR 90000 million [P3]. Before that, two bonus issues increased the share count, which changes what every per-share figure before them meant. So the record of what was returned is clear and current in its own right. But the question is not just what was paid; it is out of what. The matched payout against an earnings window comes from P9, which is not in the pack [P1]. I cannot say whether the SAR 0.34 dividend was 50% of earnings or 90%, or whether it was paid out of a loss [P3] [P4]. The amounts are there, the earnings window is not. Without the payout calculation, I have a list of cheques but no ledger. So my answer is that the dividend history is current and well-documented, but the other half of my mandate, the earnings it was drawn from, is missing. That is half a snapshot. The franchise may be intact, but I cannot tell you whether the dividend is a sign of confidence or a strain on the business.

data.headline: News and peer data are dated months apart; P9 limitations are absent.
data.text: I am answerable for the company against its sector and for what it has disclosed. The newest news item is dated 2026-08-04 and the newest disclosure 2026-03-09, a buyback of 350M shares for an employee plan [P6]. Both categories are flagged stale in [P1]. The peer data carries dates of 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-12 [P5]. So the news is from August, the disclosure from March, and the peers from August. That is not one date. The percentiles in [P2] exist only for debt_equity at 54.0 and current_ratio at 68.4; the other metrics carry none, which means no ranking, not a low one [P2]. I cannot say how this company ranks on profitability or valuation within its sector because those rankings are absent. The P9 limitations are not in the pack, so I cannot say whether any peer class is wrong. I am being asked to judge a company against its sector with a partial ranking, stale news, and no visibility on whether the peer group itself is correctly drawn. The company has disclosed a buyback and a bond issuance, but the most recent disclosure is seven months old. For a long-horizon investor, that is not recent enough to call current. So my answer is that the sector picture is a mosaic of different dates with missing rankings, and the disclosure record is dated. That is not a single snapshot.

data.headline: The data does not share one date and cannot be read as a single snapshot
data.answer:
The pack holds datasets with different dates. The quote is as of 2026-10-13 and the 1-year and 5-year price summaries end on the same day [P1][P7][P8]. The technicals and prices category are as of 2026-08-11, the news as of 2026-08-04 and the disclosures as of 2026-03-09 [P1]. The fundamentals are as of 2026-08-12 and are the only category not flagged stale [P1]. The council votes are dated 2026-08-07 and flagged stale [P4]. The dividend history runs to a payment on 2026-08-27 [P3].

The room agrees on the central point. Buffett opened by reading everything as one 2026-10-13 snapshot and withdrew it once Marks and Lynch pointed to the freshness entries [P1]. Dalio added that a price-over-earnings ratio such as the P/E of 14.47 mixes a price date with an earnings window the pack does not state [P1].

The pack also refers to a P9 statement dataset that is not present. No income statement, balance sheet or quarterly record is available. Buffett could not name a denominator or window for ROE of 26.75% and ROA of 15.86% [P2], Dalio could not date the debt_equity of 0.20 and current_ratio of 2.00 [P2], Lynch counted zero quarters, and Alwaleed had no matched payout. Marks listed ev_ebitda, ps, roic, net_margin, interest_coverage and payout as having no value [P2].

The data cannot say how current the underlying earnings are, only when each category was last refreshed. Read as separate dated items, the price figures are the most recent, the fundamentals and dividend record come next, and the disclosures and news are oldest.

data.headline: The sector comparison does not show the shares are cheap; it shows they are expensive.
data.text:
The sector comparison in [P5] clearly shows that Al Rajhi Bank is not cheap relative to its peers. The bank trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 14.51 [P1], which is the highest among the eight listed peers. Saudi National Bank (SNB) trades at a P/E of 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, and Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82 [P5]. The market is assigning Al Rajhi a significant premium, valuing its earnings at nearly double the multiple of some of its largest competitors. This is the very first thing the price is telling us: the consensus is willing to pay more for a unit of Al Rajhi's earnings than for a unit of any other bank's earnings in the group.

The price-to-book ratio reinforces this. At 3.19 [P1], the market values the bank at more than three times its stated book value. This is a rich valuation, suggesting the market believes the bank's assets are worth far more than their accounting value or that its future profitability will be exceptional. The bank's return on equity of 23.49% [P1] is strong, which justifies a premium over book value, but the price is already compensating for that quality.

On the income side, Al Rajhi's dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is the lowest in the peer group. The other banks offer yields from 3.1% (Alinma Bank) up to 6.02% (Saudi Awwal Bank) [P5]. An investor seeking current income would find the shares less attractive than almost every alternative. The price is not assuming a high payout; it is assuming growth.

The five-year price history in [P8] shows the shares have returned 34.24%, but the one-year return is a decline of 11.54%. The price is now 14.92% below its 52-week high and sits below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1]. This could be a sign that the pendulum of sentiment has begun to swing away from its extreme.

What this evidence cannot answer is crucial. The data pack does not provide earnings growth rates, so we cannot assess whether the high P/E is justified by a superior growth trajectory. The pack also does not show the net interest margin or cost-to-income ratio, which are fundamental drivers of bank profitability. We do not know what the return on assets of 2.53% [P1] looks like relative to peers, as that comparison is absent. The price is assuming a lot of good things will happen; we simply do not have the data here to know if those assumptions are reasonable.

data.text: The quarterly record in P9 is not in the pack, so I cannot read the trend. The question asks whether the sector comparison shows the shares are cheap. I can read the price tag and the peer list. Al Rajhi Bank last traded at 62.10 SAR [P1]. Over the last year the price fell 11.54 percent, from 70.20 to 62.10 SAR [P7]. Over five years it rose 34.24 percent, from 46.26 to 62.10 SAR [P8]. Price and earnings should travel together, and with the earnings history absent I am left comparing the price multiple. The P/E is 14.51 [P1]. The eight bank peers listed in P5 carry P/Es from 7.78 at Riyad Bank to 11.94 at Bank Albilad, every one below 14.51 [P5]. The dividend yield tells the same story: 2.6 percent for Al Rajhi Bank [P1] against a sector range of 3.1 to 6.02 percent [P5]. That reads as dearer than the sector on the numbers I have. I cannot call it cheap when the earnings multiple is the highest in the room and the cash return to owners the lowest. A good bank can deserve a higher multiple, but the data here gives me no quarterly earnings to check whether it is earning the premium. Without P9 I cannot count the quarters, so I stop at what the comparison shows: not cheap.

The peer list in P5 shows P/Es from 7.78 to 11.94 and dividend yields from 3.1 to 6.02 percent, all more favourable on those yardsticks than Al Rajhi Bank's 14.51 and 2.6 percent [P5][P1]. The matched-window payout from P9 is not in the pack, so I cannot say what proportion of earnings was paid out over which window. verdict.headline: On the sector table, the shares look dearer than peers, not cheaper
verdict.answer: The sector comparison in the pack does not show the shares as cheap. headline: Peer data shows a mid-range multiple but is too thin to confirm or refute the valuation.
answer:
The peer comparison in the pack does not settle whether Jarir's valuation is supported. It holds two columns per peer, P/E and dividend yield [P5]. Jarir trades at a P/E of 18.43 and a yield of 5.16% [P1]. Of the five peers with a published P/E, United Electronics is lower at 10.43, while Aldrees at 26.07, Abo Moati at 33.62, Al-Saif at 37.30 and SACO at 41.45 are higher [P5]. Three peers have no P/E [P5]. On yield, only United Electronics is higher, at 7.65% [P5]. No sector percentile for P/E is published [P2].

The room agrees on the facts. Jarir is neither the cheapest nor the dearest name, and the balance sheet is strong: debt-to-equity is 0.0, at the 89.7th sector percentile, and the current ratio is 1.37 [P2]. Jarir's ROE is 67.25% and its price-to-book is 12.28 [P1]. Buffett reads the gap to United Electronics as the decisive comparison. Lynch, Dalio, Marks and Al-Rumayyan read the range as a scatter. Alwaleed and Lynch weigh the dividend record, and Buffett weighs the book multiple.

The pack gives no peer ROE, ROA, book value, growth rate, sector median, or Jarir's own P/E history. Without them the room cannot say whether the premium over United Electronics is earned or whether the discount to the others is deserved. Lynch also notes that quarterly earnings are absent. The one-year price change is 24.95% and the five-year change is -13.87% [P7][P8], which gives context but not a peer test.
gaps: Peer ROE, ROA, ROIC and price-to-book figures are absent, so the premium cannot be tested against peer quality.
Jarir's own historical P/E range and a sector median multiple are not in the pack.
Quarterly earnings and growth rates are missing, so the P/E cannot be tied to an earnings trend.
disagreements: Whether the closest peer or the whole peer range is the right benchmark - The P/E figures are not in dispute: 10.43 for United Electronics against 18.43 for Jarir, with four peers higher [P5][P1]. Which peer is the right benchmark depends on peer returns on capital and growth, which the pack does not hold, and no sector percentile for P/E is published [P2].

Whether the yield and returns justify the premium - Jarir's 5.16% yield and 67.25% ROE are in the pack [P1], but no peer ROE or ROA is given [P5]. Without a peer counterpart the premium can be neither confirmed nor refuted. ROIC, payout and net margin are also unpublished for Jarir [P2].
