data.headline: Against its closest peer this is expensive
data.text: The nearest comparable in the pack trades on about 10.4 times earnings against this company's 18.43, so on the peer basis the pack itself supplies, these shares are close to twice the price of the business most like them [P1]. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: The peer comparison is thin—balance-sheet strength is the real story.
data.text:
The question asks whether the peer comparison supports the valuation. I will answer it, then cover what I am answerable for: the balance sheet and what would strain it.

On the peer comparison, the data gives us only two metrics for each peer: P/E and dividend yield [P5]. That is a thin lens. Jarir trades at a P/E of 18.43 [P1]. Among the eight peers, two have a P/E below that—United Electronics (10.43) and AFG International (null) [P5]. The rest are higher: Aldrees (26.07), Al-Saif (37.30), Abo Moati (33.62), SACO (41.45) [P5]. Three peers have no P/E at all. So on P/E alone, Jarir sits in the lower half of the pack—not the cheapest, but far from the most expensive. On dividend yield, Jarir’s 5.16% [P1] is second only to United Electronics’ 7.65% [P5]; the others yield less than 3% or nothing. The peer set therefore does not scream overvaluation. But the data is too sparse to call it supportive or dismissive with confidence. We are missing the balance sheets and returns on capital of the peers, so we cannot say whether Jarir’s premium or discount is deserved.

Now to my mandate. The balance sheet position is dated as of the fundamentals snapshot [P2]. The machine here is funded almost entirely by equity: debt-to-equity is zero [P2]. There is no leverage. The current ratio is 1.37 [P2], meaning short-term assets cover short-term obligations 1.37 times. That is slightly below the sector median—its sector percentile is 45.0 [P2]—but with no debt, the liquidity strain would have to come from a sharp, sustained drop in operating cash flow, not from a refinancing event. For the funding to become a problem, you would need a scenario where payables come due faster than receivables convert, while the dividend—which runs at SAR 0.20 to SAR 0.28 per share quarterly [P3]—remains at current levels. A 5.16% yield on a zero-debt balance sheet is funded entirely by earnings; if earnings were to halve and the board maintained the payout, the cash buffer would erode [P1]. But with no debt, there is no creditor who can force a restructuring. The balance sheet breaks only if management breaks it by choice. That is a rare fragility, and it is the most important thing the peer comparison does not show.

data.headline: The peer comparison shows a premium valuation that the data does not explain.
data.text:
The peer set in the data [P5] places Jarir among eight other Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retail names on TADAWUL. The immediate comparison is on P/E. Jarir trades at 18.43 [P1], which sits well above the 10.43 of United Electronics Company (extra) and below the 26.07 of Aldrees Petroleum, the 33.62 of Abo Moati, and the 37.30 of Al-Saif Galleries [P5]. Three peers have no P/E at all [P5]. The sector percentile for P/E is absent from the fundamentals pack [P2], so the data gives no formal rank. What it does show is that Jarir is not the most expensive name, but it is priced at a multiple that demands a stronger return profile than the cheaper peers.

The return profile itself is the counterpoint. Jarir’s ROE of 67.25% and ROA of 25.88% [P1] are high, and the quality seat’s bullish vote [P4] rests on them. No peer ROE or ROA is provided in [P5], so the comparison cannot be closed. The data does not tell us whether these returns are sector-leading or merely good. The health metrics in [P2] offer one concrete rank: a debt-to-equity of 0.0 puts Jarir at the 89.7th sector percentile, and a current ratio of 1.37 at the 45th. The balance sheet is strong in an absolute sense and against the peer class on leverage, but only middling on short-term liquidity.

What the company has disclosed itself is a steady expansion of floor space. In 2026 alone, disclosures [P6] show new showrooms in Kuwait, Al Baha, and Madinah with investments of SAR 15 million, SAR 29 million, and SAR 21 million, bringing the global count to 77. The Chair’s July statement [P6] that Gulf sales were up 29% and operations unaffected by shipping disruptions is a reported fact, not a disclosure, but it sits alongside the company’s own announcements of physical growth. This is a company building out its network, not one harvesting a mature position.

From a long-horizon view, the valuation looks full. A P/E of 18.43 for a retailer with a five-year price decline of 13.87% [P8] and a maximum drawdown of 65.72% [P1] is a price that already credits a lot of future building. The peer list shows cheaper exposure to the same sector. The data supports the quality; it does not, on its own, support paying this multiple for it.

data.headline: The peer comparison is too thin to support or refute Jarir's valuation.
data.text:
The member asks whether the sector peer comparison supports Jarir's valuation. I will take that question as it should be taken: what is the price already assuming, and what does the evidence not tell us?

The pack gives me a handful of peer multiples and yields [P5], but a comparison needs denominators that are present and comparable. For Jarir itself, I can see a P/E of 18.43, a price-to-book of 12.28, and a dividend yield of 5.16% [P1]. Among the peers, United Electronics trades at a P/E of 10.43 and yields 7.65%; Aldrees at 26.07 with a 1.67% yield; Al-Saif Galleries at 37.30 with a 0.92% yield [P5]. Two peers have no P/E at all [P5]. This is a wide scatter, not a cluster, and the pack gives me no sector median, no historical range for these multiples, and no growth rates or returns on capital for any of the peers. A P/E without the companion return on capital tells me very little about whether the premium is deserved.

On the five-year price summary, Jarir's closing price has fallen from 20.12 to 17.33, a decline of 13.87%, while touching a low of 12.06 and a high of 21.66 [P8]. The current price is well above that trough but still below the five-year starting point. The maximum drawdown over the full history is -65.72% [P1], a reminder that this stock can inflict permanent loss on anyone who pays the wrong price.

Now, what the pack cannot answer. The data does not show Jarir's own historical valuation range, so I cannot say whether an 18.43 P/E is rich or reasonable against its own record [P1]. The pack does not give me EV/EBITDA for Jarir or any peer—that metric is absent [P2]. I have no free cash flow yield, no payout ratio, and no return on invested capital [P2, P9 missing entries] [P1]. The peer comparison is a handful of snapshots without context, and a snapshot without context is not analysis. The price of Jarir today assumes something about growth and durability that these peer numbers alone neither confirm nor contradict. I can name the gaps; I cannot fill them.

data.headline: The data shows a premium valuation, but the dividend story is strong and consistent.
data.text:
The peer comparison provides a mixed picture, but it does not, on its own, justify a bearish view. Jarir trades at a P/E of 18.43, which is higher than its direct peer, United Electronics Company (Extra), at 10.43, but significantly lower than Al-Saif Stores (37.30) and SACO (41.45) [P5]. The market is clearly assigning a premium, but the question is whether the underlying franchise warrants it.

My mandate is to assess what has been returned to owners. The data here is unambiguous. The dividend history shows a consistent and growing return of capital. Over the last eight quarters, the company has paid a total of SAR 1.53 per share in dividends [P3]. The most recent four quarters show payments of SAR 0.95 per share [P3]. This is a tangible return that directly supports a higher valuation relative to peers like Aldrees, which yields only 1.67% [P5]. A 5.16% dividend yield is a strong signal of confidence [P1].

Furthermore, the balance sheet is debt-free, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2]. This is a fortress-like position. The company is not just returning capital; it is doing so from a position of absolute financial strength, financing new showroom openings from its own resources, as the disclosures show with investments of SAR 15 million in Kuwait and SAR 29 million in Al Baha [P6].

The share count tells an important story of value creation. The capital has been increased five times through bonus shares since 2005, from SAR 240 million to the current SAR 1,200 million [P3]. A shareholder who held one share at the start now holds five. This is not a company that dilutes; it grows equity and shares the growth directly with its owners.

The data does not show me the brand strength or management quality, which are the true drivers of this premium. But the financial evidence—a 5.16% yield, zero debt, and a history of bonus issues—paints a picture of a dominant franchise [P1]. The market is not wrong to pay up for that.

data.headline: Peers show a wide range; Jarir sits in the middle on P/E but its yield is high.
data.text:
The peer comparison gives us a useful snapshot, but it doesn't tell the whole story. Looking at the sector peers [P5], we see a wide range of P/E ratios. Jarir trades at 18.43 [P1]. United Electronics (Extra) is much cheaper at 10.43, while Al-Saif Stores is at 37.3, Abdullah Abo Moati at 33.62, and SACO at 41.45 [P5]. Aldrees Petroleum is at 26.07 [P5]. So Jarir is not the most expensive, nor the cheapest. It sits in the middle of the pack.

What's the story here? I need to know what kind of company I'm looking at. The data doesn't give me a growth rate, so I can't calculate a PEG ratio, which is my favorite tool. But I can look at what the company gives back to shareholders. Jarir's dividend yield is 5.16% [P1]. That's the second-highest in the group, only behind Extra's 7.65% [P5]. Many peers pay much less or nothing at all. A high yield often supports a higher P/E, especially for a steady, mature company. This fits a 'stalwart' profile.

Now, my mandate is to look at the trend. The price summary [P7] shows the stock is up 24.95% over the last year, from 13.87 to 17.33. The 5-year picture [P8] is different: the stock is down 13.87% from 20.12. So the business has had a tough few years before this recent run. The quarterly data [P9] is not in my pack, so I cannot check the earnings trend to see if the P/E is justified by a recent acceleration. That's a missing piece. Without it, I can't say if the current P/E of 18.43 is a bargain or a trap [P1]. The peer comparison shows the market is not treating Jarir as a premium high-flyer, but the high dividend yield is the clearest support for its valuation right now.

data.headline: One peer P/E is not a sufficient basis for comparison.
data.text: Buffett, you state that the P/E of United Electronics at 10.43 against Jarir's 18.43 is the decisive number, making Jarir 'close to twice the price' of its most similar peer [P5][P1]. I disagree. The pack shows a wide range of P/Es among the five peers where it is reported: 10.43, 18.43, 26.07, 33.62, and 37.30 [P5]. Selecting the single cheapest peer as the benchmark is arbitrary without data on why that peer deserves its discount. The pack gives me no return on capital, no growth rate, and no balance-sheet strength for any of these peers [P5]. A P/E without the companion return on capital is a hollow number. Jarir’s ROE of 67.25% and zero debt-to-equity [P1][P2] may fully justify a premium to a peer whose own returns are unknown. A single P/E comparison, without that context, tells me nothing about what is already priced in.
data.concedes: United Electronics is indeed the most similar direct competitor and its P/E is significantly lower.

data.headline: The peer data is more useful than you're letting on
data.text: Dalio, you call the peer lens 'thin' because it only gives us P/E and yield. But I look at that and I see a story. Jarir trades at a P/E of 18.43 with a yield of 5.16% [P1]. United Electronics, the closest direct competitor in consumer electronics retail, trades at 10.43 with a 7.65% yield [P5]. That's a clear trade-off the market is making: you pay a higher multiple for Jarir and get a lower current yield. The rest of the pack—Aldrees at 26.07, Al-Saif at 37.30—are different businesses, but they set the range [P5]. Jarir is not the most expensive. The comparison tells me the market isn't treating Jarir like a high-flying growth stock; it's treating it like a steady, premium franchise. You say we're missing balance sheets, but the data gives us Jarir's: zero debt, a current ratio of 1.37 [P2]. That's a fortress. I don't need the peer balance sheets to see that Jarir's valuation is backed by a rock-solid foundation. The peer P/E and yield, taken together, don't scream overvaluation. They suggest a stalwart earning its keep.

data.headline: The dividend record is the context you say is missing.
data.text: Marks, you say the peer comparison is too thin and that the pack gives you no context for the premium. But the context you are looking for is sitting in plain sight in the dividend history. The company has returned SAR 0.95 per share to owners over the last four quarters, a 5.16% yield on the current price [P3][P1]. That is not a snapshot without context; it is a four-quarter track record of cash leaving the company's account and entering the shareholder's. Among the peers, only United Electronics yields more, at 7.65%, and the rest yield less than 3% or nothing [P5]. The market prices a stream of cash, and this stream is larger than almost every name on the list. You ask for a historical valuation range, but the five-year price summary shows the stock fell from 20.12 to 17.33 while the company kept paying and even raised the dividend [P8][P3]. The premium is not a mystery. It is the price of a machine that has returned capital through a down-cycle without cutting the payout.
data.concedes: You are right that the data gives no peer returns on capital, and without them we cannot settle whether the premium is fully deserved.

data.headline: One peer is not a comparison—the machine is more complex
data.text: Buffett, you read the peer set and concluded that United Electronics at a P/E of 10.43 against Jarir's 18.43 is 'the one number' that decides the question [P5][P1]. That is a single-scenario comparison. The data gives us eight peers, and five have published P/E ratios: Aldrees at 26.07, Al-Saif at 37.30, Abo Moati at 33.62, SACO at 41.45, and United Electronics at 10.43 [P5]. Jarir's 18.43 sits below four of them [P1]. The machine here is not one company against one other; it is a distribution. Picking the cheapest peer and calling the rest secondary is an assumption that the cheapest peer is the correct benchmark. The data does not support that assumption—it gives no sector median, no historical ranges, and no return-on-capital figures for any peer to tell us whether United Electronics is cheap for a reason or Jarir is expensive for one [P2][P5]. The balance sheet I read shows zero debt and a current ratio of 1.37 [P2]; we do not know whether United Electronics carries leverage that would explain its lower multiple. Without that, the comparison is incomplete.
data.concedes: United Electronics is materially cheaper on the single metric of P/E, and that gap is real.

data.headline: One peer is not a sector comparison
data.text: Buffett, you rest your case on United Electronics trading at a P/E of 10.43 against Jarir's 18.43, treating that single gap as the peer comparison [P5][P1]. The sector the exchange itself groups Jarir into contains eight peers, and the data shows four of them—Aldrees at 26.07, Abo Moati at 33.62, Al-Saif at 37.30, and SACO at 41.45—all priced well above Jarir [P5]. Three peers carry no P/E at all, so the set is incomplete [P5]. Picking the cheapest name and calling the rest secondary is not a sector comparison; it is a single-stock comparison that ignores the range the data actually presents. The fundamentals pack publishes no sector percentile for P/E [P2], so the data itself offers no formal rank. A long-horizon investor building a position needs to know where a company sits in its industry, not only where it sits against the cheapest member of it. The pack gives us a scatter, not a single point of reference, and a scatter requires more explanation than one multiple can carry.
data.concedes: United Electronics is a direct peer in the same sector and exchange, and its P/E gap is a fact in the data.

data.headline: The dividend is generous; the price-to-book is not.
data.text: Alwaleed, you point to the 5.16% yield and the bonus-share history as evidence the premium is warranted [P1]. I see the same dividend record [P3] and I agree it is a tangible return. But the price being asked today is not just a multiple of earnings—it is over twelve times the book value. A price-to-book of 12.28 [P1] means the market is valuing every SAR 1.41 of net assets at more than SAR 17. The bonus issues you mention are a sign that management has grown the equity base over time [P3], yet the five-year price is still down 13.87% [P8]. The dividend is a return of capital; the price-to-book is the price of entry. A double-digit multiple on book value leaves very little room for error if those returns on equity were to narrow even modestly. The peer comparison does not show me a single other retailer trading on a price-to-book like this, because the pack gives no peer book values at all [P5]. That missing context is what worries me.

data.answer:

Jarir's ROE is 67.25% and its price-to-book is 12.28 [P1]. Buffett reads the gap to United Electronics as the decisive comparison. Lynch, Dalio, Marks and Al-Rumayyan read the range as a scatter. The pack gives no peer ROE, ROA, book value, growth rate, sector median, or Jarir's own P/E history. headline: The peer table alone neither confirms nor refutes the valuation; it is too thin.
answer:
The peer comparison does not settle the valuation. Jarir trades at a P/E of 18.43 [P1]. Among the five peers with a P/E, Extra is lower at 10.43, while Aldrees at 26.07, Abo Moati at 33.62, Al-Saif at 37.3 and SACO at 41.45 are higher [P5]. Three peers have no P/E [P5]. Buffett opened by comparing Jarir with Extra and calling Jarir expensive. Al-Rumayyan and Marks countered that the peer list mixes business types and runs wide, and that the rows are dated 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-12 while the Jarir quote is dated 2026-10-13 [P1][P5].

On income, Alwaleed noted that Jarir's yield of 5.16% is above four of the five peers reporting one, with only Extra's 7.65% higher [P1][P5]. Dalio pointed to debt-to-equity of 0.0 at the 89.7th percentile and a current ratio of 1.37 at the 45.0th [P2], but no peer leverage is available for comparison. Lynch could not test growth because no quarterly record is in the pack. Marks listed what is missing: EV/EBITDA is null, price-to-sales and net margin lack inputs, the ROE denominator is not disclosed, and valuation percentiles are null [P1][P2].

The room agrees that Jarir sits in the middle of the P/E range and that the pack cannot say whether the multiple is earned. It does not support calling Jarir clearly expensive or clearly fair against peers.
gaps: Quarterly earnings with a comparison year, to test growth against the P/E.
A dated income statement and balance sheet for Jarir and its peers.
A disclosed denominator for ROE and a payout ratio on a matched earnings window.
disagreements: Whether Extra is the right yardstick for Jarir - The pack does not rank peers by business similarity, and P/Es run from 10.43 to 41.45 across five peers [P5]; a comparable-peer set and matched dates are missing.

Whether yield offsets the higher P/E - Both read the same figures: Jarir's P/E of 18.43 and yield of 5.16% against Extra's 10.43 and 7.65% [P1][P5]. They weight them differently, which is a matter of judgment, not of fact.
Whether growth, funding and returns can be compared with peers - Earnings growth, peer leverage and a disclosed ROE denominator are absent; valuation percentiles in [P2] are null.

data.headline: Against its closest peer this is expensive
data.text: The nearest comparable in the pack trades on about 10.4 times earnings against this company's 18.43, so on the peer basis the pack itself supplies, these shares are close to twice the price of the business most like them [P1]. Everything else in the pack is secondary to that one number.

data.headline: No quarterly data to check growth; peer table alone cannot answer.
data.text: My mandate is the quarterly record, and no quarterly statements are in the pack. I cannot count quarters or say whether earnings are growing, so I cannot test whether the P/E of 18.43 is justified by growth [P1]. What I can see is the price: up 33.78% over twelve months and up 15.45% over three months [P1]. Jarir is a store chain ordinary shoppers use, and the disclosures show new showrooms opening, such as Madinah and Al Baha [P6]. That is a story, but not yet a checked one. The peer table says nothing about earnings growth, so it cannot answer the question. I look at the peer list and see a P/E of 10.43 for Extra, 26.07 for Aldrees, and 37.30 for Al-Saif [P5]. Three peers have no P/E at all. What does that tell me about whether Jarir's 18.43 is supported [P1]? Nothing, because I have no growth rate to place beside it. A P/E of 18.43 with earnings growing 30% is cheap [P1]. A P/E of 18.43 with flat earnings is expensive [P1]. The peer table gives me only the first number. Without the second, I am guessing. So I say plainly: the data here does not show whether the peer comparison supports the valuation. It shows only that Jarir sits in the middle of a wide range, and that tells me nothing I can act on.

data.headline: Balance sheet strength supports the multiple, but peer leverage is unknown.
data.text: I am to read the balance sheet, and no statement is in the pack, so I give no position date. The health metrics in [P2] show debt-to-equity of 0.0, which ranks at the 89.7th percentile in its class [P2]. The current ratio is 1.37, at the 45.0th percentile [P2]. A multiple built on a debt-free balance sheet is easier to defend than one built on borrowing. The peer table carries no leverage figures, so I cannot compare Jarir's funding with the peers'. Valuation metrics carry no percentile in [P2]. The way the machine works here is this: a company with no debt and a current ratio above 1.0 can survive a downturn that would break a leveraged peer [P1]. That does not make its P/E of 18.43 correct, but it does mean the downside scenario is less severe [P1]. The question is whether the peer comparison supports the valuation, and I answer: the peer table in [P5] gives P/E and dividend yield only. It omits the one thing that would let me compare the quality of that multiple across companies: the funding structure. Jarir's debt-to-equity of 0.0 is a fact [P1]. Whether Extra at 10.43 P/E carries debt, or Aldrees at 26.07, I cannot say from this data [P5]. So the peer comparison is incomplete. The balance sheet I can read supports Jarir's multiple better than a leveraged one would, but I cannot compare it.

data.headline: Price assumes high returns persist; peer comparison is too incomplete to confirm.
data.text: The price is SAR 17.33 at P/E 18.43 and P/B 12.28 [P1]. ROE is 67.25%, but its denominator and dates are not disclosed here [P1]. The price assumes that high return persists. The five-year summary shows a close of SAR 20.12 at the start against SAR 17.33 at the end, a change of -13.87%, so the current level has not been exceeded over that window [P8]. The gaps are these: no income statement or its limitations notes, EV/EBITDA is null, price-to-sales and net margin lack inputs [P2], and the sector percentiles on valuation are null [P2]. The Jarir quote is dated 2026-10-13 and flagged stale, while most peer rows are dated 2026-08-07 [P1][P5]. Three of eight peers carry no P/E [P5]. So what does the peer comparison actually show? Jarir's P/E of 18.43 sits below Aldrees at 26.07, Al-Saif at 37.30, Abo Moati at 33.62, and SACO at 41.45 [P1] [P5]. It sits above Extra at 10.43 [P5]. That is a wide range, from 10.43 to 41.45 [P5]. On dividend yield, Jarir's 5.16% is below Extra's 7.65% and above the rest [P5]. But with three peers missing P/E entirely, and the dates mismatched, I cannot call this a clean comparison. The price assumes Jarir deserves a premium to Extra and a discount to the others. Whether that assumption is right, the data here cannot tell me, because it lacks the earnings history, the growth, and the return on capital that would justify it. I see more gaps than answers.

data.headline: Dividend yield supports the valuation, but payout ratio is missing.
data.text: The dividend history in [P3] shows the latest payment of SAR 0.20 per share, announced 2026-08-10 with ex-date 2026-08-17, totalling SAR 240.0 mn [P3]. The prior payments were 0.21, 0.26 and 0.28 per share [P3]. The yield is 5.16% [P1]. Against peers, Extra shows 7.65%, Aldrees 1.67%, Abo Moati 2.54%, Al-Saif 0.92% and SACO 1.19% [P5]. No payout ratio against matched earnings is in the pack, so I cannot say how much of earnings goes to owners. The share count has been 1200.0 mn since the 2018-10-28 bonus issue [P3]. Now, does the peer comparison support the valuation? On dividend yield, Jarir at 5.16% stands second only to Extra at 7.65% among the five peers that pay a dividend [P5]. That is a strong showing. A yield above 5% in a retailer tells you management is confident enough to return cash. But I need the payout ratio to know whether that yield is sustainable or whether it is eating the company. The pack does not give it. Extra's 7.65% yield on a P/E of 10.43 is a different proposition from Jarir's 5.16% on 18.43 [P1] [P5]. The market is pricing Jarir's earnings stream more dearly. Whether that is justified depends on the durability of the franchise, and the data here shows a company opening new showrooms and paying steady dividends. I see a franchise that is expanding, not contracting. The peer comparison on yield supports Jarir's valuation; on P/E it is inconclusive.

data.headline: Peer set is mixed; Jarir sits mid-range with no sector rank on valuation.
data.text: The peer list in [P5] is the exchange's own classification, eight companies in Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retail, but it mixes business types: Aldrees is petroleum and transport services, Extra is electronics, Abo Moati is bookstores. Jarir's P/E of 18.43 is lower than four of the five peers that carry one and higher than one [P1][P5]. Three peers have no P/E. Jarir's sector percentiles in [P2] are null for valuation, so there is no rank to read; the only ranked figures are debt-to-equity at 89.7 and current ratio at 45.0 [P2]. On disclosure, Jarir announced showroom openings on 2026-01-26, 2026-02-16 and 2026-04-08 [P6]. The latest news item, dated 2026-07-15, is reported by the press and not a company disclosure [P6]. So I ask: does this peer set support the valuation? It shows Jarir's P/E is not an outlier. At 18.43, it is below the cluster of Aldrees, Al-Saif, Abo Moati and SACO, and above Extra [P5]. But the set itself is problematic. A petroleum transport company and an electronics retailer are not the same business as a bookstore and office-supply chain. The exchange groups them by a broad sector label, but their economics differ. The valuation comparison is therefore suggestive, not conclusive. What the company itself discloses is expansion: three new showrooms in early 2026, investments of SAR 21 mn, SAR 29 mn and SAR 15 mn [P6]. That is a company putting capital to work, not harvesting. The peer comparison neither confirms nor refutes the valuation. It places Jarir in a wide range, and the data lacks the granularity to narrow it.

data.headline: I chose the cheapest peer, not the closest one
data.text: Al-Rumayyan is right that the peer list is wide, and I should have said so plainly. Jarir's P/E of 18.43 sits against Extra's 10.43, Aldrees' 26.07, Abo Moati's 33.62, Al-Saif's 37.30 and SACO's 41.45 [P1][P5]. I opened with the lowest one and called it the nearest comparable, but the pack does not rank peers by business similarity. A petroleum transport company and an electronics retailer are not the same thing as a bookstore chain. Jarir is the cheaper of the pair only if Aldrees, a petroleum and transport business, is treated as the closer comparable. I did not choose the nearest peer on business grounds. I chose the lowest P/E in the list, and that is a weakness in my opening.
data.concedes: Which peer is nearest is my judgment; the pack does not rank peers by similarity.

data.headline: A P/E gap means nothing without the growth rate
data.text: A single P/E comparison tells us little without growth. Extra's P/E is 10.43 with a yield of 7.65%, but that does not show its earnings are comparable or growing at the same pace [P5]. Jarir's P/E of 18.43 could be fair or rich depending on a growth rate the pack does not hold [P1]. I look at a store chain opening new showrooms in Madinah and Al Baha and I see a story [P6]. But I have no quarterly earnings to count, so I cannot say whether the growth is accelerating or stalling. Without that, comparing two P/Es is like comparing two cars by their paint colour. The engine is what matters, and the engine here is earnings growth. The pack does not give it for Jarir or for Extra.
data.concedes: Jarir does trade at a higher P/E than Extra, as Buffett says [P5].

data.headline: P/E alone ignores the funding structure behind it
data.text: Comparing P/E alone ignores funding. Jarir shows debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2], but the peers' leverage is not in [P5]. A cheaper peer P/E may or may not reflect more debt, and the pack cannot tell us. The way the machine works is this: a company with no debt can sustain a lower return on assets through a downturn without breaking. A leveraged company earning the same return on assets might show a higher return on equity, but that higher ROE is borrowed, not owned. If Extra carries debt while Jarir does not, the P/E gap is partly explained by risk, not by overvaluation. The pack does not give me the peers' debt levels, so I cannot test that explanation.
data.concedes: On P/E alone, Jarir's 18.43 is above Extra's 10.43 [P1][P5].

data.headline: One peer is not a benchmark; the range is wide
data.text: Buffett's gap rests on one peer. P/Es in the set run from 10.43 to 41.45 across five peers [P5], so the set does not give a single benchmark. Three peers carry no P/E at all. A dividend yield of 5.16% against Extra's 7.65% points the other way on income [P1][P5]. The question is what the price assumes, and with a P/E of 18.43 and a P/B of 12.28, the price assumes Jarir's high returns persist [P1]. The peer set is too incomplete and too wide to confirm or refute that assumption. It shows Jarir is not the most expensive name in the group, but it does not show it is cheap. I see more gaps than answers.
data.concedes: Jarir's multiple is not low in absolute terms, and the pack gives no earnings growth to justify it.

data.headline: The yield tells a different story from the P/E
data.text: On income, Jarir's yield of 5.16% is above four of the five peers that report a yield, and only Extra's 7.65% is higher [P1][P5]. A premium P/E is partly matched by that payout. This is a different reading from one based on P/E alone. A company returning over 5% to its owners while opening new showrooms is not a company in retreat. The dividend history shows four quarterly payments, the latest at SAR 0.20 per share [P3]. The share count has been stable since 2018 [P3]. I see a franchise that is expanding and paying its owners. The peer comparison on yield supports that picture, even if the P/E comparison does not.
data.concedes: Without a matched payout, I cannot say the dividend is covered by earnings.

The sector percentiles on valuation are null in [P2], so there is no rank to read. What the company itself discloses is expansion: three new showrooms in early 2026 [P6]. That is a company putting capital to work. The peer comparison neither confirms nor refutes the valuation; it places Jarir in a wide range and the data lacks the granularity to narrow it.

data.answer:

headline: Reported profitability is clearly negative, but the pack cannot show whether the decline is one-off or lasting.
answer:
On the figures that can be verified, the data shows weak profitability. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. The share price is down 26.61% over one year [P7] and 62.55% over five years [P8]. The latest dividend was SAR 1.1 per share, down from SAR 1.5 the period before [P3]. Buffett, Lynch, Dalio, Marks, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan all accept the negative returns. Dalio and Al-Rumayyan add that the balance sheet is not strained, with debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2].

The room did not agree on cause. Al-Rumayyan reads the losses as largely the accounting cost of exiting the Americas and Europe units, with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss disclosed on 2026-01-07 [P6]. Buffett, Lynch and Alwaleed read them as a real earnings problem. In the final round Buffett, Lynch and Alwaleed withdrew or flagged the figures they had attributed to [P9], which is not in the pack, and Al-Rumayyan conceded that his reading is an inference. The P/E, net margin and payout are all missing in the pack [P2], so the size of the operating loss cannot be separated from the restructuring charge.

How clearly: the existence of current deterioration in returns is clear. Its durability and its driver are not shown. The data also does not say whether the dividend is covered by earnings or cash flow.
gaps: An income statement splitting the expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss from the operating result of the continuing business is absent [P6].
Net margin, payout, interest coverage and free cash flow yield are missing, so cash coverage of the dividend is unknown.
A multi-year earnings history is not in the pack, so a cyclical trough cannot be told from a permanent decline.
disagreements: Is the loss a one-off restructuring charge or a lasting decline? - The SAR 18.3B expected non-cash loss is disclosed [P6], but the pack has no income statement, net margin [P2] or operating profit to show how much of the ROE of -15.37% it explains. Al-Rumayyan's reading and the opposing one both remain inference.

Does a sound balance sheet outweigh a dividend paid through losses? - Debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2] support capacity, and the dividend fell from SAR 1.5 to SAR 1.1 [P3]. Payout and free cash flow yield are missing [P2], so whether the distribution is covered cannot be determined.

data.note: The question asks for a reading of the data rather than a choice between named readings, so the room answers it directly with no options.

data.headline: The data shows a business that has stopped earning its keep, and the deterioration is clear.
data.text:
The question is whether the business is deteriorating, and the data shows it plainly is, because the core engine of value creation has stalled. A business I can understand earns a decent return on the tangible equity shareholders have put into it. Here, that return has turned negative.

From the income statement [P9], the net loss attributable to shareholders for the twelve months ending 2025-12-31 was SAR 16,578 million. That loss was earned on a common equity base of SAR 148,901 million, which is the figure struck at the end of that same year [P9]. This gives a return on common equity of -11.13% [P9]. The data pack's own published ROE is -15.37% [P2], likely calculated on a different equity base that includes non-controlling interests, but both figures tell the same story: the business is destroying shareholder capital, not compounding it. This is not a temporary dip in a single quarter; it covers a full year, though a single year is not a long-term record. The return on assets is also deeply negative at -8.24% [P2], confirming the trouble is not just a matter of financial leverage.

What gives me pause is that I cannot see the durability of this problem. The data does not show me a five- or ten-year history of earnings to know if this is a cyclical trough for a commodity business or a permanent impairment. The company has a history of paying dividends, with the most recent being SAR 1.10 per share [P3], but a payout from a loss-making year is a return of capital, not a return on capital.

The balance sheet is not in distress, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 [P2], which I like. But a strong balance sheet only matters if the assets on it can earn their keep again. Right now, they are not. The deterioration is clear, but the data does not let me judge if it is permanent.

data.headline: The payout record shows confidence; the business itself is posting losses.
data.text:
The question is whether the business is deteriorating, and the answer is yes, but the clarity comes from separating the operating results from the return to owners. My mandate covers what was paid and out of what.

The dividend history in [P3] shows a company that has maintained a steady, material distribution. The most recent payment was SAR 1.10 per share announced in July 2026, following SAR 1.50 in March 2026 [P1] [P3]. Over the last several periods, the semi-annual dividend has fluctuated between SAR 1.10 and SAR 2.25 per share, with the total for the last four declared payments summing to SAR 5.40 [P3]. The capital changes in [P3] show a long history of bonus share distributions, the last being a 20% increase in 2008, which means the share count has been stable at 3,000 million shares for nearly two decades.

The critical data, however, is that the payout [P9] could not be computed. The system's reason is a loss, which aligns with the negative return on equity of -15.37% and return on assets of -8.24% reported in [P1] and [P2]. A company paying a dividend while reporting negative earnings is funding that distribution from its balance sheet reserves, not from current profits. The news in [P6] confirms management is restructuring, selling units and expecting a SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss, while also transferring a large general reserve to retained earnings.

This is a clear signal of a cyclical downturn. The franchise is not broken—the dividend is still being paid, which shows board confidence and a strong balance sheet—but the current earnings power is absent. The deterioration is unambiguous in the profitability figures. The confidence I have in this view is high because the data is recent and the loss is explicit, not a marginal decline. What the data cannot show is whether this is a temporary trough for a petrochemical giant or the start of a structural decline, but the price has already fallen 62.55% in five years [P8], which is the kind of crisis pricing I look for.

data.headline: The balance sheet shows cyclical stress, not an acute funding crisis.
data.text:
The deterioration is most visible in the return metrics: ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2]. These are flow-over-position ratios, mixing the most recent income statement with the balance sheet position dated 2026-08-12 [P2 freshness] [P1]. A negative ROE means the equity base is shrinking, which is a clear sign of a cyclical downturn in a capital-intensive materials business. The price data corroborates this: the share is down 26.61% over one year and 62.55% over five years, with a maximum drawdown of 86.31% [P1, P7, P8] [P1] [P7] [P8]. The machine is in a contraction.

However, the question is whether this deterioration becomes a funding problem, which is my mandate. The balance sheet is funded conservatively. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.26, placing it at the 50.5th percentile in its sector [P2]. The current ratio is 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. These numbers, struck as of the last filing, show a cushion of liquid assets over short-term liabilities and a capital structure that is not reliant on heavy leverage.

The dividend yield of 5.86% [P1] is a significant cash outflow. The recent dividend history shows a declining trend: from 2.25 SAR per share in H1 2022 to 1.1 SAR in H1 2026 [P3]. The company is adjusting its cash distributions to the cycle, which is a rational response that preserves the balance sheet.

For the funding to become a problem, the operating losses would need to persist and widen to the point where they consume the cash buffer, causing the current ratio to fall sharply toward 1.0, or where additional debt is taken on to cover the dividend, pushing the debt-to-equity ratio significantly higher [P1]. The data does not contain interest rates or a free cash flow yield, so I cannot assess the exact pressure from servicing the existing debt. What the data shows is a machine with cyclical earnings stress, but one that is funded with a prudent amount of equity and is actively reducing cash distributions. The deterioration is clear, but a funding crisis is not the most likely scenario based on this balance sheet.

data.headline: The disclosed financials show a loss-making year, but the strategic moves are reshaping the company for the long term.
data.text:
The data shows a business in the middle of a deliberate, deep restructuring, not simply a cyclical deterioration. The financial figures are stark: the company is currently unprofitable, with a negative return on equity of -15.37% and a negative return on assets of -8.24% [P2]. This is not a marginal decline but a year in the red. However, the disclosures in [P6] provide the crucial context that changes the story from a business in freefall to one being actively reshaped.

The most significant disclosure, from 2026-01-07, is the planned sale of the Americas and Europe units, which the company itself expects will result in a non-cash loss of SAR 18.3 billion [P6]. This explains the negative profitability. It is a one-off accounting charge for exiting geographies, not an operational collapse. This is consistent with the earlier sale of the 20.62% stake in Alba to Maaden for SAR 3.6 billion, a transaction the company stated aligns with its strategy to 'optimize its portfolio and focus on core businesses' [P6].

When I look at the company against its sector peers in [P5], I see a giant in transition. SABIC's market capitalization of SAR 151.65 billion [P1] dwarfs all peers except Maaden. This scale matters for a patient investor. The balance sheet supports this transformation: a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26, which is at the 50.5th percentile in its sector [P2], and a current ratio of 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2], show a company with the financial capacity to weather a strategic overhaul. The 5-year price decline of -62.55% [P8] is severe, and the market is clearly punishing the uncertainty. But I see this as a company using its balance sheet strength to absorb a large, self-inflicted loss today to build a more focused and, one hopes, more profitable business for the next decade. The data is very clear that the business is being intentionally dismantled in parts to be rebuilt, not simply deteriorating.

data.headline: The quarterly record shows a clear, multi-year earnings deterioration that the market has already reflected.
data.text:
The quarterly record in [P9] lays out a clear story of deterioration, but it's a story that's been unfolding for years, not just a recent stumble. I count eight consecutive quarters of reported net losses, from Q3 2024 through Q2 2026 [P1] [P3]. That's not a blip; that's a sustained trend.

The revenue line shows the cyclical pressure. After peaking at SAR 39.84 billion in Q2 2022, the top line has steadily compressed, with the most recent quarter, Q2 2026, bringing in just SAR 26.34 billion [P1] [P3]. That's a significant drop in demand or pricing power over four years. The gross profit margin has been crushed, turning negative in the last three reported quarters. A company that can't sell its products for more than the cost to make them, before even paying the overhead, is in a tough spot.

The market has been reading the same story. The price chart in [P7] shows a 26.61% decline over the past year, and the five-year view in [P8] is a brutal 62.55% drop. The price isn't just reacting to headlines; it's been tracking the fundamental deterioration quarter by quarter. The fact that the stock is trading near its 52-week low [P1] and below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1] tells me the market's verdict on the recent quarters is firmly negative.

So, is the business deteriorating? Yes, and the quarterly data shows it with a high degree of clarity. The only thing the data here does not show me is whether these massive losses are mostly non-cash charges. That disclosure about an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss from the Americas and Europe unit sale [P6] casts a long shadow over the recent quarters. That's a crucial piece of the story I'd need to dig into to see if the core operations are bleeding this badly on a cash basis.

data.headline: The data shows financial deterioration, but the price already reflects deep distress.
data.text:
The data presents a picture of a business under significant strain, but we must separate what has happened from what the price is already assuming. On the financials, the return on equity stands at -15.37% and return on assets at -8.24% [P2]. This is a clear sign of current unprofitability, and the quality seat in our rule-based council registers a bearish vote on this basis [P4]. The five-year price summary is stark: the shares have fallen from SAR 121.0 to SAR 45.32, a decline of 62.55% [P8]. The maximum drawdown is an even deeper -86.31% [P1]. This is the market's verdict on a deteriorating earnings picture, a verdict that has been severe and prolonged.

However, my primary role is to ask what this price has to be assuming. At SAR 45.32, the shares trade at 1.24 times book value [P1]. This is not a distressed multiple on its face, but the book value itself has likely been impaired by the very losses we are seeing. The company has been taking significant actions: a disclosure from January 2026 notes an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss from selling its Americas and Europe units [P6]. This is a major restructuring, and the market is pricing in the uncertainty of that transformation.

What we do not know is crucial. The price-to-earnings ratio cannot be computed because the earnings are negative [P1]. This is a fundamental gap in our evidence. We cannot gauge the degree of over- or undervaluation on an earnings basis. The dividend yield of 5.86% [P1] offers a return while we wait, but the most recent dividend was cut to SAR 1.1 from SAR 1.5 in the prior period [P3], a signal that management is conserving cash in a difficult environment.

The pendulum of sentiment has clearly swung to fear, as evidenced by the stock trading below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages and sitting just 6.22% above its 52-week low [P1]. The deterioration is clear in the reported returns and the dividend cut. The price, however, already reflects a high degree of pessimism. The key question the data does not answer is whether this restructuring marks the beginning of a turnaround or a prelude to further value destruction. We can see the storm, but not its end.

lines.title: One-off restructuring charge or lasting decline?
lines.text: Al-Rumayyan reads the negative ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2] as largely the effect of the expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss on the Americas and Europe sale [P6]. Buffett, Lynch and Alwaleed treat the losses as a real earnings problem, and the pack has no income statement, net margin or interest coverage [P2] to show how much of the loss is non-cash or linked to that sale.
