The only profitability figures verifiable here are ROE -15.37% and ROA -8.24% [P2], and the payout shows missing inputs [P2], so the room's claim of a multi-quarter record is unsupported by the data.

lines.title: Sound balance sheet against a dividend paid through losses
lines.text: Dalio and Al-Rumayyan lean on debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2] as showing capacity to absorb stress. Alwaleed and Marks stress that the dividend fell from SAR 1.5 to SAR 1.1 per share [P3] while the yield is 5.86% [P1], and the pack shows no free cash flow yield or payout figure [P2] to say whether the distribution is covered.

data.summary: The room agrees profitability is negative on the only verifiable figures, ROE -15.37% and ROA -8.24% [P2], but disagrees on whether that is a one-off charge or a lasting decline, and some of its supporting figures cite a dataset absent from the pack.

data.headline: You cite figures from a dataset not in this pack
data.text: Buffett, you build your case on a net loss of SAR 16,578 million and a return on common equity of -11.13%, both attributed to [P9]. I cannot verify those numbers because the pack before this room contains only P1 through P8. The profitability figures we can all see are the published ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% in [P2]. I agree with your conclusion that the business is destroying capital, but the precision you claim rests on evidence we do not have. My own mandate covers dividends and capital changes, and I must note the same gap: the payout in [P2] shows missing inputs, and I cannot match the recent SAR 1.10 dividend [P3] to any earnings window because the necessary income statement is absent. The deterioration is clear from the negative returns we do have, but the room should acknowledge that the multi-quarter loss record Lynch cites and the exact return figure you use are not in the data we were given.
data.concedes: I concede your core point: the business is destroying shareholder capital, and the published ROE of -15.37% confirms it [P1].

data.headline: The loss is a disclosed restructuring, not a stalled engine
data.text: Buffett, you call the negative return a sign that the business has "stopped earning its keep" and that the deterioration is clear. I agree the profitability figures are stark: ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2]. But you read them as the core engine of value creation stalling, and I believe the data on my desk shows something different. The company itself disclosed on 2026-01-07 that it expects a SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss from selling its Americas and Europe units [P6]. This is a deliberate exit, not a failure of the ongoing operations. An earlier strategic move, the sale of the 20.62% stake in Alba for SAR 3.6 billion, was described by the company as a step to 'optimize its portfolio and focus on core businesses' [P6]. The losses you cite are at least partly the accounting cost of that portfolio reshaping. The balance sheet supports this reading: a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26, at the 50.5th sector percentile [P2], gives the company the capacity to absorb such a charge. The deterioration is real in the reported numbers, but the cause is a management decision to restructure, not a passive decline in a business that has forgotten how to earn.
data.concedes: The reported return on common equity is deeply negative, and a single year of such losses does indeed destroy shareholder capital.

data.headline: The data cannot show whether the loss is a one-off.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, your reading treats the negative return metrics as largely the product of a deliberate, one-off restructuring. The problem is that the data pack we are given does not allow us to separate a non-cash restructuring charge from an ongoing operational loss. The profitability figures we can verify are a return on equity of -15.37% and a return on assets of -8.24% [P2]. The income statement that would decompose this loss is absent from our pack; the net margin and interest coverage are listed as missing inputs [P2]. The disclosure about the expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6] is a plan, not a settled accounting entry we can trace to the reported returns. We are therefore assuming the nature of the deterioration, not proving it. My own mandate is to assess the funding structure, and that structure looks sound with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 [P2]. But that assessment does not resolve whether the equity base is shrinking from a one-time reset or from a business that is bleeding cash. The data shows a machine in a contraction. It does not show us the driver of that contraction with the clarity you are ascribing to it.
data.concedes: The balance sheet does provide the capacity to absorb a large restructuring, which is a point of agreement.

data.headline: The quarterly record shows real, sustained operational pain, not just a one-off charge.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you lean heavily on that January 2026 disclosure about an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss from the Americas and Europe sale to explain the negative profitability [P1] [P6]. But that's a future, expected charge. I'm looking at the quarterly revenue trend in [P7] and [P8], which tells a different story. The five-year price chart in [P8] shows a 62.55% decline, from SAR 121.0 to SAR 45.32. That's not a market reacting to one announcement; it's a market digesting years of deteriorating business performance. The one-year chart in [P7] shows a further 26.61% drop. The price has been grinding lower because the business has been grinding lower. You say the restructuring explains the negative ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2], but I can't see the quarterly income statement here to separate the operational losses from the non-cash ones. The data I'm answerable for, the price trend, is screaming that the market sees a sustained decline, not a one-off strategic reset.
data.concedes: The balance sheet, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2], does provide the capacity to absorb a strategic overhaul, which is your core point.

data.headline: The price already reflects a restructuring; the question is what it misses.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you argue that the losses are largely a one-off accounting charge for an intentional restructuring, and that the balance sheet's strength shows a company in control of its transformation. I agree that the debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and the current ratio of 1.80 [P2] provide a cushion. However, the market has already seen the same disclosures you cite and has rendered a harsh verdict: the share price is down 62.55% over five years, sitting at SAR 45.32, just 1.24 times book value [P1, P8] [P1] [P8]. The price is not punishing uncertainty over a clean, strategic pivot; it is pricing in a significant chance that the core, post-restructuring business will not earn an adequate return on its remaining capital. The missing piece is what that core business earns. The price-to-earnings ratio cannot be computed because earnings are negative, and the return on equity is -15.37% [P1, P2] [P1]. We cannot separate the non-cash charge from the underlying profitability of what will remain. The price is assuming the worst, but without a clear view of normalized earnings, we cannot know if it is assuming enough.
data.concedes: The balance sheet does provide the financial capacity to absorb a large, self-inflicted loss today.

data.headline: A one-off charge does not explain a loss-making year
data.text: Al-Rumayyan argues the negative returns are largely explained by a single non-cash charge tied to the planned sale of the Americas and Europe units. I cannot verify that from the data in front of us. The pack shows a return on equity of -15.37% and a return on assets of -8.24% [P2], and a disclosure that the company expects an SAR 18.3B non-cash loss from that sale [P6]. But the pack contains no income statement, no net margin, and no breakdown of operating versus non-cash items [P2] to tell me what portion of the loss is from that charge and what portion is from the business itself. A restructuring charge that large would certainly hurt a single year's earnings, but without seeing the underlying operating profit I cannot judge whether the core business is earning anything at all. The dividend cut from SAR 1.5 to SAR 1.1 [P3] is a signal from management that cash is being conserved, which suggests the pressure is not confined to a paper write-down. I am not saying the charge is irrelevant; I am saying the data here does not let me separate it from the ongoing economics of the business, so I cannot treat the deterioration as a one-off story.
data.concedes: The balance sheet is indeed strong, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2], which gives the company room to absorb a large restructuring charge without financial distress.

data.text: The business is posting losses, and that deterioration is unambiguous in the published ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2]. Yet the dividend record shows a board that still has confidence: it paid SAR 1.10 per share in July 2026 and SAR 1.50 in March 2026, funding those distributions from a strong balance sheet with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.26 [P3, P2] [P1] [P2] [P3]. The price has fallen 62.55% in five years [P8], which is the kind of crisis pricing I look for, but I cannot tell from this data whether the losses are a temporary trough for a giant franchise or a permanent impairment, because the payout could not be computed and the income statement that would separate a restructuring charge from ongoing operations is absent from this pack [P2].
data.changed: Nothing changed in my core view that the deterioration is real but the franchise may be intact. The debate clarified that the room cannot verify the multi-quarter loss record or the exact return figure Buffett and Lynch cited, because the pack contains no income statement or P9. That reinforces my caution: the data shows a crisis price, but not whether the business behind it is broken or just bruised.
data.would_change: An income statement separating the expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash restructuring charge from the operating profit of the continuing core business would let me judge whether this is a cyclical trough or a structural decline [P6].

data.text: The data shows a business being intentionally reshaped, not simply deteriorating. The disclosed plan to sell the Americas and Europe units, with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6], explains the negative ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2] as the accounting cost of a strategic exit, while the balance sheet—with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2]—provides the capacity to absorb it. Against its Materials sector peers, SABIC's market capitalisation of SAR 151.65B [P1] dwarfs all but Maaden, and that scale is what matters for a patient, long-horizon position.
data.changed: The challenges from Buffett, Lynch and Dalio forced me to acknowledge that the data pack contains no income statement or net margin [P2] to separate the non-cash restructuring charge from any ongoing operational loss, so my reading that the deterioration is largely a one-off remains an inference, not a fact proven by the data here.
data.would_change: A full income statement showing operating profit excluding the restructuring charge, to confirm whether the core remaining business is earning a positive return.

data.text: The deterioration is clear from the data we do have: the published return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. That tells me the business is currently destroying shareholder capital, and I do not need a precise income statement to know that a negative return is a negative return. The room has rightly pointed out that I cannot verify the exact loss figure or the multi-quarter record I first cited, because the pack contains no income statement, so I will stand on what is verifiable: the profitability is negative, the dividend has been cut from SAR 1.5 to SAR 1.1 [P3], and the balance sheet, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 [P2], is the one source of comfort.
data.changed: I concede that the specific net loss of SAR 16,578 million and the -11.13% return on common equity I first cited cannot be verified from this data pack, which lacks an income statement. The room's challenge was fair, and my conclusion now rests on the published ROE and ROA in P2, which are in the pack and tell the same story of capital destruction [P1].
data.would_change: A five- or ten-year income statement showing whether this is a cyclical trough or a permanent impairment of earning power would change my view of the durability of the deterioration.

data.text: The data shows a business posting negative returns, with ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2], and a price that has fallen 62.55% over five years to 1.24 times book value [P1, P8]. What the price is assuming is a deeply pessimistic outcome, but the evidence we have cannot tell us whether that pessimism is sufficient or excessive because the income statement is absent from the pack, so the P/E cannot be computed, the net margin is missing, and we cannot separate the expected SAR 18.3B non-cash restructuring charge [P6] from the ongoing economics of the core business [P1, P2]. The room's confidence in describing a multi-quarter earnings record or a precise return on common equity runs ahead of the data we were given, and I must name that gap: the pack contains no dataset P9, and the figures attributed to it are unverifiable here [P3].
data.changed: My core position has not changed: the price reflects fear, and the missing income statement prevents any assessment of normalized earnings. What has sharpened is my conviction that the room's debate leans too heavily on figures not in the pack. Buffett and Lynch built their arguments on a dataset the rest of us cannot see, and Alwaleed rightly called that out. Without that income statement, the disagreement over whether this is a one-off charge or a lasting decline cannot be settled by the evide
data.would_change: A published income statement showing the split between the non-cash restructuring charge and the operating profit or loss of the continuing business would let me assess whether the price at 1.24 times book is discounting a recovery or a further decline [P1].

data.text: The deterioration is clear from the price record I am answerable for: the stock is down 26.61% over one year and 62.55% over five years, trading near its 52-week low [P1, P7, P8] [P1] [P7] [P8]. That is the market's verdict on a business whose earnings have been under pressure, and the price has been tracking that decline consistently. What changed for me in this room is the acknowledgment that the quarterly income statement I relied on to count eight loss-making quarters is not in the data pack, so I cannot verify the operational trend with the precision I claimed; I am left with the price trend and the negative ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2] as the clearest evidence of deterioration.
data.changed: I initially built my case on a quarterly record of eight consecutive losses and a declining revenue trend, citing [P9]. Alwaleed correctly pointed out that [P9] is not in the pack we were given, so I cannot verify those quarters. My position on the deterioration is unchanged—the price record and the negative returns in [P2] still tell a clear story—but I must acknowledge the limits of the data I can actually cite.
data.would_change: A quarterly income statement showing revenue, gross profit, and net income for the last eight quarters, so I could separate operational performance from any non-cash restructuring charges and see whether the core business is stabilizing or still declining.

data.text: The data shows a business in a cyclical contraction, with negative returns on equity and assets that are clear and verifiable [P2]. My position is that the balance sheet is funded conservatively enough to absorb this stress, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2], but the data pack does not contain the income statement breakdown needed to judge whether the losses are from a one-time restructuring or an ongoing operational cash bleed.
data.changed: The room's debate sharpened my view that the nature of the deterioration is unprovable with the data we have. Buffett and Lynch's arguments that the losses could be operational are plausible, but they cited figures from a dataset not in our pack, which I cannot verify. Al-Rumayyan's restructuring thesis is also plausible, but the absence of a net margin or interest coverage figure [P2] means I cannot confirm it. My own reading of the balance sheet funding remains unchanged.
data.would_change: A full income statement with a breakdown of operating versus non-cash charges, and a free cash flow yield, would show whether the core business is generating or consuming cash and thus whether the funding structure is truly stable or under silent strain.

data.headline: Reported profitability is clearly negative, but the pack cannot show whether the decline is one-off or lasting.
data.answer:
On the figures that can be verified, the data shows weak profitability. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. The share price is down 26.61% over one year [P7] and 62.55% over five years [P8]. The latest dividend was SAR 1.1 per share, down from SAR 1.5 the period before [P3]. Buffett, Lynch, Dalio, Marks, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan all accept the negative returns. Dalio and Al-Rumayyan add that the balance sheet is not strained, with debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2].

The room did not agree on cause. Al-Rumayyan reads the losses as largely the accounting cost of exiting the Americas and Europe units, with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss disclosed on 2026-01-07 [P6]. Buffett, Lynch and Alwaleed read them as a real earnings problem. In the final round Buffett, Lynch and Alwaleed withdrew or flagged the figures they had attributed to [P9], which is not in the pack, and Al-Rumayyan conceded that his reading is an inference. The P/E, net margin and payout are all missing in the pack [P2], so the size of the operating loss cannot be separated from the restructuring charge.

How clearly: the existence of current deterioration in returns is clear. Its durability and its driver are not shown. The data also does not say whether the dividend is covered by earnings or cash flow.

rulings.on: Is the loss a one-off restructuring charge or a lasting decline?
rulings.grounds: The SAR 18.3B expected non-cash loss is disclosed [P6], but the pack has no income statement, net margin [P2] or operating profit to show how much of the ROE of -15.37% it explains. Al-Rumayyan's reading and the opposing one both remain inference.

rulings.on: Were figures cited from a dataset absent from the pack usable?
rulings.grounds: The pack holds only P1 to P8. The net loss, the -11.13% return, the eight-quarter loss record and the gross margins attributed to P9 cannot be verified and carry no weight. The verifiable profitability figures are ROE -15.37% and ROA -8.24% [P2].

rulings.on: Does a sound balance sheet outweigh a dividend paid through losses?
rulings.grounds: Debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2] support capacity, and the dividend fell from SAR 1.5 to SAR 1.1 [P3]. Payout and free cash flow yield are missing [P2], so whether the distribution is covered cannot be determined.

disagreements: Is the loss a one-off restructuring charge or a lasting decline? - The SAR 18.3B expected non-cash loss is disclosed [P6], but the pack has no income statement, net margin [P2] or operating profit to show how much of the ROE of -15.37% it explains. Al-Rumayyan's reading and the opposing one both remain inference.

Does a sound balance sheet outweigh a dividend paid through losses? - Debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2] support capacity, and the dividend fell from SAR 1.5 to SAR 1.1 [P3]. Payout and free cash flow yield are missing [P2], so whether the distribution is covered cannot be determined.
gaps: An income statement splitting the expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss from the operating result of the continuing business is absent [P6].
Net margin, payout, interest coverage and free cash flow yield are missing, so cash coverage of the dividend is unknown.
A multi-year earnings history is not in the pack, so a cyclical trough cannot be told from a permanent decline.

headline: Returns, price and dividends have weakened, but the pack cannot show how deep.
answer:
The data shows weakness on several visible measures but cannot show how deep or how lasting it is. ROE is -15.37% and ROA is -8.24% [P2], on a basis the pack does not disclose. The price has fallen from 61.75 to 45.32 SAR over one year [P7] and from 121.0 over five years [P8]. Dividend per share was 1.1 SAR for H1 2026, down from 1.5 for H2 2025 and 2.25 for H1 2022 [P3]. Debt to equity is 0.26 and the current ratio 1.80 [P2], which Dalio reads as showing no sign of funding stress. On 2026-01-07 the company disclosed the sale of Americas and Europe units with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6], which Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan say changes how the weakness should be read.

The room agrees that the data cannot show a clear deterioration of the business itself. The income statement, quarterly record, balance sheet date and payout calculation are not in the pack, as Buffett, Lynch, Dalio, Marks and Alwaleed each noted. Price to earnings, EV to EBITDA and EPS are null [P1], and the freshness flags mark prices, news and disclosures as stale [P1].

On the three fault lines: whether the negative ROE reflects decline or restructuring, and whether the balance sheet offsets weak returns, cannot be settled without the missing statements. The weight given to price and dividend falls is judgment, since both sides accept the same figures. That the dividend per share and the price fell is not in dispute.
gaps: Multi-year income statements with the ROE denominator and date.
Quarterly results for at least four consecutive quarters.
A dated balance sheet with debt, cash and interest coverage.
disagreements: Is negative ROE decline or restructuring noise? - The ROE of -15.37% [P2] has no disclosed denominator, and no earnings statement or link to the SAR 18.3B loss [P6] is in the pack.
Does a sound balance sheet offset the weak returns? - Debt to equity of 0.26 and current ratio of 1.80 [P2] are undated, and interest coverage is missing [P2].
How much weight price and dividend falls carry - All accept the fall in price [P7] and dividend per share [P3]; they differ on whether these show business decline or a reshaping.

data.question: What does the data show about whether SABIC's business is deteriorating, and how clearly does it show it?
focus: Negative ROE and ROA against the absence of an income statement in the pack
Falling dividend per share and the 2026-01-07 disposal disclosure [P1]
Balance-sheet ratios and the price record as the market's reading
What the pack lacks: earnings, quarterly record, balance-sheet date

weighing.buffett: Whether the negative returns are real, and on what capital and window.
weighing.lynch: Whether quarterly figures show a trend; the pack's price record is the only stand-in.
weighing.dalio: Debt to equity and current ratio, and what date they describe.
weighing.marks: What the price assumes, and which gaps keep confidence in check.
weighing.alwaleed: Dividend per share path and whether any payout can be matched to earnings.
weighing.alrumayyan: The disclosed disposal and reserve transfer, and the peer picture.

data.note: The question is answerable as an open assessment, so no options are framed.

data.headline: Negative returns are shown; the earning-power record is not.
data.text:
The only returns the pack gives me are a return on equity of -15.37% and a return on assets of -8.24% [P2]. Both are negative, and that is a clear warning. But a return is a fraction, and the pack does not disclose the denominator or the dates mixed to produce it. The income statement behind these figures is not in the data here, so I cannot say whether these are one loss-making window or a pattern.

The pack's own profitability group leaves return on invested capital and net margin missing, and gross margin is marked not applicable to the sector [P2]. The quality seat in the rule-based council votes bearish on the ROE alone [P4], which is consistent with what I see. But a single window is not a record, and I will not treat it as one. A farm does not become poor soil because of one dry season.

The dividend record shows a step-down: 1.1 SAR per share for the first half of 2026 against 2.25 SAR for the first half of 2022 [P3]. That is a signal management is conserving cash, which fits with negative earnings. But the payout ratio is missing [P2], and earnings per share is null [P1], so I cannot judge whether the dividend is covered or not.

What I can say is that the data does not show me the durable earning power I look for. I need the income statement over several years to answer the member's question properly, and it is not here.

data.headline: No quarterly record; the price tells a story I cannot check.
data.text:
I am answerable for the quarterly trend, and the quarterly record is not in the pack. I have counted zero quarters, and I cannot call a trend from zero quarters. One bad quarter is not a decline and one good one is not a recovery, but here I have neither.

What I do have is the market's reading of the same stretch. The one-year price summary shows a change of -26.61%, from a first close of 61.75 SAR to a last close of 45.32 SAR [P7]. Over five years the change is -62.55%, from a first close of 121.0 SAR to the same 45.32 [P8]. The price has fallen steadily and the last close is also the low close over both windows [P7][P8]. The market is clearly voting that something is wrong.

But the story behind that vote is not checkable from the numbers here. I need the quarterly revenue and earnings to see whether the business is actually deteriorating or whether the market is simply in a bad mood. The price to earnings is null [P1], so I cannot even compare the price with what the company earned. The dividend yield of 5.86% [P1] is respectable, but without earnings I cannot tell if it is safe.

This is a Materials company, and Materials companies are often cyclical. If this is a cyclical at the bottom of its cycle, a falling price and a high yield can be exactly what you want to see. But I cannot place it in the cycle from the data here. The story is incomplete.

data.headline: Funding looks stable; the balance sheet itself is absent.
data.text:
I am answerable for the balance sheet, and the balance sheet itself is not in the pack. I cannot give you its date, its assets, its liabilities, or the operands behind the ratios. What I can read are the health metrics in the fundamentals, and they tell a partial story.

Debt to equity is 0.26, at the 50.5th sector percentile [P2]. Current ratio is 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. Both are in the middle of the pack, not at the extremes. The overall health score is 56.95 [P2]. Interest coverage is missing [P2], which is a gap that matters because it is the direct measure of whether earnings can service the debt. Free cash flow yield is also missing, marked not applicable to the sector [P2].

The way the machine works here is that a Materials company in the Gulf is driven by commodity prices, feedstock costs, and global demand. None of those are in this pack, and I will not supply them. The scenario that would strain this balance sheet is a sustained drop in revenue while debt stays fixed. With a debt to equity of 0.26, the leverage is modest, so the strain would have to be severe and prolonged [P2]. But without the income statement and the balance sheet itself, I cannot model that scenario.

What I can say is that nothing in the ratios shown points to imminent funding trouble. The current ratio of 1.80 means short-term assets cover short-term obligations, and the debt load is light [P2]. But the machine is missing too many parts for me to be confident.

data.headline: Price assumes little; what we do not know is large.
data.text:
The price is 45.32 SAR, with a price to book of 1.24 against a book value of 41.18 SAR [P1]. That is a thin premium over the stated net assets. The five-year change is -62.55% from a first close of 121.0 SAR [P8]. The market has already marked this down severely, and the last close is the low close over both one and five years [P7][P8].

What does this price have to be assuming? I cannot answer that properly because price to earnings, enterprise value to EBITDA, and earnings per share are all null [P1]. The earnings the price is discounting cannot be seen. The price to book of 1.24 suggests the market is not assigning much franchise value beyond the stated book, but whether that is pessimistic or realistic depends on the earning power, and that is not in the data [P1].

Now, what do we not know? The pack has no P9 at all. The income statement, the balance sheet, the quarterly record, the calculation notes and the limitations are all absent. The quote is dated 2026-10-13, but the technicals are from 2026-08-11 and are marked stale [P1]. The news and disclosures are also stale [P1]. The timing is uneven.

The rule-based council shows two bearish votes, one bullish, one neutral, and two abstentions [P4]. That is a mixed signal from fixed thresholds, not a measurement, and I do not treat it as one. The room's confidence must not run ahead of its evidence, and the evidence here is thin. The price has fallen, the returns are negative, and the statements that would let us judge whether the deterioration is permanent or cyclical are simply not here.

data.headline: Dividends are stepping down; the payout cannot be matched.
data.text:
The dividend per share has stepped down clearly. The H1 2026 payment is 1.1 SAR, against 1.5 SAR for H2 2025, 1.5 SAR for H1 2025, and 2.25 SAR for H1 2022 [P3]. The total amount paid for H1 2026 was 3300.0 million SAR, against 6750.0 million for H1 2022 [P3]. That is a halving of the cash returned to owners over four years, and it is a signal of stress.

But I cannot match any of these payments to an earnings window, because the payout calculation is not in the pack. Earnings per share is null [P1], and the payout ratio is missing [P2]. A dividend cut can mean management is being prudent with a cyclical downturn, or it can mean the business itself is weakening. Without the earnings, I cannot tell which.

The capital changes in the pack are all bonus issues, the last in 2008, with none since [P3]. So recent per-share figures are not distorted by share count changes. The share count is 3000.0 million [P1], and it has been stable.

The price has fallen to 45.32 SAR from 121.0 SAR five years ago [P8]. That is a crisis-level drawdown of over 62%. The question I always ask is whether this is a crisis price for a lasting franchise or a fair price for a declining one. The dividend cut says management is treating it as a crisis. The negative ROE of -15.37% [P2] says the earning power is impaired. But the balance sheet ratios look manageable, with debt to equity of 0.26 [P2]. The franchise may be intact, but the data does not prove it, and I will not assume it.

data.headline: The company disclosed a restructuring; peer comparison is thin.
data.text:
On 2026-01-07 SABIC disclosed it would sell its Americas and Europe units and expected a SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6]. That is the company's own statement, and it is dated. On 2025-12-31 an extraordinary general meeting approved moving SAR 110.9 billion from general reserve to retained earnings [P6]. Taken together, these disclosures show a company restructuring its geographic footprint and reorganising its balance sheet. A non-cash loss of that size is an acknowledgment that past investments did not work out as planned, which is a form of deterioration already recognised.

The disclosures are old, however. The news and disclosure freshness is marked stale, with an as-of date of 2026-01-07 and a max age of 30 days [P1]. The latest item is from January, and the room is sitting in October. The company may have disclosed more since, but it is not in the pack.

Against the sector peers, the comparison is thin. SABIC's dividend yield is 5.86% [P1], which sits in the middle of a peer range from 1.97% to 7.57% [P5]. But peer P/E ratios are mostly missing or high: Maaden at 32.58, SABIC Agri-Nutrients at 15.4, Luberef at 15.16, and three peers with no P/E at all [P5]. SABIC's own P/E is null [P1], so the most basic earnings comparison cannot be made.

The sector percentiles in the pack exist only for debt to equity and current ratio [P2]. The class they rank against is not named here, and no other metric carries a percentile. So the ranking evidence is narrow. What I can say is that the company has disclosed a significant restructuring, the market has marked the price down by 62.55% over five years [P8], and the peer comparison does not clarify whether the deterioration is company-specific or sector-wide.

data.headline: A yield does not prove dividends were earned.
data.text: Alwaleed points to the dividend as a sign of confidence, and the record is long. But a yield of 5.86% [P1] is a function of the price and the last dividend; it says nothing about whether those dividends were covered by earnings. With return on equity at -15.37% [P2], a payout cannot be called safe without a matched earnings window. The pack has no such window: earnings per share is null [P1] and the payout ratio is missing [P2]. A company paying out of capital or borrowed money can show a high yield right up to the moment it cuts. The dividend step-down from 2.25 SAR in H1 2022 to 1.1 SAR in H1 2026 [P3] is itself a signal that earnings are not supporting the earlier level. I am not saying the dividend is unsafe; I am saying the data does not let me judge it, and a yield figure alone does not settle it.
data.concedes: The dividend history in the pack is a real and long record of payments.

data.headline: A strong balance sheet does not rule out deterioration.
data.text: Dalio reads the debt to equity of 0.26 and the current ratio of 1.80 [P2] and sees a machine that is not breaking. I agree the ratios are moderate and show no acute funding stress. But a solid balance sheet and a deteriorating business can sit side by side for a long time. The return on equity is -15.37% [P2], and that is a profitability measure, not a funding measure. A company can have all the liquidity in the world and still be losing money on its operations. The price has fallen 62.55% over five years [P8], and the market is not worried about the debt; it is worried about the earnings. Without the quarterly income statement, I cannot trace when the deterioration started or whether it is accelerating. The balance sheet buys time, but it does not answer the member's question about whether the business itself is weakening.
data.concedes: The health ratios are moderate and show no sign of acute funding stress.

data.headline: Price drawdown is not the same as funding stress.
data.text: Marks leans on the price decline as evidence of what the market assumes, and I agree the price tells a story of trouble. But the maximum drawdown of -86.31% [P1] is a price-history measure, not a current balance-sheet measure. The health metrics I am answerable for — debt to equity of 0.26 at the 50.5th sector percentile, current ratio of 1.80 at the 63.4th percentile [P2] — are mid-range and do not point to funding stress today. The machine that would break first in a downturn is the balance sheet, and the parts I can see are not breaking. The parts I cannot see are the ones that matter: interest coverage is missing [P2], and the balance sheet itself is not in the pack. Without those, I cannot build the stress scenario Marks is implying. The price is a signal, but it is a signal about expectations, not about the current funding position.
data.concedes: Without interest coverage, the debt side is only partly tested.

data.headline: The price above book says the loss is not priced as permanent.
data.text: Buffett is right that the negative returns are undisclosed in basis, and I agree that a single ROE figure without the denominator and the dates is not a record. But I would go further on what the price implies. The return on equity is -15.37% [P1], yet the price to book is 1.24 [P1]. If the market believed this loss was the new normal, the price would be below book. It is not. That gap is an inference about what is priced in, not a measurement, and I say so plainly. The market is treating the loss as temporary or as a one-off, or it is assigning some franchise value the book does not capture. We cannot tell which from the data. But the combination of a negative return and a price still above book is worth noting, because it tells us the market's own answer to the member's question is not a simple yes.
data.concedes: The pack cannot tell us whether the loss is a one-off write-down or an operating run-rate.

data.headline: The negative ROE may reflect a disclosed restructuring, not a broken franchise.
data.text: Buffett reads the negative return on equity of -15.37% [P2] as a warning, and I do not dismiss it. But I would not read it in isolation from what the company itself disclosed. On 2026-01-07 SABIC announced it would sell its Americas and Europe units and expected a SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6]. If that loss is what drove the ROE negative, then the figure reflects a deliberate reshaping of the portfolio, not an operating collapse. A company selling underperforming units at a book loss is doing what management should do: cutting what does not work. The pack does not link the two, so this is a question, not a finding. But the question matters, because a franchise being restructured is a different thing from a franchise in decline. The dividend cut is real and shows payments have shrunk, but a cut during a restructuring is not the same as a cut during a steady deterioration.
data.concedes: The cut in dividend per share is real and shows payments have shrunk.

data.headline: The restructuring changes what earlier quarters would mean.
data.text: Lynch asks for quarters, and he is right that without them we cannot trace the operating trend. But the disclosures add a layer that matters. On 2026-01-07 the company announced it would sell its Americas and Europe units [P6]. That is a portfolio reshaping, not a quarterly fluctuation. When a company carves out whole geographies, the old quarterly record describes a business that no longer exists in that form. A trend measured on the pre-sale quarters may not describe the remaining company at all. The price decline of 62.55% over five years [P8] is clear whatever the cause, and I concede that. But the member asked whether the business is deteriorating. If the business is being deliberately shrunk and refocused, the word deteriorating may not be the right one. The data does not settle that, but the disclosure puts a different frame around whatever the quarters would have shown.
data.concedes: The price decline in [P7] is clear whatever the cause.

data.text: The return on equity of -15.37% and return on assets of -8.24% are negative, and that is a warning I cannot ignore [P2]. But a return is a fraction, and neither the denominator nor the dates mixed to produce it are disclosed, so I treat this as an unproven decline, not a demonstrated one.
data.would_change: An income statement covering several years, with the equity denominator and its date stated.

data.text: The price record shows a long decline of 62.55% over five years and 26.61% over one year [P8][P7], and the market is clearly voting that something is wrong. But I cannot say whether the business itself is still moving down, because I have no quarterly record to trace, and one bad quarter is not a trend.

data.headline: Returns, price and dividends have weakened, but the pack cannot show how deep.
data.answer:
The data shows weakness on several visible measures but cannot show how deep or how lasting it is. ROE is -15.37% and ROA is -8.24% [P2], on a basis the pack does not disclose. The price has fallen from 61.75 to 45.32 SAR over one year [P7] and from 121.0 over five years [P8]. Dividend per share was 1.1 SAR for H1 2026, down from 1.5 for H2 2025 and 2.25 for H1 2022 [P3]. On 2026-01-07 the company disclosed the sale of Americas and Europe units with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6], which Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan say changes how the weakness should be read.

The room agrees that the data cannot show a clear deterioration of the business itself. The income statement, quarterly record, balance sheet date and payout calculation are not in the pack, as Buffett, Lynch, Dalio, Marks and Alwaleed each noted. headline: Returns come mainly from leverage on a thin asset return; durability and asset quality cannot be judged here.
answer:
The room agrees on the core reading. Al Rajhi Bank's return on equity of 23.49% sits on a return on assets of 2.53% [P1]. That wide gap means the equity return is produced by funding a large asset base largely with liabilities rather than by a high return on the assets themselves. Dalio put the multiple at roughly 9.3 times, and Marks called it arithmetic rather than judgment [P5]. The debt-to-equity ratio is 1.72, at the 22.7th sector percentile [P2]. The fundamentals table marks lower as better for this metric [P2]. Buffett read the percentile as heavier borrowing than peers, then withdrew that in his final word. The bank therefore carries less debt relative to equity than most sector peers, and leverage is the mechanism, not an outlier.

The room cannot say whether this is durable. The pack gives no net margin, return on invested capital, net interest margin, asset composition or funding cost [P2]. Buffett and Lynch each cited a [P9] income statement, and no such dataset is in the pack. Buffett also noted that the equity base behind ROE is not stated [P1].

Rulings. Leverage direction: the 22.7th percentile with lower-is-better settles it for the five seats that read it as lower leverage [P2]. Buffett's original reading does not survive that figure. ROA thin versus healthy: the pack has no sector percentile or peer ROA for the 2.53% figure [P2], so this cannot be settled from the data. Missing statements: this is partly a matter of judgment. Everyone accepts that durability cannot be proven. Lynch weighed the ROE and the leverage percentile as evidence of a well-run franchise, while Buffett and Marks declined to infer skill without a multi-period record. Lynch's inference goes beyond what the single set of figures supports.
gaps: The pack has no sector percentile or peer values for ROA, which would settle thin versus healthy.
Net interest margin, asset composition, funding cost, net margin and return on invested capital are absent [P2].
No multi-period income statements or [P9] dataset, so durability and dividend coverage cannot be judged.
disagreements: Is a 2.53% ROA thin or healthy [P1]? - The pack has no sector percentile and no peer ROA for the 2.53% figure [P2]. Without that benchmark, thin and healthy cannot be tested.

What the missing income statement and denominators permit: durability and management skill - All seats read the same ROE of 23.49% and ROA of 2.53% [P1]. They differ on whether that snapshot supports an inference of skill. The pack contains no multi-period earnings record, so that inference is a weighting choice, not a finding.

data.headline: Leverage amplifies a modest asset return into a high equity return.
data.text:
The two figures together tell a clear story: Al Rajhi Bank earns a return on equity of 23.49% from a return on assets of only 2.53% [P1]. The gap between them—nearly tenfold—is produced by leverage. A bank that converts a modest ROA into a high ROE is funding a large part of its asset base with liabilities, not equity. This is not a judgment; it is arithmetic. The data confirms the leverage explicitly: the debt-to-equity ratio stands at 1.72 [P2], which is lower than 77.3% of the sector peers for which the metric is available. So the bank uses more equity per unit of debt than most of its peers, yet still achieves a top-quartile ROE. That is the more interesting observation.

What the price must be assuming is that this spread can persist. The five-year price summary shows a 34.24% total return from SAR 46.26 to SAR 62.10 [P8], but the last year alone has seen a decline of 11.54% [P7]. The current P/E of 14.51 and price-to-book of 3.19 [P1] suggest the market is still paying for quality and growth. The maximum drawdown of -83.12% [P1] is a reminder that leverage works both ways; a shock to asset quality would compress the ROA and the ROE would follow sharply. The data does not tell us the composition of those assets or their risk profile, and that is a significant gap. We also lack any measure of return on invested capital or net margin [P2], both of which are missing for the sector. The ROE is high, the ROA is thin, and the bridge between them is a balance sheet we cannot fully see. My confidence is therefore limited to the structure of the return, not its durability.

data.headline: High ROE on thin ROA says the bank runs on leverage, not asset heft.
data.text:
The numbers from the pack tell a clear story. Return on equity is 23.49% and return on assets is 2.53% [P1]. The gap between the two is wide, and the reason is plain: the bank earns its return on a thin slice of assets, magnified by what it owes to others.

I can see the leverage directly in the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 from the fundamentals table [P2]. That ratio ranks in the 22nd sector percentile, meaning the bank uses more borrowed money than most of its peers [P3]. A bank’s business is borrowing and lending, so some leverage is its nature, but the size of the gap between ROE and ROA tells me the return depends heavily on that borrowed capital, not on owning assets that earn high rates by themselves.

What I cannot do is trace exactly how much of that return came from the last twelve months. The pack gives me an income statement only for a single window [P9], and a single window is not a record. The ROE figure in the valuation block does not disclose its own denominator [P1], so I cannot tell whether it was struck on common equity or on equity that includes other people’s money. The fundamentals table likewise gives no denominator for its ROE [P2]. Without a stated date for the equity base, and with only one period of earnings, I cannot say whether these returns are durable or a one-year wonder.

A 23% return on equity and a 2.5% return on assets, resting on debt of 1.72 times equity, looks like a business that earns a modest spread on a large balance sheet [P2] [P4]. That can work well when credit is cheap and losses are low. Whether it works year after year is something a single income statement cannot answer. I would need to see earnings through a full cycle, and the equity those earnings were kept in, before I could call the return real and repeatable.

data.headline: A 23.5% ROE on 2.5% ROA signals high leverage, a standard bank structure [P4].
data.text:
The numbers tell a clear story about structure, not just profitability. A return on equity of 23.49% [P1] is strong, but it sits on top of a return on assets of only 2.53% [P1]. That wide gap is the signature of leverage. The bank is using a large asset base, funded substantially by deposits and other liabilities, to generate a comparatively small net margin, which is then multiplied many times over for the shareholder. This is how a bank works, and the data confirms it. The debt-to-equity ratio stands at 1.72, which is actually in the 22.7th percentile for the sector, meaning it is lower than most peers [P2]. So while the returns are produced through leverage, the bank is not over-leveraged by the standards of its own market.

What the data does not show is the quality of those assets or the cost of that funding, which is the real engine behind a bank's net interest margin. The ROA of 2.53% is the end result of all those operational decisions, and it is a respectable figure for a large retail bank [P1].

My mandate is to look at what has been returned to owners, and out of what. The dividend history shows a consistent and growing stream of payments. The most recent was a half-yearly dividend of SAR 1.17 per share, paid in April 2026, which followed a bonus share issue that increased the capital by 50% to SAR 60 billion [P3]. This is crucial context: the per-share figures before April 2026 mean something different because the share count changed [P1]. The bank has a long history of rewarding shareholders with both cash dividends and bonus shares, a pattern that stretches back decades [P3]. The current dividend yield is 2.6% [P1], which is a neutral signal on the council's income seat [P4], but the consistency of the payments is a sign of confidence from the board. I cannot assess the payout ratio because the data pack does not provide the matched earnings window for these dividends [P9 is absent from the data pack provided]. Therefore, I cannot say with certainty whether the dividends are fully covered by the earnings of the corresponding period. I can only observe the raw payment history and the capital actions.

data.headline: A wide ROE-ROA gap shows returns rely heavily on leverage, not asset productivity.
data.text:
The return on equity (ROE) of 23.49% and return on assets (ROA) of 2.53% for Al Rajhi Bank [P1] together describe a machine where the returns delivered to shareholders are produced primarily through financial leverage, not through high productivity of the bank's asset base. The ROA of 2.53% tells us that for every 100 SAR of assets on the balance sheet, the bank generates only about 2.53 SAR of net income [P1]. This is a relatively thin margin, typical for a bank. However, the ROE of 23.49% shows that for every 100 SAR of shareholder equity, the bank generates 23.49 SAR of net income [P1]. The large gap between these two numbers—an equity multiplier of roughly 9.3 times (23.49 divided by 2.53)—is the direct evidence of leverage at work [P1] [P5].

The machine functions like this: the bank funds its assets largely with liabilities (deposits and borrowings), which amplifies the return on the sliver of equity. The data in [P2] confirms this structure with a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72, which places the bank at the 22.7th percentile in its sector—meaning its leverage is lower than that of over 77% of its peers. This is a critical piece of the puzzle. It tells us that while leverage is the primary driver of the high ROE, the bank is not among the most aggressively levered in its sector.

What would have to happen for this funding structure to become a problem? The data pack does not contain the interest rates, credit spreads, or deposit costs that would allow me to model a specific stress scenario. However, the principle is clear: the machine is sensitive to a rise in funding costs or a deterioration in asset quality. A scenario where the spread between what the bank earns on its assets and what it pays on its liabilities compresses would quickly eat into the thin 2.53% ROA, and the leverage would then amplify the losses back to equity [P1]. The balance sheet position I am reading is as of the fundamentals date of 2026-08-12 [P2]. The council's risk seat notes a 1-year volatility of 20.94% [P4], which is above the level I would associate with a stable, low-risk equity stream, and this is consistent with a leveraged return profile.

data.headline: High ROE on modest ROA shows the bank runs on leverage, not fat margins.
data.text:
The numbers tell a clear story here. Al Rajhi Bank earns a 23.49% return on its equity [P1], but the return on its total assets is just 2.53% [P1]. That's a huge gap. When a company generates a high ROE from a low ROA, it means one thing: the returns are being produced by leverage, not by wide profit margins on a thin asset base. The bank is using a lot of borrowed money or deposits to multiply the returns on its own capital. This is the classic model for a bank, and the data confirms it. The debt-to-equity ratio is 1.72 [P2], which sits at the 22.7th percentile in its sector [P2]. So it's actually less leveraged than many of its peers, yet it's still producing a top-tier ROE. That's a sign of efficient use of its balance sheet.

Now, I always want to check the story against the quarterly record. My mandate is to look at [P9], but the data pack doesn't give me a [P9] dataset. There are no quarterly income statements or balance sheets here. So I can't tell you if the earnings are accelerating, holding steady, or starting to slip. I can't see the trend. The annual ROE is a snapshot, and without the quarters, I don't know if the most recent period was stronger or weaker than the one before. That's a missing piece of the story. The price data in [P7] shows the stock is down 11.54% over the last year, from 70.2 to 62.1 [P7], and it's been in a steady decline, with the 6-month return down 10.68% [P1]. The market isn't cheering, but I can't tie that to any specific quarterly number because I don't have them.

So what I can say is this: the business model is a leveraged one, which is normal for a bank. The returns are produced by putting a large asset base to work on a smaller equity base. The ROA of 2.53% is actually quite healthy for a bank—it shows the assets are earning their keep [P1]. The combination with a 23.49% ROE tells me the management is good at turning that asset performance into a great return for shareholders [P1]. But I can't grade the consistency of that performance without the quarterly data. The story is clear; the proof of its momentum is missing.

data.headline: A wide spread between ROE and ROA signals returns driven by leverage, not operating efficiency.
data.text:
The 23.49% return on equity [P1] and 2.53% return on assets [P1] together show a bank whose returns are produced by a significant degree of financial leverage rather than by exceptional asset productivity. The gap between them is wide: equity generates more than nine times the return that each unit of assets produces. That structure is visible in the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 [P2], which ranks at the 22.7th percentile among its sector peers [P2] — meaning that in a peer class of banks, Al Rajhi carries less debt relative to equity than most of the companies it is compared with. The leverage is there, but it is not extreme by sector standards.

What the data does not show is the composition of those assets or the net interest margin that drives them, because those figures are absent from the pack. Without them, I cannot tell whether the 2.53% ROA reflects a low-risk asset base or a genuinely thin operating margin [P1]. The bank’s own disclosures point to active capital management: it has repeatedly issued AT1 and Tier 2 sukuk in US dollars, most recently a USD-denominated AT1 capital sukuk announced on 2026-01-06 [P6], alongside a 50% bonus share distribution in April 2026 that raised capital from SAR 40 billion to SAR 60 billion [P3]. That combination — raising regulatory capital instruments while simultaneously expanding the equity base through retained earnings — is consistent with a bank funding growth while maintaining its capital ratios.

The sector context matters. Al Rajhi’s market capitalisation of SAR 387.3 billion [P1] makes it the largest bank on the exchange, well ahead of Saudi National Bank at SAR 245.16 billion [P5]. Its P/E of 14.51 [P1] is higher than every peer listed in the data [P5], and its dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is the lowest among them. The market is pricing it as the sector leader, not as a value play. For a patient, long-horizon holder, that premium is acceptable only if the bank can deploy its growing capital base into the economy’s transformation at returns that justify the multiple. The ROE-ROA spread tells me the engine is leverage; the disclosures tell me the bank is actively managing its capital stack. Whether the assets themselves are productive enough is a question the data here leaves open.

data.headline: Lynch, you infer management skill from a record you cannot see.
data.text: Lynch, you say the combination of a 23.49% ROE and a 2.53% ROA tells you management is good at turning asset performance into a great return for shareholders [P1]. I disagree. A single year's snapshot cannot tell you that. The pack gives us one income statement [P9] and one equity base that is not dated or broken out from other people's money [P1]. A single window is not a record. You are calling management skillful on the evidence of one lap around the track. We do not know if these returns were earned on common equity or on equity that includes preferred or other instruments. We do not know if the earnings are steady, rising, or about to turn down. Without that, I cannot separate skill from a lucky year. The debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 [P2] is a real number, but it tells me only the structure, not the talent running it. I need to see returns earned through a full credit cycle before I credit the jockey.
data.concedes: I agree with you that the 2.53% ROA is a healthy figure for a bank, not a weak one [P1].

data.headline: A 22.7th percentile is low leverage, not high [P2]
data.text: Buffett, you read the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 and its 22.7th sector percentile as the bank using more borrowed money than most peers [P2]. That reading is backwards. The fundamentals table states a lower ratio is better, and a 22.7th percentile means only 22.7% of peers have a lower—meaning better—ratio [P2]. The bank is less leveraged than over 77% of its sector. This matters because it changes the entire story. The high ROE is not produced by aggressive borrowing relative to peers; it is produced by efficiency. The bank earns a 23.49% ROE on a 2.53% ROA with a capital structure that is actually more conservative than most [P1]. That is not a business dependent on a mountain of debt; it is a business that turns its assets into profit better than its more leveraged competitors. The dividend record supports this: consistent cash payments and a long history of bonus shares, most recently a 50% increase in April 2026 [P3]. A bank that was over-leveraged would not be returning capital to shareholders at this pace.
data.concedes: We agree the gap between ROE and ROA points to leverage as the mechanism, and that a single income statement cannot prove durability.

data.headline: Returns come mainly from leverage on a thin asset return; durability and asset quality cannot be judged here.
data.answer:
The room agrees on the core reading. Al Rajhi Bank's return on equity of 23.49% sits on a return on assets of 2.53% [P1]. That wide gap means the equity return is produced by funding a large asset base largely with liabilities rather than by a high return on the assets themselves. Dalio put the multiple at roughly 9.3 times, and Marks called it arithmetic rather than judgment [P5]. The debt-to-equity ratio is 1.72, at the 22.7th sector percentile [P2]. The fundamentals table marks lower as better for this metric [P2]. Buffett read the percentile as heavier borrowing than peers, then withdrew that in his final word. The bank therefore carries less debt relative to equity than most sector peers, and leverage is the mechanism, not an outlier.

The room cannot say whether this is durable. The pack gives no net margin, return on invested capital, net interest margin, asset composition or funding cost [P2]. Buffett and Lynch each cited a [P9] income statement, and no such dataset is in the pack. Buffett also noted that the equity base behind ROE is not stated [P1].

Rulings. Leverage direction: the 22.7th percentile with lower-is-better settles it for the five seats that read it as lower leverage [P2]. Buffett's original reading does not survive that figure. ROA thin versus healthy: the pack has no sector percentile or peer ROA for the 2.53% figure [P2], so this cannot be settled from the data. Missing statements: this is partly a matter of judgment. Everyone accepts that durability cannot be proven. Lynch weighed the ROE and the leverage percentile as evidence of a well-run franchise, while Buffett and Marks declined to infer skill without a multi-period record. Lynch's inference goes beyond what the single set of figures supports.

data.headline: High ROE, low ROA points to leverage; the pack lacks the window and denominator.
data.text:
The pack gives return on equity of 23.49% and return on assets of 2.53% [P2]. That is a wide gap, and in my experience it usually means one thing: a lot of leverage. A bank can show a high return on the equity shareholders put up because it is also using a great deal of other people's money — deposits and borrowings — to earn that return. The assets earn a modest return, but the equity slice is thin, so the return on that slice looks large.

But I cannot take either figure at face value. P2 does not state a denominator or a date for either return, and the income statement and the calculations in P9, which would tell me what window the earnings cover and what common equity the return was struck on, are not in this pack [P3]. A published return on equity that does not disclose its own denominator is a number without a receipt. I need to know whether it is common equity or includes preferred and minority interests, and whether it is a single year, a trailing twelve months, or something else.

One published figure is not a record. A durable earning power shows itself over years, not in one snapshot. The pair of numbers is consistent with a heavily leveraged balance sheet, as any bank's would be, but the pack does not let me show that, size it, or judge whether the leverage is prudent. I can only say the pattern is what I would expect, and that I cannot go further without the statements that are missing.

data.headline: Zero quarters counted; price fell but that is not earnings evidence.
data.text:
My job here is the quarterly record, and P9 — the dataset that carries the quarters — is not in the pack. I counted zero quarters. Without the quarter-by-quarter numbers I cannot tell you whether the returns on equity and assets are rising, falling, or holding steady. A single annual figure is not a trend. I need to see at least four or five quarters to say which way the business is moving, and I do not have them.

What the pack does show is the market's reading of the same stretch. P7 gives a one-year price change of -11.54%, from a first close of 70.2 SAR on 2025-09-29 to a last close of 62.1 SAR on 2026-10-13 [P7]. That is a decline. But a falling price is not evidence that earnings fell. The market can mark down a share for many reasons — a higher interest rate, a sector rotation, a general mood — that have nothing to do with the business's own earning power. The five-year picture in P8 shows a 34.24% rise from 46.26 SAR to 62.1 SAR [P8], so the longer arc is still positive, but again that is price, not earnings.

I cannot connect the returns to the price without the quarterly earnings that would let me plot them side by side. The story the annual figures imply — high ROE, low ROA — is a story about a leveraged bank. Whether the quarters support that story or are starting to weaken it is something this pack cannot tell me.

data.headline: The gap between ROE and ROA points to leverage; balance sheet absent.
data.text:
The machine here is straightforward in principle. A return on equity of 23.49% and a return on assets of 2.53% [P2] are connected by leverage. The equity is earning roughly nine times what the assets earn. That means for every unit of equity, there are many units of assets funded by liabilities — deposits, borrowings, sukuk. That is how a bank works. The equity is a thin layer on top of a large asset base, and a modest return on those assets becomes a high return on that thin layer.

But I cannot size the machine from this pack. My mandate is the balance sheet and its calculations, and P9 is absent. The only funding measure in the pack is a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72, with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. That tells me this bank is less indebted than most of its peers — a lower percentile on a metric where lower is better — but P2 does not show the operands, the date the ratio was struck, or even the peer class it was ranked in. For a bank, the relevant measures are not just debt-to-equity but the full leverage ratio, the funding structure, the liquidity coverage. None of that is here.

The scenario that would make the funding a problem is one where the asset return shrinks while the liability costs stay fixed. A 2.53% return on assets leaves very little room before the equity return turns negative [P1]. But I cannot say what interest rates, deposit costs or asset yields are, because the pack carries none of them. I can only point to the link between the two returns and say the balance sheet that would let me test it is not in front of us.

data.headline: Price assumes the return persists; large gaps limit what we know.
data.text:
The price as of 2026-10-13 is 62.1 SAR, with a price-to-earnings of 14.51 and a price-to-book of 3.19 [P1]. A price-to-book of 3.19 means the market is paying more than three times the accounting value of the equity [P1]. That only makes sense if the return on that equity is high and expected to stay high. The published return on equity of 23.49% [P2] is indeed high, and the market is pricing it as though it is durable.

But what we do not know is large. P9, with its limitations and calculations, is missing from this pack [P3]. The return on equity in P2 carries no stated denominator, no date, and no window — we do not know whether it is a single year, a trailing figure, or what equity it was struck on. Net margin is flagged as missing inputs, and return on invested capital as not applicable to the sector [P2]. So the profitability picture is incomplete even before we consider the price.

The prices themselves are flagged stale in P1, and the one-year return is -11.54% [P7]. The maximum drawdown is -83.12% [P1], which tells me this has been a volatile ride. A high return on equity that cannot be verified against a stated denominator, a price that assumes it persists, and a drawdown that shows what happens when the assumption falters — that is the shape of the risk. I am not saying the return is not real. I am saying the evidence to judge it is not all here, and the price is not asking a cautious question.

data.headline: Dividend paid, bonus shares issued; payout ratio cannot be computed.
data.text:
The latest dividend is 1.17 SAR per share, announced 2026-01-27, with an ex-date of 2026-04-20 and payment on 2026-04-30, for the second half of 2025 [P3]. That is a substantial payment — 7000 million SAR in total [P3] — and it follows a 0.50 SAR interim dividend for the first half of 2025 and a 0.97 SAR final dividend for the second half of 2024 [P3]. The bank has been paying twice a year, and the amounts have been rising.

But the return on equity and return on assets are not directly about dividends. They are about earnings. The payout ratio — how much of those earnings was returned to owners — comes from P9, which matches each dividend to the earnings window it was paid out of [P3]. P9 is not in this pack, so I cannot state the payout ratio. I can see the dividends, but I cannot see what they were paid from.

On the same ex-date as that latest dividend, 2026-04-20, the bank issued bonus shares at 50%, raising capital from 40000.0 million SAR to 60000.0 million SAR [P3]. That is one new share for every two held. A bonus issue does not change the total equity or the total earnings, but it does change what every per-share figure before that date meant. An earnings per share of 4.42 before the bonus [P1] would be restated downward if compared on the new share count. The returns on equity and assets are ratios of totals, so the share count does not affect them directly. But any per-share reading of the returns — and the market thinks in per-share terms — must account for that change.

data.headline: No sector ranking for ROE or ROA; peers trade at lower multiples.
data.text:
The pack gives no sector percentile for return on equity or return on assets in P2. The only ranked metric is debt-to-equity at 22.7, and P2 does not name the peer class that ranking was computed against [P2]. The absence of a ranking is not a low rank — it means the data does not tell us where this bank sits among its peers on the two returns the member is asking about.

What we can see is how the market ranks them. In P5, the peer banks trade at price-to-earnings ratios from 7.78 for Riyad Bank to 11.94 for Bank Albilad [P5]. Al Rajhi Bank trades at 14.51 [P1]. That is a premium — the market is paying more for each unit of this bank's earnings than for any of the peers listed. Whether that premium is justified by the returns is a question the missing rankings would help answer, but they are not here.

The disclosures in P6 show a bank that has been active in capital markets. On 2026-01-06 it issued USD-denominated AT1 capital sukuk, and on 2025-09-09 it completed a $1 billion Tier 2 social sukuk offering at 5.65% per annum with a 10.5-year maturity [P6]. These are capital-raising exercises — strengthening the balance sheet, not returning cash to shareholders. They are consistent with a bank that is growing its asset base and needs the regulatory capital to support that growth. That growth, in turn, would be one way to produce a high return on equity from a modest return on assets: keep adding assets, fund them with deposits and sukuk, and let the leverage do the work. But the disclosures do not give us a return figure, and the sector ranking that would let me compare the returns directly is absent.

data.headline: One return without a window is not durability.
data.text: Marks, you pair the 23.49% return on equity with a price-to-book of 3.19 and conclude the market is pricing durability [P1]. That treats the return as a settled fact. But P2 gives no window for that return and no denominator. I cannot tell whether it is a single year, a trailing twelve months, or something else. A number without a receipt cannot carry the weight of a durable earning power. A bank can show a high return on equity in one year because credit losses were low or because it added leverage. Calling that durable requires a record — several years of returns struck on the same measure of common equity — and this pack does not provide it. The gap between the 23.49% return on equity and the 2.53% return on assets is consistent with leverage, but I cannot size it or judge its prudence without the statements [P1].
data.concedes: The valuation figures are published and current to 2026-10-13 [P1].

data.headline: A bonus issue breaks the per-share record.
data.text: Alwaleed, you flagged the 50% bonus issue on 2026-04-20 that took capital from 40000.0 to 60000.0 million SAR [P3]. That matters for any per-share reading. An earnings per share of 4.42 before that date [P1] is not comparable with one after it unless you restate the old figure for the new share count. The market knows this — the price adjusts too. But my job is the quarterly trend, and with P9 absent I have zero quarters to count. I cannot say whether the earnings that produced those returns were rising or falling, or whether the bonus issue came at a moment of strength or weakness. A bonus issue in a rising business is a different signal from one in a business where earnings per share are already slipping. Without the quarters, I cannot tell you which one this is.
data.concedes: The bonus issue is a real distortion to any per-share history.

data.headline: The leverage link is inference, not measurement.
data.text: Buffett, you want the denominator named, and I agree. But the pack has no balance sheet at all — no assets, no equity, no deposits, no borrowings. P9 is absent. So neither of us can name what the returns were earned on. The link between the 23.49% return on equity and the 2.53% return on assets [P2] is an inference from the gap, not a measurement from the statements. I can say that a gap of that size points to leverage, and the debt-to-equity of 1.72 with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2] is consistent with a bank that uses less debt than most of its peers. But that ratio alone does not describe a bank's funding structure. A bank's machine runs on deposits, interbank lines, and capital instruments — none of which are in this pack. The scenario I would want to test is one where the asset return compresses, and I cannot build it from what we have.
data.concedes: The debt-to-equity figure alone does not describe a bank's funding.

data.headline: A premium multiple does not prove sector-leading returns.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you set Al Rajhi Bank against peers trading at price-to-earnings ratios from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5]. The bank's own multiple is 14.51 [P1]. That is a premium, and I agree the peer list in P5 is usable. But P2 gives no sector percentile for either return on equity or return on assets. So we have a ranking of prices, not a ranking of returns. A higher multiple can mean the market believes the returns are better, or more durable, or less risky — or it can mean the market is simply paying more for the same thing. Without a peer ranking of the returns themselves, the premium multiple does not show that the 23.49% return on equity is sector-leading [P1]. It shows only that the market has priced it as though it is. Those are different things.
data.concedes: The peer list in P5 is an exchange classification and is usable.

data.headline: Bonus issues complicate the equity side of the equation.
data.text: Dalio, you infer leverage from the gap between the two returns. But the capital history shows equity growing through bonus issues, not through retained earnings or new capital. The 2026-04-20 bonus issue moved capital from 40000.0 to 60000.0 million SAR [P3]. Before that, a 60% bonus issue in 2022 took it from 25000.0 to 40000.0 million [P3]. These are book entries — a transfer from reserves to capital — not new funds. They change the equity denominator used in any return calculation without adding a single riyal of new assets. That complicates any reading of how the returns are produced from the equity side. A high return on equity that is partly a function of a capital base that has been restated through bonus issues is not the same as one earned on capital that grew through retained profits.
data.concedes: No matched payout is computable from this pack, so I cannot say how much of earnings was returned.

data.headline: We cannot rank the returns, only the price.
data.text: Marks, you read the premium multiple as an assumption about persistence, and I agree that a price-to-book of 3.19 [P1] is asking a lot. But my point is simpler. The peer table in P5 gives us multiples and dividend yields for eight banks. It gives us no peer returns on equity or assets. P2 gives no percentile for either return. So I cannot say whether the 23.49% return on equity is high, ordinary, or low for this sector [P1]. The market has ranked the bank at the top of the peer set by price-to-earnings, but that is a ranking of what the market is willing to pay, not a ranking of what the bank earns. The two may align, or they may not. Without the peer returns, I cannot tell you which it is.
data.concedes: P2 gives no percentile for either return, so there is no peer ranking of the returns.

verdict.headline: The two returns are published, but the pack cannot show how they were produced.
verdict.answer:
The pack publishes a return on equity of 23.49% and a return on assets of 2.53% [P2]. P2 states no denominator or date for either, and the P9 statements and calculations that would give them are not in the pack. So the room can report the two figures but cannot decompose them.

Dalio's reading is that a gap this wide between the two returns points to leverage as the link between them, as a bank's balance sheet would. The only funding figure available is a debt-to-equity of 1.72 with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2], and its operands are not shown, so the inference cannot be measured. Buffett and Lynch both note that there is no income statement window and no quarterly record, so nothing shows whether the returns are a record or a single period. Counting quarters gives zero.

Marks points to the valuation: a price-to-earnings of 14.51 and a price-to-book of 3.19 at 62.1 SAR on 2026-10-13 [P1] assume the return persists, while net margin and return on invested capital are not available [P2]. Al-Rumayyan adds that P2 gives no ranking for either return, so the room cannot say how they compare with peers, though the peer banks in P5 trade at lower earnings multiples. Alwaleed notes a 1.17 SAR dividend with ex-date 2026-04-20 and a 50% bonus issue on the same date taking capital from 40000.0 to 60000.0 mn [P3]; the matched payout is not computable here. The price fell 11.54% over the year to 2026-10-13 [P7], which is a market reading and not an earnings one.

What is agreed: the returns are published, and their basis is undisclosed. What the data cannot tell: how much comes from margin and how much from leverage, over what period, and whether it is steady.
