headline: Price sits modestly above book, while the pack's profitability figures are negative and the earnings behind the book are missing.
answer:
The pack shows a last price of SAR 45.32 against a book value of SAR 41.18 per share, a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P1][P2]. On the pack's own figures, the market pays a modest premium to stated equity.

The pack's figures do not contradict one another. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. Buffett, Dalio, Marks and Lynch all read a premium to book alongside negative returns as a warning, not a bargain. Debt-to-equity is 0.26 and the current ratio is 1.80, so Dalio is right that the balance sheet is not under funding strain [P2]. There is no P/E, no EPS and no payout ratio, and the pack says several metrics are missing inputs [P1][P2].

The room's context: the shares are down 62.55% over five years and sit at the five-year low [P8]. The dividend has fallen from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 per share [P3]. Al-Rumayyan and Marks point to the disclosed sale of the Americas and Europe units, with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss, as a reason the stated book is a pre-reset figure [P6].

Rulings. On whether negative ROE makes book unreliable (Dalio, Al-Rumayyan, Buffett), the evidence cannot settle it: the ROE window and denominator are not disclosed, and no post-disposal book value is given [P2][P6]. On the 5.86% dividend (Marks, Alwaleed, Lynch), the evidence is only partly decisive [P1]. The cut from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 is in the pack, but coverage cannot be tested without a payout ratio or EPS [P1][P2][P3]. On what the 1.24 multiple implies (Marks, Dalio, Lynch), this is judgment: all three read the same price-to-book and negative returns, and the pack holds no earnings or loss-driver data to test a recovery bet against a shrinking-book reading [P1][P2].
gaps: The measurement window and equity denominator behind ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% are not shown [P1].
The pack has no P/E, EPS, payout ratio or free cash flow, so dividend coverage cannot be tested.
No post-disposal balance sheet shows the book value per share after the SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6].
disagreements: Does negative ROE make the stated book value unreliable? - The ROE of -15.37% has no disclosed measurement window or denominator, and the book value after the SAR 18.3B disposal loss is not in the pack [P2][P6].

Is the 5.86% dividend a cushion or a warning [P1]? - The fall from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 per share is documented [P3], but coverage cannot be tested because the pack has no payout ratio, EPS or free cash flow [P1][P2].

What does the 1.24 price-to-book imply about market expectations [P1]? - All three weigh the same price-to-book of 1.24 and ROE of -15.37% [P1][P2]. They differ on whether the premium signals a recovery bet or an overpriced shrinking book, and no P/E or quarterly trend exists to test either.

data.headline: Price below book, but negative profitability says the book may be overstated.
data.text:
The machine here is simple: the market prices SABIC at SAR 45.32 per share while the balance sheet reports a book value of SAR 41.18 per share [P1]. That yields a price-to-book ratio of 1.24x [P2]. In isolation, a ratio just above one could suggest the market sees the assets as worth roughly what is on the books, with a small premium. But the other gears in this machine tell a different story.

Profitability is negative. The return on equity (ROE) is -15.37%, and the return on assets (ROA) is -8.24% [P2]. A company earning negative returns on its equity is destroying its book value, not building it. When a business consistently loses money, the assets on its balance sheet are likely worth less than their stated carrying value because they are not generating adequate returns. The book value of SAR 41.18 is a historical accounting number, not a liquidation value, and these negative returns suggest it is eroding [P1]. Therefore, a P/B of 1.24x cannot be read as confirmation that the shares are worth more than book; rather, the book itself may be too high [P1].

The health metrics provide the next piece of the machine. The debt-to-equity ratio is a manageable 0.26, which is right at the sector median with a percentile of 50.5 [P2]. The current ratio is 1.80, at the 63rd percentile in its sector [P2]. This means the balance sheet is not under immediate liquidity strain from creditors. The funding is conservative, with equity, not debt, carrying the weight of the negative returns. The problem is not a funding crisis; it is an earnings crisis that slowly consumes the equity base.

So, the pack's figures do agree with each other, but they agree on a warning. The market price is above book value, yet the company's own profitability shows that book value is shrinking. The most important scenario to consider is that if these negative returns persist, the book value per share will continue to fall, making the current SAR 45.32 price look increasingly expensive relative to a deteriorating asset base [P1]. The data here does not show the drivers of these losses—commodity prices or operating leverage—so I cannot say when the cycle turns, only that the current state is one of value destruction.

data.headline: Price sits modestly above book, but negative profitability undermines the book's foundation.
data.text:
The market price of SAR 45.32 exceeds the reported book value of SAR 41.18 per share by a narrow margin, producing a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P1]. This ratio is not, by itself, an endorsement of value. The book value is an accounting construct, and its reliability rests on the company's ability to generate a return on that equity. The data here shows an ROE of -15.37% and an ROA of -8.24% [P1][P2]. When a business is destroying shareholder capital at that rate, the book value is not a floor; it is a figure that is shrinking. The market is, in effect, pricing the shares as if it expects the book value to decline.

Looking at the company against its sector, the peer list places SABIC as the largest by market capitalization at SAR 151,650 million, more than double the next-largest materials peer, Maaden, at SAR 235,075 million [P5]—a point I must correct: the data shows Maaden's market cap is larger at SAR 235,075 million, which makes SABIC the second-largest in this peer set. The company's debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 sits at the 50.5th percentile in its sector, and its current ratio of 1.80 is at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. These are the hallmarks of a balance sheet with capacity, which is what matters for a long-horizon position. The capacity is there; the immediate returns are not.

As for what the company has disclosed, the most recent item is from 2026-01-07, noting the planned sale of its Americas and Europe units with an expected non-cash loss of SAR 18.3 billion [P6]. This is a significant restructuring that will reshape the book value itself when it closes. An earlier disclosure from 2025-12-31 shows the transfer of SAR 110.9 billion from general reserve to retained earnings [P6], a move that changes the composition of equity but not its total. The price-to-book ratio today is a snapshot of a balance sheet in transition, and the negative profitability figures tell me the market is not misreading it.

data.headline: Price just above book, but the quarterly record is deeply negative.
data.text:
The market price of SAR 45.32 sits only 10% above the book value of SAR 41.18 per share [P1]. That slim premium makes sense when you check the profitability figures. An ROE of -15.37% and an ROA of -8.24% [P2] are destroying that book value, not building on it. A company trading at 1.24 times book while earning a negative return on that equity is a story of capital erosion, not a bargain [P1].

My job here is to look at the trend, and the quarterly record in [P9] is missing from the pack. I cannot say whether the negative annual profitability is from one bad quarter or a steady decline. The price summary shows the market has been reading this story negatively for a while: the stock is down 26.61% over the past year and 62.55% over five years, with the 5-year range showing a high of SAR 139.0 and a low of SAR 45.32 [P8]. That’s a brutal drawdown, and the current price is sitting right at that 5-year low [P7][P8]. The market has clearly been repricing a deteriorating business.

Without the quarterly data, I can’t tell you if the worst is behind or still coming. The dividend record shows a steady payout, with H1 2026 at SAR 1.1 per share, down from SAR 1.5 in both halves of 2025 [P3]. That cut is a real-world signal from management that cash flow is tighter. So, while the price-to-book ratio looks low, the negative returns and the missing quarterly proof mean I can’t call this a value story yet. The numbers I do have agree: the company is earning less than its cost of capital, and the price reflects that trouble.

data.headline: Price is a modest premium to a book value whose earning power is deeply negative.
data.text:
The pack gives a last price of SAR 45.32 and a book value of SAR 41.18 per share, so the market is paying about SAR 1.10 for each SAR 1 of stated equity [P1]. The price-to-book ratio is 1.24 [P2]. That is not an expensive multiple on its face, but the real question is what that equity can earn.

I start with what the business returns on the capital it keeps. The pack reports a return on equity of -15.37% and a return on assets of -8.24% [P2]. Those figures are negative. A business that loses money on its owners' capital is destroying value, not compounding it. The pack does not tell me the exact window those returns were measured over, nor does it disclose the denominator used for the ROE calculation, so I cannot see whether it is common equity or total equity including others' money. A single window of negative returns is a snapshot, not a record, and I would not treat it as one.

The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.26, which is moderate [P2]. The current ratio is 1.80, so the company appears liquid [P2]. That is some comfort, but if the assets cannot earn their keep, the balance-sheet strength only delays the reckoning.

The dividend yield of 5.86% catches the eye, but the pack shows no payout ratio and no earnings-per-share figure to tell me whether that dividend is covered by current earnings [P1][P2]. The latest dividend was SAR 1.10 per share announced in July 2026, down from SAR 1.50 six months earlier [P3]. A falling dividend alongside negative returns is not the profile of a business with a durable competitive advantage.

In short, the book value is there, but the earning power behind it is absent. I cannot tell from these figures alone whether the price is a bargain or a trap, only that the returns on that book value are poor.

data.headline: Price below book, but negative returns and a shrinking payout test the franchise.
data.text:
The market price of SAR 45.32 sits 10.1% above the book value of SAR 41.18 per share, giving a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1]. That is not a distressed multiple on its face, but I do not look at book value in isolation. I look at what the company earns on that book, and what it returns to me as an owner.

The pack shows a return on equity of -15.37% and a return on assets of -8.24% [P2]. A business destroying its own capital is not one I can value on book alone. The dividend yield of 5.86% [P1] signals confidence, but the trend is what matters.

That is where my own mandate comes in. The dividend history [P3] shows the per-share payout has been cut steadily: H1 2022 paid SAR 2.25, H2 2023 paid SAR 2.00, H1 2024 paid SAR 1.70, and the last two distributions were SAR 1.50 and SAR 1.10. The most recent, announced 2026-07-29 for H1 2026, is half what it was four years ago [P1] [P3]. The data pack does not give me a payout ratio computed against a matched earnings window [P9], so I cannot say what portion of earnings these dividends represent. That is a gap: a 5.86% yield means little if it is not covered [P1].

The capital history shows only bonus shares, the last in 2008, taking the capital from SAR 25 billion to SAR 30 billion [P3]. No dilutive issuance since then, which I like. But a steady dividend decline alongside negative returns tells me the franchise is under pressure, not just the share price. I would want to know whether the restructuring disclosed in January 2026—the planned sale of Americas and Europe units with an expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6]—is a cleanup that restores earning power or a retreat from markets it could not win. The data does not answer that.

data.headline: The price reflects real distress, and the figures agree on that.
data.text:
The market price of SAR 45.32 sits just 10% above the reported book value of SAR 41.18 per share, giving a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P1]. On its face, that is not a demanding multiple. But the question is what this price has to be assuming, and on that point the pack's own figures are consistent in a sobering way.

The book value is an accounting number, and its relevance depends entirely on the earning power of the assets. Here, both return on equity and return on assets are deeply negative: ROE sits at -15.37% and ROA at -8.24% [P1]. A company that is destroying its own equity does not deserve to trade at book value, let alone a premium to it. The 1.24x multiple, in this context, is not a sign of undervaluation; it is a sign that the market is betting the asset base will eventually earn its keep again, or that the assets could be worth more in someone else's hands [P1]. The five-year price summary shows the market has been steadily losing confidence: the shares have fallen from SAR 121.00 to SAR 45.32, a decline of 62.55%, with the current price marking the five-year low [P8]. The pendulum has swung far toward pessimism.

Do the figures agree with each other? The profitability metrics are uniformly negative, which is consistent with a price that has collapsed. The dividend yield of 5.86% [P1] might appear to offer a cushion, but a yield is only as safe as the earnings and cash flows that support it. The pack does not show us the payout ratio or free cash flow, so we cannot judge the dividend's durability. This is a critical gap. We also lack a P/E ratio because the unit of the trailing earnings is unconfirmed [P1], and several other valuation and profitability metrics are missing [P2]. We are making an assessment with incomplete information, and I must name that aloud: we do not know the normalized earnings power, we do not know the free cash flow, and we do not know the outcome of the planned asset sales. The price is assuming a difficult road ahead, and on the evidence we have, that assumption looks warranted.

lines.title: Does negative ROE make the book value unreliable?
lines.text: Dalio and Al-Rumayyan read ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% as evidence that the SAR 41.18 book value is eroding or overstated, while Buffett treats the returns as one snapshot whose window and denominator the pack does not disclose [P1][P2]. The dispute turns on the missing measurement period and on whether the January 2026 disposal loss of SAR 18.3B will reset book value [P6].

lines.title: Is the 5.86% dividend a cushion or a warning [P1]?
lines.text: Marks and Alwaleed say coverage cannot be judged because the pack shows no payout ratio, free cash flow or EPS, while Lynch and Alwaleed read the fall from SAR 1.50 to SAR 1.10 per share as a signal of tighter cash [P1][P2][P3]. They differ on how much a missing payout figure limits that reading.

lines.title: Does the 1.24 price-to-book mean the market expects recovery [P1]?
lines.text: Marks reads the premium to book as a bet that the assets will earn again or be worth more to others, Dalio reads it as a price above a shrinking book, and Lynch reads it as a fair reflection of capital erosion [P1][P2]. The data shows no P/E, no quarterly earnings trend and no loss drivers, so none of these readings can be tested against it [P2].

data.summary: The advisors agree the pack's figures are consistent: price SAR 45.32 against book SAR 41.18 with negative ROE and ROA, but they split on what the premium implies and on how far the missing earnings, payout and window data limit any reading [P1].

data.headline: A single loss does not make the whole book unreliable
data.text: Dalio, you say that because the ROE is negative, the book value itself is likely overstated and eroding. I would be slower to write off the whole book. The pack gives us one return figure, -15.37%, and does not tell us over what window it was measured [P2]. A single bad year, or even two, does not mean the assets are permanently impaired. A farm has a bad harvest now and then; the land is still there. The debt-to-equity ratio is a modest 0.26, so the losses are not being magnified by heavy borrowing [P2]. The current ratio of 1.80 says the company is liquid [P2]. The book value of SAR 41.18 per share is an accounting number, yes, but I cannot call it unreliable from one negative return whose measurement period the pack does not disclose [P1]. I concede that if these losses persist for years, the book will shrink, but the data here shows me only a snapshot, not a trend.
data.concedes: A business that consistently loses money will see its book value erode over time.

data.headline: The dividend cut is a stress signal, not just a data gap
data.text: Lynch, you say the quarterly record is missing and that you cannot call this a value story without it. I disagree with that hesitation. The dividend record I am answerable for tells you the trend plainly enough. The per-share payout has been cut from SAR 2.25 in H1 2022 to SAR 1.10 in H1 2026 [P3]. A management team does not halve the dividend over four years unless the earnings power has weakened. That is the quarterly signal, delivered in cash. You also note the 62.55% five-year price decline and the 26.61% one-year decline [P8][P7]. A price at a five-year low, coupled with a shrinking dividend, is exactly the crisis moment I look for. The question is not whether the worst is behind; the question is whether the franchise is intact. The data does not show me brand strength, but it does show a balance sheet with a debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2], which can carry it through a restructuring. The planned sale of the Americas and Europe units [P6] is the kind of move that resets a business. I would want to own it before the quarterly numbers turn, not after.
data.concedes: You are right that without a payout ratio or EPS, the dividend coverage cannot be confirmed from this pack.

data.headline: The book value's funding base is sound; the earnings erosion is the risk.
data.text: Buffett, you say the balance-sheet strength only delays the reckoning, but I think that understates what the health metrics tell us about the funding structure itself. The machine here is funded conservatively: the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.26, right at the 50.5th sector percentile, and the current ratio is 1.80, at the 63.4th percentile [P2]. The balance sheet, struck at the date in [P9]—which the pack does not provide here, so I must note that gap—is not under liquidity strain from creditors. Equity, not debt, is absorbing the negative ROE of -15.37% [P2]. The reckoning is not a credit crunch; it is a slow erosion of the equity base. The most important scenario is that if these negative returns persist, the book value of SAR 41.18 per share will continue to fall, making the current SAR 45.32 price increasingly expensive against a deteriorating asset base [P1]. The funding is not the problem; the earnings power that determines whether that funding becomes a problem is.
data.concedes: You are right that the window and denominator for the ROE calculation are not disclosed in the pack, so I cannot say how long this erosion has been underway or whether it is accelerating.

data.headline: Book value is not a machine; it is a historical record.
data.text: Dalio, you frame the book value as a figure that is currently shrinking and potentially overstated, and you are right that negative ROE erodes equity. But I must push back on the certainty with which you state the book value is 'too high.' An accounting book value of SAR 41.18 is a historical cost-based snapshot, not a real-time liquidation appraisal [P1]. The market, at SAR 45.32, is paying a slim premium [P1]. The data here shows the company is restructuring: the planned sale of Americas and Europe units will crystallize a non-cash loss of SAR 18.3 billion [P6]. That suggests the current book value is not yet written down to reflect the reality that management itself sees. The price-to-book of 1.24 may be the market's acknowledgment that the stated book is stale, not that the assets are worthless [P1]. The negative ROE tells us the assets are not earning; it does not, by itself, tell us the precise gap between carrying value and economic worth. We would need the post-restructuring balance sheet to judge that, and the data does not yet give it to us.
data.concedes: I agree with your core point that negative returns make the current book value a poor anchor for valuation.

data.headline: The machine is missing a key gear
data.text: Dalio, you call the machine simple and say the figures agree on a warning, but your machine is running without the gear I am answerable for: the quarterly trend. You say the book value is eroding because ROE is -15.37% and ROA is -8.24%, but the pack does not tell you whether that is one terrible quarter dragging down an otherwise profitable year, or a steady grind lower [P1]. Without [P9], I cannot say, and neither can you. A single negative annual figure is a snapshot, not a trend. You also say the debt-to-equity of 0.26 and current ratio of 1.80 mean the problem is an earnings crisis, not a funding crisis [P2]. I agree the balance sheet has capacity. But calling it an earnings crisis requires showing the earnings are consistently in crisis, quarter after quarter. The price summary I do have shows a 62.55% five-year decline to SAR 45.32, right at the five-year low [P8]. That market vote is loud. But the quarterly proof of whether the losses are accelerating or steady is absent. Your machine is missing that gear, and without it, the warning is half-built.
data.concedes: I agree the balance sheet has capacity, with a manageable debt load and a current ratio above 1.8 [P2].

data.headline: A single window of losses tells less than the disclosed restructuring.
data.text: Buffett reads the negative ROE as a snapshot and says the pack does not disclose the window. I agree the window is absent, but the company has disclosed events that explain why the book value and returns are in flux. On 2025-12-31, SABIC transferred SAR 110.9 billion from general reserve to retained earnings, and on 2026-01-07 it announced the planned sale of its Americas and Europe units with an expected non-cash loss of SAR 18.3 billion [P6]. These are not ordinary-course items; they are deliberate, disclosed restructurings that will reset the book value per share when they close. The negative ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2] are therefore not a mystery snapshot of a steady-state business but a picture of a company in the middle of a portfolio transformation. The balance sheet has capacity: a debt-to-equity ratio at the 50.5th sector percentile and a current ratio at the 63.4th [P2]. The book value of SAR 41.18 [P1] is a pre-restructuring number, and the market price of SAR 45.32 is pricing a post-restructuring reality that has not yet landed on the balance sheet.
data.concedes: The pack does not give the measurement window for the ROE and ROA figures, so we cannot see how much of the loss is tied to the disclosed non-cash charge.

data.text: The price of SAR 45.32 is a modest premium to a book value of SAR 41.18 that is currently earning nothing for its owners [P1]. The pack shows a return on equity of -15.37%, but does not disclose the window it was measured over or the denominator used, so I cannot treat it as a record of durable earning power [P2]. I would need a multi-year history of returns on common equity, struck on consistent dates, to judge whether the business compounds value or destroys it.
data.changed: I have not changed my view. Dalio and Al-Rumayyan read the negative ROE as proof the book value is eroding, but the pack still does not tell me over what period that return was earned, and a single snapshot is not a record. Marks rightly notes the restructuring will reset the book, which only deepens my caution.
data.would_change: A five- or ten-year record of return on common equity, with the denominator and measurement dates clearly stated, would let me judge whether the business has a durable competitive advantage.

data.text: The balance sheet is funded conservatively: debt-to-equity is 0.26 at the sector median and the current ratio is 1.80, so equity—not creditors—absorbs the negative ROE of -15.37% [P2]. The funding structure is not the immediate problem; the problem is that the book value of SAR 41.18 per share is being eroded by persistent losses, making the market price of SAR 45.32 a premium over a shrinking asset base [P1]. The most important scenario is that if these negative returns continue, the book value will fall further and the current price will look increasingly expensive against it.
data.changed: Marks challenged my certainty that the book value is 'too high,' and I now acknowledge that the SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss from the planned Americas and Europe sale means the stated book is pre-restructuring and not yet written down to the reality management itself sees [P6]. The negative ROE tells us the assets are not earning; it does not tell us the precise gap between carrying value and economic worth until the restructuring closes.
data.would_change: The post-restructuring balance sheet and a matched ROE window over several quarters would show whether the book value has been reset to a level the business can earn on.

data.text: Price at SAR 45.32 against book of SAR 41.18 is not the question [P1]. The question is whether the franchise can earn again, and the dividend record I am answerable for says it is under real pressure: the per-share payout has been cut from SAR 2.25 in H1 2022 to SAR 1.10 in H1 2026 [P3]. A 62.55% five-year price decline to a five-year low, a balance sheet with a debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80, and a disclosed restructuring that will crystallize a SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6]—this is the crisis setup I look for, but only if the core franchise survives the cleanup [P8][P2]. The data does not show me brand strength or post-restructuring earning power, so I cannot call the bottom, only that the price is pricing distress and the dividend trend confirms it.
data.changed: Lynch and Marks pressed me on the missing payout ratio, which I concede: without a matched earnings window [P9], I cannot say whether the SAR 1.10 dividend is covered or is being paid out of reserves. That tempers my confidence that the dividend cut alone proves the franchise is intact rather than bleeding. I still read the steady cuts as a stress signal, but I now acknowledge the data gap limits how far I can take that reading.
data.would_change: A payout ratio computed against a matched earnings window [P9] would tell me whether the dividend is covered, and post-restructuring financials showing the book value and returns after the Americas and Europe disposal would tell me whether the franchise reset has worked.

data.text: My position remains that the price of SAR 45.32 reflects real distress, and the pack's own figures are consistent in showing a business that is currently destroying its book value, not compounding it [P1]. The 1.24x price-to-book multiple is not a bargain signal; it is a slim premium that the market is paying over an equity base that is being eroded, and that premium likely reflects a bet on the disclosed restructuring rather than current earning power [P1]. What changed for me in this room was the reinforcement from Al-Rumayyan's reading of the restructuring disclosures: the planned SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss and the reserve transfer tell me the current book value of SAR 41.18 is a pre-reset number, and the market is already pricing a post-reset reality that we cannot yet measure [P1] [P6].
data.changed: My conviction that the book value is stale, not just eroding, was strengthened by Al-Rumayyan's focus on the disclosed restructuring events, which I had noted but now see as the primary reason the market is paying any premium at all.
data.would_change: A post-restructuring balance sheet showing the new book value per share, alongside a normalized earnings figure that tells me whether the remaining assets can earn an adequate return, would change my assessment of what the price is assuming.

data.text: SABIC holds the scale and balance-sheet capacity to matter to its sector—it is the second-largest materials peer by market capitalisation at SAR 151,650 million, with a debt-to-equity ratio at the 50.5th sector percentile and a current ratio at the 63.4th—but its negative ROE of -15.37% and the disclosed restructuring, including the planned sale of Americas and Europe units with an expected SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss, tell me the book value of SAR 41.18 per share is a pre-transformation figure that will be reset, and the market price of SAR 45.32 is pricing a post-restructuring reality that has not yet landed on the balance sheet [P1][P2][P5][P6].
data.changed: Nothing material changed in my position. The room reinforced that the negative ROE is a snapshot whose measurement window the pack does not disclose, which I conceded, but the disclosed events—the reserve transfer of SAR 110.9 billion and the unit sales—remain the structural facts that explain why the book value is in transition and why a simple price-to-book comparison is insufficient [P6].

data.text: I came in looking for the quarterly trend, and the pack simply does not give it to me. The price summary shows a brutal 62.55% five-year decline to SAR 45.32, right at the five-year low, and the dividend has been cut from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 over four years—that is a real-world signal of earnings trouble, not just a data gap [P8][P3]. But I cannot do my job without the quarterly record in [P9] to tell me whether the negative ROE of -15.37% is from one bad quarter or a steady grind [P2]. My position is that the price-to-book of 1.24 reflects capital erosion, and I cannot call it a bargain or a trap until I see the quarter-by-quarter earnings trend that either confirms or breaks the story [P1].
data.changed: Alwaleed pushed me hard on the dividend record, and he is right: a halved payout over four years is a signal you can read even without the quarterly P&L. I still insist that the quarterly trend is the proof I need, but I concede the dividend cuts are a legitimate proxy for deteriorating earnings power when the P&L detail is missing.
data.would_change: The quarterly revenue and net income trend from [P9] would tell me whether the losses are accelerating, steady, or reversing, and that would change whether I see the current price as a falling knife or a potential turnaround.

data.headline: Price sits modestly above book, while the pack's profitability figures are negative and the earnings behind the book are missing.
data.answer:
The pack shows a last price of SAR 45.32 against a book value of SAR 41.18 per share, a price-to-book ratio of 1.24 [P1][P2]. On the pack's own figures, the market pays a modest premium to stated equity.

The pack's figures do not contradict one another. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. Buffett, Dalio, Marks and Lynch all read a premium to book alongside negative returns as a warning, not a bargain. Debt-to-equity is 0.26 and the current ratio is 1.80, so Dalio is right that the balance sheet is not under funding strain [P2]. There is no P/E, no EPS and no payout ratio, and the pack says several metrics are missing inputs [P1][P2].

The room's context: the shares are down 62.55% over five years and sit at the five-year low [P8]. The dividend has fallen from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 per share [P3]. Al-Rumayyan and Marks point to the disclosed sale of the Americas and Europe units, with an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss, as a reason the stated book is a pre-reset figure [P6].

Rulings. On whether negative ROE makes book unreliable (Dalio, Al-Rumayyan, Buffett), the evidence cannot settle it: the ROE window and denominator are not disclosed, and no post-disposal book value is given [P2][P6]. On the 5.86% dividend (Marks, Alwaleed, Lynch), the evidence is only partly decisive [P1]. The cut from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 is in the pack, but coverage cannot be tested without a payout ratio or EPS [P1][P2][P3]. On what the 1.24 multiple implies (Marks, Dalio, Lynch), this is judgment: all three read the same price-to-book and negative returns, and the pack holds no earnings or loss-driver data to test a recovery bet against a shrinking-book reading [P1][P2].

rulings.grounds: The ROE of -15.37% has no disclosed measurement window or denominator, and the book value after the SAR 18.3B disposal loss is not in the pack [P2][P6].

rulings.grounds: The fall from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 per share is documented [P3], but coverage cannot be tested because the pack has no payout ratio, EPS or free cash flow [P1][P2].

rulings.on: What does the 1.24 price-to-book imply about market expectations [P1]?
rulings.grounds: All three weigh the same price-to-book of 1.24 and ROE of -15.37% [P1][P2]. They differ on whether the premium signals a recovery bet or an overpriced shrinking book, and no P/E or quarterly trend exists to test either.

disagreements: Does negative ROE make the stated book value unreliable? - The ROE of -15.37% has no disclosed measurement window or denominator, and the book value after the SAR 18.3B disposal loss is not in the pack [P2][P6].

Is the 5.86% dividend a cushion or a warning [P1]? - The fall from SAR 2.25 to SAR 1.10 per share is documented [P3], but coverage cannot be tested because the pack has no payout ratio, EPS or free cash flow [P1][P2].

What does the 1.24 price-to-book imply about market expectations [P1]? - All three weigh the same price-to-book of 1.24 and ROE of -15.37% [P1][P2]. They differ on whether the premium signals a recovery bet or an overpriced shrinking book, and no P/E or quarterly trend exists to test either.

The pack has no P/E, EPS, payout ratio or free cash flow, so dividend coverage cannot be tested.
No post-disposal balance sheet shows the book value per share after the SAR 18.3B non-cash loss [P6].

headline: Book value is reported, but the figures do not reconcile and earnings evidence is missing
answer:
The pack reports a last price of 45.32 SAR, book value of 41.18 SAR per share and a published price-to-book of 1.24 [P1]. Marks notes that these three do not visibly reproduce one another, and the pack states no date or basis for each; the quote is dated 2026-10-13 and fundamentals 2026-08-12 [P1]. So the room cannot confirm that its own figures agree.

Buffett and Marks both point to the return on equity of -15.37% and return on assets of -8.24%, published without a denominator [P2]. That makes book value a weak yardstick for what the shares are worth. Alrumayyan adds that SABIC disclosed on 2026-01-07 an expected SAR 18.3B non-cash loss from selling Americas and Europe units [P6]. The pack does not link that loss to the negative return.

On the market's side, the price fell from 121.0 to 45.32 SAR over five years and by 26.61% over one year [P8][P7]. Dividends stepped down from 1.5 to 1.1 SAR per share for H1 2026 [P3]. Dalio finds debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 moderate [P2], but they come without a dated balance sheet.

The earnings, quarterly and balance sheet dataset, P9, is absent from this pack, so the five advisors who depend on it could report only what P1 to P3 and P5 to P8 show [P3]. P/E, EV/EBITDA and trailing EPS are missing [P1]. Nothing here says the shares are worth more or less than book value; it shows only that the pack's own figures do not settle the point.
gaps: P9's income statement, quarters and balance sheet are not in the pack.
The dates and basis behind book value and price-to-book are not stated.
P/E, EV/EBITDA and EPS are missing, and no price-to-book percentile is given.
disagreements: Do price, book value and price-to-book agree? - The pack gives no date or basis for the 41.18 SAR book value or the 1.24 ratio [P1], so reconciliation cannot be tested.
Is the loss one event or a pattern? - Quarterly and multi-window income figures from P9 are absent; the 2026-01-07 disclosure gives a loss expectation but no earnings window [P6].
Is the dividend step-down earned by earnings? - The matched-window payout from P9 is absent, so the dividends in P3 cannot be set against earnings.

data.headline: A loss-making return on undisclosed equity against a book value I cannot verify.
data.text:
I am answerable for earning power, but the income statement in P9 is not in this pack. So I cannot name a window of earnings or a return struck on common equity. What I have is P2's published return on equity of -15.37% and return on assets of -8.24% [P2]. P2 does not disclose the denominator for either figure. A single published ratio, without the date, the equity it was earned on or the period it covers, is not a record of earning power — it is a number without the story behind it.

Book value is reported at 41.18 SAR per share [P1]. Against a loss-making return, a book value is a weak anchor. The assets that make it up are worth what they can earn, and what they are earning now is negative. I cannot call the shares cheap at 1.24 times book [P1] when I do not know what those assets have earned over any window I can check.

If I had P9, I would look at the return on the common equity struck on a stated date and matched to a stated income period [P3]. I would ask whether that return has been steady over years, earned with little debt, and paid out sensibly. The dividend record in P3 suggests management has returned cash to owners, but a dividend paid from a loss-making business is a different thing from one paid from steady earnings. On the evidence in front of me, I cannot say the book value is a sound measure of worth.

data.headline: Without quarterly figures I cannot say whether the business or the mood declined.
data.text:
I am answerable for the trend, but P9's quarters are not in this pack. I cannot count quarters or say which way earnings are moving. That leaves me with the market's own reading. P7 shows a one-year change of -26.61%, from a first close of 61.75 to a last close of 45.32 SAR [P7]. P1 gives a three-month return of -17.67% [P1]. The price has been falling for a while.

But a price record is not a business record. A share can fall because earnings are shrinking, or because the market's mood has turned, or both. Without quarterly figures I cannot separate the two. I cannot sort this company into a kind — is it a cyclical at the bottom, a turnaround, or a slow grower that has stumbled? Each kind is judged differently, and I need the quarters to tell.

The book value of 41.18 SAR sits below the last price of 45.32 [P1]. That is a narrow cushion. If the business is losing money, as P2's negative ROE of -15.37% suggests [P2], book value can shrink. I would want to see whether the quarterly losses are widening or narrowing before I called 1.24 times book a bargain or a trap [P1]. On what is here, I cannot call it either.

data.headline: The balance sheet is absent; the ratios I have show moderate leverage but no stress test.
data.text:
I am answerable for the balance sheet, but P9 is not in this pack. I have no balance-sheet date, no asset or liability lines, and no operands to trace. What I have are two ratios from P2: a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2]. The debt-to-equity sits at the 50.5th sector percentile and the current ratio at the 63.4th, yielding a composite health score of 56.95 [P2]. That is a middling reading — neither strong enough to dismiss risk nor weak enough to sound an alarm.

The strain scenario I would test is this: continued losses eroding the equity that stands behind that 0.26 ratio [P2]. P2's return on equity is -15.37% [P2]. If losses persist, equity shrinks, the debt-to-equity ratio rises, and what looks moderate today can become strained. But I cannot put numbers on that without the balance-sheet lines and the income statement in P9.

Interest coverage is missing from P2 [P2]. That is a gap that matters, because it is the first measure to flash when earnings cannot service the debt. The book value of 41.18 SAR per share [P1] is the equity per share, and at 1.24 times book [P1] the market is pricing it just above that equity. Whether that is cheap or dear depends on whether the equity is intact or being consumed. The pack does not give me the pieces to answer that.

data.headline: The three figures do not visibly agree, and the pack gives no single date or basis.
data.text:
I am answerable for what the price assumes and for what we do not know. Let me start with the gaps. P/E, EV/EBITDA and trailing EPS are all missing from P1. EPS is absent because its unit is unconfirmed [P1]. P9 and its limitations are absent altogether, so I cannot name what the source itself says it cannot show. The council's rule-based votes in P4 are thresholds, not measurements, and I will not cite them as figures.

Now the question. The pack reports a last price of 45.32 SAR, a book value of 41.18 SAR per share and a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1]. Those three numbers do not visibly reproduce each other. 45.32 divided by 41.18 is roughly 1.10, not 1.24 [P1] [P3]. The pack does not give a single date or basis for the three. The quote is dated 2026-10-13 and the fundamentals 2026-08-12 [P1]. A price-to-book ratio that mixes a price from one date with a book value from another is not a measurement of one moment.

The five-year price summary tells a sobering story: the close fell from 121.0 to 45.32 SAR [P8]. The market has marked this company down by more than half over five years. At 1.24 times book, the price is not demanding much from the assets, but what it is assuming is that the book value itself is sound [P1]. With a return on equity of -15.37% [P2], that assumption is what needs to be questioned. A book value that earns nothing, or loses money, is not worth what it cost. The price may look modest against book, but we do not know what the book is worth.

data.headline: Dividends have been paid but are shrinking; the matched-window payout is absent.
data.text:
I am answerable for what has been returned to owners and out of what. P3 shows a dividend record that has been shrinking. The H1 2026 dividend was 1.1 SAR per share, totalling 3,300.0 million SAR, with an ex-date of 2026-08-11 [P3]. The two prior half-years were 1.5 SAR each [P3]. Go back to the H1 2022 payment and it was 2.25 SAR [P3]. That is a steady step-down: 2.25, then 1.8, 1.6, 1.7, 1.7, 1.5, 1.5, and now 1.1 [P2] [P3]. The direction is clear.

But I will not assemble a payout ratio from this list. P9's matched-window payout is absent from the pack, and counting a dividend against the wrong earnings window is how a payout that is four-fifths of earnings reads as a whole one. Without P9, I cannot say what share of earnings these dividends represent [P3]. A dividend paid from a loss-making business is a return of capital, not a return on capital, and P2's return on equity of -15.37% [P2] suggests that is the case here.

The latest capital change in the record is the bonus issue of 2008-03-29 [P3]. No recent change distorts the per-share figures, so the book value of 41.18 SAR per share [P1] and the dividends per share are comparable over the window shown. The company has a long history of returning capital to owners through bonus issues, but that history stopped in 2008 [P3]. What it has done lately is pay cash dividends, and those dividends are shrinking. That is the fact the book-value question must reckon with.

data.headline: No sector ranking exists for price-to-book; the company disclosed a large reserve transfer and a unit sale.
data.text:
I am answerable for the company against its sector and for what it has disclosed. P2 reports a price-to-book of 1.24 with no sector percentile attached [P2]. That is not a low ranking — it is no ranking at all. The peer list in P5 gives P/E ratios for the Materials group ranging from 15.16 for Luberef to 58.93 for Yansab, and SABIC has no P/E at all [P5][P1]. So the two most common ways of comparing price to the balance sheet — price-to-book ranking and price-to-earnings — are both absent for this company.

What the company has disclosed is more instructive. On 2026-01-07, SABIC announced it would sell its Americas and Europe units and expects an SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6]. That is a material restructuring, and a non-cash loss of that size will flow through the book value. On 2025-12-31, it disclosed shareholder approval to transfer an SAR 110.9 billion general reserve to retained earnings [P6]. That is an accounting move, not a cash event, but it changes the composition of equity and may affect how book value per share is calculated going forward.

Both disclosures are dated well before the latest quote of 2026-10-13 [P1]. They tell me the book value the market is pricing today is not a steady figure. A large reserve transfer and a pending unit sale with an expected loss mean the 41.18 SAR per share [P1] is a number in motion. The price-to-book of 1.24 is a snapshot of a moving picture, and the sector offers no benchmark to judge it against [P1].

lines.text: Marks flags that 45.32 SAR, 41.18 SAR and 1.24 do not visibly reconcile and have unstated dates [P1]. Buffett says the negative return on equity makes book value a weak anchor anyway [P2].

data.summary: The room disagrees on how to read book value and the loss, and the earnings data that would settle it is missing.

data.headline: Book value is not worth much if it earns nothing.
data.text: Marks treats the price against book as the central test of what is priced in. I understand that instinct, but it puts the cart before the horse. A book value of 41.18 SAR per share [P1] is only the balance sheet's claim on the assets. What those assets are worth depends on what they earn, and what they are earning now is a return on equity of -15.37% [P2]. That is a negative number, and a negative return on capital means the capital is shrinking, not compounding. I cannot tell from this pack whether that loss is a single window or a pattern, because the income statement in P9 is absent. But a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1] is not cheap if the book itself is melting. The price of 45.32 SAR and the book value of 41.18 SAR are the right starting figures, and I concede that [P1]. But the question is not whether they agree; it is what the book can earn.
data.concedes: The pack's price of 45.32 SAR and book value of 41.18 SAR are the right starting figures [P1].

data.headline: The dividend is shrinking, but is it following earnings?
data.text: Alwaleed is right to point to the dividend history, and I concede it is a real record of what was paid. A dividend of 1.1 SAR per share for H1 2026, against 1.5 for H2 2025 and H1 2025, shows payouts shrinking [P3]. That is a fact. But without quarterly earnings I cannot say whether the cut follows the earnings or runs ahead of them. A company can cut a dividend because earnings have already fallen, or because management sees trouble coming and wants to conserve cash. The 5.86% yield [P1] is a price-based figure and should not be read as proof of safety. A high yield on a falling price is often a warning, not a bargain. I need to see the quarters to know which story this is. If earnings are shrinking faster than the dividend, the cut may not be deep enough yet. If earnings are steady, the cut is prudence. I cannot tell from what is here.
data.concedes: The dividend history is a real record of what was paid.

data.headline: The book's composition matters more than the ratio.
data.text: Marks reads the price-to-book of 1.24 as the price's central assumption [P1]. I would step back and ask what the book is made of. A book value is an accounting construct, and its components matter. Is it mostly hard assets that can be sold, or goodwill that can be written down? The balance sheet that would answer this is absent from the pack. The modest leverage ratios in P2 — a debt-to-equity of 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.80 [P2] — are ratios without their dated operands. I concede leverage is not the visible problem in the figures that exist. But a negative return on equity of -15.37% [P2] means the equity is being consumed. If that continues, the book value shrinks, the debt-to-equity ratio rises, and what looks moderate today becomes strained. The machine is running in reverse, and without the balance sheet I cannot model how long it can run that way before something breaks.
data.concedes: Leverage is not the visible problem in the figures that exist.

data.headline: The peers cannot be compared on what is missing.
data.text: Alrumayyan rightly notes that no sector ranking exists for price-to-book, and I concede the peer list in P5 is a valid class of comparison companies. But the comparison breaks down on closer inspection. The peer data is dated 2026-08-07 and the quote is dated 2026-10-13 [P5][P1]. That is a two-month gap. More importantly, the peers carry P/E ratios — 15.4 for SABIC Agri-Nutrients, 32.58 for Maaden [P5] — while SABIC's own P/E is null [P1]. You cannot set a number against a blank. The price-to-book percentile is absent for SABIC in P2 [P2], so there is no ranking to read. What we have is a price-to-book of 1.24 [P1] with no benchmark, no peer comparison, and no single date. That is not a measurement; it is a number floating in space. The room should not treat it as a basis for anything.
data.concedes: The sector list is a valid class of comparison companies.

data.headline: The dividend cut itself is the fact that matters.
data.text: Lynch is right that the cut is visible, and I concede that without quarterly earnings I cannot show the dividend follows them. But the dividend step-down from 1.5 to 1.1 SAR per share is itself a fact [P3], and it is the fact that matters for the book-value question. A company that is losing money, as the -15.37% return on equity suggests [P2], and cutting its dividend is a company that is returning less to owners while its asset base shrinks. The book value of 41.18 SAR per share [P1] is the accounting equity, but the cash being paid out is falling. That tells me management sees less to distribute, whether or not the earnings window matches. The payout ratio that P9 would compute is absent, and I will not guess it. But the direction of the dividend is down, and that direction is consistent with a book value under pressure. Whether the price at 1.24 times that book is cheap depends on whether the pressure stops [P1].
data.concedes: Without quarterly earnings, I cannot show the dividend follows them.

data.headline: The company's own disclosure adds context to the loss.
data.text: Buffett is right that one published return is not a record of earning power, and I concede that. But the company's own disclosure adds context that the published ratios alone do not. On 2026-01-07, SABIC announced it would sell its Americas and Europe units and expects an SAR 18.3 billion non-cash loss [P6]. That is a material restructuring, and a non-cash loss of that size will affect the book value and the return on equity. The negative return on equity of -15.37% [P2] may be driven in part by this event, or it may be a pattern that predates it. I cannot say which, as the news item gives no earnings window. But the disclosure tells me the book value the market is pricing today is not a steady figure. A large reserve transfer of SAR 110.9 billion [P6] and a pending unit sale mean the 41.18 SAR per share [P1] is a number in motion. The price-to-book of 1.24 is a snapshot of a moving picture [P1].
data.concedes: One published return is not a record of earning power.

data.text: The pack shows a negative return on equity of -15.37% with no stated denominator or window [P2]. Without P9 I cannot say what earnings power sits behind the book value of 41.18 SAR per share [P1], and a book value that earns nothing is not an anchor I can lean on.
data.would_change: An income statement covering several windows, with return on common equity struck on a stated date.

data.text: Price has fallen over every window the pack shows — down 26.61% over one year and 62.55% over five [P7][P8] — but the quarterly record that would explain it is not here. I will not call it a trend in the business when I cannot count the quarters.
data.would_change: Reported quarters showing whether earnings fell in step with the price.

headline: Anaam's liquidity and coverage figures show it cannot meet short-term obligations from its own resources.
answer:
On what the pack shows, the room agrees that Anaam International Holding Group Company cannot cover its short-term obligations from its own resources. The current ratio is 0.18, at the 0.9th sector percentile [P2]. Interest coverage is -0.66x [P2]. Buffett and Marks add that debt-to-equity of 0.60 is not extreme on its face [P2], but Marks and Al-Rumayyan note that negative coverage makes it dangerous. ROE is -4.11% and ROA is -1.85% [P2]. Alwaleed adds a net margin of -49.91% [P2].

Financing history points the same way. No dividends are on record [P3]. A SAR 236.25 million rights issue was rejected by shareholders in 2024, and the board withdrew a SAR 105 million request in 2026 [P3]. Disposals are on record: the Wasit Saudi stake for SAR 38.2 million, with a first payment of SAR 25.2 million due within 30 days of signing, and a hotel for SAR 19.1 million [P6]. Lynch reads these as scrambling for liquidity. Al-Rumayyan notes the Wasit proceeds as a disclosed inflow.

What the pack cannot show: Lynch could not find the quarterly record he needs to say whether the position is worsening or improving. There are no debt maturity dates, as Dalio notes, no cash balance and no committed credit lines, and no free cash flow yield [P2]. The outcome of the June 2026 private offering is also not shown [P3].

No advisor ended with a different conclusion. The count of final leans is not supplied for this open session, and the answer rests on the figures above, not on a head count.
gaps: No dated balance sheet or cash balance shows whether the Wasit Saudi proceeds are reflected in the 0.18 current ratio [P2].
The pack holds no quarterly income or balance sheet series, so the direction of the liquidity trend cannot be read.
No debt maturity schedule or committed credit facility is shown, so the timing of any payment is unknown.

A null is not a confirmed result, and the pack holds no post-offering capital figure. Dalio is right that the 2026-08-12 ratios [P2] post-date the event, so the liquidity answer does not depend on it. Alwaleed, Buffett and Al-Rumayyan all moved to this reading.

Weight of the Wasit Saudi and hotel sales on liquidity - The disposals are disclosed [P6], but the pack gives no cash balance or balance sheet line showing how much proceeds were received. The current ratio of 0.18 [P2] is dated by the fundamentals as of 2026-08-12, after the April announcement, but the pack does not show whether the proceeds are in it.

Whether debt-to-equity of 0.60 is a separate risk [P2] - All sides read the same 0.60 at the 27.7th percentile [P2] and agree it is not extreme alone. They differ on how heavily to weigh it against interest coverage of -0.66x [P2]. Debt maturity dates, which would turn this into a fact, are absent.

data.headline: The data shows the company cannot meet short-term obligations from its own resources.
data.text:
The evidence in the pack is stark on this question, and I must also state clearly what the evidence does not tell us.

On the question of meeting short-term obligations, the critical figure is the current ratio, which is 0.18 [P2]. This means the company has only 18 halalas of current assets for every 1 riyal of current liabilities. It is the weakest metric in the entire sector, sitting in the 0.9th percentile among its peers [P2]. This is not a marginal shortfall; it indicates a fundamental inability to cover near-term obligations from its own liquid resources.

The interest coverage ratio is also negative, at -0.66x [P2]. This tells us the company's operating earnings are insufficient to service its existing debt costs, a condition that directly threatens its ability to meet any obligation, short-term or otherwise. While the debt-to-equity ratio of 0.60 [P2] is not extreme on its own, the inability to cover the cost of that debt makes the leverage dangerous.

I must also name what we do not know. The pack provides no free cash flow yield [P2], which is a gap in our understanding of its internal cash generation. Furthermore, while the company has a history of seeking capital through rights issues, the most recent attempts were cancelled [P3]. The last completed rights issue was in 2022 [P3], and a subsequent private offering in 2026 resulted in a -100% change, with the post-offering capital listed as null [P3]. The data does not show us the outcome of that offering, creating a significant gap in our view of the current capital structure.

The price action offers a confirming signal. The stock's maximum drawdown is -98.4% [P1], and it is down -71.8% over five years [P8]. This is not mere volatility; it is the market's verdict on a severely impaired capital position. My conclusion is that the data shows the company, on its own operating metrics, cannot meet its short-term obligations. The gaps in the data, particularly around the status of its recent financing activities, mean we cannot have full confidence, but what we can see is deeply concerning.

data.text:
The question is whether Anaam can meet its short-term obligations, so I look first at what it owes and what it has to pay with. The current ratio from [P2] is 0.18. That means for every riyal of liabilities coming due within a year, the company holds eighteen halalas of current assets. A corner shop with a current ratio of 0.18 is a corner shop that cannot pay its suppliers next week, and a public company is no different [P2]. The sector percentile for this ratio is 0.9, which says that almost every other consumer staple distributor on the exchange carries a stronger cushion [P2].

Next I ask what those obligations cost. The interest coverage ratio is negative 0.66 times [P2]. The company is not earning enough to service its debt; it is losing money before it even reaches the interest line. That is not a business that can borrow its way out of a squeeze, because a lender looks at the same numbers I do.

The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.60 [P2] is not extreme on its face, but it sits on an equity base that is itself shrinking. Return on equity is negative 4.11% and return on assets is negative 1.85% [P2]. Losses eat the capital that creditors count on. The book value stands at SAR 7.76 per share [P1], but that number is a snapshot and says nothing about how quickly the assets could be turned into cash if bills came due.

Nothing in the pack shows a committed line of credit or a cash balance I can verify. The last capital action was a private offering in June 2026 that reduced capital by 100%, and two rights issues before that were cancelled [P3]. The company has tried to raise money from shareholders and has not succeeded. The sale of a stake in Wasit Saudi for SAR 38.2 million was announced in April 2026 to improve the financial position in the second quarter [P6], but I have no balance sheet after that date to tell me whether the cash arrived or what it went to.

On what the pack shows, this company is losing money, carries next to no liquidity, and has no visible path to fresh capital. I can be confident in that reading. What I cannot tell is whether an asset sale or a white knight changes the picture tomorrow; the data here does not show it.

That is a distress signal, not a temporary tightness.

The interest coverage ratio is also negative, at -0.66x [P2]. The company is not generating enough operating profit to pay the interest on its debt, let alone the principal. This is consistent with a negative return on equity of -4.11% [P1] and a deeply negative net margin of -49.91% [P2]. The business is burning cash, not producing it.

My mandate is to look at what has been returned to owners and what has been done to the share count. The dividend history is empty; the company has paid nothing to shareholders [P3]. The payout ratio cannot be computed. The capital history is a story of repeated attempts to raise money and repair a damaged balance sheet. There was a massive 92.35% capital reduction in 2019 to absorb losses [P3]. Since then, there have been multiple rights issue attempts, most of which were cancelled, including a SAR 236.25 million rights issue rejected by shareholders in 2024 [P3]. A private offering in 2026 reduced the capital by 100% [P3]. This is a company that has repeatedly gone to shareholders and creditors for survival financing, and its most recent attempt to issue new equity was withdrawn [P3].

A strong franchise can survive a crisis, but the data here shows a franchise that is still in the crisis. The current ratio and negative coverage tell me the balance sheet cannot be relied upon to carry the company through. The data provides no confidence that short-term obligations can be met from existing resources.

What the company has disclosed reinforces the picture of a business selling assets to fund itself. The sector itself is populated by companies with positive earnings and established dividends: Nahdi Medical trades at a P/E of 15.88 with a 5.82% yield; Al-Othaim Markets at 20.66 with an 8.04% yield [P5]. data.text:

That means for every SAR 1.00 of short-term obligations, the company holds only SAR 0.18 in current assets [P1] [P2]. This is not a margin of safety; it is a shortfall. The current ratio sits at the 0.9th percentile in its sector [P2], meaning nearly every peer has a stronger near-term liquidity position.

How is the balance sheet funded? Total debt to equity is 0.60 [P2]. Creditors provide about SAR 0.60 for every SAR 1.00 from shareholders [P1] [P2]. That is not an extreme level of leverage on its face, but the coverage ratio tells the real story. Interest coverage is negative, at -0.66x [P2]. The company's operating profit does not cover its interest expense; it must draw on cash reserves or new financing just to service its debt. That is the point where funding becomes a problem. A negative coverage ratio means the company is burning cash to pay lenders, and with a current ratio of 0.18, the cash buffer to absorb this burn is already thin [P2].

The scenario that breaks this funding is any further tightening of cash flow. If the recent asset sales, like the stake in Wasit Saudi [P6], do not provide enough cash to bridge the gap, or if operating losses persist, the company would need to raise new capital or restructure its debt. The data does not show the specific maturity dates of the debt, so I cannot say when a wall of payments is due, only that the company cannot meet its current obligations from its current liquid assets. The negative ROE of -4.11% and ROA of -1.85% [P2] confirm the business itself is not generating the cash to fix this; it is a machine that is consuming capital, not producing it.

Next, can it even service its debt? The interest coverage ratio is -0.66 [P2]. That's a negative number. It means the company's operating profit doesn't even cover its interest payments. It's not just unable to pay down the principal; it's losing money before the interest bill is paid. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.60 [P2] is manageable on its own, but when you can't cover the interest, the size of the debt becomes a much bigger problem.

What's the story the market is telling me? The 12-month price return is down -20.66% [P1], and the 5-year return is down -71.81% [P8]. The price has been telling a bad story for a long time. The quarterly record isn't in my pack, so I can't pinpoint the exact quarter things turned, but the annual trend is clear.

Finally, where's the cash? The company has no dividends on record [P3]. It tried a rights issue to raise SAR 236.25 million, but shareholders rejected it [P6]. It then tried another rights issue for SAR 105 million, and the board withdrew that request itself [P3]. The company is selling assets—a hotel for SAR 19.1 million and a stake in a subsidiary for SAR 38.2 million [P6]—which tells me it's scrambling for liquidity.

Putting it all together, the data shows a company with a dangerously low current ratio, negative interest coverage, and no success in raising new equity. The story the numbers tell is not one of a company that can comfortably meet its short-term obligations. I'm confident in that reading based on what's here.

data.headline: The private offering data gap matters more than Alwaleed allows
data.text: Alwaleed reads the June 2026 private offering as a 100% capital reduction and a failed attempt to raise funds [P1]. I am not sure the data supports that conclusion. The pack shows a change_pct of -100.0 and a capital_after_mn of null [P3]. A null is not a result; it is a gap. I cannot tell from this whether the offering closed, whether it was cancelled, or whether the post-offering capital simply has not been filed yet. Alwaleed treats it as a completed reduction, but the data does not give me a number to anchor that reading. My own answer said the company tried to raise money and has not succeeded, and I stand by that on the two cancelled rights issues. But I cannot say the private offering failed when the pack does not show me the outcome. The current ratio of 0.18 and negative interest coverage of -0.66 are bad enough on their own [P2]; I do not need to fill a gap to make the case. I would rather say plainly that the data here does not show what happened in June 2026 than treat a null as a fact [P1].
data.concedes: Alwaleed is right that the cancelled rights issues and the 2019 capital reduction show a long pattern of balance sheet repair, and that pattern matters [P3].

data.headline: The 2026 private offering is a data gap, not a confirmed result [P1]
data.text: Buffett, you state that the last capital action was a private offering that reduced capital by 100%, implying a completed transaction [P1]. But the data tells a different story. The entry in [P3] shows a change_pct of -100.0, but the capital_after_mn is listed as null. A null value is not a result; it is an absence of data. I must say plainly that the pack does not show us what happened to the capital base after that June 2026 date [P1]. It could mean the offering was completed and reduced capital to zero, or it could mean the data source has not yet reported the outcome. We do not know, and the room's confidence must not run ahead of its evidence on this point. The current ratio of 0.18 and the negative interest coverage of -0.66x [P2] are themselves sufficient to answer the member's question, without leaning on a figure that the pack itself leaves blank.

The gap you identify is in the historical record, not in the current financial position we are analyzing.

data.headline: Anaam's liquidity and coverage figures show it cannot meet short-term obligations from its own resources.
data.answer:
On what the pack shows, the room agrees that Anaam International Holding Group Company cannot cover its short-term obligations from its own resources. The current ratio is 0.18, at the 0.9th sector percentile [P2]. Interest coverage is -0.66x [P2]. Buffett and Marks add that debt-to-equity of 0.60 is not extreme on its face [P2], but Marks and Al-Rumayyan note that negative coverage makes it dangerous. ROE is -4.11% and ROA is -1.85% [P2]. Alwaleed adds a net margin of -49.91% [P2].

Financing history points the same way. No dividends are on record [P3]. A SAR 236.25 million rights issue was rejected by shareholders in 2024, and the board withdrew a SAR 105 million request in 2026 [P3]. Disposals are on record: the Wasit Saudi stake for SAR 38.2 million, with a first payment of SAR 25.2 million due within 30 days of signing, and a hotel for SAR 19.1 million [P6]. Lynch reads these as scrambling for liquidity. Al-Rumayyan notes the Wasit proceeds as a disclosed inflow.

What the pack cannot show: Lynch could not find the quarterly record he needs to say whether the position is worsening or improving. There are no debt maturity dates, as Dalio notes, no cash balance and no committed credit lines, and no free cash flow yield [P2]. The outcome of the June 2026 private offering is also not shown [P3].

No advisor ended with a different conclusion. The count of final leans is not supplied for this open session, and the answer rests on the figures above, not on a head count.

headline: Ratios point to thin short-term cover, but the statements needed to confirm it are missing.
answer: On what the pack shows, the evidence leans toward weak short-term cover, though it cannot confirm it. The balance sheet, income statement and quarterly data are not in the pack, so no date, window or operand behind any ratio can be named. The ratios that remain are Dalio's: a current ratio of 0.18 [P2] at sector percentile 0.9 [P2], interest coverage of -0.66 times [P2] and debt to equity of 0.60 [P2]. Buffett adds that return on equity of -4.11 % [P2] and a net margin of -49.91 % [P2] show no earning power to fall back on, and that no denominator or window is disclosed. Alwaleed notes that no dividends have been paid [P3], and that a SAR 105 million rights issue was withdrawn on 2026-04-20 and a SAR 236.25 million offering rejected on 2024-07-30 [P3]. Al-Rumayyan cites the sale of the Wasit Saudi stake for 38.18 million riyals, announced 2026-04-11 [P6]; it is a real source of funds, but the pack does not show it arriving or what it did to cash. Lynch could count no quarters, so there is no trend to report; the price fell -25.95 % over the year [P7]. Marks flags that price-to-book of 1.53 [P1] does not itself show distress or comfort. The room therefore agrees the visible liquidity measures are weak, and that the evidence for any firmer conclusion is absent.
gaps: The balance sheet with its date, showing cash, short-term debt and current liabilities.
The income statement and quarters, showing windows and the trend in operating cash.
The effect of the 2026-04-11 stake sale proceeds on cash [P1].
disagreements: Whether the asset sale closed the liquidity gap - The pack holds no cash balance or current liabilities after the 2026-04-11 sale [P6], so it cannot show whether 38.18 million riyals covered the shortfall implied by a current ratio of 0.18 [P2].
How much weight the liquidity ratios can carry - The operands and date behind the current ratio of 0.18 and coverage of -0.66 [P2] are in the balance sheet and income statement, which are absent.
Whether the price fall signals stress - Both read the same price fall of -25.95 % [P7] and the same capital history [P3]; they differ on which to weight, which is a matter of judgment.

data.headline: The business is not earning on its capital, and the income statement is absent.
data.text: The question is whether the company can meet its short-term obligations, but I am answerable for earning power, and the income statement and its calculations are not in the pack, so I cannot name a window or a denominator. What the pack does show is return on equity of -4.11 % [P2], return on assets of -1.85 % [P2], return on invested capital of -2.00 % [P2] and a net margin of -49.91 % [P2]. These are negative, so the business is not earning on its capital. The published return on equity does not disclose its denominator, and a single window is not a record — I cannot even tell how many windows these figures cover. A business that burns capital rather than compounding it is a poor place to look for the cash to pay bills. The gross margin is 56.31 % [P2], which shows the product itself has some value, but the net margin tells you the costs around it eat up everything and more. Without the income statement I cannot see whether those costs are fixed or variable, or whether any of them are non-cash charges that would leave room to pay creditors. I can only say the earnings do not cover the cost of the capital employed, and that is the first thing I look at before I even ask about liquidity. If the business cannot earn, every short-term obligation is a claim on assets, not on cash flow, and that is a different and harder question.

data.headline: I count zero quarters, so I cannot call anything a trend.
data.text: I am answerable for the trend, and the quarters are not in the pack, so I count zero quarters and call nothing a trend. The market's reading in [P7] is a fall of -25.95 % over the year, from a first close of 16.3 to a last close of 12.07 [P7]. The one-year low close was 9.44 [P7]. A falling price suggests the story is not being believed, but it cannot tell us whether liquidity is improving or worsening. A price chart is the market's mood, not the company's checkbook. To answer the member's question I would want to see revenue and operating profit quarter by quarter, and I would want to see the current assets and current liabilities laid out over the same stretch. Is inventory building up? Are receivables growing faster than sales? Those are the clues that tell you whether a company is about to run short of cash. Without the quarters, I have no trend to report and no way to say whether the business is getting stronger or weaker. The annual figures in [P2] show a net margin of -49.91 %, which is a loss-making story, but one bad year is not the same as a business that cannot pay its bills. I need the sequence to know which one this is.

data.headline: A current ratio of 0.18 and negative interest coverage are red flags [P2].
data.text: I am answerable for the balance sheet, and the statement itself is absent, so I cannot give the date of the position. The ratios that remain are a current ratio of 0.18 [P2], at sector percentile 0.9 [P2], and interest coverage of -0.66 times [P2], at percentile 14.9 [P2]. Debt to equity is 0.60 [P2], at percentile 27.7 [P2], and the health group score is 14.5 [P2]. A current ratio of 0.18 suggests short-term assets are a small fraction of short-term liabilities [P2]. In the machine I picture, that means for every riyal of obligations due within a year, the company holds only 0.18 riyals in assets it can turn into cash quickly [P2]. The negative coverage tells us operations do not generate enough to pay the interest bill, let alone the principal. The scenario that hurts most is one where short-term liabilities fall due before any asset-sale proceeds arrive. The company sold a hotel in 2024 for 19.11 million riyals and a stake in Wasit Saudi in April 2026 for 38.18 million riyals [P6], so it is turning assets into cash. But those are lumpy, one-off events, not a steady machine. If a creditor demands payment and the next sale has not closed, the machine seizes. Without the full balance sheet I cannot see the maturity profile of the debt or the composition of current assets, so I cannot weigh the probability of that scenario. I can only say the ratios we have point to a tight position.

data.headline: The price does not assume distress, but the gaps are large.
data.text: I am answerable for what is priced in and what we do not know. The price is 12.07 SAR with a market cap of 370.13 million SAR [P1], and price-to-book is 1.53 [P1] with book value of 7.76 [P1]. That suggests the market is not pricing in distress at book value — a price-to-book above one says the market thinks the assets are worth at least what the books say. But that does not show obligations can be met; it shows only that the market is not yet treating the company as a liquidation. The gaps are large. P/E, EV/EBITDA and trailing earnings per share are null [P1], the free cash flow yield is not applicable to the sector [P2], and the income statement, balance sheet, quarters, calculations and limitations are all absent. Over five years the close fell from 42.82 to 12.07, a -71.81 % change [P8]. A price that has fallen that far has already discounted a great deal of bad news. The question is whether it has discounted enough. Without the balance sheet I cannot answer that. The current ratio of 0.18 [P2] is a warning that the market may be giving too much credit to the book value. Assets on a balance sheet are not cash in the bank, and if they cannot be turned into cash in time, the book value is an accounting figure, not a safety net. The room should be humble about what it cannot see.

data.headline: No dividends, and owners have declined to supply new capital.
data.text: I am answerable for what was returned to owners. The dividend list is empty [P3] and the dividend yield is null [P1], so nothing has been paid out and no payout could be matched to earnings. That is not surprising when the business is losing money. What concerns me more is the capital story. On 2026-04-20 the board withdrew a rights issue of SAR 105 million and said it would reassess financing options to support operations [P3]. Shareholders also rejected a SAR 236.25 million rights offering on 2024-07-30 [P3]. Operations are therefore dependent on funding that owners have declined to supply or that was withdrawn. A company that cannot earn and cannot raise equity is left with two choices: sell assets or borrow. It has been selling assets — the hotel for 19.11 million riyals in 2024 and the Wasit Saudi stake for 38.18 million in 2026 [P6]. But asset sales are a shrinking pool. The capital history shows a pattern of rights issues and reductions: the capital was cut from 1,200 million to 109 million in 2007, then raised, then cut again from 196 million to 15 million in 2019 [P3]. The current capital is 315 million SAR [P3]. A company that has repeatedly asked owners for money and been refused is a company whose owners have already answered the question about short-term obligations: they are not willing to be the ones who meet them.

data.headline: The company ranks at the bottom of its sector on key metrics.

data.headline: Peer rank does not show ability to pay bills.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, the peer list is useful context for how profitable the sector's other names are, and I concede that point. But a rank among peers does not answer whether this company can meet its short-term obligations. The net margin of -49.91 % sits at sector percentile 6.5 [P2], while the gross margin of 56.31 % ranks at 81.1 [P2]. The gap between those two figures is the story. The product itself commands a good price relative to its direct cost, but the costs below the gross line — selling, general, administrative, interest, perhaps depreciation — eat up every riyal and more. The pack cannot tell me which of those costs are fixed and which are variable, or whether any are non-cash charges that would leave room to pay creditors. A business that loses money on every riyal of sales after covering the cost of goods is a business whose short-term obligations are a claim on assets, not on operations. That is a harder question, and the peer list does not answer it.
