data.headline: A falling price is a clue, not proof of stress.
data.text: Marks, you are right that the missing statements limit every conclusion in the room, and I concede that. But a price that fell -25.95 % over a year [P7] is still a clue worth reading. It does not prove the company cannot pay its bills, and I never said it did. A price chart is the market's mood, not the company's checkbook. The price-to-book of 1.53 [P1] tells me the market is still paying above book value, which is not what you see when the crowd thinks a default is coming. But without quarterly data I cannot say whether the decline reflects obligations coming due or just poor earnings. A company can lose money for years and still pay its bills if it has cash or assets to sell. The one-year low close was 9.44 [P7], and the price is now 12.07 [P1], so the market has already seen worse and pulled back. That is a mood swing, not a balance sheet. data.text: Al-Rumayyan, the sale is a real source of funds, and I concede that the second instalment of 3.25 million riyals falls due a year after signing [P6]. headline: Quarterly dividends sum to a steady annual figure; the pack's own yield is the one it states.
answer:
The dividend records show Q3 2025 at SAR 0.33 per share, then Q4 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 each at SAR 0.34 [P3]. Those four quarters add to SAR 1.35 per share, the annual figure on these records. The pack states no annual dividend per share of its own; this is arithmetic on its per-share records. The pack's stated dividend yield is 5.01% [P1][P2], struck against a last price of SAR 25.78 dated 2026-10-13 [P1]. Buffett began at SAR 1.34 and Alwaleed wrote SAR 1.36 in his opening line. Both corrected to SAR 1.35 once the Q4 2025 record was checked [P3].

The room agrees on the quarterly pattern and on quoting the pack's 5.01% yield [P1]. Lynch notes no cuts and one small step up from SAR 0.33 to SAR 0.34 [P3]. Al-Rumayyan notes that 5.01% is the highest yield among the Energy peers listed, against Bahri at 3.22% and ADES at 2.48% [P5].

What the data cannot tell is how the pack built its 5.01% [P1]. SAR 1.35 against SAR 25.78 does not reproduce it, and the pack gives no calculation basis [P1]. It also cannot tell whether earnings or cash cover the dividend. Buffett set the dividend against EPS of SAR 1.84 [P1], but Marks observed that the payout ratio and free-cash-flow yield are listed as missing [P2]. The rulings below take each disputed point in turn.
gaps: The pack does not show how its 5.01% dividend yield was calculated or which dividends it covers [P1].
The pack gives no payout ratio or free-cash-flow figure matched to the dividend's period, so coverage cannot be judged.
The income statement and full balance sheet are not in the pack, so the earnings and funding behind the dividend cannot be read directly.
disagreements: Whether to quote the pack's 5.01% yield or a self-computed one [P1] - The pack gives 5.01% [P1][P2] but no calculation basis and no annual dividend per share, so the gap to a hand-computed yield cannot be reconciled. The pack's figure is the only stated yield; its construction is not shown.

Whether earnings or cash cover the dividend - Payout and free-cash-flow yield are missing in [P2]. Buffett's payout inference from EPS of SAR 1.84 [P1] cannot be confirmed because the earnings window behind that EPS is not shown.

data.headline: Trailing four quarters sum to SAR 1.34 per share, yielding 5.01% at the last price [P1].
data.text:
I read the machine by looking at the flows that reach the shareholder. The dividend records in [P3] show four quarterly payments that together make up the most recent trailing twelve months. The latest four announced dividends are Q2 2026 at SAR 0.34 per share (announced 2026-08-04), Q1 2026 at SAR 0.34 (2026-05-10), Q4 2025 at SAR 0.34 (2026-03-10), and Q3 2025 at SAR 0.33 (2025-11-04) [P1] [P3]. Summing these gives an annual dividend per share of SAR 1.35. I note that the Q3 2025 payment of SAR 0.33 included a performance-linked component of SAR 820 million, while the three subsequent payments of SAR 0.34 did not carry that note, suggesting the base dividend has been raised slightly [P3]. The yield the pack provides in [P1] and [P2] is 5.01%, and that is the only yield figure the data gives us; it is computed on the trailing dividend the pack's own engine used, which may differ slightly from my simple sum if the engine used a different trailing window or adjusted for the ex-date timing. The last price used for that yield is SAR 25.78 as of 2026-10-13 [P1].

My mandate is the balance sheet and what would put its funding under strain. The fundamentals in [P2] give a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20, which is low and sits at the 54th sector percentile, and a current ratio of 2.00 at the 68th percentile. data.headline: Yield is 5.01%, but coverage and capital are unknown here [P1].
data.text:
The published dividend yield for Saudi Aramco is 5.01% [P1]. That is the figure the data gives us, and it is a useful starting point. But a yield is only as good as the earnings that support it, and the income statement and its calculations are not in the pack. I cannot see what the dividend was paid out of, or on what capital it was earned.

Return on equity is published at 26.75% [P2], which looks strong at a glance. But the data does not disclose the denominator used for that ROE, and the pack's own note says so on its face. Without the balance sheet and income statement, I cannot strike my own return on the common equity, and I cannot say whether that 26.75% is real or a figure that mixes two dates [P1].

What I can say is what was declared. The dividend list shows 0.34 SAR per share for Q2 2026, 0.34 for Q1 2026, 0.34 for Q4 2025, and 0.33 for Q3 2025 [P3]. Those are quarterly declarations, not an annual figure, and I will not add them myself into something the pack does not give. The payout ratio against a matched earnings window is not in the pack either, so I cannot tell you whether these dividends are covered by the earnings of the same period.

A yield of 5.01% on a last price of 25.78 SAR [P1] is what the market sees. Whether it is sustainable is a question the data here does not answer.

data.text:
The dividend yield is 5.01% [P1], and the last price is 25.78 SAR [P1]. The P/E is 14.47 [P1]. Those two numbers together tell me the market is paying about 14.5 times earnings for a 5% yield, which on its face is not an unreasonable combination. But I cannot do my real work here, because the quarterly earnings record is not in the pack.

I can see the dividend pattern. The company declared 0.34 SAR per share for Q2 2026, 0.34 for Q1 2026, 0.34 for Q4 2025, and 0.33 for Q3 2025 [P3]. That is four quarters of fairly steady payments, with a small step up from 0.33 to 0.34 [P3]. In 2024 the quarterly amounts were 0.48, including large performance-linked dividends [P3]. So the run rate has come down, but the base dividend has been stable.

What I cannot do is count the quarters of earnings and call a trend. The quarterly income statement is not here. I cannot say whether earnings are growing, shrinking, or holding steady. I cannot compare the P/E to the earnings growth rate, because I have no growth rate. The price moved 3.16% over the past year [P7], but price without earnings is half the story.

If the earnings were in front of me, I would look at whether the dividend is covered quarter by quarter, and whether the earnings trend supports the current payout. Without that, I can only say the dividend history looks consistent, and the yield is what it is.

data.text:
The dividend yield is 5.01% [P1]. That is a flow to shareholders, and to understand what it means I need to see the balance sheet it flows from. The balance sheet is not in the pack, so I cannot give you a position date or say how the funding of this company would be strained.

What I do have are two health metrics. The debt to equity is 0.200619170560779, and the current ratio is 1.9985889009180524 [P2]. Those numbers suggest a company that is not heavily borrowed and has short-term assets roughly twice its short-term obligations. But I cannot see the operands behind them, or the date the balance sheet was struck. A ratio without its components is a summary without the story.

The dividend company total for Q2 2026 is 82,060.0 million SAR [P3]. That is a cash outflow I would normally set against the cash and debt lines on the balance sheet, and against the operating cash flow from the income statement. None of those lines are here. I cannot tell you whether the dividend is being paid out of free cash flow, out of borrowing, or out of asset sales.

In a scenario where revenue falls, the question is whether the balance sheet can absorb the shock while still paying this dividend. The debt-to-equity figure suggests some room, but without the absolute amounts of debt and cash, and without knowing the maturity profile, I am guessing. The machine is missing too many parts.

data.headline: Declared amounts are real, but durability is unproven
data.text: Alwaleed, the quarterly per-share amounts in the dividend list are indeed the right starting point. I have no quarrel with them as declarations. But a list of declarations is not a record of earning power. The step from 0.48 per share in 2024 to 0.33 in 2025 [P3] tells us the payout is not fixed, and the performance-linked portion fell from 40,390 million SAR to 820 million SAR [P3]. That is a meaningful change in what the business chose to distribute. Without a matched earnings window I cannot say whether the current 0.34 [P3] is covered by the earnings of the same period, or whether it rests on capital that was earned in a different year. One published yield of 5.01% [P1] is a single figure, not a record I can hang a judgment on. A durable dividend is one that can be paid through a bad year without strain. The data here does not let me test that.
data.concedes: The quarterly per-share amounts in the dividend list are the right starting point.

data.headline: Four steady quarters is a fact, not a forecast
data.text: Marks, I take your point about the earlier cut. The 0.48 per share in 2024 [P3] is a different animal, and I cannot pretend it is not there. But what I am looking at is the last four declarations: 0.33, 0.34, 0.34, 0.34 [P3]. That is four quarters of payments that barely moved. Four data points is not a long trend, and I will not call it one. It is four points, and they are steady. If I had the quarterly earnings to set against them, I could say whether the business is earning its way into that steadiness or just holding the payout flat while earnings wobble. I do not have those quarters, so I cannot. The yield basis is uncertain, as you say. But the dividend pattern over the most recent stretch is not erratic. It is the one piece of the story I can read from the data we have.
data.concedes: The earlier cut from 0.48 [P3] means the steadiness is recent only.

data.headline: The bond issuance cannot be linked to dividends
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you rightly note the disclosures. The $4 billion bond issuance dated 2026-02-02 [P6] is a fact. But the pack does not tell us what that debt funded. It could have refinanced maturing obligations, funded the Jafurah gas processing deal, or gone into general corporate purposes. The summary says nothing about dividends. To draw a line from that issuance to the dividend payout would be inference, not reading the data. The machine works by tracing flows: cash in, cash out, and the obligations between them. Without the balance sheet I cannot see the cash position before or after the issuance, and without the income statement I cannot see the operating cash flow that funds the dividend. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 [P2] suggests room on the balance sheet, but I do not know the absolute debt level or its maturity. The dividend and the bond are two separate parts of a machine whose other parts are not in the pack.
data.concedes: The disclosures confirm the company has market access.

data.headline: Four points do not make a steady dividend
data.text: Lynch, the last four declared amounts are close together, I grant you that. But four quarters is a short window, and the step from 0.48 per share in 2024 to 0.33 in 2025 [P3] sits right behind it. A dividend that was nearly fifty percent higher two years ago is not steady; it is recently stabilised after a cut. Calling it steady on four points ignores the larger arc. And the yield of 5.01% [P1] depends on a price whose basis is not disclosed and a quote flagged stale as of 2026-10-13 [P1]. I do not know whether that yield uses the last price, an average, or something else. A yield is a ratio, and the denominator matters as much as the numerator. We are being asked to read a figure whose components we cannot verify. That is not a small gap. It is the gap that sits between what the data shows and what we are being asked to conclude.
data.concedes: The last four declared amounts are close together.

data.headline: The step-down is documented, not a mystery
data.text: Buffett, you are right that I cannot show you a matched payout ratio, and I will not pretend otherwise. But the per-share declarations stand on their own, and the reason for the step-down is in the data. The 2024 amounts of 0.48 per share included performance-linked dividends of 40,390 million SAR in Q3 2024 alone [P3]. By 2025 that performance-linked portion had fallen to 820 million SAR [P3]. The base dividend actually edged up from 0.33 to 0.34 [P3]. That is a documented fact, not an inference. The company chose to return less of the windfall and hold the base. Whether that base is covered by current earnings is a question the data does not answer, and I concede that freely. But the story of what happened to the dividend is in the dividend list itself. The performance-linked piece shrank, and the ordinary piece held. That is what the numbers say.
data.concedes: Without a matched payout I cannot say whether earnings covered the amounts.

data.headline: The peer comparison is loose, and I accept that
data.text: Marks, you are right to point out the dates. The peer yields come from a sector file dated 2026-08-07 [P5], while the quote I used for the yield is dated 2026-10-13 [P1]. Those are two different moments, and I should not have set them side by side without noting the gap. The peers themselves are also much smaller companies. The National Shipping Company has a market cap of 27,906.98 million SAR, and ADES Holding is at 19,973.07 million SAR [P5], against Aramco's 6,413,000 million SAR [P1]. Comparing yields across companies of such different scale is loose at best. What I can say without stretching the data is that Aramco paid a dividend in every quarter shown, and the base amount held steady at 0.34 for the last three declarations [P3]. The peer list confirms that few others in the sector pay anything at all. That much is clear.
data.concedes: The yield comparison mixes dates and very different company sizes.

data.headline: No, bonus issues break comparability; dividends show steady per-share growth.
data.text:
No, they are not comparable across the whole period without adjustment, and the reason is right in the capital changes I am answerable for [P3]. The company issued bonus shares twice: a 25% bonus in May 2022, and a 20% bonus in May 2023 [P3]. When a company gives you one extra share for every ten you hold, the per-share figures before that date are not the same as the ones after. The earnings and dividends from 2022 are spread over more shares today, so a straight comparison makes the old numbers look bigger than they really were on the current share count [P3]. The secondary offering in June 2024 did not change the capital, so it does not affect per-share comparability [P3].

Now look at what was actually paid. The dividends show a clear pattern: the quarterly dividend per share increased from SAR 0.33 to SAR 0.34 in the most recent quarters, and before that it was SAR 0.48 [P3]. That is a cut, but the notes tell you the earlier SAR 0.48 included a large performance-linked component, while the current SAR 0.34 is the base dividend with only a small top-up [P3]. The base dividend is growing. The company has paid every quarter without fail in the history shown, and the total amounts are enormous—over SAR 80 billion each quarter [P3]. This is a sign of confidence from a company that thinks like an owner.

The data pack does not provide the payout ratio computed against the matched earnings window, so I cannot tell you what fraction of profits this represents. That is a gap, and it matters because a dividend paid out of borrowed money is not the same as one paid from earnings. But the direction is clear: the per-share payout is edging up, and the bonus issues mean every shareholder now holds more shares than they did in 2022 [P3]. That is a return of value, even if the raw per-share figures need the bonus ratio applied to make them speak the same language.

data.headline: No, bonus shares changed the per-share basis, requiring adjustment for comparability.
data.text:
The per-share figures in the pack are not directly comparable across the full period covered because of two bonus share issues that altered the share count without a corresponding change in the company's underlying equity. The machine here is straightforward: when the number of shares changes, any metric quoted 'per share' is mechanically reset, making a simple comparison across the event misleading.

Looking at the capital changes in [P3], we see two key events. On 2022-05-12, the company issued bonus shares at a rate of 1 for every 10, increasing the capital from SAR 60,000.00 million to SAR 75,000.00 million [P3]. Then, on 2023-05-08, another bonus issue at the same 1-for-10 rate increased the capital further from SAR 75,000.00 million to SAR 90,000.00 million [P3]. Each of these events increased the number of shares outstanding by 20% and 20% respectively, cumulatively increasing the share count by 50% from the pre-2022 base [P3] [P4]. A per-share metric like earnings per share (EPS) of SAR 1.84, which is a trailing twelve-month figure as of the latest date [P1], is calculated on the current share count. This figure cannot be directly compared to a dividend per share (DPS) from, say, Q1 2024, which was SAR 0.48 [P3], without knowing if the EPS figure has been retrospectively adjusted by the data provider, which the pack does not state.

My mandate is to examine the balance sheet, and this question cuts to the core of how it is funded. The equity base was expanded not by new cash but by capitalizing SAR 15.00 billion of retained earnings in each bonus issue [P3]. This is a cosmetic change to the equity account, moving funds from retained earnings to share capital. It does not reflect new money coming into the business. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 [P2] and book value per share of SAR 6.49 [P1] are struck at a point after these changes. The risk is that an investor looking at a long-term chart of book value per share would see a mechanical drop at each bonus issue date, mistaking it for value destruction. The data here does not provide adjusted per-share figures for prior periods, so I can only flag the break and state that direct comparison is not valid. The confidence in this assessment is high, as the capital change events are clearly dated and quantified.

data.headline: No; bonus shares and a large secondary offering break direct per-share comparability.
data.text:
The per-share figures in the pack are not directly comparable across the full period it covers. The data records two bonus share issues and a substantial secondary offering, all of which alter the share count and therefore the per-share metrics without a corresponding change in the company's underlying value at the time of the event.

Specifically, the capital changes in [P3] show a 20% bonus issue (1 for 10 shares) in May 2023, which increased the capital from SAR 75.00 billion to SAR 90.00 billion, and a 25% bonus issue (also 1 for 10 shares) in May 2022, increasing capital from SAR 60.00 billion to SAR 75.00 billion. These are scrip issues that mechanically dilute all per-share figures—earnings, dividends, and book value—from before those dates. An investor comparing today's trailing EPS of SAR 1.84 [P1] to a figure from 2022 would be misled unless the historical number is adjusted for these issues.

Furthermore, in June 2024, the Saudi Government sold 1.545 billion shares, representing 0.64% of the company's total shares, in a secondary offering at SAR 27.25 per share [P3]. While this did not change the company's total capital, it increased the public float and the number of shares trading, which can influence market-based per-share metrics like trading volume and price dynamics.

Regarding my own mandate, the peer comparison in [P5] shows Saudi Aramco's scale is in a different league, with a market cap of SAR 6,413,000 million versus the next largest peer, Bahri, at SAR 27,906.98 million. This weight matters. On disclosures, the company has been active, communicating a share buyback for an employee plan, a $4 billion bond issuance, and the strategic $11 billion Jafurah gas processing deal with BlackRock's GIP [P6]. These actions, dated from early to mid-2026, signal a company actively managing its capital structure and investing in its long-term gas strategy, which is the kind of sector-building commitment I look for [P1].

data.headline: They are broadly comparable, but bonus shares require the reader to adjust perspective.
data.text:
The member asks a question that goes to the heart of analysis: can we trust the numbers to mean the same thing over time? Looking at the data, the answer is nuanced.

The per-share figures in [P1], such as the EPS of 1.84 and book value of 6.49, are current metrics. Their comparability backward is directly affected by the capital changes detailed in [P3]. The company issued bonus shares twice: a 20% increase in May 2023 and a 25% increase in May 2022 [P3]. A standard data provider will retroactively adjust prior per-share data to reflect these splits, making the series comparable on a like-for-like basis. However, the pack does not state this explicitly, and we must note the gap: we do not see the historical EPS or book value series to confirm the adjustment was made [P9].

A more subtle point is the secondary offering in June 2024 [P3]. This increased the number of shares outstanding by 0.64% without a corresponding increase in the company's assets [P3]. This means the pie was sliced into slightly more pieces; the current share count of 242 billion is the denominator for today's per-share figures, but any historical per-share data from before that date would have been based on a slightly smaller share count. The difference is minor but real.

What this price has to be assuming is that the earnings power and book value are stable enough to make the current P/E of 14.47 and P/B of 4.1 [P1] defensible. What we do not know is the full historical context for these multiples. The five-year price summary shows a decline of 10.52% from a close of 28.81 to 25.78 [P8], a period that encompasses both bonus issues. This decline, alongside a maximum drawdown of over 40% [P1], tells me the pendulum of market sentiment has swung from optimism to something more cautious. The current valuation may be less demanding than it once was, but without the historical P/E and P/B bands—a key limitation [P9]—we cannot quantify how much of that caution is now embedded in the price.

data.headline: The share count changed three times; per-share figures are not directly comparable.
data.text:
The per-share figures are not comparable across the whole period because the number of shares outstanding changed materially, and the pack tells us exactly when and by how much. I count three capital changes that affect the share base [P3]. In May 2022, a 1-for-10 bonus issue increased the capital by 25%, from SAR 60,000 million to SAR 75,000 million [P1] [P3]. In May 2023, another 1-for-10 bonus issue increased it by 20%, from SAR 75,000 million to SAR 90,000 million [P1] [P3]. Then, in June 2024, the government sold 1.545 billion existing shares in a secondary offering; the company's total capital stayed at SAR 90,000 million, but the float increased by 0.64% [P3].

What does this mean for the numbers? Any per-share figure—earnings, book value, dividends—calculated before a bonus issue counts more shares today than it did back then. The 2022 bonus alone means one old share is now 1.10 shares; after the 2023 bonus, one pre-2022 share is 1.32 shares [P3]. The dividend history shows this plainly. The quarterly dividend per share was SAR 0.48 in early 2024, then dropped to SAR 0.33 from Q4 2024 through Q1 2026, and just ticked up to SAR 0.34 in Q2 2026 [P3]. That drop is not a cut—the bonus shares simply spread the same total payout over more shares. The total amount paid each quarter, around SAR 80–116 billion, tells the real story of the cash being returned.

The valuation sheet gives us a book value of SAR 6.49 and an EPS of SAR 1.84 [P1]. Those numbers are correct for today's share count—242,000 million shares [P1]—but you cannot line them up against a pre-bonus EPS from an old report without adjusting. The pack does not give us restated historical per-share figures, so I cannot do the adjustment myself. The quarterly record I am answerable for [P7] shows the price moving from a close of SAR 28.81 five years ago to SAR 25.78 today [P8], but that price series already reflects the bonus issues because the exchange adjusts historical prices downward on the ex-date. So the price chart is comparable; the per-share fundamentals are not, unless you restate them yourself. That is the story the numbers tell.

data.headline: The bonus issues break direct per-share comparability; adjust for them.
data.text:
The per-share figures are not directly comparable across the whole period the pack covers, and the reason sits in the capital-changes table [P3]. In May 2022 the company gave shareholders one new share for every ten held (a 20% increase in shares outstanding), and in May 2023 it gave another one for every ten (a further 25% increase on the already-higher base) [P3]. Both were bonus shares, funded by capitalising retained earnings, so the number of shares a single certificate represented grew while the underlying equity was simply re-labelled, not enlarged by new money.

When you compare an earnings-per-share figure from before those dates with one from after, you are dividing the same or similar total earnings by a larger number of shares. The older per-share number will look higher than it would if it were restated for the bonus, and the newer one will look smaller than it would if the bonus had never happened. The data pack does not itself restate the older periods; the EPS of 1.84 reported in [P1] is a trailing twelve-month figure struck after the last bonus, so it already reflects the current share count, but it cannot be laid side-by-side with a pre-2023 EPS taken at face value.

A secondary offering by the government in June 2024 did not change the number of shares outstanding – it merely moved some from one owner to another – so that event does not disturb per-share comparability [P3]. The bonus issues are the only capital changes that do. For my own work I would want to see the old per-share numbers recast as if the bonus had already happened, but that work is not in the pack we have. What we can say is that the dividend-per-share record shows a steady 0.33 to 0.34 SAR per quarter in recent periods, all paid after the last bonus, so those figures are comparable among themselves [P3].

Turning to my own part of the evidence, the return on equity published in [P2] is 26.75%, but the pack does not disclose the denominator used for that number. The balance sheet in [P9] is absent – that dataset holds an error for this company – so I cannot strike an ROE myself on a stated date using common equity. The same missing balance sheet means I cannot read the debt-to-equity ratio or the current ratio with my own eyes, though [P2] reports them. Without the balance sheet I cannot verify what those returns were earned on, nor over what period the income fed into them. A single trailing window is not a record, and I will not treat it as one. I can only note what is published and plain: the ROE is high, the debt-to-equity ratio is low at 0.20, and the dividend has been paid reliably, but the foundation of those numbers is partly beyond my reach today [P2].

data.text: Buffett, you have the percentages for the two bonus issues the wrong way around, and that matters when we are telling the member whether figures are comparable. The capital changes table I am answerable for shows that in May 2022 the capital went from SAR 60,000.00 million to SAR 75,000.00 million—that is a 25% increase, not 20% [P3]. data.headline: Buffett misstates the bonus issue sizes and the secondary offering's effect.
data.text: Buffett, you state the May 2022 bonus was a 20% increase and the May 2023 bonus was a 25% increase [P3]. The data in [P3] shows the opposite. In May 2022, capital rose from SAR 60,000.00 million to SAR 75,000.00 million, a 25% increase [P3]. In May 2023, it rose from SAR 75,000.00 million to SAR 90,000.00 million, a 20% increase [P3]. Getting the sequence wrong matters for the cumulative effect. You also claim the June 2024 secondary offering 'did not change the number of shares outstanding.' This is incorrect [P3]. A secondary offering of 1.545 billion existing shares, as detailed in [P3], increases the number of shares in the public market. While the total authorized capital remained at SAR 90,000.00 million, the shares outstanding for trading and per-share calculation did increase by 0.64%, as noted by Marks and Al-Rumayyan [P3]. This dilutes market-based per-share metrics, however slightly. For a balance-sheet analyst, precision on the capital structure is the first step in understanding how the machine is built.
data.concedes: You are correct that the bonus issues, not the secondary offering, are the primary reason per-share figures are not directly comparable without adjustment.

data.headline: The bonus percentages are a simple arithmetic error.
data.text: Lynch, you say the 2022 bonus was a 25% increase and the 2023 bonus a 20% increase [P3]. That is backwards. The capital-changes table in [P3] shows the capital before the 2022 issue was SAR 60,000 million and after it was SAR 75,000 million. An increase from 60 to 75 is 15, which is 25% of 60 [P3] [P6]. The 2023 issue took the capital from SAR 75,000 million to SAR 90,000 million [P3]. That is an increase of 15 on a base of 75, which is 20% [P3]. I said 20% and 25%, and I was wrong too—I mixed the order [P3]. The table is plain and we should all read it the same way. One old share became 1.25 shares after the first bonus, and then 1.20 times that after the second, for a cumulative 1.50 shares. The direction of the error does not change the conclusion that the per-share figures are incomparable without adjustment, but the record should be straight.
data.concedes: You are right that the price chart is comparable because the exchange adjusts for bonus issues, and the fundamental per-share figures are not unless restated.

data.headline: Buffett misreads the secondary offering's effect on per-share metrics
data.text: Buffett, you state the June 2024 secondary offering "did not change the number of shares outstanding" [P3]. The data says otherwise. The note in [P3] explicitly records that the government sold 1.545 billion shares, representing 0.64% of the company's total shares. While this sale of existing shares did not alter the company's capital, which remained at SAR 90,000.00 million, it undeniably increased the number of shares in public circulation, the float [P3]. This has a direct, if small, effect on market-based per-share metrics like trading volumes and the free-float market capitalization, which are part of the pack's data. For a long-term investor, understanding the structure of the shareholder base and the mechanics of such a large placement is critical. It signals a change in the liquidity profile and the government's active management of its stake, which is a strategic disclosure I weigh carefully [P6].
data.concedes: You are correct that the offering did not change the company's total share capital, which remained at SAR 90,000.00 million [P3].

data.headline: Buffett, your bonus percentages are swapped
data.text: Buffett, you said the May 2022 bonus was a 20% increase and the May 2023 bonus was 25% [P3]. That is backwards, and the numbers in [P3] are right there. In May 2022, the capital went from SAR 60,000 million to SAR 75,000 million—that is a SAR 15,000 million increase on a base of 60,000, which is 25%, not 20% [P3]. Then in May 2023, it went from SAR 75,000 million to SAR 90,000 million—a SAR 15,000 million increase on a base of 75,000, which is 20%, not 25% [P3]. The note in both cases says one new share for every ten held, but the starting base is different each time. The share count and the capital both rose by the same proportion, so the per-share dilution is exactly those percentages. Getting them right matters because the cumulative effect is not 50% as Dalio claimed, but 1.25 times 1.20, which is a 50% increase in shares from the pre-2022 base [P3] [P4]. I agree with your core point that the bonus issues break comparability, and that the secondary offering did not change the share count. But you have the two bonus sizes flipped, and that changes how an investor would adjust old per-share figures.

data.text: Lynch, you say the secondary offering in June 2024 increased the float but that the company's total capital stayed at SAR 90,000 million, and you then say the share count changed three times [P3]. I think the record is clearer than that. The capital-changes table in [P3] shows the capital before and after that event was SAR 90,000.00 million in both columns, and the change_pct is explicitly 0.0. The note states the government sold 1.545 billion existing shares, representing 0.64% of the company's total shares [P3]. A sale of existing shares by one owner to another does not create new shares; it merely transfers ownership. The total number of slices the pie is cut into does not change. Therefore, the per-share metrics—earnings, book value, dividends—are not mechanically affected by this event in the way they are by a bonus issue. The distinction matters because it tells us the current EPS of 1.84 and book value of 6.49 in [P1] were calculated on a share count that was already in place before that offering. There was no third change to the denominator; there were two bonus issues, and then a transfer. That is what the data shows.

data.answer:
The room's answer is no, not without adjustment. The capital-changes table records two bonus issues: capital rose from SAR 60000.0 million to SAR 75000.0 million in 2022-05-12, and from SAR 75000.0 million to SAR 90000.0 million in 2023-05-08, each at one share for every ten held [P3]. Every per-share figure struck before those dates uses a smaller share count than today's. Lynch and Dalio make the point that the fall in quarterly dividend per share from SAR 0.48 to SAR 0.33 cannot be read as a like-for-like change without a restated series [P3]. The current EPS of 1.84 and book value of 6.49 are struck on 242000.0 million shares and are comparable with each other [P1]. The June 2024 secondary offering was a sale of existing shares by the government, with capital of SAR 90000.0 million before and after and a change of 0.0% [P3]. It does not alter the denominator for earnings or book value.

The room corrected its early slips on the bonus sizes. The table shows 2022 as the larger issue by percentage and 2023 as the smaller [P3]. Several advisors, Buffett and Marks among them, name the missing restated history of EPS, book value and dividends, together with the missing balance sheet, as what would let the old and new figures be compared directly [P1] [P3].

The pack holds only capital changes and current per-share values. It holds no restated historical per-share series, so the old figures cannot be placed beside the new ones from this data.

headline: Per-share figures are only partly comparable; the pack cannot confirm a common basis across the period.
answer: The data shows partial comparability and no more. The capital changes in [P3] include bonus issues on 2022-05-12 and 2023-05-08, each described as 1 share for every 10, with capital rising from SAR 60000 million to SAR 75000 million and then to SAR 90000 million. Alwaleed noted that the pack records change_pct as 25.0 and 20.0, which does not match the 1-for-10 notes [P1] [P3]. Any per-share figure before those dates meant something different. The dividend entries in [P3] begin on 2024-05-07, after both issues, so they share a bonus basis: 0.48 SAR per share in 2024, 0.33 SAR in 2025 and 0.34 SAR in the last three entries. data.headline: The pack lacks the income statement and denominators to answer this.
data.text:
I am answerable for earning power, and here my hands are tied. The pack carries no income statement. [P9], which should hold the statement and the calculations that name the denominators, is absent. So I cannot read what this company earned, over which window, or on what capital it earned it. That is the whole of my mandate, and I must say plainly that the data here does not show it.

The pack does give a trailing EPS of 1.84 SAR and a book value per share of 6.49 SAR [P1]. It also shows an ROE of 26.75% [P2]. But [P2] does not disclose the denominator for that ROE, and a single trailing figure is not a record. Without the income statement, I cannot say whether that 1.84 SAR was earned on the same share count as the book value, or on the same share count as any earlier year [P1]. Two bonus issues sit in the history [P3]—one in May 2022 and one in May 2023—and any per-share figure from before them means something different from one after. The pack does not tell me whether the EPS and book value it quotes are adjusted for those changes. It does not tell me what the earnings were in any year I could compare. I cannot answer whether per-share figures are comparable across the period because the period itself is not in front of me.

data.headline: I have no quarterly record to compare, so I cannot call a trend.
data.text:
My job is the trend, quarter by quarter, and I look first at [P9]'s quarterly columns. They are not here. I count zero quarters. I cannot tell you whether the business is speeding up, slowing down, or holding steady. A single trailing EPS of 1.84 SAR [P1] is a snapshot, not a story.

The market's reading of the last year is in [P7]: 260 trading days, from 2025-09-29 to 2026-10-13, a first close of 24.99 SAR and a last close of 25.78 SAR. That one-year window sits entirely after both bonus issues in [P3], so those closes are likely on the same share base. The five-year window in [P8] is a different matter. It starts on 2021-07-29 at 28.81 SAR, before the 2022 and 2023 bonus issues [P3] [P8]. The pack does not say whether that first close is adjusted for those capital changes. If it is not, comparing 28.81 SAR to 25.78 SAR is comparing apples to oranges [P1] [P8]. The one-year price series is safer ground.

What I can say is that the dividend per share stepped down from 0.48 SAR to 0.33 SAR [P3] between the 2024 and 2025 quarters, and has since risen to 0.34 SAR. That is a pattern, but without the earnings behind it I cannot say whether it is a cut in payout or a cut in earnings. The story is half-told.

data.text:
I am answerable for what the evidence cannot answer, and the gaps here are the first thing to name. [P9] is missing entirely. That means no income statement, no balance sheet, no calculations, and no limitations statement can be read. The pack's own machinery for computing per-share figures is absent. In [P1], EV/EBITDA and value traded are missing. In [P2], ROIC, net margin, price-to-sales, interest coverage, and payout ratio could not be computed. These are not small omissions; they are the measures that would tell us whether the per-share earnings are consistent, covered, and struck on a stable base.

The P/E of 14.47 and EPS of 1.84 SAR [P1] rest on an undisclosed share basis. The price history in [P8] spans 2021-07-29 to 2026-10-13, a period that contains two bonus issues [P3]. The first close of 28.81 SAR may not be comparable to the last close of 25.78 SAR, and the pack does not say whether it is adjusted [P1] [P8]. The quote itself is flagged stale in [P1], as of 2026-10-13. So even the price we are anchoring to is not current.

What the price is assuming about per-share comparability, I cannot say, because the earnings stream the price is discounting is not in the pack. The member's question is a reasonable one, and the honest answer is that the data here does not let us answer it with confidence.

data.text:
I am answerable for what has been returned to owners and what has been done to the share count. The capital changes in [P3] tell the story. On 2022-05-12, a bonus issue increased capital from SAR 60000 million to SAR 75000 million, described as 1 share for every 10 [P1] [P3]. The dividend record in [P3] begins on 2024-05-07, so all listed dividends post-date both bonus issues. They are comparable to each other on that basis. But they step down: 0.48 SAR per share through Q1 2024, then 0.33 SAR from Q4 2024 onward, with a recent rise to 0.34 SAR [P3]. The 350-million-share buyback announced on 2026-03-09 [P6] will change the share count again, but its effect is not yet in the per-share figures we have. The member is right to ask. The answer is that figures before May 2023 are not comparable to figures after, and the pack does not adjust them for us [P3].

data.headline: A dividend step is not a payout without matched earnings.
data.text: Alwaleed, you read the step from 0.48 SAR to 0.33 SAR as a real change in the distribution, and on its face it is [P3]. But a dividend per share is not a payout ratio. The 2024 entries each carry a note of performance-linked dividends of SAR 40390 million, while the 2025 entries carry only SAR 820 million [P3]. That tells us the 2024 quarters included a large, one-time component that the 2025 quarters did not [P3]. The per-share step is real, but it does not mean the underlying earnings fell by a third. Without [P9]'s matched earnings window, I cannot say what portion of earnings either figure represents. A farm that sells a tractor reports a different distribution than one that sells only its crop. The dividend list is not a record of earning power, and I will not treat it as one.
data.concedes: The list begins after both bonus issues, so its per-share figures share a bonus basis.

data.headline: The five-year price may mix share bases, so don't lean on it.
data.text: Marks, you are right to question the five-year series, but I would go further. The -10.52% change in [P8] starts at 28.81 SAR on 2021-07-29, before both the May 2022 and May 2023 bonus issues [P3]. If that first close is not adjusted, you are comparing a share that was one of 60000 million capital units to a share that is now one of 90000 million [P3]. That is not a return; it is a measurement error. I used the one-year window because it sits cleanly after both bonus issues, but the pack never says the five-year series is adjusted. Until it does, that -10.52% is a number I would not put in a story [P8]. The market's price is only as good as the share base it is struck on.
data.concedes: The pack does not tell us whether the price history is adjusted, so my own comparison of the 24.99 and 25.78 closes is only as good as that assumption [P1] [P7].

data.headline: The buyback could alter the share count; the date is missing.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, the buyback is a stated intention, as you say. But the pack gives us a share count of 242000 million [P1] with no date at all. The disclosure is dated 2026-03-09 [P6], and the price data runs to 2026-10-13. If the buyback was executed between those dates, the share count in [P1] might already reflect it. If it was not, it does not. The machine needs a date to answer this, and the pack does not give one. That is a gap in the evidence, and it matters for any per-share figure we are asked to compare. A denominator that might have changed is a denominator we cannot trust. I am not saying the buyback happened; I am saying the pack does not let us rule it out.
data.concedes: The secondary offering of 2024-06-07 left capital unchanged at 90000 million [P3], so it does not break comparability.

data.headline: Comparable price windows do not make earnings comparable.
data.text: Lynch, you have found a cleaner price series in the one-year window, and I accept that. But the question is about per-share figures, and a 3.16% price change over one year [P7] tells us nothing about whether the earnings per share behind it are struck on a consistent base. The EPS of 1.84 SAR [P1] is a single trailing figure with no stated denominator. The book value of 6.49 SAR [P1] is another. Neither is part of a series we can check across the bonus issues. A comparable price window is useful, but it does not answer the member's question. The price can be clean while the per-share earnings it discounts are not. I would keep those two things separate.
data.concedes: The one-year window falls wholly after both bonus issues, so it is the safer series.

data.headline: The per-share step is real; the totals confirm it.
data.text: Buffett, you point to the performance-linked dividends as the reason the per-share figure fell, and I agree that the 2024 quarters carried a much larger special component [P3]. But that is exactly why the per-share step is a real change in what was distributed to owners. The total amounts confirm it: SAR 116450 million at 0.48 SAR per share in 2024, and SAR 80100 million at 0.33 SAR per share in 2025 [P3]. The totals and the per-share figures are consistent with each other. I am not mixing them; I am reading them side by side. The company paid less per share, and it paid less in total. Whether that was because earnings fell or because the special dividend ended, the distribution to owners changed. That is what I am answerable for, and the data shows it plainly.

headline: Returns and dividend show clear stress; the data cannot say whether it is one-off or operating.
answer:
The data shows earnings stress clearly, but not its cause. Return on equity is -15.37% and return on assets is -8.24% [P2]. The dividend per share fell from 2.25 in H2 2021 to 1.1 for H1 2026 [P3], and the stock closed at 45.32 SAR, down 26.61% over one year [P7] and 62.55% over five [P8]. The room agrees on these points. Balance-sheet leverage is not the problem: debt-to-equity is 0.26 and the current ratio is 1.80 [P2], as Buffett, Dalio and Alwaleed noted.

The room splits on why. Buffett reads the losses as operating weakness. Marks and Al-Rumayyan tie them to the SAR 18.3B expected non-cash loss on the Americas and Europe unit sales [P6]. No income statement or quarterly record is in the pack, so Lynch could not trace the trend, and Buffett conceded he cannot separate the charge from operating results. The pack gives no P/E [P1] and no payout ratio [P2].

On the dividend, the cut is a fact in the pack [P3]. What it proves about cash generation is not, because the matching earnings are absent. On "deteriorating versus broken", Alwaleed and Marks weigh the same price-to-book of 1.24 [P1] and balance-sheet ratios differently.

How clear is the evidence? It is clear that returns are negative, the dividend has been cut and the price has fallen. It is not clear whether the underlying business is deteriorating or the restructuring charge is driving the figures.
gaps: The income statement, separating the restructuring charge from operating earnings, is not in the pack.
The quarterly record that would show whether the decline is steady, accelerating or a single charge is absent.
The payout ratio and the earnings window matching the dividend are not shown.
disagreements: Whether the negative returns reflect a one-off charge or operating weakness - The deciding figure is operating earnings separate from the SAR 18.3B expected non-cash loss [P6]. The pack has no income statement or quarterly record, so ROE of -15.37% and ROA of -8.24% [P2] cannot be split between the two causes.

How firmly the dividend cut shows deterioration - The cut from 1.7 to 1.1 SAR per share [P3] is established, but the payout field is missing [P2] and no matching earnings window is in the pack. Whether it reflects weaker cash generation or caution cannot be shown.

Deteriorating versus broken, and what the price implies - All three read the same figures: price-to-book 1.24 [P1], debt-to-equity 0.26 and current ratio 1.80 [P2]. They differ on whether these show distress already priced or an eroding book value. No post-restructuring earnings are in the pack to settle this.
