headline: The data cannot confirm that earnings and returns support the valuation; the premium is visible, its justification is not.
answer:
What the data shows: Al Rajhi Bank trades at 62.1 SAR (as of 2026-10-13, flagged stale) on a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19, with a published ROE of 23.49%, ROA of 2.53%, EPS (TTM) of 4.42 and a dividend yield of 2.6% [P1][P2]. Against eight listed bank peers, whose P/Es run from 7.78 to 11.94 and yields from 3.1% to 6.02% [P5], the bank is priced higher and yields less (Al-Rumayyan). Over five years the share rose from 46.26 to 62.1 SAR (34.24%) [P8], while over the year the close fell from 70.2 to 62.1 SAR (-11.54%) [P7].

Where the room agrees: the strong ROE is the main support for the multiple (Buffett, Marks), and nobody could verify it. The statement dataset [P9], which holds the income statement, balance sheet, quarters, payout calculations and limitations, is not in the pack. That leaves the earnings record, the ROE denominator and date, the quarterly direction (Lynch), the funding position (Dalio) and the matched payout (Alwaleed) all unread. Marks added that the pack mixes dates: prices to 2026-10-13, technicals to 2026-08-11 and peers to 2026-08-07 [P1].

What the data cannot tell: whether earnings are growing, stable or falling, what capital the 23.49% was earned on, and how the bank's funding would hold under strain [P1]. A 50% bonus issue on 2026-04-20 [P3] also means per-share comparisons across that date need care (Alwaleed). The council's rule-based votes are thresholds, not measurements, and are not evidence here.

The answer to the member is that the valuation premium is documented but its support is unproven on this pack.
gaps: The multi-year income statement and the equity denominator with its date for the ROE of 23.49% [P1].
Quarterly earnings with a comparison year, to show the direction of the business.
The balance sheet with its date and the bank's funding and leverage measures.
disagreements: Is the premium to peers earned by returns? - The ROE denominator and date, the earnings history and peer ROE figures are missing; the P/E gap (14.51 against 7.78 to 11.94) is visible but its justification is not [P1] [P5].
Is the weak price a trend or a window effect? - The 12-month return of 2.46% [P1] and the 1-year change of -11.54% [P7] cover different windows, and no quarterly earnings are present to compare.
Does the low yield mean low payout? - The matched-window payout is missing from [P2] and [P9] is absent; the yield of 2.6% against peers' 3.1% to 6.02% is a fact, but its cause is not.

data.note: The question asks about support for the valuation rather than what to do; the room answers it as an open assessment of the data.

data.headline: I cannot test the earnings record; the income statement is missing.
data.text:
I am meant to look at what this bank earned, over which window, and on what capital it earned it. The data pack does not give me the income statement or the calculations in [P9], so I cannot do that work. The only return figures I have are a published ROE of 23.49% and ROA of 2.53% [P2]. Those look high, but the pack does not state the equity denominator or the date it was struck. A single published ratio is not a record of earnings across years, and I will not treat it as one.

The price is 62.1 SAR, which gives a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19, with EPS (TTM) of 4.42 and book value of 20.11 [P1]. A business that earns a high return on the equity it keeps can justify a price above book value, and a 23.49% ROE would be consistent with that [P1]. But I cannot confirm that those returns are durable, that they are earned with little debt, or that they rest on common equity rather than on equity that includes other people's money. The debt-to-equity ratio is 1.7165 [P2], which is not light, but without the balance sheet I cannot say what it is made of.

The dividend record shows payments going back several years [P3], which is a sign of confidence, but I cannot check the payout ratio because [P2] lists it as missing. A bank that pays a dividend and keeps enough earnings to grow its capital at a good rate is one I would want to study further. On what is in front of me, I can say the valuation assumes high returns, and I cannot say whether those returns are real or lasting.

data.headline: No quarterly data means no trend; the share has drifted lower.
data.text:
I am supposed to count the quarters and tell you which way the business is moving. The quarterly data is in [P9], and [P9] is not in this pack. I counted zero quarters, so I call no trend. One quarter does not make a trend, and zero quarters certainly does not.

The market's reading of the last year is in [P7]. The close went from 70.2 SAR to 62.1 SAR, a change of -11.54% over 260 trading days [P7]. That is a drift lower, not a crash. The five-year change is 34.24%, from 46.26 to 62.1 SAR [P8], with a high close of 76.52 and a low close of 42.34. The share has given back some of its gains but is still above where it was five years ago.

What I cannot do is set that price against what the business earned quarter by quarter. The P/E is 14.51 and EPS (TTM) is 4.42 [P1]. A P/E of 14.5 is not stretched for a bank if earnings are growing, but I have no growth figure to compare it against. The pack gives me no quarterly revenue, no quarterly net income, no year-ago quarter to measure against. Without that, I cannot say whether the -11.54% price drop is the market overreacting to a flat quarter or correctly pricing a slowdown [P7]. The story is incomplete. The bank pays a 2.6% dividend yield [P1], which is something, but it is not a substitute for knowing which way the earnings are headed. I need the quarters to do my job, and they are not here.

data.headline: The balance sheet is absent; I cannot read the funding structure.
data.text:
I am answerable for the balance sheet: what this company owns, what it owes, who funded it, and what would put it under strain. The balance sheet in [P9] is not in this pack, so I cannot state a position date, the funding mix, or the leverage measures I would use for a bank. For a bank, I read the leverage and funding measures in [P9]'s calculations, not a current ratio, which is not defined for a balance sheet with no current split. Those calculations are not here.

The only health figure I have is a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.7165, with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. A percentile of 22.7 means the ratio is lower than roughly 77% of its sector peers, which is a relative strength [P2]. But without the operands behind it, I cannot say what the debt is or what the equity is, and for a bank the debt-to-equity ratio is not the same measure of leverage it is for an industrial company. I will not treat it as one.

The disclosures give me some clues about how the bank funds itself. It issued a USD-denominated AT1 capital sukuk announced on 2026-01-06 [P6], and earlier completed a $1 billion Tier 2 social sukuk offering in September 2025 and a $1.5 billion AT1 sukuk in January 2025 [P6]. That is recurring capital market activity, which tells me the bank accesses international investors to fund its capital layers. What I cannot see is the size of those instruments against the total balance sheet, the deposit base, the loan book, or the maturity profile. The machine's parts are hidden. I cannot build a scenario for what would cause funding strain because I cannot see the lines that would break first.

data.headline: The price assumes high returns persist; the gaps are large.
data.text:
The price of 62.1 SAR, dated 2026-10-13 and flagged stale [P1], gives a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19, with a dividend yield of 2.6% [P1]. A P/B above 3 for a bank says the market expects the 23.49% ROE [P2] to continue. If that return fades toward the cost of capital, the price would have to adjust. The question is whether the data supports that assumption.

Over five years the share rose from 46.26 to 62.1 SAR, a 34.24% gain [P8], against a high close of 76.52. The last twelve months show a decline of 11.54% [P7]. The market has already taken something off the price, but it is still paying a premium to book value.

Now the gaps. [P9] is missing from this pack. That means I have no income statement, no balance sheet, no calculations, and no limitations statement. The ROE denominator is undisclosed. EV/EBITDA, P/S, net margin, and the payout ratio are all unavailable [P2]. The dates in the pack are mixed: the price is from 2026-10-13, the technicals from 2026-08-11, and the fundamentals from 2026-08-12 [P1][P2]. I am reading a snapshot whose pieces were taken at different moments.

The rule-based council in [P4] gives one bullish vote, three neutral, and one bearish. I treat that as a rough gauge of what simple thresholds see, not as a measurement. The momentum seat is bearish, the value seat neutral. None of them had the full statements either.

What this price assumes is that the bank's high returns are durable. What we do not know is whether the earnings behind those returns are real, what they were earned on, and over what period. That is a large gap to carry into any judgment.

data.headline: The dividend is modest; the share count has doubled on bonus issues.
data.text:
I am meant to look at what has been returned to owners and out of what. The dividend history shows a payment of 1.17 SAR per share for the second half of 2025, with an ex-date of 2026-04-20, and 0.5 SAR for the first half of 2025 [P3]. The yield at the current price is 2.6% [P1]. That is a modest return of cash to shareholders, not a generous one.

The matched-window payout calculation from [P9] is not in this pack, and [P2] lists the payout ratio as missing. I will not assemble a payout myself from the dividend list, because counting a dividend that falls outside the earnings window is how a payout reads wrong. Without that matched figure, I cannot say what portion of earnings is being distributed.

The capital changes tell a story of their own. A 50% bonus issue took the capital from SAR 40000 million to SAR 60000 million on 2026-04-20 [P3]. That is one share for every two held. Before that, a 60% bonus issue in May 2022 took capital from SAR 25000 million to SAR 40000 million [P3]. The share count has been rising steadily through bonus issues for decades, from SAR 750 million in 1991 to SAR 60000 million today [P3]. Shares outstanding now stand at 6000 million [P1].

A bonus issue does not change the value of the whole business, but it changes what every per-share figure before it meant. A dividend of 0.97 SAR declared in January 2025 was on a smaller share base than the 1.17 SAR declared in January 2026 [P1] [P3]. The per-share figures are not comparable across those dates without adjustment. The bank has chosen to capitalise earnings rather than pay them all out, which is consistent with a business that sees opportunities to reinvest. Whether those opportunities earn good returns is what the missing income statement would show, and it is not here.

data.headline: The bank trades at a premium to every listed peer on P/E.
data.text:
I am answerable for how this company sits against its sector. Against the eight listed bank peers in [P5], Al Rajhi Bank trades at a P/E of 14.51 [P1]. That is above every peer P/E in the list: Saudi National Bank at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, Alinma Bank at 10.97, Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82, Banque Saudi Fransi at 9.30, Arab National Bank at 8.49, Bank Albilad at 11.94, and The Saudi Investment Bank at 9.03 [P5]. The premium is not small. The closest peer on P/E is Bank Albilad at 11.94, and the bank is still more than two and a half turns above it [P5].

The dividend yield tells the same story from the other side. The bank's 2.6% yield [P1] is below every peer yield: Saudi National Bank at 5.26%, Riyad Bank at 5.08%, Alinma at 3.10%, Saudi Awwal at 6.02%, Banque Saudi Fransi at 5.23%, Arab National Bank at 5.94%, Bank Albilad at 4.04%, and Saudi Investment Bank at 5.01% [P5]. The market is paying more for each riyal of earnings and accepting less in cash return.

I must note the dates. The peer figures are as of 2026-08-07 [P5] and the bank's own valuation is as of 2026-10-13 [P1]. That is a gap of over two months, so the comparison mixes two points in time. The sector percentiles for valuation and profitability in [P2] are null, which means no ranking exists in that dataset. That is not the same as a low rank; it is an absence.

The disclosures show a bank that is active in capital markets: an AT1 sukuk issuance announced 2026-01-06, a Tier 2 sukuk completed September 2025, and an earlier AT1 sukuk in January 2025 [P6]. None of these is a forecast. The most recent item, dated 2026-08-02, is about Saudization MoUs [P6], which speaks to the bank's role in the wider economy but does not change the valuation question. The market is assigning this bank a premium over its peers. Whether that premium is supported depends on earnings that the missing statements would show.

data.headline: A peer P/E gap without peer ROE is half a comparison
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, the peer P/E figures you cite — from 7.78 for Riyad Bank to 11.94 for Bank Albilad [P5] — do show that Al Rajhi trades at a higher multiple than every other bank in the list. But a multiple by itself is a price tag, not a verdict. The question is whether the earnings behind that tag are better, and the pack does not give us the peers' return on equity. The bank's own ROE is 23.49% [P2], and that is the figure the market is presumably paying for. If the peers earn 10% on equity, a premium is earned; if they earn 20%, it is not [P1] [P3]. We have no way to tell. I agree with you that the multiple gap is real on the figures shown — the bank is priced higher, and that is a fact. But I cannot call that premium unearned without knowing what the other banks earn on their capital, and that figure is not in this room.
data.concedes: The premium to peers is real on the figures shown.

data.headline: Two return windows, two different stories
data.text: Marks, you are right to flag the disagreement between the 12-month return of 2.46% [P1] and the one-year summary change of -11.54% [P7]. I see the same thing. The 12-month return ends on 2026-10-13, the date of the quote [P1], while the one-year summary runs from 2025-09-29 to 2026-10-13 [P7]. Those are different windows — one is a trailing twelve months, the other a fixed calendar stretch — and they land on different numbers because they start at different prices. Neither is a trend. A trend needs quarters, and I have none. What I can say is that a 2.46% gain over twelve months and a 11.54% loss over roughly the same stretch cannot both be right as a story unless the starting point shifts the answer [P1] [P7]. Without the quarterly earnings to match against these price moves, I would not build a case from either number. The room is looking at two snapshots of a share that has drifted, not at a record of what the business earned while it drifted.
data.concedes: Without earnings history the room cannot say price and earnings are travelling together.

data.headline: High ROE without the leverage breakdown is incomplete
data.text: Buffett, you noted the 23.49% ROE [P2] and called it high, which it is on its face. But for a bank, return on equity is partly a function of how much leverage sits underneath it. A bank that earns 23% on equity with a thin capital cushion is a different machine from one that earns it with thick equity. The only leverage-type figure in this pack is the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.7165 [P2], and I cannot interpret it properly for a bank. A bank's balance sheet is funded by deposits, wholesale borrowing, and capital instruments — the debt-to-equity ratio does not separate those layers. The AT1 and Tier 2 sukuk issuances in the disclosures [P6] tell me the bank uses capital market instruments, but without the balance sheet I cannot see the deposit base, the loan book, or the risk-weighted assets that sit behind that ROE. I do not discredit the published ROE — it is what it is. But I cannot say whether it is earned on a sound funding structure or a leveraged one, and that matters for whether it can persist through a cycle.
data.concedes: The ROE is a published value I cannot discredit.

data.headline: Two clashing numbers, neither a trend
data.text: Lynch, you make the right point about the two return figures. The 12-month return of 2.46% [P1] and the one-year summary change of -11.54% [P7] disagree, and the most likely reason is that the windows end on different dates and started from different price levels. A 2.46% gain and an 11.54% loss cannot both describe the same stretch unless the starting point moves [P1] [P7]. Neither should be read as a trend until the dates are reconciled, and I agree with you that without quarterly earnings the room cannot say which number fits the business better. I will add one thing: the six-month return of -10.68% [P1] is consistent with a fall in the price, and it covers a shorter and more recent window. That does not make it a trend either — six months is not a record — but it does line up with the direction of the one-year summary more than the twelve-month return does. The price has been coming down, and we cannot say whether earnings are coming down with it.
data.concedes: The six-month return of -10.68% [P1] is consistent with a fall in the price.

data.headline: The yield gap partly reflects shares, not stinginess
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, the peer yields you list — from 3.10% for Alinma to 6.02% for Saudi Awwal Bank [P5] — do put this bank's 2.6% yield [P1] at the bottom of the sector. But a yield is two numbers: the dividend per share divided by the price. The price is 62.1 SAR [P1], which is higher than every peer price in the list except Saudi National Bank at 40.86 [P5]. A higher price mechanically lowers the yield. The other half is the dividend itself. The bank paid 1.17 SAR for the second half of 2025 and 0.50 SAR for the first half [P3], and those amounts sit on a share count that doubled through the 50% bonus issue on 2026-04-20 [P3]. A bonus issue does not change the total dividend paid, but it spreads it over more shares, and that lowers the per-share figure. The yield gap partly reflects a larger share count, not necessarily a smaller payout. Without the matched payout ratio from [P9], I cannot say what share of earnings was returned, and I will not guess.
data.concedes: Without a payout figure, I cannot say what share of earnings was returned.

data.headline: The multiple gap is visible; the return gap is not
data.text: Buffett, you are right that the peer P/E comparison is incomplete without the peers' ROE. The bank's P/E of 14.51 sits above every peer P/E in the list, from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5], and that gap is clear. What is not clear is whether the earnings behind that multiple are better enough to justify it. The bank's ROE of 23.49% [P2] is a strong figure on its face, and I do not dispute that. But the room cannot see the peers' ROE — the sector percentiles in [P2] are null for profitability — so we cannot say whether 23.49% is exceptional or merely good. A premium multiple over peers requires a premium return over peers, and we have only one side of that equation. The disclosures [P6] show a bank that accesses international capital markets regularly, which speaks to its standing, but standing is not a return figure. The valuation question turns on a comparison the data does not complete, and I accept your point that the multiple gap alone does not settle it.
data.concedes: A 23.49% ROE [P2] is a strong figure on its face.

verdict.headline: The data cannot confirm that earnings and returns support the valuation; the premium is visible, its justification is not.
verdict.answer:
What the data shows: Al Rajhi Bank trades at 62.1 SAR (as of 2026-10-13, flagged stale) on a P/E of 14.51 and a P/B of 3.19, with a published ROE of 23.49%, ROA of 2.53%, EPS (TTM) of 4.42 and a dividend yield of 2.6% [P1][P2]. Against eight listed bank peers, whose P/Es run from 7.78 to 11.94 and yields from 3.1% to 6.02% [P5], the bank is priced higher and yields less (Al-Rumayyan). Over five years the share rose from 46.26 to 62.1 SAR (34.24%) [P8], while over the year the close fell from 70.2 to 62.1 SAR (-11.54%) [P7].

Where the room agrees: the strong ROE is the main support for the multiple (Buffett, Marks), and nobody could verify it. The statement dataset [P9], which holds the income statement, balance sheet, quarters, payout calculations and limitations, is not in the pack. That leaves the earnings record, the ROE denominator and date, the quarterly direction (Lynch), the funding position (Dalio) and the matched payout (Alwaleed) all unread. Marks added that the pack mixes dates: prices to 2026-10-13, technicals to 2026-08-11 and peers to 2026-08-07.

What the data cannot tell: whether earnings are growing, stable or falling, what capital the 23.49% was earned on, and how the bank's funding would hold under strain. A 50% bonus issue on 2026-04-20 [P3] also means per-share comparisons across that date need care (Alwaleed). The council's rule-based votes are thresholds, not measurements, and are not evidence here.

The answer to the member is that the valuation premium is documented but its support is unproven on this pack.

headline: Trailing earnings cover the dividend on the pack's figures, but safety across a cycle cannot be shown.
answer:
On trailing figures the dividend is covered. Earnings per share are SAR 1.84 [P1], and the last four declared dividends in [P3] are three payments of SAR 0.34 and one of SAR 0.33. Buffett, Lynch, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan each put the payout at roughly 73% to 74% of earnings. Marks and Dalio accept that arithmetic but note that the pack holds no published payout ratio, and none of the other cash-flow lines are populated [P2].

The room agrees on three points. First, current earnings exceed the dividend. Second, leverage is low, with debt-to-equity of 0.20 and a current ratio near 2.0 [P2]. Third, the return on equity is 26.75% [P2].

The room does not agree on how far that shows safety. Buffett, Dalio and Marks point out that the pack has no multi-year earnings history, no cash or debt-maturity lines and no free cash flow yield [P2]. They also cite the five-year maximum drawdown of -40.14% [P1]. Lynch, Alwaleed and Al-Rumayyan read the balance-sheet ratios as a fortress. Their final statements concede that safety under stress is an assumption.

The data therefore shows coverage today and a conservative balance sheet. It does not show whether the payout survives a sharp fall in earnings.

The Chair's rulings on the three fault lines are set out below.
gaps: The pack has no published payout ratio, free cash flow or interest coverage, so cash coverage of the dividend cannot be measured directly.
The pack has no multi-year earnings history, so durability through an earnings downturn cannot be tested.
The pack has no cash, retained earnings or debt-maturity lines, so the balance-sheet buffer under stress cannot be modelled.
disagreements: Whether the pack proves coverage or only implies it - Both sides read the same figures: EPS of SAR 1.84 [P1] and the dividends in [P3]. The payout ratio and free cash flow yield are missing in [P2]. The dispute is whether a hand-computed ratio counts as proof, which is a question of standard, not of data. Both sides agree the computed ratio sits near 73% to 74%.

How much safety the balance sheet and history support - The ratios in [P2] are low debt-to-equity at 0.20 and a current ratio near 2.0. The figures that would test a downturn are absent: multi-year earnings, cash, debt maturities, free cash flow yield and interest coverage, all missing in [P2]. The pack therefore cannot decide between the two readings.

data.headline: Earnings cover the dividend, the quarterly record shows it's steady.
data.text:
Let's check the story: the annual earnings per share is SAR 1.84 [P1]. Over the last four quarters, the dividends declared add up to SAR 1.35 per share (0.34 + 0.34 + 0.34 + 0.33) [P3]. That is a payout ratio of roughly 73% from earnings, which means the dividend is covered with a cushion. That's a good start.

The quarterly record I'm answerable for tells me more about the trend. Looking at the last eight quarters of dividends [P3], the base dividend has been steady at SAR 0.33 or SAR 0.34. The company has also layered performance-linked dividends on top in earlier quarters, but the core payout hasn't been cut. I count eight quarters of this consistency. A dividend that stays flat or rises quarter after quarter while earnings cover it is a sign of a steady large company, not a cyclical in trouble.

Now, what the data doesn't show me is the quarterly earnings per share, so I can't see if earnings dipped in any single quarter. The annual EPS of SAR 1.84 [P1] is the only earnings figure I have. The balance sheet, which I can see, supports the safety: debt-to-equity is just 0.20 and the current ratio is near 2.0 [P2]. That's a fortress. A company with that kind of financial health can maintain a dividend through a rough patch.

The market's reading over the past year shows the price is up about 10% with a 5% dividend yield [P1]. That tells me the market isn't pricing in a cut. The news mentions a $4B bond issuance and an $11B gas deal [P6], so the company is investing for the future, but the balance sheet suggests it can do that and pay the dividend. I'd sleep well owning this for the dividend, based on the steady quarterly payouts and the strong financials I can see.

data.headline: Earnings cover the dividend, but a one-year window is not a record of safety.
data.text:
The data shows a dividend of SAR 0.34 per share for each of the last three quarters, which annualises to SAR 1.36 [P3]. Against trailing twelve-month earnings per share of SAR 1.84 [P1], the dividend is covered. The payout ratio implied by these two figures is about 74%. That is a substantial distribution, but it is covered by current earnings.

My own mandate is to look at the earning power behind that number. The published return on equity is 26.75% [P2], a high figure. But [P2] does not disclose what denominator it used. The income statement in [P9] is absent from the pack. Without it, I cannot see the actual common equity figure, nor the net income from which the ROE was struck, nor the date of that equity. I can see that the book value per share is SAR 6.49 [P1], which gives a return on that book value of 28.3% against the SAR 1.84 of earnings. That is a fine return on tangible capital, and the company carries very little debt to achieve it, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 [P2].

But here is the catch. These returns are drawn from a single trailing twelve-month window. A single year tells you almost nothing about the durability of a business. An oil company's earnings can swing wildly with the price of the commodity it sells, and this data pack provides no income history at all. I cannot see what this company earned five or ten years ago, or what it earned on the capital it employed then. Without that record, I cannot judge whether the current dividend is a permanent feature of a wide-moat business or a cyclical high. The dividend is covered today. Whether it will be covered in a year when oil prices are lower is a question the data here does not answer.

data.headline: The dividend is covered by strong earnings, and the company's disclosures and sector position support its durability.
data.text:
The dividend is covered, and the data shows a company positioned to sustain it. Earnings per share over the last twelve months stand at SAR 1.84 [P1]. The most recent four quarterly dividends total SAR 1.34 (three payments of SAR 0.34 and one of SAR 0.33) [P3]. This gives a payout ratio of approximately 73% from the available figures, which is fully covered by earnings. The return on equity is 26.75%, a figure that suggests the remaining earnings reinvested into the business are being deployed productively [P2].

Looking at the sector, Saudi Aramco's market capitalization of SAR 6,413,000 million makes it the dominant player, far exceeding peers like The National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia at SAR 27,906.98 million and Petro Rabigh at SAR 26,936.52 million [P5]. This scale is a form of safety in itself. The company's debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 and a current ratio near 2.00 provide a strong balance sheet, ranking in the 54th and 68.4th percentiles of its sector respectively, showing a financial health score of 61.2 [P2]. This capacity is critical for a dividend payer.

The company's own disclosures reinforce this picture. The dividend record shows a steady base distribution, with performance-linked dividends of SAR 820 million added in several quarters through early 2026, before a new base of SAR 0.34 was established in Q1 2026 [P3]. A disclosure from 2026-03-10 confirms a 350 million share buyback for an employee plan, a signal of confidence in the company's cash position [P6]. The 2025 acquisition of a 22.5% stake in Petro Rabigh, disclosed on 2025-10-09, demonstrates a strategy of strengthening the sector ecosystem, which supports long-term stability [P6].

What the data does not show is the specific free cash flow yield, which is absent from the pack [P2]. This is a direct measure of dividend coverage that I would prefer to see. However, the combination of covered earnings, a fortress balance sheet, and a dominant sector position gives me confidence that the dividend is secure on the available figures.

data.headline: The dividend is well covered and looks secure on the data we have.
data.text:
The data shows a dividend that is well supported by earnings. My mandate is to examine what has been returned to owners, and out of what. Looking at [P3], the company has paid a steady quarterly dividend. Over the last four declared quarters—from Q3 2025 to Q2 2026—the dividend per share (DPS) has been SAR 0.33 for three quarters and then increased to SAR 0.34 in the most recent quarter [P3]. This is a total of SAR 1.33 per share over the trailing twelve months. Against this, the company reported trailing twelve-month earnings per share (EPS) of SAR 1.84 [P1]. This implies a payout ratio of roughly 72%, a very comfortable level for a company of this stature. The dividend is clearly covered by earnings.

The capital changes also offer a strong signal of confidence. The company has consistently increased its capital through bonus share issues—20% in 2023 and 25% in 2022—by capitalizing retained earnings [P3]. This is a direct return of value to shareholders and a sign that the company prefers to distribute its substantial profits rather than hoard them. The recent increase in the quarterly dividend from SAR 0.33 to SAR 0.34, announced in August 2026, is another positive signal [P3].

The safety of the dividend looks solid. The company’s profitability is exceptional, with a return on equity (ROE) of 26.75% [P2]. A business generating that level of return has ample room to maintain its distributions. The balance sheet is also robust, with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.20 [P2]. This fortress-like financial position means the dividend is not being funded by debt. The data does not show a payout ratio calculated against a matched earnings window [P9], so I must rely on the simple trailing figures, which tell a clear story. The only thing the data cannot show is the future oil price, which ultimately drives Aramco's earnings. But with this level of coverage and a rock-solid balance sheet, the dividend looks secure against all but the most severe, sustained downturn.

data.headline: Earnings cover the base dividend, but the balance sheet shows the payout is the main drain on equity.
data.text:
The question requires looking at the earnings stream and then at the balance-sheet machine that must fund any gap. The data shows a trailing P/E of 14.47, which implies earnings per share of 1.84 SAR [P1]. The latest quarterly dividend is 0.34 SAR per share [P3], which annualises to roughly 1.36 SAR. On that arithmetic, the base dividend is covered by trailing earnings.

However, the balance sheet I am answerable for tells a more complete story. The position is struck at the date of the last fundamentals update, 2026-08-12 [P2 freshness] [P1]. The company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 [P2], which is low and sits at the 54th sector percentile [P2]. The return on equity is 26.75% [P1][P2], a high number that shows the earnings machine is productive. But here is the critical part of the machine: the dividend is the main thing draining equity. The data in [P9] is absent from this pack. Without the balance-sheet lines themselves, I cannot see the cash, the retained earnings, or the total equity base against which the 82,060 million SAR quarterly payout [P3] is drawn. I also cannot see the operating cash flow or the free cash flow, because the interest coverage and free-cash-flow yield fields are marked as missing inputs in [P2].

What would have to happen for the funding to become a problem? The machine would need two things to occur together. First, a sustained drop in earnings that pushes the payout ratio above 100% of net income [P1]. Second, a balance sheet that is already lean on liquid assets, forcing the company to borrow or cut the dividend. The current ratio of 2.0 [P2] suggests short-term liquidity is comfortable, but without the cash and debt maturity lines from [P9], I cannot stress-test that. The recent 4 billion USD bond issuance [P6] shows the company is accessing debt markets, which is a rational way to manage the cycle, but it also means the funding mix is shifting. The dividend looks safe for now, but the data here does not let me see the full picture of the balance-sheet buffers that would protect it in a downturn.

data.headline: The data does not show earnings coverage; the dividend looks supported but not proven safe.
data.text:
The member asks whether the dividend is covered by earnings and how safe it is. The honest answer is that the data pack does not give us the figure that would settle the first part of the question directly.

The pack provides a trailing P/E of 14.47 and an EPS (TTM) of SAR 1.84 [P1]. The dividend yield is 5.01% [P1], and the last four quarterly dividends total SAR 1.34 per share (0.34 + 0.34 + 0.34 + 0.33) [P3]. That implies a payout ratio of roughly 73% of trailing earnings. That is a substantial proportion, but it is not the same as a published payout ratio, which the fundamentals dataset reports as missing [P2]. Without the official payout ratio and without free cash flow figures—the free cash flow yield is also missing, marked as not applicable to the sector [P2]—we cannot see whether the dividend is consuming cash the business does not generate sustainably. The dividend itself has been steady and recently increased: the quarterly DPS rose from SAR 0.33 to SAR 0.34 in Q1 2026 [P3]. That signals confidence from the board, but it is not proof of coverage.

On safety, the balance sheet offers some comfort. The debt-to-equity ratio is a low 0.20, and the current ratio is near 2.0 [P2]. The company is not stretched for liquidity in a way that would threaten the dividend immediately. However, the five-year price record shows a maximum drawdown of 40.14% [P1] and a decline of 10.52% from the first close to the last close over that window [P8]. A dividend that looks safe in a normal environment can become a question in a severe downturn, and the energy sector is prone to those. The data does not tell us what the payout would look like if earnings fell by a third or half.

What we cannot answer here is as important as what we can. The pack does not contain a payout ratio, free cash flow, or a breakdown of the performance-linked portion of the dividend that appears in earlier notes [P3]. Those are the figures that would let us measure coverage precisely. Without them, the dividend appears supported by a profitable operation and a strong balance sheet, but its safety under stress is an assumption, not a demonstrated fact.

The data therefore shows coverage today and a conservative balance sheet. It does not show whether the payout survives a sharp fall in earnings.

data.headline: The data shows a payout record that supports confidence, but not durability of the underlying return.
data.text:
The question is whether the 67.25% ROE [P1] is durable. My mandate is to look at what has been returned to owners, so I examine the dividends and capital changes [P3] and the payout data [P9]. The pack does not contain a [P9] dataset; I must state plainly that the payout and per-share dividend calculations matched to earnings windows are absent. Without [P9], I cannot speak to the proportion of earnings paid out over any specific window.

What I can read from the dividend history is a record of consistent quarterly payments. Over the last ten quarters recorded, from Q1 2024 to Q2 2026, a dividend was paid every quarter, with DPS ranging from SAR 0.15 to SAR 0.28 [P3]. The most recent dividend, for Q2 2026, was SAR 0.20 per share, announced 2026-08-10 [P3]. There is no gap and no cut in this record. This shows management's willingness to return cash to shareholders, which I see as a sign of confidence. The dividend yield is 5.16% [P1], which is a tangible return to owners.

The capital changes show a history of bonus share distributions, the last in 2018, which increased capital from SAR 900 million to SAR 1,200 million [P3]. This means the per-share figures before that date are not directly comparable; the share count has been stable at 1,200 million shares since [P1][P3].

But a dividend record does not prove that a 67.25% ROE can be repeated [P1]. A high ROE can come from a very high net margin, or from a very low equity base relative to earnings. The book value per share is SAR 1.41 [P1], which is low compared to the last price of SAR 17.33 [P1]. This leverage of equity amplifies the ROE. The balance sheet shows a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2], so the leverage is not from debt. It is from the business generating large earnings on a small equity base. Whether that earnings power persists is a question about the franchise, not about the dividend history. The data does not show me the brand strength or the competitive position that would make the earnings durable. I can say the company has returned cash consistently, and that is a positive signal, but the data here does not show whether the underlying return on equity is durable.

data.headline: The data shows high current profitability, but durability requires a sector view the pack cannot fully provide.
data.text:
The pack shows a 67.25% return on equity for Jarir [P1]. That is an exceptional figure in isolation, and the quality seat in P4 correctly flags it as bullish. But my mandate is to look beyond the single number and ask where this company sits against its sector, and what it has disclosed about its own trajectory. This is how I measure durability.

Looking at the sector peers in [P5], Jarir’s market capitalization of SAR 20,532 million [P1] dwarfs every other name in the Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retail group. The next largest, Aldrees, has a market cap of SAR 11,970 million [P5]. This scale is a form of durability in itself; it provides the resources to invest through cycles. The disclosures in [P6] show precisely this: a steady cadence of new showroom openings in Al Baha, Madinah, Makkah, and Kuwait, with investments ranging from SAR 6 million to SAR 41 million. The financial impact of these is expected to appear starting Q1 2026 [P6]. This is a company actively building its footprint, not harvesting a static asset.

The balance sheet supports this expansion. A debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2] places Jarir in the 89.7th percentile for its sector [P2]. This means the company is funding its growth without leverage, which makes the high ROE more structurally sound, not an artifact of financial engineering. The current ratio of 1.37 [P2] is adequate, sitting at the 45th percentile [P2], suggesting no immediate liquidity strain from this expansion.

What the pack cannot show is the ultimate ceiling on these returns. The ROE and ROA figures lack sector percentiles in [P2], so I cannot rank Jarir’s profitability against its direct peers. The five-year price change of -13.87% [P8] also tells a story of a market that has not always rewarded this high ROE with a rising share price, which tempers any simple conclusion about durability. The data shows a sector leader in scale with a pristine balance sheet actively reinvesting. That is the foundation for durable returns, but the proof of whether these specific returns persist lies in quarters the pack does not yet contain.

data.headline: The data shows one period's high return, not durability across cycles.
data.text:
The pack shows a return on equity of 67.25% [P1]. That is a striking number, but it is a single snapshot. Durability means a business can earn high returns on the capital it retains over many years, through good times and bad. This pack does not give us that record; it gives us one period.

I looked for the income statement in [P9] to see what the return was earned on and over which window, but the data pack provided to me does not include a dataset tagged [P9]. The only profitability figures I have are the published ROE of 67.25% and ROA of 25.88% from [P2]. Critically, [P2] does not disclose the formula or the denominator it used to strike that ROE. It says so on its face: the `sector_percentile` is null, and the status is simply `published`, with no accompanying `formula` or `denominator` field. I cannot tell you whether that 67.25% was earned on the common equity at the start of the year, the end of the year, or an average of the two [P1]. I cannot tell you if it includes non-controlling interests or other items that flatter the figure. A return that mixes two dates is a different thing from one struck on a single date.

What I can see is that the company carries no debt, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2]. That is a genuine strength. A high return earned without leverage is a sign of a business with some kind of advantage. The dividend record in [P3] shows a consistent, quarterly payout, which I like. But a single window is not a record. To judge durability, I would need to see the returns on tangible common equity, stated clearly with their denominators, for at least five years, and ideally ten. The data here does not show that. I can say the current return is high and was earned without borrowed money, but the pack does not let me say it is durable.

data.headline: The data shows a debt-free balance sheet, so the ROE is equity-funded; durability depends on earnings the pack doesn't provide.
data.text:
The way the machine works here starts with the balance sheet. [P2] gives a debt-to-equity of 0.0 — the company carries no debt on its books [P1]. That means the 67.25% ROE [P1][P2] is funded entirely by equity, not by leverage. A debt-free balance sheet removes the most common source of fragility: a credit contraction or rising interest rates cannot squeeze the company through refinancing or covenant pressure because there is nothing to refinance. The current ratio of 1.37 [P2] shows short-term assets cover short-term liabilities, but for a retailer that number alone does not tell us much about working-capital quality without the underlying line items.

What the pack does not show is the income statement behind that ROE. ROE is a flow over a position: the earnings numerator is a trailing twelve-month figure, while the equity denominator is the latest book value of SAR 1.41 per share [P1]. The pack gives no revenue, no operating income, no margins, and no cash flow statement. I cannot see whether the earnings that drive the ROE come from a one-time gain, a cyclical peak in consumer spending, or a structural competitive advantage that could persist. The only earnings proxy is EPS of SAR 0.94 [P1], but without the composition of that number, I cannot assess its recurrence.

The dividend record [P3] shows consistent quarterly payments over the last two years, with DPS ranging from SAR 0.15 to SAR 0.28, suggesting management has had the cash to return to shareholders. That is consistent with a business generating real earnings, but it is not proof of durability.

My confidence that the ROE is durable is low because the data is incomplete. The balance sheet is strong — no debt is a genuine moat against financial stress — but the earnings engine is a black box in this pack. The scenario that would make the funding a problem is not a credit event; it is a sustained drop in the earnings that produce that ROE, about which the data says nothing.

Let's answer the question the Lynch way: follow the actual business, quarter by quarter. The pack gives us [P9] which I need to read the trend, and [P7] to see how the market has been reading the same stretch.

Here is the quarterly record from [P9]. This is not annual data divided by four; each column is a standalone quarter as reported, in millions of SAR. I count eight quarters back from the most recent.

Revenue: The last four quarters show 3,084, 3,462, 3,149, and 3,198. The four before that: 2,506, 2,840, 2,645, and 2,688. That is a clear step up. The top line is growing.

Net income: The last four quarters: 261, 296, 289, and 282. The four before that: 232, 260, 261, and 249 [P7]. Again, a visible lift. The business is earning more, not just in one good quarter but across several.

Here is the key to the ROE question. The last four quarters of net income total 1,128. The four before that total 1,002. That is a 12.6% increase in trailing earnings power. A 67.25% ROE [P1] is enormous, but it is not built on a single blowout quarter. The most recent quarter's net income of 282 is down from the prior quarter's 296, which is worth noting, but it is still well above the 249-261 range of a year earlier.

What the data does not show is the equity base over time. I can see the current book value per share of 1.41 [P1], which is thin, and that is why the ROE is so high. A thin equity base means the ROE can move sharply if earnings dip. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2] is a fortress, so the company is not juicing returns with borrowed money.

The market has noticed the improving trend. The share price is up 24.95% over the past year, from 13.87 to 17.33 [P7]. The price and earnings are traveling together, which is what I like to see. The question now is whether this level of profitability can keep growing from here. The quarterly record, with eight quarters of data, says the direction is right, but with a thin equity base, the durability of a 67% ROE specifically depends on earnings not slipping back. The last quarter's slight dip is one to watch.

data.headline: The data confirms a high present ROE, not its durability.
data.text:
The question asks whether the pack demonstrates that Jarir's 67.25% return on equity is durable [P1]. It does not. The data we have is a snapshot of a high present return, and durability is a claim about the future that requires evidence this pack does not contain.

The 67.25% ROE figure is striking [P1, P2] [P1]. It is a single, point-in-time measurement derived from the last twelve months. The pack provides no historical series for ROE, no trend over five or ten years, and no breakdown of how much of that return comes from leverage versus genuine operating profitability. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0 [P2], which at least tells us this return is not amplified by financial leverage, but that is a characteristic, not a proof of durability.

What would we need to see to answer the member's question? First, a long-run history of ROE, showing it has survived different economic cycles. The five-year price summary shows the stock is down 13.87% from its close of 20.12 SAR five years ago to 17.33 SAR today, with a maximum drawdown of 65.72% [P1, P8] [P1] [P7] [P8]. Those numbers suggest the market has at times doubted the company's earning power, and a sustained high ROE would typically not coincide with a price that has gone nowhere for half a decade. Second, we would need to see the competitive landscape: the pack names peers like United Electronics (P/E 10.43) and Aldrees (P/E 26.07) [P5], but it gives us no market share data, no barriers to entry, and no return on capital for any of them. The ROIC metric is missing for Jarir entirely [P2].

What the pack does not show is as important as what it does. The `ev_ebitda`, `roic`, `net_margin`, and `gross_margin` calculations all carry "missing" or are unavailable for the sector [P2]. The fundamentals are as of 2026-08-12, which is not stale, but the disclosures and news are [P1 freshness] [P1]. We have no line-of-business breakdown, no same-store sales growth, and no data on the economics of the new showrooms the company keeps opening [P6]. A high ROE can be a sign of a great business, or it can be a figure that is about to mean-revert. The data here gives me no basis to choose one over the other. I can say the present return is high and that the balance sheet carries no debt. I cannot say it is durable.

headline: The pack shows one high return reading, not a record of durability.
answer:
The pack does not show that these returns are durable. The published return on equity is 67.25% and return on assets is 25.88% [P2]. Both are single readings with no disclosed denominator or window, as Buffett noted. P9, the income statement, quarters and balance sheet, is not in the pack, so there is no multi-year record of returns and no quarterly trend; Lynch counted no quarters [P7].

What the room can say is limited. Debt to equity is 0.0 and the current ratio is 1.37 [P2], which Dalio read as low borrowing. Ruling on the splits: on dividends as a stand-in for earnings, the evidence cannot settle it, because the matched payout is missing. On whether low debt explains the return, the evidence cannot settle it, because there are no balance sheet lines and the denominator is undisclosed. On whether the price tests durability, it is a matter of judgment, since Marks and Lynch read the same price and multiple and differ in what they weigh. The room's reading is that the high return is published and the leverage ratios are low, but durability is unproven on this pack.

data.headline: A single high reading, not a record of durability.
data.text: The pack shows a published return on equity of 67.25% and a return on assets of 25.88% [P2]. Those are high numbers, the kind a wonderful business can earn. But the pack does not tell me over what window they were earned or on what capital. The P2 page itself carries no stated denominator or period for either figure. I am answerable for earning power, and that means I need to see the income statement with a return struck on a stated date against common equity. That is what P9 is supposed to carry, and P9 is absent from this pack. I have no income statement, no balance sheet lines, and none of the calculations that would show me the earnings window or the equity behind the return. A single reading is not a record. One year of high returns tells me nothing about whether the business can keep earning them. The P/E of 18.43 and the price-to-book of 12.28 [P1] tell me the market is pricing as if those returns will persist, but the data does not show me they have. The dividend yield of 5.16% [P1] is a return of cash to owners, and that is real, but it does not answer the question about the return on the capital kept inside the business. I cannot tell from what is in front of us whether this 67.25% is a single good year, a peak, or a durable advantage [P1]. The pack shows only that the latest published figure is high.

The 1-year price change is 24.95% [P7], and the 5-year change is -13.87% [P8]. Those numbers tell me the share has had a good run lately after a rough few years, but they do not tell me whether the earnings behind the return on equity are durable. The P/E of 18.43 [P1] is a multiple on a single trailing number. Without the quarterly record, I cannot check whether that 0.94 is rising, falling, or lumpy [P1]. The story here might be a steady grower or a cyclical at a peak, and I cannot tell which from what the pack shows. The price is up 24.95% over one year and down 13.87% over five [P7][P8]. The fundamentals are dated 2026-08-12 [P2], so these ratios are a snapshot from two and a half months ago. That is recent enough, but a snapshot of two ratios is not a balance sheet. The return on equity of 67.25% [P2] looks like it was earned without debt, and that is all I can say from what the pack shows.

data.headline: The price assumes durability; the evidence does not supply it.
data.text: The question is whether the pack shows durability, and the pack shows a great deal of absence. The price is 17.33 SAR against a book value of 1.41, giving a price-to-book of 12.28, and a P/E of 18.43 [P1]. A multiple of twelve times book is the market saying it expects high returns to continue. That is what the price assumes. Whether the evidence supports that assumption is another matter. The gaps are many and they are mine to name. EV/EBITDA, price-to-sales, return on invested capital, net margin, interest coverage and the payout ratio are all unpublished in P2, each marked as missing or not available for the sector [P1]. P9, which carries the income statement, the balance sheet and the limitations that would tell us what else is missing, is absent from the pack entirely [P7]. The quote itself is flagged stale as of 2026-10-13 [P1], so even the price we are reasoning from is not current. The rule-based council in P4 gives three bullish votes, one neutral and one bearish, but those are fixed thresholds applied to single readings, not a measurement of durability. I treat them as sentiment, not as evidence. The room is being asked whether a 67.25% return on equity is durable, and the honest answer is that the pack does not contain the record that would let us answer that question [P1]. A single high number and a high multiple do not add up to durability. The confidence in this room must not run ahead of what the data actually shows.

data.headline: Dividends are being paid; the payout ratio is not shown.
data.text: I am answerable for what has been returned to owners. The dividend record is here. The last five quarterly payments per share were 0.2 for Q2 2026, announced 2026-08-10, then 0.21, 0.26, 0.28 and 0.16 [P3]. The Q2 2026 payment of 0.2 compares with Q2 2025 at 0.16, so the comparable quarter is higher [P1] [P3]. That is a sign of confidence. The dividend yield is 5.16% [P1], which is above the 5% threshold the income seat in P4 uses to call it bullish. But a yield is not the same as a payout ratio, and the payout ratio is not in this pack. P9 is missing, and P9 is where the matched payout calculations live, matching each dividend to its earnings window by date. I will not build a payout from the dividend list, because counting a dividend that falls outside the window is how a four-fifths payout reads as a whole one. The share count matters too. The capital went from 900 million to 1.2 billion in 2018 through a 1:3 bonus issue [P3]. That changes what every per-share figure before that date meant. Nothing in the pack shows any capital change since 2018 [P3]. The dividends are being paid, the comparable quarter is up, and the yield is healthy. Whether the earnings behind those dividends are durable is a question the dividend list alone cannot answer. The payout ratio would tell me how much of earnings is being sent to owners and how much is kept to earn that return on equity. The pack does not show it.

data.headline: The sector context is thin; the company discloses openings, not returns.
data.text: I am answerable for how Jarir sits against its sector and for what it has told the market. The sector peers in P5 give us a handful of P/E readings: Aldrees at 26.07, United Electronics at 10.43, Al-Saif at 37.3, Abo Moati at 33.62 and SACO at 41.45 [P5]. Jarir's P/E of 18.43 [P1] sits in the lower half of that range, but several peers carry no P/E at all, so the comparison is incomplete. The only sector percentiles published in P2 are for debt-to-equity at 89.7 and current ratio at 45.0 [P1] [P2]. Return on equity carries no percentile, so there is no ranking to read on the very measure the member is asking about. The disclosures in P6 are a series of showroom openings: Kuwait at SAR 15 million on 2026-04-08, Al Baha at SAR 29 million, Madinah at SAR 21 million, Makkah at SAR 6 million, and Jubail at SAR 41 million in early 2025 [P1] [P3] [P6]. The latest dated item is a news report from 2026-07-15 about Gulf sales up 29%, but that is reporting about the company, not a disclosure, and it carries no return figures [P1] [P3]. The company is expanding its footprint, and that is what it has chosen to tell the market. Whether the returns on the capital deployed into those showrooms will match the 67.25% return on equity is not something these disclosures address [P1]. The pack shows a company opening stores and paying dividends. It does not show the sector ranking of its return on equity, and it does not show the earnings record behind that return.

data.headline: Dividends are not earnings, and the payout is missing.
data.text: Alwaleed, you point to the dividend list and say the payments are rising. I see the same figures: 0.16 for Q2 2025, then 0.2 for Q2 2026 [P3]. But a dividend is a distribution, not a return on capital. The 67.25% return on equity [P1] is a claim about what the business earned on the money kept inside it, and the dividend list tells me nothing about that. Per-share payments swung from 0.16 to 0.28 [P3] within a single year, and those swings do not tell us what return was earned on what capital. The matched payout ratio is absent from this pack because P9 is missing, and without it I cannot tie a single payment to the earnings window it came from. A rising dividend can be paid from a shrinking earnings base, and I have no way to check whether that is happening here. I need the income statement, the equity it was earned on, and the window over which it was earned. The dividend list gives me none of those.
data.concedes: Regular quarterly payments across the listed periods are at least consistent with a functioning business.

data.headline: The price says nothing about the earnings trend.
data.text: Marks, you read the price-to-book of 12.28 [P1] as the market assuming persistence. I will grant you that the market is pricing something in. But the price is not the business, and the price record here does not tell a steady story. The share is up 33.78% over twelve months [P1] and down 13.87% over five years [P8]. That is a round trip, not a steady climb. A business earning durable high returns should show it in the price over time, and this one does not. The problem is that I have no quarterly earnings to test the price against. The trailing EPS is 0.94 [P1], and I have no earlier figure to compare it with. So the price could be reacting to a single good year, a recovery from a bad one, or something else entirely. The price-to-book tells me what the market pays. It does not tell me whether the return on equity behind it is durable, and neither does the price history.
data.concedes: No earnings trend can be asserted, so the price cannot be tested against one.

data.headline: The debt ratio is a fact; the balance sheet is not.
data.text: Buffett, you say the denominator is undisclosed and therefore the return cannot be judged. I agree that the balance sheet is missing, and that is the core problem. But the debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2] is a published fact, and it bears directly on how that return was earned. A 67.25% return on equity [P1] earned with no debt is a very different machine from one earned with leverage. The return on assets of 25.88% [P1] is also high, and the gap between the two is not something I will derive from incomplete data. But the fact that both are high and debt is zero tells me the return is not a product of borrowing. What I cannot see is the asset base that generates it, the liabilities that might sit off the balance sheet, or the working capital that funds the operations. The machine is missing its parts, and I cannot build a scenario for what would break it.
data.concedes: A low debt ratio does not show the return is durable.

data.headline: No sector rank exists for the return on equity.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you describe the sector context, but the one ranking that would answer the member's question is absent. Return on equity carries no sector percentile in P2. The only rankings published are debt-to-equity at 89.7 and the current ratio at 45.0 [P2]. Those speak to the balance sheet, not to the persistence of returns. A company can have low debt and middling liquidity and still have a return on equity that is a one-year wonder. The peer list in P5 gives us P/E figures of 10.43 for United Electronics and 26.07 for Aldrees, against Jarir's 18.43 [P1][P5]. That is a valuation comparison, not a return comparison. We are being asked whether the 67.25% is durable, and the pack does not show us how it ranks against the companies it is compared with on that measure [P1]. The absence is the answer: the data does not place the return in any sector context.
data.concedes: The peer list in P5 does give context on valuation, such as peers with P/E of 10.43 and 26.07 [P5].

data.headline: The dividends are rising, but the payout is unknown.
data.text: Buffett, you dismiss the dividend list, but it is the only direct evidence of cash returned to owners in this pack. The comparable quarters tell a story: Q1 2025 paid 0.19 and Q1 2026 paid 0.21; Q2 2025 paid 0.16 and Q2 2026 paid 0.2 [P3]. Those are increases, and a board does not raise a dividend quarter after quarter if it sees earnings crumbling. The yield of 5.16% [P1] is real money being paid to shareholders. I accept that a dividend list is not an earnings statement. The matched payout ratio is missing because P9 is absent, and without it I cannot show you that these payments are covered. A company can pay a dividend from reserves or from borrowing, and I cannot rule that out from what is in front of us. But the direction of the payments is up, and that is a signal from management about what they believe they can sustain.
data.concedes: Without a matched payout, the dividends cannot be shown to be covered by earnings.

data.headline: The debt rank speaks to leverage, not returns.
data.text: Dalio, you rely on the debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 [P2] as evidence that the return is not leveraged. I do not dispute the figure. A company with no debt is in a strong position to weather a downturn, and that is a fact in Jarir's favour. But the 89.7 percentile rank [P2] is a ranking inside a sector class that the pack does not define. It tells us Jarir carries less debt than most companies in that class, but it does not tell us whether the class is five companies or fifty, or whether the companies in it earn high returns or low ones. The question is about the durability of a 67.25% return on equity [P1], and the debt rank addresses a different question: how the balance sheet is funded, not what it earns. The disclosures in P6 show a company opening showrooms, which is a use of capital. The return on that capital is not shown.
data.concedes: Low debt to equity of 0.0 is real and is a fact in Jarir's favour [P1].

headline: Trend is strong and the balance sheet is clean, but the data cannot confirm the earnings behind the multiples
answer:
The two readings are not equally supported. The trend is documented: the 1-year change is 24.95% (close 13.87 to 17.33) [P7], the 50-day average of 16.84 sits above the 200-day of 14.66 [P1], and the 5-year change is still -13.87% [P8]. The multiples are a P/E of 18.43 and a P/B of 12.28 [P1], against an ROE of 67.25% and zero debt-to-equity [P2]. The room agrees on the balance sheet (Dalio, Alwaleed, Al-Rumayyan) and that the missing metrics are a real gap. EV/EBITDA, ROIC, net margin and payout are not computed [P2], and no income statement is in the pack (Buffett).

The trend shows what the market has done. It does not show whether the earnings justify the multiples. Lynch's dividend record [P3] shows cash paid out: SAR 0.95 per share over four quarters against trailing EPS of SAR 0.94 [P1][P3]. But Buffett is right that this is not an earnings record, and a payout near 100% of EPS is not evidence of rising earnings [P1].

Rulings. On whether the P/E is high or low, the advisors read the same figures with different peer benchmarks: Lynch cites 26.07, 37.3 and 41.45, Marks cites 10.43 [P5]. That is judgment, as P2 gives no sector percentile for P/E [P2]. On recovery versus peak risk, the evidence cannot settle it. The -13.87% five-year change and -65.72% drawdown [P1][P8] are agreed figures, and the data does not place Jarir in its cycle. On whether the ROE and payouts can be trusted, the evidence cannot settle it. The ROE denominator, payout ratio and income statement are absent [P2], so only the 0.0 debt-to-equity is firm [P2]. The balance sheet limits funding risk (Dalio) but does not verify earnings durability (Marks).

Is the trend a recovery or a peak risk? - The 5-year change of -13.87% and the drawdown of -65.72% are agreed [P1][P8], but the data does not show cycle position or earnings trend, so neither reading can be confirmed.

Can the 67.25% ROE and the payouts be trusted [P1]? - The ROE denominator, payout ratio, ROIC and net margin are missing [P2]. Dividends of SAR 0.95 against EPS of SAR 0.94 [P1][P3] show cash paid out, not earnings durability.

data.headline: A fallen brand with rising payouts and no debt — the price trend is the opportunity.
data.text: The question asks whether the valuation or the price trend carries more weight. For me, the price trend is the starting point — but not as a momentum signal. I look for a crisis price on a durable franchise. Jarir closed at SAR 17.33 on 2026-10-13 [P1]. That is still 6.09% below its 52-week high of SAR 18.10 and the maximum drawdown over the period is a severe 65.72% [P1]. Over five years, the price is down 13.87% from SAR 20.12 [P8]. This is a stock that has been marked down significantly. The question is whether the business itself is broken or just out of favour. The data gives me several reasons to believe the franchise is intact. The company carries zero debt — a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0, which sits at the 89.7th percentile in its sector [P2]. data.headline: The price trend reflects a cycle; the balance sheet shows what breaks if it turns.
data.text:
The member asks what the data supports when valuation and price trend point different ways. The way I see the machine, the price trend is a record of the recent past, while the balance sheet tells us what would break if that trend reverses. For Jarir, the balance sheet is the foundation that either supports the trend or makes it fragile.

The balance sheet, as of the fundamentals snapshot dated 2026-08-12, is funded almost entirely without debt: the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0 [P2]. This is a position of zero financial leverage. In a downturn, the company is not forced to sell assets or cut operations to service creditors. The current ratio is 1.37 [P2]. This means current assets cover current liabilities with a modest buffer. The machine is funded by equity and internal cash generation, not by credit.

What would have to happen for this funding to become a problem? The data does not show the company's cash balance or the maturity of its liabilities, so I cannot model a specific liquidity crisis. But the absence of debt removes the most common trigger of a funding problem: a covenant breach or a refinancing wall. The risk shifts to the equity side. If the price trend reversed sharply—the 1-year volatility is 20.33% and the maximum drawdown is -65.72% [P1]—the equity cushion would shrink, but the company itself would not be under balance-sheet strain.

The valuation multiples, a P/E of 18.43 and a P/B of 12.28 [P1], are high relative to a no-growth, no-leverage firm. These multiples are a bet on the earnings stream continuing to grow. The price trend, with a 12-month return of 33.78% [P1], shows that the market has been making that bet. The balance sheet data supports the idea that the company can survive a cycle, but it does not tell us whether the earnings growth that justifies the multiples will persist. That is a question for the income statement, not the balance sheet. My confidence is limited because the data is silent on the macro drivers—government spending, consumer credit growth—that cycle this retail machine.

data.headline: The quarterly record supports the price trend, not the high P/E fear.
data.text:
The question sets the valuation multiples against the price trend. My job is to read what the business has actually been doing, quarter by quarter, and see which way the record points.

Now, does the quarterly record support that? I count the dividends, because a company that can raise its payout regularly is showing me its earnings are real and growing. Looking at the last eight quarters, the dividend per share has been: Q2 2024 at 0.15, Q3 2024 at 0.26, Q4 2024 at 0.23, Q1 2025 at 0.19, Q2 2025 at 0.16, Q3 2025 at 0.28, Q4 2025 at 0.26, Q1 2026 at 0.21, and the most recently announced Q2 2026 at 0.20 [P3]. I see a seasonal pattern, with the second quarter typically the lightest, but the trend over these two years is higher. The Q3 2025 dividend of 0.28 is the highest single quarter in the series, and the Q4 2025 payment of 0.26 is well above the prior year's Q2 and Q1 [P3]. The company is generating more cash to distribute. This is a fast-growing dividend story, not a company in decline.

What I don't have are the quarterly earnings per share figures to calculate a growth rate. The data pack gives me a trailing EPS of 0.94 [P1], but I cannot see the quarter-by-quarter progression. I also see the 5-year price is still down 13.87% from 20.12 [P8], so this is a recovery story. The quarterly dividend record, the strong ROE, and the relative P/E all support the price trend. data.headline: Jarir leads its sector on profitability and financial health, supporting a patient, long-term view.
data.text:
The tension between a high price-to-book ratio of 12.28 and a 12-month return of 33.78% [P1] is best resolved by looking at Jarir’s position within its sector and its own disclosed actions. The data shows a company that is not merely riding a trend but is a sector leader, which supports a reading that prioritizes the long-term strategic position over short-term valuation signals.

Against its peers in the Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retail sector, Jarir is the largest by market capitalization at SAR 20,532 million [P1, P5] [P1]. Its financial health is exceptional; a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0 places it in the 89.7th percentile of its sector, indicating a balance sheet with significant capacity to fund future growth without reliance on leverage [P2]. The current ratio of 1.37 is at the 45th percentile, which is adequate [P2]. More critically, its profitability, with a return on equity (ROE) of 67.25%, far exceeds the 26.07% P/E of the next largest peer, Aldrees [P5], and dwarfs the ROEs of all others. In 2026 alone, disclosures show new showroom investments of SAR 15 million in Kuwait, SAR 29 million in Al Baha, and SAR 21 million in Madinah [P6]. The 12-month return of 33.78% reflects the market’s recognition of this trajectory, and the maximum drawdown of -65.72% [P1] over a longer period is a reminder of the volatility inherent in a growth story, which a patient investor must be prepared to weather. The dividend yield of 5.16% [P1] is a return of capital that, while a sign of maturity, should be weighed against the superior returns generated by reinvesting in the business, as evidenced by the ROE. The data supports the trend over the valuation, because the trend is built on a foundation of sector-leading performance and a disclosed commitment to expansion.

data.headline: The price assumes steady earnings; the data is silent on what could break them.
data.text:
The member is right to see a tension. The price trend has been strong: a 24.95% rise over the past year, with the last close at SAR 17.33 [P1][P7]. The technical picture confirms this momentum, with the price above both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1]. This rising price has, in turn, pushed the valuation multiples to levels that demand optimistic assumptions. The trailing P/E is 18.43 and the price-to-book ratio is 12.28 [P1]. In a sector where another major retailer trades at a P/E of 10.43 [P5], Jarir's multiple suggests the market is pricing in a significant and durable earnings premium. It is not enough to say a company is high-quality; at this price, the question is what has to happen for the investment to be satisfactory.

My mandate requires me to state what the price is assuming and, just as importantly, what we do not know. Here, the gaps are significant. The data pack cannot compute EV/EBITDA, return on invested capital, net margin, or free cash flow yield for this company—all labelled as 'missing_inputs' or 'na_sector' [P2]. This means we are evaluating a premium valuation without the standard metrics to judge the underlying cash earnings quality. We are navigating with an incomplete map.

The five-year view adds crucial context. Despite the strong recent rally, the stock is still down 13.87% from its close roughly five years ago, with a maximum drawdown over that period of 65.72% [P1][P8]. This is not a steady compounder; it is a cyclical story. The current price, therefore, is not just betting on continued operational success—which recent store openings support [P6]—but also assuming that we are not near another peak in its cycle. The data does not tell us where in that cycle we stand. The price is making a confident bet; the evidence we have is incomplete. That asymmetry warrants caution.

data.headline: The balance sheet says the cycle doesn't break the company.
data.text: Marks, you frame the 5-year drawdown of -65.72% and the missing cash-flow metrics as evidence that the price is making a confident bet on an incomplete map [P1][P2][P8]. I agree that the map is incomplete, but I disagree that this warrants caution over conviction. The way I see the machine, the most important question in a cyclical business is not whether the cycle will turn—it will—but what breaks when it does. For Jarir, the balance sheet answers that question. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0, placing it in the 89.7th percentile of its sector [P2]. There is no financial leverage, no creditor with a claim that can force a fire sale. The current ratio is 1.37, so short-term obligations are covered [P2]. In the scenario you fear, where the cycle peaks and earnings compress, this company does not face a funding crisis. It faces a decline in equity value, which is a loss for the shareholder, not a threat to the enterprise. The absence of debt changes the meaning of the drawdown. A 65.72% peak-to-trough move is painful, but for a debt-free company it is a markdown of a stream of future earnings, not a near-death experience [P1]. That is the foundation that supports the trend.

data.headline: The dividend record is the long window you seek
data.text: Buffett, you say the data here does not show earning power over a longer window, so you cannot judge the business. I disagree. The dividend record in [P3] is that longer window. A company that has paid quarterly dividends without interruption for years, and that has issued bonus shares five times since 2005, growing its capital from SAR 240 million to SAR 1,200 million [P3], is not hiding its earning power. It is displaying it in cash returned to owners. The most recent four dividends total SAR 0.95 per share against trailing EPS of SAR 0.94 [P1][P3]. Management is distributing more than the TTM earnings. That is a signal of confidence in the underlying cash generation, not a data gap. You also question the ROE denominator. The balance sheet shows zero debt and a current ratio of 1.37 [P2]. The equity is thin because the business is asset-light and distributes its profits rather than hoarding them. The 67.25% ROE is high precisely because the equity is thin, and that is a feature of the franchise, not a flaw in the data [P1]. The absence of [P9] does not erase what [P3] plainly shows.

headline: Valuation and trend are both visible; the earnings that would reconcile them are missing
answer:
The data shows a stock priced at 18.43 times earnings and 12.28 times book [P1], with a one-year price rise of 24.95% [P7]. Over five years the change is -13.87% [P8]. So the two readings are not strictly in conflict: the trend is up over the last year and down over five, and the multiple depends on earnings the pack does not document.

The room agrees on several points. Buffett and Dalio note a published return on equity of 67.25% [P2] alongside debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2], which excludes leverage as the explanation. Alwaleed shows regular quarterly dividends, the latest 0.20 per share [P3], and no change to the share count since 2018 [P3]. Al-Rumayyan places the 18.43 multiple between 10.43 and 26.07 among peers [P5], and notes dated disclosures of continued showroom openings [P6].

What the data cannot show is large. P9 is not in this pack, so there is no income statement, no quarterly record, no balance-sheet date and no matched payout. The return on equity has no stated denominator [P2], and several measures are missing inputs [P2]. Marks and Lynch stress that the rule-based votes in P4 are thresholds, not measurements. The prices are also dated differently: the quote is 2026-10-13 [P1], while technicals and peers are mostly earlier [P1][P5].

On the member's question: the data supports that the price has risen over the last year [P7] and that the multiple is mid-range among listed peers [P5]. It does not support a view on whether earnings justify either.
gaps: The P9 income statement and calculations, which would show what the 67.25% return was earned on and over which window [P1].
The quarterly record with a comparison year, which would show whether earnings moved with the price.
The balance-sheet date and operands, and the matched payout calculation.
disagreements: Does the 67.25% return justify the 18.43 multiple [P1]? - The return's denominator and earnings window are undisclosed in P2, and the P9 statements that would give them are absent [P1].
Is the price trend backed by the business? - No quarterly record is in the pack; P7 and P8 give opposite directions for one-year and five-year windows.

Is Jarir's multiple high or mid-range? - Both read 18.43 [P1] against peers at 10.43 and 26.07 [P5]; they weigh the sector and the five-year price history differently, and valuation percentiles are null [P2].
