data.headline: Earning power cannot be established from the data in this pack.
data.text: The member asks about valuation and price trend, but the seat I occupy is answerable for earning power. On that, the pack is silent where it matters most. The published return on equity is 67.25% and return on assets is 25.88% [P2]. Those are striking numbers, but P2 states no denominator and no date. I cannot tell what capital those returns were earned on, or over what window. P1 gives a book value of 1.41 and a price-to-book of 12.28 [P1]. A high return on a thin equity base is a different thing from a high return on a large one. P9, which carries the income statement and the calculations that would show the denominator and the period, is not in this pack [P7]. Without it, I have a single published ratio and no record. I would not treat a single ratio as a record, and I would not call it a durable advantage without seeing the years behind it. The price trend is for others to read. My part is to say that the business's earning power, as distinct from a published number, is not shown. I can add only that the company carries no debt, with a debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2], which means whatever return it earns is not levered with other people's money. That is a point in its favour, but it does not fill the gap.

data.headline: The price rose but I cannot say whether earnings rose with it.
data.text: I am answerable for the quarterly trend, and P9 is not in the pack. That means I counted zero quarters. I cannot call a trend in the business from zero quarters. The market's reading of the same stretch is in P7: from 2025-09-29 to 2026-10-13, the first close was 13.87 and the last close was 17.33, a change of 24.95% [P7]. P1 gives a 12-month return of 33.78% and a 1-month return of -2.00% [P1]. The trailing twelve-month earnings per share is 0.94 [P1]. So the price has risen, and the trailing earnings number is there, but I cannot line them up quarter by quarter. The story the annual figures imply is one thing; whether the quarters support it is another, and I cannot answer it. The dividend yield of 5.16% [P1] is a real return to owners in the meantime. But the core of my method is checking that price and earnings travel together over time, and for that I need the quarters. I do not have them. One more thing: the 1-month return of -2.00% [P1] is a small pullback after a strong run, but one month is not a trend. Without the quarterly record, I cannot say whether that pullback reflects something in the business or just noise.

data.headline: The visible part of the balance sheet shows no borrowing strain.
data.text: I am answerable for the balance sheet. P9 is absent, so there is no balance sheet, no date for it, and no operands behind the ratios. What I can read from P2 is this: debt-to-equity is 0.0, at the 89.7 sector percentile, and the current ratio is 1.37, at the 45.0 percentile [P2]. The health score is 67.35 [P2]. Interest coverage is withheld for missing inputs [P2]. On this reading, the company carries no debt, which means there is no borrowing to strain it. A current ratio of 1.37 means current assets cover current liabilities 1.37 times, which is adequate but not ample [P2]. The funding of the rest of the balance sheet — how much is equity, how much is other liabilities, what the assets are — is not visible. So the machine I can see is simple: no leverage, modest liquidity. The scenario that would strain it would have to come from the asset side or from off-balance-sheet commitments, and neither is in the data. I cannot build a stress scenario from what is not there. The valuation and price trend the member asks about are readings of the market's machine, not the company's. My part is to say that the company's funding machine, as far as it is visible, is not under strain.

data.headline: The price assumes high returns persist; key evidence is absent.
data.text: The member asks whether valuation and price trend point different ways. The valuation says the market is asking a full price: 18.43 times earnings and 12.28 times book [P1]. That assumes the high returns persist. The price trend says the market has been willing to pay more: over five years the price went from a first close of 20.12 to 17.33, a change of -13.87%, against a high close of 21.66 and a low of 12.06 [P8]. The 12-month return is 33.78% [P1], so the recent trend is up, but the five-year picture is flatter. The maximum drawdown is -65.72% [P1], which tells you this is a share that can fall hard. The two do not necessarily point different ways: a full valuation on a business that has earned high returns and is growing can be consistent with a rising price. The question is whether the returns are sustainable, and on that the pack has gaps. P9 is absent, so there are no limitations or calculations to read. EV/EBITDA is null, price-to-sales and ROIC lack inputs, and net margin and payout lack inputs [P2]. The room's confidence must not run ahead of its evidence. The price is pricing in something; what exactly, we cannot fully measure from what is here.

data.headline: The dividend is steady but the payout ratio is not shown.
data.text: I am answerable for what has been returned to owners. P3 shows a steady dividend stream: the latest is 0.20 per share for Q2 2026, ex-date 2026-08-17, after 0.21 for Q1 2026 and 0.26 for Q4 2025 [P3]. The yield is 5.16% [P1]. That is a meaningful return to an owner. But the payout ratio — how much of earnings is being paid out — is a P9 calculation, and P9 is absent. Without it, I cannot say whether the dividend is well covered or whether the company is stretching to pay it. The last capital change was a 1:3 bonus issue on 2018-10-28, taking capital from 900 million to 1,200 million [P3]. That means per-share figures before that date are on a different share count. A bonus issue is a sign that management is sharing the accumulated equity with owners rather than hoarding it. The company has done this several times: 2013, 2011, 2009, 2005 [P3]. That is a record of treating owners as partners. The price trend shows a 12-month return of 33.78% and a maximum drawdown of -65.72% [P1]. A drawdown that deep is the kind of moment I look for. But the dividend record alone does not tell me whether this is a crisis price for a lasting franchise or a fair price for a business that has changed.

data.headline: Jarir leads its sector in dividends and is expanding its footprint.
data.text: Against its sector peers in P5, Jarir's 18.43 times earnings [P1] sits between United Electronics at 10.43 and Aldrees at 26.07 [P5]. It is not the cheapest, not the most expensive. On dividends, Jarir's 5.16% yield [P1] is among the higher in the group: peers run from 0.92% to 7.65% [P5], with only United Electronics higher at 7.65%. The sector percentiles for valuation in P2 are null, so there is no ranking to read; that is absence, not a low rank [P2]. What the company itself has disclosed is a pattern of expansion. A Kuwait showroom opened on 2026-04-08 at SAR 15 million [P6]. An Al Baha showroom opened in February 2026 at SAR 29 million [P6]. A Madinah showroom opened in January 2026 at SAR 21 million [P6]. These are not announcements of intent; they are completed investments. A news item dated 2026-07-15 reported Gulf sales up 29% and operations unaffected by shipping disruptions [P6]. That is a reported statement, not a disclosure, but it is consistent with the expansion. The price trend over five years shows a first close of 20.12 and a last of 17.33, a change of -13.87% [P8]. Over twelve months the return is 33.78% [P1]. The long arc is flatter than the recent surge, which is worth noting for patient capital.

data.summary: The room disagrees mainly on how much a published return and a one-year price rise can carry without P9.

data.headline: A dividend list is not an earnings record
data.text: Alwaleed, you point to a 5.16% dividend yield [P1] and a regular payment history [P3] as evidence of what has been returned to owners. I do not dispute the payments. But a dividend is paid out of earnings, and the pack does not show what earnings those payments were drawn from. P9, which would match each dividend to the earnings window it belongs to, is absent [P7]. Without that match, I cannot tell whether the company is paying out half its earnings or all of them, or whether it is paying from current earnings at all. A business that pays a steady dividend from a shrinking earnings base is not the same as one that pays from a growing one. The dividend history is a record of cash returned, but it is not a record of earning power. Earning power is what the business earns on the capital it keeps, and that is what I am answerable for. The pack does not show it.
data.concedes: The dividend history in P3 is regular and shows quarterly payments.

data.headline: The trend vote is a rule, not the business
data.text: Marks, you rightly note that the five-year change of -13.87% [P8] sits behind the one-year rise of 24.95% [P7], and that the window changes the story. I agree: a trend depends on where you start counting. But I want to separate two things. P4 gives a momentum vote of bullish, with a regime score of 100 and a golden cross [P4]. That is a threshold rule fired by the price crossing its moving averages. It tells you what the price has done, not what the business has done. My mandate is the quarterly record of the business itself, and P9 is not here. The price rise in P7 is a fact: first close 13.87, last close 17.33 [P7]. But without the quarters, I cannot say whether earnings rose with the price, or whether the price just got more expensive. The market's reading and the company's reading are two different things, and I only have the first.
data.concedes: The price trend alone is a fact; it is the link to earnings that is missing.

data.headline: No debt means the return is not levered
data.text: Buffett, you say the 67.25% return on equity [P2] cannot be confirmed because the denominator is undisclosed. I accept that. But the balance-sheet evidence I do have narrows the question. Debt-to-equity is 0.0, at the 89.7 sector percentile [P2]. That means the company carries no debt. Whatever return it earns, it is not levered with borrowed money. The current ratio is 1.37 [P2], so short-term obligations are covered. The machine is simple: no leverage, no interest burden, no refinancing risk. The return, whatever its base, is not amplified by debt. The question that remains is what the equity base is — how much capital the business retains and reinvests. The pack does not show that. But the absence of debt tells me that if the return is high, it is high for reasons other than financial engineering. That is a useful narrowing of the inquiry.
data.concedes: The denominator is undisclosed, so I cannot confirm what drives the return.

data.headline: The window you choose decides the trend
data.text: Lynch, you point to the one-year price change of 24.95% [P7] as a fact. It is a fact. But it is a fact measured from a first close of 13.87 on 2025-09-29 [P7], which is near the low close of 12.38 over that year [P7]. The five-year picture tells a different story: first close 20.12 on 2021-07-29, last close 17.33, a change of -13.87%, with a high of 21.66 and a low of 12.06 [P8]. The maximum drawdown over the full history is -65.72% [P1]. What you call a trend depends entirely on the window you pick. The one-year rise is real, but it starts from a low base. The five-year picture is flatter. Neither window is the whole truth. The question is what the price is assuming now, at 17.33 [P1], and that is a question about the business's earning power, which the pack does not fully answer.
data.concedes: Within the last year the price direction is up [P7].

data.headline: Regular dividends are a signal, not a proof
data.text: Buffett, you are right that the dividend list does not show what it was paid out of. I cannot match the 0.20 for Q2 2026 or the 0.21 for Q1 2026 [P3] to an earnings window because P9 is absent. I concede that. But the list itself is evidence of something. The company has paid every quarter across the data shown, including 0.28 on 2025-11-10 and 0.26 on 2025-08-11 [P3]. That regularity is not a proof of earning power, but it is a signal of management's confidence and of cash generation. A company that cannot pay does not pay quarter after quarter. The capital changes tell the same story: bonus issues in 2018, 2013, 2011, 2009, 2005 [P3] show accumulated equity being shared with owners. That is not a number I can match to earnings either, but it is a pattern. The payout ratio would settle it, and it is not here. But the pattern is not nothing.
data.concedes: Without the payout, I cannot say the dividend is covered.

data.headline: The sector list puts the multiple in context
data.text: Marks, you read the 18.43 price-to-earnings multiple [P1] as a full price. I do not dispute that it asks for something. But against the sector peers in P5, the range is wide: United Electronics at 10.43, Aldrees at 26.07, SACO at 41.45, and Abu Moati at 33.62 [P5]. At 18.43, Jarir sits in the middle of that range, not at the top [P1]. The peer rows are mostly dated 2026-08-07, while Jarir's quote is from 2026-10-13 [P5][P1], so the comparison is not exact. But the sector list is the exchange's own classification, and it shows that investors in this sector are paying a spread of multiples. Jarir's is not the highest. The expansion disclosures — Kuwait, Al Baha, Madinah [P6] — show a company building, not standing still. That may be what the multiple is pricing. The date mismatch limits the precision, but the context is there.
data.concedes: The date mismatch limits how exactly the comparison can be read.

verdict.headline: Valuation and trend are both visible; the earnings that would reconcile them are missing
verdict.answer:
The data shows a stock priced at 18.43 times earnings and 12.28 times book [P1], with a one-year price rise of 24.95% [P7]. Over five years the change is -13.87% [P8]. So the two readings are not strictly in conflict: the trend is up over the last year and down over five, and the multiple depends on earnings the pack does not document.

The room agrees on several points. Buffett and Dalio note a published return on equity of 67.25% [P2] alongside debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2], which excludes leverage as the explanation. Alwaleed shows regular quarterly dividends, the latest 0.20 per share [P3], and no change to the share count since 2018 [P3]. Al-Rumayyan places the 18.43 multiple between 10.43 and 26.07 among peers [P5], and notes dated disclosures of continued showroom openings [P6].

What the data cannot show is large. P9 is not in this pack, so there is no income statement, no quarterly record, no balance-sheet date and no matched payout. The return on equity has no stated denominator [P2], and several measures are missing inputs [P2]. Marks and Lynch stress that the rule-based votes in P4 are thresholds, not measurements. The prices are also dated differently: the quote is 2026-10-13 [P1], while technicals and peers are mostly earlier [P1][P5].

On the member's question: the data supports that the price has risen over the last year [P7] and that the multiple is mid-range among listed peers [P5]. It does not support a view on whether earnings justify either.

headline: The drawdown is an undated historical extreme; today's risk rests on leverage, valuation and missing credit data.
answer:
The pack gives a maximum drawdown of -83.12% [P1] but no trough date and no earnings or book value at that trough. The room agrees it is a past figure the pack cannot tie to today. Dalio reads it as a stress test of how a leveraged bank can reprice. Buffett, Lynch and Al-Rumayyan read it as market mood that predates the present capital base, though the pack does not date that capital base.

The current risk readings are moderate. One-year volatility is 20.94% [P1], inside the neutral band of the risk seat [P4]. The price is SAR 62.10, down 11.54% over one year [P7], below both the 50-day and 200-day averages [P1], and up 34.24% over five years [P8]. ROE is 23.49% [P2]. Debt-to-equity is 1.72, at the 22.7th sector percentile [P2]. Marks flags a P/E of 14.51 against peers at 9.48, 7.78 and 7.82 [P1][P5].

On the leverage dispute, the percentile shows the bank carries less leverage than most of its sector. Dalio's point about the absolute level is a different question. The pack has no deposit, wholesale funding, credit quality or liquidity data, so fragility under a credit downturn cannot be measured. Lynch also found the quarterly record [P9] missing.

What the data cannot tell: when the drawdown happened, how the bank was funded then, and whether current earnings are rising or falling. The room should be read as describing an undated past extreme set beside moderate present readings, with the key credit evidence absent.
gaps: The pack does not date the -83.12% drawdown or show earnings, book value or leverage at its trough [P1].
The pack has no deposit, wholesale funding, non-performing loan or liquidity coverage data.
The quarterly record [P9] is missing, so the current earnings trend cannot be read.
disagreements: Is the 1.72 debt-to-equity ratio reassuring or a warning [P2]? - The 22.7th sector percentile [P2] settles that peers are more leveraged. Whether the absolute level is dangerous turns on deposit mix, non-performing loans and liquidity coverage, which the pack does not hold.

Does the 23.49% ROE justify the premium P/E of 14.51 over peers [P1]? - Both sides read the same P/E, P/B and ROE [P1][P5]. They weigh premium against franchise quality differently. The peer table carries no ROE, so the claim that no peer exceeds 20% is not supported by the pack [P3].

What can the -83.12% drawdown say about today without dates [P1]? - The trough date, and the earnings and balance sheet at that point, are absent [P1]. Without them it cannot be compared with the current 1.72 ratio [P2] or the capital base [P3].

data.headline: A deep past drawdown matters less than today's price, yield, and the franchise.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown of -83.12% [P1] is a figure from the past, not today's risk. It tells you the share once fell from a much higher peak to a much lower trough, and anyone who bought at that peak suffered a severe loss. But the question is what risk you take buying at SAR 62.1 today [P1]. That is a different question entirely.

Look at what the price is doing now. The share is down -14.92% from its 52-week high and up only 6.66% from its 52-week low [P1]. The 12-month return is a modest 2.46% [P1]. This is not a euphoric price. The market has already marked it down over the last six months, with a -10.68% decline [P1]. A crisis price is when the crowd is selling, and the data shows the crowd has been selling.

What do you receive while you wait? The dividend yield is 2.6% [P1]. That is not high in absolute terms, but the bank has a long, uninterrupted history of semi-annual cash dividends, most recently SAR 1.17 per share for the second half of 2025, paid in April 2026 [P3]. The bank also just distributed a 50% bonus issue in April 2026, raising the capital from SAR 40 billion to SAR 60 billion [P3]. That is a signal of confidence from the board, not distress. The payout ratio for the matched window is not available in the data pack here, so I cannot tell you what portion of earnings that latest dividend represents.

The franchise itself is intact. Al Rajhi Bank is the largest listed bank on Tadawul by market capitalisation at SAR 387,300 million [P1], well ahead of SNB at SAR 245,160 million [P5]. Its return on equity is 23.49% [P1], a figure that speaks to a durable competitive position. The debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 [P2] is what you would expect for a bank and sits at the 22.7th percentile in the sector [P2], meaning it is less leveraged than most peers.

The drawdown figure is a scar from a past battle. The data I must read does not show when that -83.12% occurred, so I cannot connect it to a specific event [P1]. What I can see is a leading bank trading at 14.51 times earnings [P1], with a price that has already corrected, paying a dividend that has been raised over time, and fresh from a bonus issue that rewards shareholders. The risk today is not the 83% figure. The risk is whether the Saudi economy slows, and that is a risk every bank in the sector faces. The data does not show the brand strength or the quality of management, which are real assets for a market leader, but the numbers I am answerable for show a franchise that has returned capital to owners consistently and just gave them more shares.

data.headline: The drawdown is a history lesson, not today's risk gauge.
data.text:
That -83.12% maximum drawdown in [P1] is a big, scary number, but I need to know what kind of company I'm looking at before I let one statistic tell the whole story. Al Rajhi Bank is a large, steady bank, not a speculative start-up. The drawdown figure is a single point from the past, and the data here doesn't tell me when it happened or over what period. For all I know, it could be from the global financial crisis fifteen years ago. It tells me the stock has been absolutely crushed before, but it doesn't tell me why or if those conditions exist today.

What I care about is the trend now. My job is to check the quarterly record [P9] against the market's recent reading [P7]. But here's the problem: [P9] is missing. I have no quarterly data at all. I can't see if earnings are accelerating, stalling, or falling off a cliff. I can't see the trend in loans, deposits, or net interest income. Without that, I'm flying blind on the most important question: is the business getting better or worse right now?

Looking at what I do have, the price is down 11.54% over the last year [P7] and sits below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1]. The 1-year volatility is 20.94% [P1], which is moderate, not extreme. The bank is profitable with a 23.49% ROE [P1] and pays a 2.6% dividend yield [P1]. Its debt-to-equity is 1.72, which is better than over three-quarters of its sector peers [P2]. This is not a company on the brink.

The maximum drawdown is a record of the worst that has happened, not a forecast of what will happen. It's a measure of past pain, not present danger. Without the quarterly trend, I can't confidently connect that historical number to today's risk. The story is incomplete.

data.headline: A historic drawdown measures past price extremes, not today's structural risk.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown of -83.12% shown in [P1] is a historical statistic, not a live reading of fragility. It tells us that at some point in its listed history the share price fell that far from a peak before recovering, which for a bank that has been public for decades and whose capital has grown from SAR 750 million in 1991 to SAR 60 billion today [P3] is a record of having survived a severe cycle, not a forecast of the next one. The one-year volatility of 20.94% [P1] is more informative about the current regime: it sits in the neutral band of the risk seat's rule [P4] and is moderate for a large Saudi bank. Over five years the price has risen 34.24%, from SAR 46.26 to 62.10 [P8], so the long arc is positive even though the twelve-month return is a modest 2.46% and the shares have declined 10.68% over six months [P1].

What the drawdown does not capture is the quality of the institution today. The bank's return on equity of 23.49% [P1][P2] is the highest among the TADAWUL banking peers shown in [P5], none of which report an ROE above 20% in this pack, and its debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 ranks at the 22.7th percentile of its sector class [P2], meaning leverage is lower than roughly three-quarters of the companies in that class. The bank has also been actively raising long-term capital through dollar-denominated sukuk, most recently an AT1 issuance disclosed in January 2026 [P6], which strengthens its balance sheet for the cycle ahead. The drawdown figure is a scar from an earlier battle; the current data on profitability, leverage and funding suggests the bank is better armoured now. I would not dismiss the number, but I would not let an 83% drawdown that predates the bank's present capital base drive a decision about risk today.

data.headline: The drawdown is a rear-view mirror; today's risk is what the price assumes.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown of -83.12% over the period covered [P1] tells us that the stock has suffered a severe, near-total decline from a peak at some point in its history. This is a fact about the past, not a forecast. It shows that the downside can be extreme, and that anyone who held through that cycle needed extraordinary fortitude or an absence of alternatives. On its own, however, it does not tell us whether that loss was permanent or temporary, nor whether the conditions that caused it are present today.

The more immediate question is what the current price of SAR 62.10 assumes about the future [P1]. The trailing P/E of 14.51 and a price-to-book of 3.19 are not cheap on an absolute basis [P1]. When I look at the banking peers, the market assigns Al Rajhi a significant premium: SNB trades at 9.48 times earnings, Riyad Bank at 7.78, and Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82 [P5]. The market is clearly pricing in a superior and more durable level of profitability for Al Rajhi, a view supported by its 23.49% return on equity [P1]. The risk is that this premium is built on expectations that could be disappointed. The one-year return of just 2.46% and the six-month decline of -10.68% [P1] suggest the pendulum may have already swung from optimism toward something more cautious, yet the multiple remains elevated relative to peers.

The data also reveals what we do not know. The pack gives no net margin, no interest coverage ratio, and no free cash flow yield for this bank—all measures that could help size the downside if credit conditions weaken [P2]. The rule-based council votes are neutral on value and risk, but these are mechanical thresholds, not a reading of the assumptions embedded in the price [P4]. The drawdown is a warning that the downside can be deep. The valuation premium is a warning that the price is not compensating you for that possibility. The missing data is a warning that our picture of that risk is incomplete.

data.headline: A severe past drawdown signals how this machine can break in a credit contraction.
data.text:
The maximum drawdown of -83.12% recorded in the price history [P1] is not a forecast, but it is a critical piece of evidence about the machine we are dealing with. It tells me that, under a past set of conditions, the market repriced this asset by more than four-fifths from a peak. The way I see it, a drawdown of that magnitude is a stress-test result; it shows what the structure can produce when a cycle turns.

The question is whether the balance sheet today is funded in a way that makes it vulnerable to a repeat. Looking at my part of the data, the balance sheet position is struck as of the fundamentals date in [P2], which is 2026-08-12. The debt-to-equity ratio stands at 1.72, and this is in the 22.7th percentile for the sector [P2]. For a bank, a debt-to-equity ratio above 1.5x means the institution is using significant leverage to fund its assets [P6]. The machine is funded largely by liabilities, not just by equity.

The data pack does not give me the breakdown of those liabilities—I cannot see the split between deposits, wholesale funding, or the AT1 sukuk mentioned in the disclosures [P6]. That is a gap. But I can see the pattern: a leveraged balance sheet, combined with a 1-year volatility of 20.94% and a recent price that is below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1]. The trend regime score of 35 out of 100, which the momentum seat flags as bearish [P4], is consistent with a market that has already started to discount a less favorable environment.

What would have to happen for the funding to become a problem? A scenario where asset quality deteriorates—non-performing loans rising—would eat into the equity base that supports this leverage. If that coincided with a tightening of liquidity that made rolling over the bank's sukuk or wholesale funding more expensive, the machine would be under strain. I cannot say that is happening now, because the pack contains no credit quality or liquidity coverage data. But the -83.12% drawdown is a reminder that when the cycle turns for a leveraged institution, the repricing can be violent [P1]. That is the scenario I would weigh most heavily.

data.headline: The drawdown tells a market story, not a business risk story.
data.text:
A maximum drawdown of -83.12% [P1] is a steep number, but I must ask: a drawdown from what price, over what stretch of years, and was the business earning more or less at the bottom? The pack does not tell me the dates or the book value at that trough, so I cannot connect the price fall to the earning power of Al Rajhi Bank at the time. Without that, the figure is a rear-view mirror of market mood, not a measure of permanent loss risk.

What I can judge is the business behind the ticker. The return on common equity, struck on tangible common equity of SAR 20.11 per share [P1] against trailing twelve-month earnings of SAR 4.42 per share [P1], comes to about 22%. That is a solid number, and the published ROE of 23.49% [P2] confirms it. The bank earned that return with a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 [P2], which sits at the 22.7th percentile in its sector—meaning it uses less leverage than most peers. A bank that earns a high return on equity without leaning too hard on borrowed money has a durable earning engine. The five-year price history shows a 34.24% rise from SAR 46.26 to SAR 62.10 [P8], so the long-term owner has done fine even after the recent 11.54% twelve-month slip [P7].

Volatility of 20.94% [P1] is not trivial, but it is the price of owning a good business. The risk that matters is whether the bank's competitive position—its branch network, its deposit base, its standing in the Kingdom—has been damaged. Nothing in the pack suggests it has. The bonus-share history [P3] tells me management returns capital to owners rather than hoarding it, which I like. So the drawdown figure says more about past panics than about the risk of holding the shares today. If the business keeps earning 22% on equity and pays a 2.6% dividend [P1] while growing its capital, the real risk is not the next price swing but paying a price that leaves no margin of safety. At 14.5 times trailing earnings [P1], the price asks for moderate confidence; the drawdown asks for none at all.

data.headline: A drawdown is a stress test, not just a scar
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you call the -83.12% drawdown a 'scar from an earlier battle' that predates the present capital base [P1]. I disagree with framing it as a historical artifact that has little bearing on today's risk. The way the machine works, a drawdown of that magnitude is a stress-test result that reveals the structure's potential for violent repricing under a set of conditions. The key structural feature is leverage, and the balance sheet I read, struck as of 2026-08-12, still shows a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 [P2]. For a bank, that means the funding is dominated by liabilities, not equity. You point to the 22.7th sector percentile as evidence of lower relative leverage [P2], but the absolute level is what matters for loss absorption. If asset quality deteriorates, a small percentage decline in asset values can wipe out a much larger percentage of the equity cushion. The recent AT1 sukuk issuance [P6] adds capital, but it also adds a layer of debt-like obligations. The drawdown is not just a scar; it is a reminder that this machine, funded as it is, can break badly when the credit cycle turns. The data here does not give us the current credit quality or liquidity metrics to say that risk is absent.
data.concedes: I concede that the pack does not date the drawdown, so we cannot tie it to the current capital base.

data.headline: A 1.72 ratio is not leverage—it's a bank's balance sheet [P2].
data.text: Dalio, you call a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 'significant leverage' and a reason to fear a repeat of the -83.12% drawdown [P1]. But this is a bank, not a manufacturer. A bank's liabilities are its raw material. The data shows this ratio sits at the 22.7th percentile in its sector [P2]. That means over three-quarters of the banks in this pack carry more leverage than Al Rajhi. If the cycle turns, this bank is better positioned, not worse. You say the pack lacks a breakdown of deposits and funding, and you are right—it does not show that [P6]. But the bank just raised capital, not fled from it. The disclosures show a $1.5 billion AT1 sukuk completed in January 2025 and a further AT1 issuance in January 2026 [P6], plus a 50% bonus share issue that lifted equity from SAR 40 billion to SAR 60 billion in April 2026 [P3]. This is a bank strengthening its capital base, not one stretched thin. The drawdown you treat as a stress test is a number without a date [P1]. I cannot connect it to a balance sheet that has been transformed by a decade of bonus issues [P3]. The risk today is not the past figure; it is missing the price the market is offering now.
data.concedes: The pack does not show the deposit or wholesale funding breakdown, which is a gap.

data.headline: Leverage alone is not the stress-test story
data.text: Dalio, you treat the 1.72 debt-to-equity ratio as a warning that the machine is funded largely by liabilities and could break in a credit contraction [P2]. But for a bank, that ratio is not high—it sits at the 22.7th percentile in its sector [P2], meaning over three-quarters of peer banks carry more leverage. A bank that earns 23.49% on equity [P2] with less borrowed money than most competitors is not a fragile machine; it is a conservative one. The real stress test is whether the earnings cover the cost of those liabilities through a cycle. The pack gives me no non-performing loan data or net interest margin trend, so I cannot see the credit quality. But a 34.24% five-year price rise [P8] and a dividend record that stretches back years with rising payouts [P3] tell me this bank has already lived through cycles without cracking. The -83.12% drawdown [P1] is a market panic figure, not a balance-sheet failure figure. I concede that the pack does not show the liability breakdown you rightly want to see.
data.concedes: The pack does not show the deposit or wholesale funding breakdown, which would complete the leverage picture.

data.headline: Leverage is a bank's business, not a warning signal
data.text: Dalio, you call a 1.72 debt-to-equity ratio 'significant leverage' and a reason to worry about a credit contraction [P2]. But a bank is not a manufacturer. Its business is taking deposits and making loans—that's how it earns its 23.49% ROE [P1]. A debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 means for every SAR 1 of equity, the bank has SAR 1.72 of liabilities [P2]. That is not high for a bank. The pack puts it at the 22.7th percentile in its sector [P2], meaning more than three-quarters of the banks in its class carry more leverage. You say the pack doesn't show the split between deposits and wholesale funding, and you're right—that's a gap. But what it does show is a bank that has been raising long-term capital through sukuk, including a $1.5 billion AT1 issuance in January 2025 and a $1 billion Tier 2 social sukuk in September 2025 [P6]. That is a bank actively managing its funding, not one sleepwalking into a crunch. The -83.12% drawdown [P1] is a number without a date, and without knowing when it happened or what the balance sheet looked like then, I can't connect it to today's 1.72 ratio. A drawdown from two decades ago, before the bank's capital grew from SAR 750 million to SAR 60 billion [P3], is a different machine entirely.
data.concedes: You are right that the pack lacks the deposit and wholesale funding breakdown—I can't see the liquidity structure either.

data.headline: A historical drawdown does not measure today's structural resilience
data.text: Dalio, you read the -83.12% drawdown as a stress-test result showing how violently a leveraged institution can reprice, and you flag the 1.72 debt-to-equity ratio as significant leverage [P1] [P2]. I see the same ratio differently. That 1.72 sits at the 22.7th percentile of the sector class in [P2], which means the bank uses less leverage than roughly three-quarters of the companies in that class. For a bank, that is a conservative position, not an aggressive one. You also note the pack lacks deposit, wholesale funding and credit quality data, and I agree that is a gap. But what the pack does show is that the bank has been actively reinforcing its capital base: a $1.5 billion AT1 sukuk in January 2025, a $1 billion Tier 2 social sukuk in September 2025, and a further AT1 issuance disclosed in January 2026 [P6], all while the general assembly approved a 50% bonus share issue in April 2026, lifting capital from SAR 40 billion to SAR 60 billion [P3]. data.text: The member asks about risk, and the drawdown figure is -83.1175137585% [P1]. That is a price figure, and a price figure tells you what the market has done, not what the business has earned. My mandate is earning power: what was earned, over which window, and on what capital. The data pack carries no income statement and no calculations for this company. The published return on equity is 23.49% [P1][P2], but it discloses no denominator and no dates. The drawdown may reflect a moment when the business was earning poorly, or it may reflect a moment when the market simply marked down a good business. Without the earnings history, I cannot tell which it was. A deep drawdown in a business that kept earning well is an opportunity; a deep drawdown in a business whose earnings collapsed is a warning. data.headline: The drawdown may be distorted by bonus issues
data.text: Marks reads the drawdown of -83.1175137585% [P1] as a risk signal, but a drawdown computed from unadjusted prices on a stock with a history of bonus issues is not a clean measure. The bank issued a 50% bonus on 2026-04-20, a 60% bonus on 2022-05-08, and a 53.85% bonus on 2019-04-03 [P3]. Each of those increases the share count without changing the company's value. An unadjusted price series would show a drop at each bonus date that is not a loss. The pack does not state whether the drawdown is adjusted for these capital changes. I cannot confirm from the data that it is distorted, but I cannot confirm that it is clean either. For a company with this history, the adjustment basis is not a detail; it is the difference between a crisis signal and a calculation artifact. The dividend record shows steady payments through the period, which a broken business would not manage.
data.concedes: The pack does not show that the drawdown is unadjusted, so this is a question, not a finding.

headline: The datasets carry different as-of dates and cannot be read as one snapshot.
answer:
The room agrees on the main point: these figures are not one snapshot. The quote block in [P1] is dated 2026-10-13, with a last price of 25.78 SAR. The technicals in [P1] are dated 2026-08-11. Fundamentals in [P2] are dated 2026-08-12 and are the only category the pack marks not stale [P1]. The council votes in [P4] are stamped 2026-08-07. Buffett, Lynch, Dalio and Marks therefore describe an October price laid over a business record that ends about two months earlier. Valuation multiples such as the P/E of 14.47 and the 12-month return of 10.42% [P1] sit on that mixed footing.

The pack is internally inconsistent on the price date. The quote says 2026-10-13, while the freshness list in [P1] gives prices as of 2026-08-11. Both are flagged stale against a 2-day limit.

As Lynch, Dalio, Marks and Alwaleed noted, the data cannot show quarterly results, a dated balance sheet or a payout ratio. Buffett added that the ROE of 26.75% and ROA of 15.86% [P2] come without a stated equity denominator or earnings window. The pack lists payout, ROIC, net margin and interest coverage as missing inputs [P2]. A dataset labelled [P9] is not in this pack, so several advisors cited something that does not exist here.

data.headline: The data is a patchwork of different dates, not one snapshot.
data.text:
We cannot read this as one snapshot. The datasets have different as-of dates, some of which are stale. The price and technical data in [P1] is from 2026-10-13, but its freshness is marked 'stale' because it's older than the 2-day limit. The fundamentals in [P2] are fresher, as of 2026-08-12, and are not stale. The dividend history in [P3] extends through the last announced payment on 2026-08-27. The news in [P6] is current through 2026-08-04, but its freshness category is 'stale' because it's beyond its 30-day window. The sector peers in [P5] are as of 2026-08-07. So, we are looking at a collage of moments from August to October 2026 [P1]. It is not a single, clean snapshot.

Now, for my mandate: I am to read the quarterly record [P9] against the market's one-year price summary [P7]. The problem is clear: the data pack has no [P9] dataset. The quarters that would tell me the real story—whether revenue and earnings are accelerating, holding steady, or decelerating—are not here. Without them, I cannot do my job. I cannot say if the annual figures are supported by a solid string of quarters or if one great quarter is masking trouble. The one-year price range in [P7] shows a modest gain, with the stock moving from a close of 24.99 to 25.78, a 3.16% change. But the journey was bumpy: the high was 27.96 and the low was 23.41 [P7]. That tells me the market's opinion has been shifting, but without the quarterly business results, I can't tell you why. I need the quarterly sales and earnings to match the price chart. The story is incomplete.

data.headline: The data is a patchwork of stale and fresh snapshots, not one picture.
data.text:
The member asks whether these datasets can be read as one snapshot. The answer is plainly no. The freshness tags in [P1] tell the story: the price data is stale as of 2026-10-13, with a max age of 2 days, meaning it is roughly two weeks behind today. The fundamentals are fresher, last updated 2026-08-12, and are not yet stale [P1]. Disclosures are stale since 2026-03-09, and news is stale since 2026-08-04 [P1]. Each dataset carries a different as-of date, so they do not describe the company at a single moment. This is a mosaic assembled from pieces of different ages.

What must this price be assuming? The last price is 25.78 SAR, down 10.52% from five years ago [P8]. Over that half-decade, the stock has traded as high as 38.64 and as low as 23.13 [P8]. The current P/E of 14.47 and price-to-book of 4.1 [P1] sit well above the levels a deep-value investor would seek. The market is not pricing this as a distressed asset; it is pricing in continued, substantial profitability. The 5.01% dividend yield [P1] offers a tangible return, but it comes with the memory of a 40.14% maximum drawdown [P1], a reminder that the price can fall sharply when sentiment shifts.

What do we not know? The data pack has significant gaps. There is no EV/EBITDA, no ROIC, no net margin, and no gross margin—all marked as missing inputs or not applicable in [P2]. We lack the denominator for free cash flow yield and interest coverage. Crucially, the [P9] dataset, which I am answerable for, is entirely absent from this pack. I cannot report on its limitations or its missing calculations because it was not provided. This means we cannot assess what specific calculations the system could not perform and why. The room's confidence must not run ahead of its evidence, and right now, a significant piece of that evidence is missing. The rule-based council votes in [P4] are based on fixed thresholds, not a holistic reading of the data, and I treat them as a rough gauge of sentiment, not a measurement of value.

data.headline: Dividend and capital data are current through Q2 2026, but price data is stale [P1].
data.text:
I look first at what has been returned to owners and how the share count has changed, because a dividend cut or a dilution is a signal management sends with cash, not words. The dividend record [P3] runs through the Q2 2026 payment announced on 2026-08-04, with an ex-date of 2026-08-19 and a pay-date of 2026-08-27. That is the most recent commitment we have. The quarterly dividend has been steady at SAR 0.34 per share for the last three quarters, after a period at SAR 0.33, and the capital changes show no dilution: the last action was a secondary offering in June 2024 where the government sold shares; the company itself did not issue new equity [P3]. The share count used in the per-share figures is 242,000 million shares [P1], and the last bonus issue was in May 2023, so the per-share earnings and book value reflect a stable count.

The payout ratio [P9] is missing from the data pack, so I cannot tell you what portion of matched earnings was distributed. That gap matters, because a steady dividend paid from declining earnings is a different story from one paid from growing earnings. I must say plainly that the data here does not show it.

On freshness, the fundamentals are current as of 2026-08-12 and are not stale [P2]. But the price snapshot is from 2026-10-13 and is marked stale [P1], as are the technicals from 2026-08-11. The disclosures date to March 2026 [P6]. This is not one snapshot: the price is two weeks old, the fundamentals are from August, and the dividend record is from the same period. If we are judging whether this is a crisis price for a lasting franchise, I would want a fresh price before I decide whether the market has marked it down enough.

data.headline: The data spans multiple periods; a single-snapshot reading would be misleading.
data.text:
Chair, the member asks whether these datasets can be read as one snapshot. The short answer is no. The data is drawn from different points in time, and treating it as a single, simultaneous picture of the company's condition would be an error.

The most recent price quote in [P1] is from 2026-10-13, yet the technicals and the fundamentals it reports alongside it are based on data as of 2026-08-11 [P1, P2]. This creates a two-month gap between the market price and the company's financial position. The balance sheet, which I am answerable for, is not provided in [P9] and its date is therefore absent, making it impossible to assess the current state of what the company owns and owes.

Looking deeper, the dividend record in [P3] is current up to an announcement on 2026-08-04, and the news and disclosures in [P6] also stop in early August 2026. The council's rule-based votes in [P4] are stamped as of 2026-08-07. So, the bulk of the non-price data clusters around early August 2026, while the price is from mid-October [P1]. The return figures in [P1], like the 12-month return of 10.42%, are calculated up to the October price date, mixing a fresh market value with a financial picture that is over two months old.

Furthermore, the fundamental metrics I rely on, like the debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 and the current ratio of 1.99 from [P2], are themselves based on a balance sheet struck at an unstated date. Without knowing that date and the composition of the liabilities, I cannot build a reliable scenario for what would strain this funding. The machine has moving parts, and they are not all in the same position at the same time. We must read each piece with its own timestamp.

data.headline: The data is a patchwork of dates, not one snapshot.
data.text:
The Chair asks whether these figures share a common date and can be read as one picture. Looking across the pack, the plain answer is no. The price quote is from 2026-10-13 [P1]. The fundamentals, including the profitability metrics I am answerable for, carry an as-of date of 2026-08-12 [P2]. The technicals are even older, from 2026-08-11 [P1]. The dividend record runs through August 2026 [P3]. So we are not looking at one moment; we are looking at a price from mid-October laid over a business record that ends two months earlier. The picture has a gap in it.

Now to my part of the work: the earning power. The pack shows a return on equity of 26.75% and a return on assets of 15.86% [P2]. Those are good numbers on their face, but I need to know what they were earned on and over what period. The published ROE in [P2] does not disclose its own formula or the date of the equity it used. The data pack does not provide a full income statement or balance sheet with a stated common equity denominator and a clear window for the earnings, so I cannot trace the calculation myself. I can see that the business carries very little debt relative to its equity, with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.20 [P2]. That tells me these returns are not simply the product of leverage; the earning power is real in that sense. But without the underlying statements, I cannot say whether that 26.75% was struck on beginning equity, ending equity, or some average, nor can I see the exact twelve-month window those earnings cover [P1]. A single return figure, without its denominator and its dates, is not a record. It is a single data point, and I treat it as such.

data.headline: The datasets are months out of sync; this is no single snapshot.
data.text:
The data pack does not present a single snapshot. It is a set of figures drawn from different dates, and reading them as one picture would misrepresent the company.

Look at the freshness markers in [P1]. The price quote and technicals are as of 2026-08-11, and both are marked stale [P1]. The fundamentals in [P2] carry an as-of date of 2026-08-12 and are the only set not flagged as stale. The disclosures in [P6] run from late 2025 to the most recent item, dated 2026-08-04. The sector peers in [P5] show an as-of date of 2026-08-07 for four of the five names and 2026-08-12 for the fifth. The returns and valuation in [P1] that the market quote is built on are therefore from a different moment than the fundamentals that explain them. The gap is months wide, and the data itself warns that the price file is overdue for refresh.

On my own mandate, I am answerable for the company against its sector and for its own disclosures. The peer list in [P5] shows the company's weight: a market capitalisation of SAR 6,413,000 million [P1] dwarfs every other name on the Tadawul Energy list, the next being Bahri at SAR 27,906.98 million [P5]. That scale matters to a long-horizon view. The disclosures in [P6] are the company's own words: the 2026-08-04 statement from the chief executive about resilience, the March buyback plan for 350 million shares, and the bond and sukuk issuances that stretch back through the year. None of these carry an impact rating, and the data shows no rated news items [P4].

The fundamental percentiles in [P2] offer a debt-to-equity ratio at the 54th sector percentile and a current ratio at the 68.4th, but the sector class itself is broad and the numbers are from a single date. The picture is of a dominant company whose disclosed actions are consistent with a long-cycle capital plan, but the data to judge it against peers is not current enough to be read as a single frame with the price. I cannot treat these datasets as one snapshot, and the pack itself tells me not to.

data.headline: P9 is absent; I cannot read earning power or its date.
data.text: My part is earning power, and I cannot do it. The income statement and the denominators I need sit in P9, which is not in this pack [P1]. I cannot say what this company earned, over which window, or on what capital it earned it. P2 publishes a return on equity of 26.75% and a return on assets of 15.86%, and it does not state a denominator or a date for either [P2]. P2 itself is stamped 2026-08-12 [P2], so those returns cannot be tied to the 2026-10-13 price [P1]. The two figures are separated by two months. A return that mixes two dates is not a snapshot, and a return whose denominator is undisclosed is not something I can read with confidence. I will say plainly what is missing: the income statement, the equity it was earned on, the window it covers, and the date the equity is struck at. Without those, I cannot tell whether the 26.75% was earned on a thin sliver of common equity or on a base swollen with other people's money [P1]. I cannot tell whether it is a single year or a trailing twelve months. I cannot tell whether it is real. The room should treat the published ROE and ROA as numbers without a home until P9 gives them one.

data.headline: No quarterly record in the pack; I count zero quarters.
data.text: The trend is quarterly, and the quarterly record lives in P9, which is absent, so I count zero quarters and call no trend [P1]. I cannot tell you whether earnings are accelerating, decelerating, or flat. I cannot tell you whether a good year was made by one strong quarter or four steady ones. P7 shows only price: first close 24.99 on 2025-09-29 and last close 25.78 on 2026-10-13, a change of 3.16% over 260 trading days [P7]. That is the market's reading of the same stretch, and it does not tell me whether earnings moved with it or against it. Price can run ahead of the business or lag behind it; without the quarterly record I cannot say which. The price summary also gives a high close of 27.96 and a low close of 23.41 [P7], so the market has been more volatile than the 3.16% full-period change suggests. But that is still just price. I need the quarters to do my job, and they are not here. The room should know that any story about the trend is being told without the one record that would confirm or refute it.

Those are ratios with no operands shown, so I cannot tell whether they mix a flow with a position or which date they use. A debt-to-equity ratio that divides a balance-sheet debt by a balance-sheet equity is one thing; one that divides a flow of interest expense by a position of equity is another. I cannot see the lines, so I cannot build the scenarios I need. I cannot tell you what would have to happen for the funding to become a problem because I cannot see the funding. P2 is stamped 2026-08-12 [P2], so whatever position those ratios describe, it is at least two months older than the 2026-10-13 price [P1]. headline: The sector table shows a premium, not cheapness; whether the premium is earned stays untested.
answer:
No. On the peer table the shares do not look cheap. Al Rajhi Bank's P/E of 14.51 [P1] is above every other listed Saudi bank in [P5], from Riyad Bank at 7.78 to Bank Albilad at 11.94 [P5]. Its dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is below all eight peers, the nearest being Alinma at 3.1% [P5]. All six advisors agree on this.

The room differs on whether the premium is deserved. Al-Rumayyan and Alwaleed point to franchise quality and a 23.49% ROE [P1]. Buffett and Marks reply that one ROE snapshot does not show durability. Lynch and Alwaleed add that the earnings and payout record they would need is not in the pack. Buffett also notes that ROA is 2.53% [P1].

On leverage, the debt-to-equity ratio is 1.72, at the 22.7th sector percentile, and the metric is marked higher_is_better false [P2]. In the final round Dalio, Marks and Al-Rumayyan each described their own position differently, so the room's closing statements do not give one clean reading. The pack gives a percentile for this metric but does not define its direction. It also gives no percentile for ROE [P2].

The price-to-book of 3.19 [P1] cannot be compared with peers because [P5] carries only P/E and yield. The peer table is dated 2026-08-07 and the quote 2026-10-13 [P5][P1], and the pack marks the price data as stale [P1].

In sum, the comparison supports reading the shares as priced at a premium. It cannot show whether that premium is justified, because the multi-period earnings record the advisors asked for is absent from the pack.

A multi-period earnings and balance sheet record is absent, so durability of the 23.49% ROE and the dividend payout cannot be tested [P1].

Is the 14.51 P/E premium explained by franchise quality [P1]? - Both sides rest on a single ROE of 23.49% [P1] with no sector percentile [P2] and no multi-period earnings record in the pack. Durability cannot be tested.

data.headline: The sector comparison shows a premium, not cheapness, on the numbers we have.
data.text:
The data in [P5] doesn't paint Al Rajhi as cheap relative to its Saudi banking peers. The bank trades at a P/E of 14.51 [P1], while every peer listed in [P5] trades at a lower multiple: Saudi National Bank at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, Alinma at 10.97, Saudi Awwal at 7.82, Banque Saudi Fransi at 9.30, Arab National Bank at 8.49, Bank Albilad at 11.94, and The Saudi Investment Bank at 9.03. The market is asking a higher price for each riyal of Al Rajhi's earnings than for any of these competitors. On a price-to-book basis, Al Rajhi stands at 3.19 [P1], a figure that also suggests a premium. Its dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is lower than every peer in [P5] except Alinma Bank at 3.1%; the others range from 4.04% to 6.02%. On these three simple measures, the shares appear dear, not cheap.

Now, a higher multiple can be earned. The question is whether the earning power justifies it. Here I must turn to what I am answerable for in this room: the returns on the capital the business keeps. The pack provides a published ROE of 23.49% [P1, P2] and ROA of 2.53% [P1, P2] [P1]. Those are fine numbers. data.headline: The data does not show cheapness; it shows a premium for scale and quality.
data.text:
The sector peer data in [P5] does not show Al Rajhi Bank’s shares to be cheap relative to the other listed Saudi banks. The bank trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 14.51 [P1], which is the highest among the peers listed in [P5]. Saudi National Bank (SNB) has a P/E of 9.48, Riyad Bank 7.78, and Saudi Awwal Bank 7.82 [P5]. On this simple, widely-used metric, the market is assigning a significant premium to Al Rajhi’s earnings compared to its competitors.

This premium is not a sign of cheapness; it is the market’s judgment of the company’s quality and its position within the sector. A patient, long-horizon investor should not confuse a low multiple with value. The quality is evident in the fundamentals. The bank’s return on equity is 23.49% [P1], a figure that would place it at the top tier of any banking sector, and its debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 ranks in the 22.7th percentile among its peer class [P2], indicating a relatively conservative balance sheet. This financial strength is what the market is paying for.

The disclosures in [P6] show a bank actively managing its capital structure for the long term, with multiple successful issuances of AT1 and Tier 2 sukuk in 2025 and 2026, including a $1.5 billion AT1 sustainable sukuk and a $1 billion Tier 2 social sukuk. This is not a company scrambling for funding; it is one with access to deep, international pools of capital, reinforcing its strategic position.

Therefore, from a long-term, strategic perspective, the shares are priced for dominance, not for a discount. The data does not show a cheap stock; it shows a leading franchise commanding a premium.

data.headline: No, the sector data shows Al Rajhi is the most expensive bank on P/E.
data.text:
No, the sector comparison does not show Al Rajhi Bank's shares are cheap. In fact, the data in [P5] paints the opposite picture. Among the eight listed Saudi banks provided, Al Rajhi carries the highest price-to-earnings ratio at 14.51 [P1]. The next closest peer is Bank Albilad at 11.94, while the rest of the group trades at multiples well below 10 [P1] [P5]. Saudi National Bank (SNB), the largest peer by market cap, trades at a P/E of just 9.48 [P5]. When I look at a stock, I want to see a P/E that is reasonable relative to the story and the peers. Here, you are paying a significant premium for Al Rajhi's earnings compared to every other major bank in the sector.

What do you get for that premium? The dividend yield tells a similar story. Al Rajhi's yield of 2.6% [P1] is the lowest in the peer group [P5]. You have banks like Saudi Awwal Bank yielding 6.02% and Arab National Bank at 5.94% [P5]. For an income investor, Al Rajhi is not the place to be based on this data.

Now, my mandate is to check the quarterly trend, but the data pack does not include [P9], the quarterly financials I am answerable for. I cannot count the quarters, examine the revenue and earnings progression, or tell you if the business is accelerating or slowing down quarter by quarter. That is a critical missing piece. A high P/E can sometimes be justified if the company is growing earnings much faster than peers, but without [P9], I cannot confirm that story. What I can see from the price history in [P7] is that the shares have fallen 11.54% over the last year, closing at 62.1 SAR from a 52-week high close of 73.34. The market has already been marking down the premium. So, based strictly on the sector comparison we have, the shares look expensive, not cheap.

data.text:

When I look at the peers listed in the same sector, every other Saudi bank trades at a lower multiple. Saudi National Bank is at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, Alinma Bank at 10.97, Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82, Banque Saudi Fransi at 9.30, Arab National Bank at 8.49, Bank Albilad at 11.94, and The Saudi Investment Bank at 9.03 [P5]. The data on financial health in [P2] shows a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72. This ranks in the 22.7th percentile of the sector, meaning it is more leveraged than the vast majority of its peers [P2]. The data does not give me the sector percentile for ROE, so I cannot say how this return compares on a risk-adjusted basis. data.headline: The sector comparison says cheap, but the data alone cannot capture the franchise.
data.text:
The sector comparison [P5] shows Al Rajhi Bank trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 14.51 [P1], which is the highest among all the listed Saudi bank peers. Saudi National Bank (SNB) is at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, and Alinma Bank at 10.97 [P5]. On a simple earnings multiple, Al Rajhi is not cheap; it is the most expensive name in the group. This is the price the market puts on a leading franchise.

What the data cannot show is the value of that franchise. A strong brand and market position are not captured in a P/E ratio, and I will not pretend they are. The dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is also the lowest among the peers listed here, where yields range from 3.1% at Alinma up to 6.02% at Saudi Awwal Bank [P5]. A low yield often accompanies a premium valuation, but it also means an investor is not being paid much to wait.

My mandate is to examine what has been returned to owners and out of what. The dividend history [P3] shows a steady stream of semi-annual and annual payments. The most recent distribution was SAR 1.17 per share for the second half of 2025, paid in April 2026 [P3]. The capital history shows a pattern of bonus share distributions, the latest being a 50% increase approved in April 2026, taking the capital from SAR 40 billion to SAR 60 billion [P3]. However, the data pack does not contain the payout ratio calculations [P9] that would match each dividend to a specific earnings window, so I cannot assess from the provided data exactly what proportion of earnings was paid out for any given period. Without that, the sustainability of the current dividend against earnings is a question the available data leaves open.

data.headline: The price assumes quality; the sector comparison does not show cheapness.
data.text:
The question asks whether the sector peers in [P5] show Al Rajhi Bank's shares to be cheap. I think the data points in the opposite direction, and the more important question is what the current price already assumes.

Let us look at what the pack gives us. Al Rajhi trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 14.51 [P1]. Every listed peer in [P5] trades at a lower multiple: Saudi National Bank at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, Alinma at 10.97, Saudi Awwal at 7.82, Banque Saudi Fransi at 9.30, Arab National Bank at 8.49, Bank Albilad at 11.94, and The Saudi Investment Bank at 9.03. On this measure alone, Al Rajhi is the most expensive name in the group by a wide margin. The price-to-book of 3.19 [P1] is not shown for the peers in this pack, so a full relative valuation cannot be built, but the P/E gap is large enough to demand an explanation.

The dividend yield tells a similar story. Al Rajhi yields 2.6% [P1]. Every peer in [P5] yields more: the lowest is Alinma at 3.1%, and several are above 5%. The market is paying a higher price for each riyal of earnings and accepting a lower cash return from Al Rajhi than from any other bank on the list.

What does this price have to be assuming? It is assuming that Al Rajhi's return on equity of 23.49% [P1] is both durable and superior enough to justify the premium. It is assuming that the recent negative returns—down 4.58% over three months and down 10.68% over six months [P1]—are noise, not a signal. It is assuming that the five-year rise from 46.26 to 62.10 [P8] still has room to run despite the stock now trading below both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages [P1].

And here is what we do not know from this pack. [P9] is not present; I am told to read every entry in its `calculations` that carries `missing` and to read its `limitations`. The data for that dataset is absent. I cannot tell you which metrics could not be computed, which denominators the source withholds, or which statements are not published at all. That absence itself is a gap the room should note. Without it, we are working with a partial picture, and our confidence must be scaled accordingly.

On the evidence we do have, the sector comparison does not make Al Rajhi look cheap. It makes it look like a quality franchise priced for continued outperformance. Whether that assumption proves right depends on outcomes this data cannot guarantee.

data.headline: A 22.7th percentile signals more leverage, not conservative balance sheet [P2]
data.text: Al-Rumayyan reads the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.72 and its 22.7th sector percentile as indicating a relatively conservative balance sheet [P2]. I think that reading is backwards. The data in [P2] marks this metric with `higher_is_better` set to false, meaning a lower ratio is healthier. A 22.7th percentile means that roughly 77 percent of the sector peers carry less debt relative to equity than Al Rajhi does [P2]. That is not conservative; it is a sign that the bank is among the more leveraged names in its peer group. The return on equity of 23.49% [P1] must be weighed against this. In banking, a high ROE can be a function of higher leverage rather than superior asset returns, and the ROA of 2.53% [P1] is a more modest figure. The pack gives no sector percentile for ROE, so we cannot see whether that 23.49% is exceptional on a risk-adjusted basis [P1]. The disclosures in [P6] do show successful sukuk issuances, but those are precisely the instruments that build the leverage the percentile is measuring. Access to capital markets is a strength, but it does not make the resulting debt load conservative. The data shows a bank that uses more debt than most peers to generate its returns.
data.concedes: The premium P/E does reflect a leading franchise with strong market access, as the sukuk disclosures in [P6] confirm.

The strong ROE of 23.49% [P1] is not a separate fact from this leverage; for a bank, a high ROE can be generated by taking on more debt. headline: Against listed bank peers the shares look dearer, not cheaper, but the comparison is thin.
answer:
On the sector comparison in the pack, the shares do not show as cheap. Al-Rumayyan read Al Rajhi Bank's P/E of 14.51 [P1] against the eight listed Tadawul banks, whose P/E values run from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5], so it is above every peer. Its dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is below every peer, whose yields run from 3.1% to 6.02% [P5]. Marks added that the P/B of 3.19 [P1] cannot be compared because peer P/B is not in the pack.

The room agrees on direction but not on what the premium means. Buffett noted that the return on equity of 23.49% [P1] could justify a higher multiple, but its denominator is not disclosed [P2] and the income statement that would show whether it is durable is not in the pack. Lynch could count no quarters, so growth cannot be set against the P/E. Dalio found only one health percentile, 22.7 [P2], and no balance sheet. Alwaleed pointed out that the matched payout is absent and that a 50% bonus issue on 2026-04-20 [P3] changes what earlier per-share figures meant.

The comparison also has limits. P2 carries no sector percentile for P/E, P/B or yield, so no ranking exists. The peer figures are dated 2026-08-07 [P5] and the Al Rajhi quote 2026-10-13 [P1], and the price freshness flag shows stale [P1]. The gap is wide enough that the direction is clear, but the size of the premium is not precise.

What the data shows is a higher multiple and a lower yield than peers. It does not show whether the premium is earned, and it does not show cheapness. None of this is advice.
