data.headline: The pack cannot confirm the returns, so the premium cannot be judged.
data.text:
The question is whether the sector comparison shows the shares are cheap. To answer that I need to know what the business earns, on what capital, and over what window. My part of the evidence is earning power, and the income statement and the calculations in P9 are not in this pack. I have no earnings history, no common-equity denominator I can name, and no window to read. The only return figure is a return on equity of 23.49% [P2], and it does not disclose its own denominator. A return that mixes two dates without saying which two is not one I can assess. A single window would not be a record in any case, and I cannot call it one.

A bank that earns a high return on equity will usually trade at a higher multiple than its peers, and Al Rajhi’s P/E of 14.51 [P1] sits above every peer in the list, whose P/E values run from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5]. That premium may be deserved or it may not, but without the earnings record I cannot say which. The price-to-book of 3.19 [P1] is also high for a bank, and that too rests on the return the book value produces. I have no peer price-to-book figures to set it against. The dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is the lowest among the peers shown, every one of which yields more [P5].

What I can say is that the pack does not give me the evidence I need to judge whether the returns that support this premium are real, durable, or earned with little debt. The debt-to-equity ratio of 1.7165 [P2] is the only health measure with a sector percentile, and at 22.7 it is the better end of its class, but without the balance sheet I cannot see what it is made of. I cannot call the shares cheap or dear on this evidence, and I will not guess.

data.headline: Without quarterly earnings I cannot call a trend or a bargain.
data.text:
My job is to look at the quarters and see which way the business is moving. The quarterly figures in P9 are not in this pack, so I counted zero quarters and I can call no trend. One good year or one bad year does not tell you whether the story is intact, and a P/E without the earnings behind it is just a number.

What I do have is the price history. Over the last year the share went from a first close of 70.2 SAR to a last close of 62.1 SAR, a change of -11.54% [P7]. The high close was 73.34 and the low was 61.95 [P7]. So the price has been falling while the question is whether it is cheap. That can happen for two reasons: earnings fell, or the multiple compressed. I cannot tell which because I have no quarterly earnings to compare.

The P/E of 14.51 [P1] is higher than every peer in the pack. Saudi National Bank sits at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, Alinma at 10.97, Saudi Awwal at 7.82, Banque Saudi Fransi at 9.3, Arab National at 8.49, Bank Albilad at 11.94, and Saudi Investment at 9.03 [P5]. The dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is the lowest of the group; the next lowest is Alinma at 3.1% and the highest is Saudi Awwal at 6.02% [P5]. On price and yield alone, Al Rajhi is the most expensive bank in the list.

But I cannot say whether that premium is justified because I cannot see the growth. A fast grower can deserve a higher P/E, and a slow grower cannot. Without the quarterly record I have no growth rate to set against the multiple. The story might be fine and the price might be fair, or the story might be weakening and the price still too high. I cannot tell which from what is in front of us.

data.headline: The balance sheet is absent, so the funding machine cannot be read.
data.text:
The question asks whether the sector comparison shows the shares are cheap. My part of the evidence is the balance sheet: what the company owns, what it owes, who funded it, and what would put it under strain. P9 is not in this pack, so I have no balance sheet date, no asset mix, no liability structure, and no leverage measures computed from the bank’s own statements. I cannot build the machine.

The one health figure I can see is a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.7165, with a sector percentile of 22.7 [P2]. A lower percentile means less debt relative to equity than most peers in whatever class that rank was computed against, and the pack does not say which class. For a bank, a debt-to-equity ratio alone tells me little without knowing what the debt is: deposits, wholesale funding, sukuk, or something else. The current ratio is marked not applicable, which is correct for a bank whose balance sheet is not split into current and non-current [P2]. Interest coverage is missing its inputs [P2].

What I would need to assess cheapness is the funding structure. A bank that funds itself with sticky retail deposits can carry more leverage safely than one that relies on short-term wholesale money. The disclosures in P6 show Al Rajhi has been active in the sukuk market: a $1 billion Tier 2 social sukuk in September 2025, a $1.5 billion AT1 sukuk in January 2025, and another AT1 sukuk announced in January 2026 [P6]. That tells me the bank uses international capital markets, but without the balance sheet I cannot see what share of its funding that represents.

The sector comparison shows Al Rajhi trades at a P/E of 14.51 against peers at 7.78 to 11.94 [P5]. Whether that premium is justified depends partly on whether its funding is more stable and cheaper than the peers’. I cannot answer that from the data I have.

data.headline: The price assumes the high ROE lasts; the gaps are large.
data.text:
The question is whether the sector comparison shows the shares are cheap. My job is to say what the price assumes and what we do not know, and on this pack the second part is the larger one.

What the price assumes: a P/E of 14.51 and a price-to-book of 3.19 [P1]. Against the eight Tadawul bank peers in the pack, whose P/E values range from 7.78 for Riyad Bank to 11.94 for Bank Albilad [P5], Al Rajhi’s multiple is the highest by a clear margin. The market is paying more for each riyal of Al Rajhi’s earnings than for any other bank’s. That premium rests on the return on equity of 23.49% [P1], which is the reason an investor would accept a higher multiple. The price is assuming that return persists.

What we do not know is large. P9 is absent from this pack, so I cannot read the limitations that dataset carries, and I cannot see which calculations returned missing values. P2 shows no sector percentile for P/E or P/B, so there is no ranking to read; that is not the same as a low ranking, it is an absence. EV/EBITDA is not applicable for a bank [P2]. The peer figures are dated 2026-08-07 [P5] and the Al Rajhi quote is dated 2026-10-13 [P1], a gap of more than two months, and the price freshness flag shows stale [P1]. The peers may have moved in that time and we would not see it. Peer price-to-book is not in the pack at all, so I cannot compare the 3.19 [P1] against anything.

The rule-based council votes in P4 are not measurements; they are thresholds applied to a few inputs, and I do not cite them as figures. The one thing the sector comparison does show is that Al Rajhi is not cheap on the measures we have. It is the most expensive bank in the list on P/E and the lowest-yielding on dividends. Whether that premium is warranted is a question the missing data cannot answer.

data.headline: The payout cannot be read, and the bonus issue complicates comparison.
data.text:
My part of the evidence is what has been returned to owners and out of what. The matched-window payout calculations in P9 are not in this pack, so I cannot state a payout ratio. I will not assemble one myself from the dividend list because a dividend that falls outside the earnings window can make a four-fifths payout read as a whole one, and that is how mistakes are made.

What I can read is the dividend history. The most recent dividend is 1.17 SAR per share, announced 2026-01-27, with an ex-date of 2026-04-20 and a pay-date of 2026-04-30, for the second half of 2025 [P3]. The one before it is 0.5 SAR per share, ex-date 2025-09-22, for the first half of 2025 [P3]. The amounts are company totals of 7000 million and 3000 million SAR respectively [P3]. The per-share figures and the totals must not be mixed.

There is also a capital change that matters for any comparison. On 2026-04-20 the bank issued a 50% bonus, one share for every two held, raising capital from 40000.0 million to 60000.0 million SAR [P3]. That bonus issue changes what every per-share figure before it meant. An older dividend per share cannot be read alongside a newer one without adjustment, and I will not attempt that adjustment here. The same applies to any peer comparison that uses per-share figures across different capital bases.

The dividend yield the pack gives is 2.6% [P1]. Set against the peers, every one of them yields more: Saudi National Bank at 5.26%, Riyad Bank at 5.08%, Alinma at 3.1%, Saudi Awwal at 6.02%, Banque Saudi Fransi at 5.23%, Arab National at 5.94%, Bank Albilad at 4.04%, and Saudi Investment at 5.01% [P5]. On the return to owners alone, Al Rajhi is the least generous of the group. Whether that is because it retains more earnings to grow, or because earnings themselves are lower than the multiple implies, is a question the missing payout ratio would answer.

data.headline: On every peer measure in the pack, Al Rajhi trades at a premium.
data.text:
My part is the company against its sector and what it has disclosed. The Tadawul classifies eight other banks alongside Al Rajhi, and on the two valuation measures the pack carries for every one of them, the comparison is straightforward.

Al Rajhi’s P/E is 14.51 [P1]. Saudi National Bank trades at 9.48, Riyad Bank at 7.78, Alinma Bank at 10.97, Saudi Awwal Bank at 7.82, Banque Saudi Fransi at 9.3, Arab National Bank at 8.49, Bank Albilad at 11.94, and The Saudi Investment Bank at 9.03 [P5]. Al Rajhi is the highest by a margin of more than two and a half points over the next highest, Bank Albilad. The average of the peers is roughly 9.3, and Al Rajhi sits more than fifty percent above that [P5].

On dividend yield the picture is the same in reverse. Al Rajhi yields 2.6% [P1]. Saudi National Bank yields 5.26%, Riyad Bank 5.08%, Alinma 3.1%, Saudi Awwal 6.02%, Banque Saudi Fransi 5.23%, Arab National 5.94%, Bank Albilad 4.04%, and Saudi Investment 5.01% [P5]. Al Rajhi is the lowest-yielding bank in the group, and the next lowest, Alinma at 3.1%, still yields more [P5].

P2 carries no sector percentile for P/E, P/B or dividend yield, so there is no ranking to read. That absence is not the same as a low ranking; it means the ranking was not computed or not published. The debt-to-equity percentile of 22.7 [P2] is the one ranking we have, and it shows the bank carries less debt relative to equity than most of its class, but the pack does not name that class.

The latest disclosure is the AT1 sukuk issuance of 2026-01-06 [P6], a capital instrument that does not bear on the valuation comparison. The only news item is dated 2026-08-02 and concerns Saudization memoranda [P6], which also does not speak to cheapness. On the evidence in front of us, the sector comparison does not show the shares are cheap. It shows they command a premium on every measure where a peer figure exists.

data.summary: The room agrees the comparison shows a premium multiple; it differs on whether that premium is earned and how reliable the comparison is.

data.headline: Peer multiples show a gap, not a bargain.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, the peer P/E figures are a fair first look, but they say nothing about the quality of earnings behind each multiple. Al Rajhi's P/E of 14.51 [P1] sits against peers from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5], and that gap alone does not show whether the price is high or the earnings are better. A bank that earns a durable 23.49% [P1] on equity deserves a higher multiple than one that earns less, and I cannot read the peers' returns from this pack. Without the income statement and a common-equity denominator I can name, I cannot judge whether Al Rajhi's return is real or repeatable, and I cannot compare it to what the other banks earn. The premium may be earned or it may not, but the P/E list by itself does not settle it.
data.concedes: The raw peer values do show Al Rajhi at a higher multiple than every listed peer.

data.headline: A premium multiple is not a verdict.
data.text: Marks, a premium multiple is not proof of a mispriced stock; it depends on growth, and the pack has none. The one-year price fall of -11.54% [P7] alongside a P/E above all peers [P5] means the market has not been paying more for it lately, whatever the multiple says. If the business were growing fast enough, a P/E of 14.51 could be cheap; if it were slowing, the same number could be dear [P1]. I have zero quarters of earnings to count, so I have no growth rate to set against that multiple. The price has been drifting down from a high close of 73.34 to a last close of 62.1 [P7], and without the quarterly record I cannot tell whether that is a multiple compressing on steady earnings or earnings falling under a steady multiple. The sector comparison shows a premium, but it does not show whether the premium is wrong.
data.concedes: Without earnings growth figures I cannot say the premium is justified.

data.headline: Price comparisons need the funding machine.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, peer P/E and yield tell us about price, not about resilience, and a cheap-looking multiple can reflect a weaker funding position. The one health percentile we have is debt-to-equity at 22.7 [P2], and P2 gives no sector percentile for P/E, P/B or dividend yield, so the ranking is absent rather than low. An absent ranking is not evidence of cheapness or dearness; it is a gap. For a bank, the funding structure is what breaks first in a downturn, and without the balance sheet I cannot see whether Al Rajhi's premium multiple is supported by a stickier deposit base or a safer liability mix than the peers'. The sukuk disclosures in P6 show the bank taps international markets, but I cannot measure that against the peers' funding. The raw P/E values in P5 are real, but they are one piece of a machine whose other pieces are missing.
data.concedes: The raw peer values in P5 are unaffected by the missing percentiles.

data.headline: The premium is the thing to explain.
data.text: Buffett, the premium need not be unearned, but it should be treated as the thing to explain, not an assumption to wave through. The bank's P/E of 14.51 [P1] is above all eight peers, whose multiples run from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5]. Its dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is below every peer's, whose yields run from 3.1% to 6.02% [P5]. On the two measures where we can compare, Al Rajhi is the most expensive bank in the group. A return on equity of 23.49% [P1] could justify some premium, and I cannot show it does not, but the burden is on the return to prove itself, and the pack has no income statement, no common-equity denominator, and no window. I also note the quote dates: Al Rajhi at 2026-10-13 [P1] and peers at 2026-08-07 [P5], a gap of more than two months. The peers may have moved, and we would not see it. The premium is real; whether it is deserved is what the missing data would answer.
data.concedes: A return on equity of 23.49% [P1] could justify some premium, and I cannot show it does not.

data.headline: Yield is a price measure, not a payout.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, the yield gap with peers, 2.6% [P1] against 3.1% to 6.02% [P5], is real but it compares a bank that has issued bonus shares repeatedly [P3] with peers whose capital history is not in the pack. Al Rajhi gave a 50% bonus in April 2026, a 60% bonus in 2022, and a 53.85% bonus in 2019 [P3]. Each bonus changes what every per-share figure before it meant, and a yield quoted on today's share count is not the same as the cash returned to an owner who held through those issues. Yield is a price measure, and it does not show how much of earnings was kept to grow the capital that produced those bonus shares. Without the matched-window payout ratio from P9, I cannot say whether the lower yield reflects a stingy payout or a deliberate retention that built the book value behind that 3.19 price-to-book [P1].
data.concedes: On the quoted yields alone, Al Rajhi pays less than every listed peer.

data.headline: The gap is wide enough to read.
data.text: Buffett, the peer list is the exchange's own classification, and the raw values stand even where percentiles are missing. The peers' data is dated 2026-08-07 [P5] while Al Rajhi's quote is dated 2026-10-13 [P1], which is a limit on precision but does not reverse a gap as wide as 14.51 against a peer maximum of 11.94 [P5, P1]. The average peer P/E is roughly 9.3, and Al Rajhi sits more than fifty percent above that [P5]. A date gap of two months cannot close a spread of that size, and the direction is clear on every measure we can compare: P/E is higher, yield is lower. I accept that without return figures for the peers I cannot say the premium is unjustified, but the question was whether the sector comparison shows the shares are cheap, and on the evidence in front of us it does not.

verdict.headline: Against listed bank peers the shares look dearer, not cheaper, but the comparison is thin.
verdict.answer:
On the sector comparison in the pack, the shares do not show as cheap. Al-Rumayyan read Al Rajhi Bank's P/E of 14.51 [P1] against the eight listed Tadawul banks, whose P/E values run from 7.78 to 11.94 [P5], so it is above every peer. Its dividend yield of 2.6% [P1] is below every peer, whose yields run from 3.1% to 6.02% [P5]. Marks added that the P/B of 3.19 [P1] cannot be compared because peer P/B is not in the pack.

The room agrees on direction but not on what the premium means. Buffett noted that the return on equity of 23.49% [P1] could justify a higher multiple, but its denominator is not disclosed [P2] and the income statement that would show whether it is durable is not in the pack. Lynch could count no quarters, so growth cannot be set against the P/E. Dalio found only one health percentile, 22.7 [P2], and no balance sheet. Alwaleed pointed out that the matched payout is absent and that a 50% bonus issue on 2026-04-20 [P3] changes what earlier per-share figures meant.

The comparison also has limits. P2 carries no sector percentile for P/E, P/B or yield, so no ranking exists. The peer figures are dated 2026-08-07 [P5] and the Al Rajhi quote 2026-10-13 [P1], and the price freshness flag shows stale [P1]. The gap is wide enough that the direction is clear, but the size of the premium is not precise.

What the data shows is a higher multiple and a lower yield than peers. It does not show whether the premium is earned, and it does not show cheapness. None of this is advice.

headline: The sector peer comparison is too sparse and scattered to confirm or refute Jarir's valuation.
answer:
The peer comparison does not settle Jarir's valuation. Jarir trades at 18.43x P/E and 12.28x P/B [P1]. The pack lists eight peers; five carry a P/E: Aldrees 26.07, United Electronics 10.43, Al-Saif 37.30, Abo Moati 33.62 and SACO 41.45, while SASCO, AFG International and Nice One show none [P5]. No peer carries a P/B, so the 12.28x figure cannot be compared with anyone in the sector [P5]. Sector percentiles for P/E and P/B are null [P2].

The room agrees on this. Marks and Alwaleed describe the P/E band as directionless rather than merely sparse: Jarir sits above one peer and below four [P5]. Dalio's simple average was withdrawn as an anchor because three high multiples pull it up.

On Jarir itself, the pack shows ROE of 67.25%, ROA of 25.88% and debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2]. Dalio's point that the capital structure carries no financial debt stands without an income statement. Buffett's point also stands: the pack does not disclose the period or equity base behind the ROE, and no peer ROE or ROA is given, so those returns cannot be tested against peers [P2] [P5]. Alwaleed confirms a steady dividend record, latest SAR 0.20 per share, but no payout ratio is available [P3]. Lynch cannot read a quarterly trend because none is in the pack. Al-Rumayyan notes the expansion disclosures and a 29% Gulf sales rise reported on 2026-07-15 [P6]; these show activity, not a verified earnings base.

The data therefore neither supports nor undermines the valuation. It leaves the comparison open.
gaps: Peer P/B ratios or book values are absent, so the 12.28x P/B cannot be compared with any peer [P1].
Peer ROE and ROA figures are absent, so Jarir's 67.25% ROE cannot be tested against the sector [P1].
The income statement and quarterly series are absent, so the earnings window, equity base, payout ratio and recent trend cannot be verified.
disagreements: Whether Jarir's 18.43x P/E sits low, middle or high among peers [P1] - The five peer P/Es run from 10.43 to 41.45 [P5]. Placement depends on whether United Electronics or the 26.07 to 41.45 cluster is the right anchor, and the pack has no sector percentile for P/E [P2] and no peer business detail to choose between them.

Whether ROE, ROA and zero debt justify a premium multiple - The 67.25% ROE and 25.88% ROA [P2] have no stated period or equity base, and no peer ROE or ROA appears in [P5], so a premium cannot be tested. The zero debt-to-equity figure [P2] is not disputed.

data.headline: The peer comparison does not settle Jarir's valuation; earning power matters more.
data.text:
The question asks whether the peer data supports Jarir's valuation of 18.43x P/E and 12.28x P/B [P1]. The pack gives me seven peers [P5], but the comparison it offers is thin. Four of those peers carry no P/E at all [P5], and only one has a P/E below Jarir's: United Electronics at 10.43x [P5]. The others range from 26.07x to 41.45x [P5]. On that narrow sample, Jarir's multiple sits in the middle, not at the top. But a P/E alone tells me nothing about the business behind it. A low multiple on a poor business can be expensive; a high multiple on a wonderful business can be cheap. The peer list does not give me the returns on equity or assets for any of these companies, so I cannot weigh the price against the quality of what it buys. The comparison is unsettled.

What I can weigh is Jarir's own earning power, which is my part of the evidence. The return on equity shown in the fundamentals is 67.25% and the return on assets is 25.88% [P2]. Those are published metrics, but the pack does not disclose the formula or denominator used to strike them [P2]. The income statement in [P9] is absent for this company; the dataset holds no data. Without it, I have no window of earnings, no stated common equity on a given date, and no way to verify what produced those returns. A single published ROE figure, without the underlying statements, is not a record I can rely on. I must say plainly that the data here does not show me the period over which these returns were earned or the exact capital they were earned on.

I also see that Jarir carries no debt [P2], which I like. A debt-to-equity of zero means the returns, whatever they are, were not juiced by borrowing. The dividend record is steady, paid quarterly, with the latest at SAR 0.20 per share [P3]. That suggests management treats shareholders as partners. But until I can see the income statement and the equity it was earned against, I cannot call these returns real. The peer comparison does not settle the valuation, and the missing income statement leaves the most important question unanswered.

data.headline: The peer data does not settle the valuation question; it is too thin.
data.text:
The question is whether the sector peer comparison supports Jarir’s valuation of 18.43x P/E and 12.28x P/B [P1]. To answer it, I look at the machine of the peer set. The pack gives me eight peers [P5]. Of those, only five have a P/E: Aldrees at 26.07, United Electronics at 10.43, Al-Saif at 37.30, Abo Moati at 33.62, and SACO at 41.45 [P5]. Three peers have no P/E at all. No peer has a P/B in the data. So the comparison for P/B is absent, and the P/E sample is small and scattered from 10 to 41 [P1] [P6]. A simple average of those five P/Es is roughly 29.8, which would make Jarir’s 18.43 look low [P1]. But that average is pulled up by three very high multiples and tells us nothing about the different drivers of each business. Without understanding what each company earns, the comparison is just numbers on a page.

Now I turn to what I am answerable for: the balance sheet. The fundamentals data shows a debt-to-equity of 0.0, meaning the company carries no financial debt [P2]. Its current ratio is 1.37 [P2]. The balance sheet here is funded entirely by equity and short-term operating liabilities; there is no leverage. For the funding to become a problem, you would need a scenario where operating cash flows stop covering those short-term obligations—perhaps a sharp and sustained drop in revenue that runs down cash faster than payables and accruals can adjust. But with zero debt, the machine has no credit-cycle vulnerability. The absence of a balance-sheet date in [P2] means I cannot pinpoint the exact moment of this position, but the zero-debt figure is the central fact. That makes the valuation debate less urgent from a survival standpoint, even if the peer data does not settle whether the price is right.

data.headline: The peer set is too thin to support or reject Jarir's valuation.
data.text:

I look at the peer table [P5] and see that the question cannot be answered with confidence from this data alone. Only three of the eight peers carry a P/E, and none carries a P/B. Aldrees trades at 26.07x, Extra at 10.43x, Abu Moati at 33.62x, and Al-Saif Galleries at 37.30x [P5]. Jarir's 18.43x sits in the middle of a wide range drawn from four names, which is too sparse to call a premium or a discount with conviction [P1]. The other five peers either show no P/E or have no P/B at all in the pack, so a comparison on book value is impossible from this data [P5].

My own mandate is what has been returned to owners and out of what earnings [P3, P9] [P3]. The dividend record shows steady quarterly payments: the last four announced dividends are SAR 0.20, 0.21, 0.26, and 0.28 per share, totaling SAR 0.95 per share over the trailing twelve months if we read the announcements from August 2026 back through November 2025 [P3]. The pack does not provide a computed payout ratio in [P9] — the dataset is absent — so I cannot state what proportion of earnings that stream represents. A payout ratio is central to judging whether a dividend yield of 5.16% [P1] is sustainable or a sign of stress. The capital changes show a history of bonus issues: the share count rose from 900 million to 1.2 billion in 2018, and earlier from 600 million to 900 million in 2013 [P3]. Those events mean every per-share figure before 2018 must be read with the dilution in mind [P3]. The data tells me Jarir has a habit of returning capital to shareholders, both in cash and in shares, but without the payout ratio I cannot say whether the current yield is well-covered. I therefore find the peer valuation question unsettled, and on my own mandate I can confirm the return of capital but not its affordability.

data.headline: The peer data is too thin to settle the valuation question.
data.text:
I look at the sector peers in [P5] and ask: what story do the numbers tell about Jarir’s 18.43 P/E and 12.28 P/B from [P1]? There are eight peers listed. Two — United Electronics at 10.43 and Aldrees at 26.07 — give us a P/E to compare [P5]. The other six either show no P/E at all or one that feels like a different story: SASCO, AFG International, and Nice One have no P/E in the data, while Al-Saif at 37.30, Abo Moati at 33.62, and SACO at 41.45 sit well above Jarir [P5]. So the pack gives us three clusters: a cheaper retailer, a much pricier group, and a set with no earnings metric to work with. That is not a clean peer set — it is a scattered one.

Jarir’s P/B of 12.28 is even harder to place because [P5] provides no book values at all. I cannot say whether the market is paying more or less for Jarir’s assets relative to anyone else in the sector. The data simply does not show it.

On dividends, Jarir’s 5.16% yield [P1] is the second-highest among the peers that report one, behind United Electronics at 7.65% [P5]. That is a real point of comparison and it tells me Jarir’s cash return to shareholders is competitive. But a dividend yield alone does not settle a P/E question — it is one piece of the puzzle.

My mandate is the quarterly trend, and here I must say plainly: the data pack contains no [P9] dataset. There is no quarterly record for me to read. I cannot tell you whether the last few quarters show revenue or earnings moving up, flattening, or turning down. Without that, I cannot answer the question I am answerable for — which way the business is moving — and that means I cannot check whether the 18.43 P/E is supported by an improving trend or stretched against a slowing one [P1]. The annual figures in [P1] give a snapshot, but I need the quarters to call a trend. They are not here.

data.headline: The peer comparison does not settle the valuation; it raises questions.
data.text:
The data provides a peer list, but the comparison it supports is incomplete and does not settle the valuation question. My mandate is to assess Jarir against its sector, and the picture is mixed.

Looking at the sector peers in [P5], Jarir trades at a P/E of 18.43 [P1]. This is lower than several direct peers: Aldrees at 26.07, Al-Saif at 37.30, and Abo Moati at 33.62 [P5]. However, its closest competitor in the consumer electronics and bookstore space, United Electronics (Extra), trades at a significantly lower P/E of 10.43 [P5]. The P/B ratio of 12.28 [P1] is a company-specific figure without a peer comparison in the pack to contextualize it. The sector percentile rankings for valuation metrics like P/E and P/B are not provided in [P2]; they are listed as 'null'. This means the data does not rank Jarir against its sector on these key valuation metrics, and we must rely on the raw peer list, which shows a wide dispersion.

On fundamentals, the data is clearer. Jarir's ROE of 67.25% and ROA of 25.88% [P2] are exceptionally high. While the pack withholds the sector percentile for these profitability metrics, the raw values dwarf what one would expect from a typical retailer. The balance sheet is pristine, with a debt-to-equity of 0.0, which ranks in the 89.7th percentile for its health group [P2]. This fortress balance sheet supports a premium valuation.

The company’s own disclosures [P6] show a clear strategy of physical expansion, with multiple new showroom openings in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait throughout 2025 and 2026, representing significant aggregate investment. A July 2026 news item notes a 29% increase in Gulf sales, suggesting this expansion is gaining traction [P1] [P3].

In summary, the peer comparison is not clean enough to declare the valuation either supported or refuted. The P/E is higher than its most direct comparable, Extra, but sits below other sector peers. The exceptional profitability and zero-debt balance sheet provide a rationale for a premium, but the data lacks the sector-wide valuation rankings needed to make a definitive judgment. The valuation is a question mark that the given peer data cannot erase.

data.headline: The peer set is too incomplete to support the valuation; the price embeds strong assumptions.
data.text:
The member asks whether the sector peer comparison supports Jarir's valuation of 18.43x P/E and 12.28x P/B [P1]. The data in [P5] gives us eight peers in the same TADAWUL sector, but the picture is fragmentary: of those eight, three peers—Saudi Automotive Services (4050), AFG International (4240), and Nice One (4193)—carry no P/E at all [P5]. That is not a neutral fact; it means the market cannot price their earnings in the same way, so they offer no anchor for Jarir's multiple. Among the five peers that do have a P/E, the range runs from 10.43x (United Electronics) to 41.45x (SACO), with Aldrees at 26.07x, Abo Moati at 33.62x, and Al-Saif at 37.30x [P5]. Jarir's 18.43x sits toward the lower end of that wide band, but the band itself tells you more about dispersion than about support: a set where the cheapest peer is 10.43x and the dearest is 41.45x does not anchor a single number; it asks what each price is assuming [P1] [P5].

Price to book is even less anchored. The pack gives no peer book values, no peer P/B ratios, and no sector percentile for P/B [P2] [P5]. So the 12.28x multiple [P1] cannot be compared to any other company in the sector from the data we have. That is a significant gap, and I must name it as such: the evidence does not show whether 12.28x is high, low, or ordinary relative to these peers [P1].

What the price is assuming is the question I am answerable for. At 18.43x earnings, the market is paying for a business that has delivered a 67.25% ROE and a 25.88% ROA [P1], with zero debt on the balance sheet—a debt-to-equity of 0.0 that sits at the 89.7th sector percentile [P2]. Those are quality characteristics, and the price almost certainly embeds an expectation that they persist. The five-year price summary adds context: the stock closed at 20.12 five years ago and at 17.33 today, a decline of 13.87%, with a high of 21.66 and a low of 12.06 [P8]. So the price has not run away from its own history; it is below where it was five years ago, even after a 33.78% twelve-month return [P1]. The maximum drawdown of 65.72% [P1] reminds us that this name can fall hard when expectations shift.

The peer comparison does not settle the valuation question—it leaves it open. The data shows a P/E that is not extreme in its peer group but is measured against a group where a third of the names cannot even be priced on earnings. The P/B comparison is entirely absent from the pack. I would say the price is assuming continued high returns on equity and a steady dividend stream—the trailing yield is 5.16% [P1]—but we cannot test that assumption against what the market is paying for similar assets, because the data does not let us make that test fully.

data.headline: You miscounted the peers, Buffett, and the data is thinner than you say.
data.text: Buffett, you say there are seven peers and four lack a P/E. The pack lists eight peers in [P5], not seven. Five carry a P/E: Aldrees at 26.07, United Electronics at 10.43, Al-Saif at 37.30, Abo Moati at 33.62, and SACO at 41.45 [P5]. Three have none: SASCO, AFG International, and Nice One. That is a different sample than the one you described. More importantly, you lean on Jarir's 67.25% ROE and 25.88% ROA from [P2] to argue the peer comparison is secondary. But the pack gives no ROE or ROA for any peer in [P5]. Without those, you cannot weigh the price against the quality of what it buys, as you rightly insist we must. You are asking us to trust Jarir's returns in isolation while dismissing the peer set for being thin. The peer set is thin—I agree—but the quality comparison you want to make is not just thin, it is absent. You cannot call the returns wonderful without seeing what the others earn on their equity.
data.concedes: You are right that the income statement is missing, which limits what any of us can verify about those returns.

data.headline: The peer count is clear; the missing statements are not my brief.
data.text: Buffett, you say the peer list gives you seven peers with four lacking a P/E. The pack lists eight peers in [P5], and five carry a P/E: Aldrees at 26.07, United Electronics at 10.43, Al-Saif at 37.30, Abo Moati at 33.62, and SACO at 41.45. Three—SASCO, AFG International, and Nice One—do not. That is not a matter of interpretation; it is a count the data settles. On the missing income statement, I agree the pack does not show the period or the capital base for the 67.25% ROE [P2], and that limits what anyone can conclude from it. But my mandate is the sector and the disclosures, and the disclosures [P6] show a company committing capital to new showrooms across the Kingdom and into Kuwait, with a chairman reporting a 29% Gulf sales increase in July 2026. That is evidence of a business building something, not just reporting a return. The peer comparison is thin, but the expansion story is not.
data.concedes: The missing income statement means the high ROE cannot be verified from the data in the pack.

data.headline: A premium needs a verified foundation, not just a rationale
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you call Jarir's 67.25% ROE and zero debt 'a rationale for a premium' and say the balance sheet supports it [P1]. But a rationale is not a fact until you can show me what produced that return. My mandate is earning power, and the pack's income statement [P9] is absent. I have no window of earnings, no common equity on a stated date, and no way to verify that 67.25% figure [P2]. The fundamentals dataset itself does not disclose the formula or denominator it used; it says so on its face. Without that, I cannot tell you whether that return was earned on a thin equity base after a write-down, or on a steadily growing book of reinvested earnings. A premium built on an unverified number is a house on sand. The zero debt is real, and I like it, but it does not make the return real. Until I see the statements, I would not hang a valuation argument on that ROE, and neither should this room.
data.concedes: The zero-debt balance sheet is a genuine strength that reduces downside risk.

data.headline: The balance sheet is not a mystery
data.text: Buffett, you say you cannot rely on the published returns because the pack does not disclose the formula or the underlying statements. I respect the discipline of wanting to see the raw numbers. But you are overlooking what the balance sheet data in [P2] does show plainly: a debt-to-equity of 0.0. That is not a derived return metric; it is a direct statement of the capital structure. A company with no financial debt, sitting at the 89.7th sector percentile on that measure, is funded entirely by equity and operating liabilities [P2]. That fact does not require an income statement to verify. The machine here has no credit-cycle vulnerability. You ask for the exact period of the ROE—the data does not give it, and I concede that gap. But the core of what I am answerable for is how the balance sheet is funded and what would break it. The answer is that it is funded without leverage, and breaking it would require an operating collapse severe enough to eat through the current ratio of 1.37 [P2], which is a much higher bar than a debt-fueled structure would face. The missing income statement does not make the capital structure unreliable.
data.concedes: The data does not show the period over which the ROE was earned or the exact equity base used.

data.headline: The peer average is not a useful anchor
data.text: Dalio, you note that a simple average of the five available P/Es is roughly 29.8, which would make Jarir's 18.43 look low [P1]. But an average drawn from a set where three names carry multiples above 33x and only one sits below 11x is not an anchor—it is a measure of dispersion [P1]. The question is not whether Jarir's multiple is below a flawed average; it is what the price is assuming. The five-year price summary shows the stock closed at 20.12 five years ago and sits at 17.33 today, a decline of 13.87%, with a high of 21.66 and a low of 12.06 [P8]. That history suggests the price has not stretched beyond its own past, even after a 33.78% twelve-month return [P1]. A peer average that is pulled upward by three very high multiples tells us more about the outliers than about Jarir. I agree with you that the peer data is too thin to settle the question, but I would go further: the average you cite is not a useful benchmark, and the price's own five-year range is a more grounded starting point for asking what expectations are embedded in 18.43x [P1].
data.concedes: I agree that the debt-to-equity of zero removes credit-cycle vulnerability, which is a central fact for the downside.

data.headline: The P/E band is wider than you say

You call it the lower end, but the midpoint of that range is near 26, which would make 18.43 look cheap, while the presence of Extra at 10.43 pulls the anchor the other way entirely [P5]. On my own mandate, the dividend stream of SAR 0.95 per share over the trailing twelve months [P3] is a tangible return to owners, but without a payout ratio from [P9] I cannot say whether it supports or strains the valuation you describe.
data.concedes: You are right that the five-year price history shows a stock below where it traded five years ago, which matters more than a single peer multiple.

data.headline: The sector peer comparison is too sparse and scattered to confirm or refute Jarir's valuation.
data.answer:
The peer comparison does not settle Jarir's valuation. Jarir trades at 18.43x P/E and 12.28x P/B [P1]. The pack lists eight peers; five carry a P/E: Aldrees 26.07, United Electronics 10.43, Al-Saif 37.30, Abo Moati 33.62 and SACO 41.45, while SASCO, AFG International and Nice One show none [P5]. No peer carries a P/B, so the 12.28x figure cannot be compared with anyone in the sector [P5]. Sector percentiles for P/E and P/B are null [P2].

The room agrees on this. Marks and Alwaleed describe the P/E band as directionless rather than merely sparse: Jarir sits above one peer and below four [P5]. Dalio's simple average was withdrawn as an anchor because three high multiples pull it up.

On Jarir itself, the pack shows ROE of 67.25%, ROA of 25.88% and debt-to-equity of 0.0 [P2]. Dalio's point that the capital structure carries no financial debt stands without an income statement. Buffett's point also stands: the pack does not disclose the period or equity base behind the ROE, and no peer ROE or ROA is given, so those returns cannot be tested against peers [P2] [P5]. Alwaleed confirms a steady dividend record, latest SAR 0.20 per share, but no payout ratio is available [P3]. Lynch cannot read a quarterly trend because none is in the pack. Al-Rumayyan notes the expansion disclosures and a 29% Gulf sales rise reported on 2026-07-15 [P6]; these show activity, not a verified earnings base.

The data therefore neither supports nor undermines the valuation. It leaves the comparison open.

data.headline: Without the income statement, earning power cannot be verified against peer valuations.
data.text: I am answerable for what Jarir earned and on what capital, and I cannot do my job with what is in front of us. The income statement that should be in [P9] is not here, so I have no window of earnings and no denominator I can check. [P2] gives me a return on equity of 67.25% and a return on assets of 25.88%, but neither figure carries a date or tells me what capital it was earned on, and both show a null sector percentile [P1]. A published ratio with no disclosed denominator is a number on a page, not a record I can rely on. The P/E of 18.43x and price-to-book of 12.28x also carry no percentile, so the peer ranking that the question asks for is absent for the very metrics that matter most. [P2] A peer comparison built on a P/E that I cannot tie to verified earning power is a comparison of prices, not of businesses. The yield of 5.16% is a single published figure with the same gap. [P1] I am not saying the business is weak; I am saying the data does not let me judge its strength. Until I can see what Jarir earned, over which period, on what common equity, and whether those returns are steady, I cannot tell you whether an 18.43x multiple is in line, above, or below what the earning power warrants [P1]. The pack does not support the peer comparison because the foundation the comparison rests on is not there.

data.headline: No quarterly record means no trend to test the peer P/E against.
data.text: I look at what the business has been doing lately, quarter by quarter, and the quarterly record in [P9] is not in this pack. I count zero quarters, so I cannot call a trend. The P/E of 18.43x and the trailing EPS of 0.94 SAR are single points, and the pack has no growth figure to set against them. [P1] I cannot say whether earnings are accelerating, slowing, or flat, and without that I cannot tell you if 18.43x is a fair price for what the company is actually doing [P1]. The market's reading over one year in [P7] shows a close moving from 13.87 SAR to 17.33 SAR, a change of 24.95%, but price alone does not tell me what earnings did underneath it. [P7] The peers in [P5] show P/Es from 10.43x at United Electronics to 41.45x at SACO, with three peers reporting no P/E at all. Jarir's 18.43x sits in the middle of that range, but a middle-of-the-pack multiple means nothing if I do not know which direction the business is headed [P1]. A company growing fast can deserve a higher multiple; one that is stalling can deserve a lower one. The quarterly record would have shown me which story fits. It is not here, so the peer comparison is a comparison of snapshots with no motion. The data does not support a conclusion about whether the valuation is in line, above, or below, because the trend that would answer that question is absent.

data.headline: Without the balance sheet, funding structure and strain scenarios cannot be compared.
data.text: I am answerable for the balance sheet, and the balance sheet that should be in [P9] is not in this pack. I cannot give you a position date or show you what Jarir owns, what it owes, and who funded it. What I do have are two ratios in [P2]: a debt-to-equity of 0.0 with a sector percentile of 89.7, and a current ratio of 1.37 with a percentile of 45.0. The debt-to-equity of zero says there is no debt on the books, which on its face is a strong position, but I cannot see the operands behind it. The current ratio is middling against the sector, and again I cannot see the current assets and current liabilities that produced it. Interest coverage and free cash flow yield are both unavailable, marked as missing inputs. [P2] A peer comparison of valuations tells me nothing about how the machine would work under strain. If one peer carries debt and another does not, the same P/E means very different things when credit tightens. I cannot build a scenario for Jarir without the balance sheet. I cannot say what would have to happen for funding to become a problem, because I cannot see the funding. The peer comparison in the pack is a comparison of prices, not of resilience, and the data I need to judge resilience is absent. My answer is that the question cannot be answered from what is here.

data.headline: The price assumes a premium, but the data lacks the rankings to confirm it.
data.text: The price of 17.33 SAR on 2026-10-13, flagged stale, carries a P/E of 18.43x and a price-to-book of 12.28x. [P1] That is what the market is assuming. The peer list in [P5] shows five companies that report a P/E: United Electronics at 10.43x, Aldrees at 26.07x, Al-Saif at 37.30x, Abo Moati at 33.62x, and SACO at 41.45x. Jarir's 18.43x sits below four of them and above one [P1]. But the dates are mixed: Jarir's quote is 2026-10-13, while most peer rows are 2026-08-07 and Al-Saif is 2026-08-12 [P1]. Comparing a stale October price with an August peer set is comparing two different moments, and the market can move in two months. More importantly, the sector percentiles for Jarir's P/E and price-to-book are null in [P2]. No ranking exists. The only percentiles we have are for debt-to-equity at 89.7 and current ratio at 45.0, which are health metrics, not valuation ones [P1] [P2]. The limitations and missing calculations that should be in [P9] are not in the pack, so I cannot tell you what earnings the price is assuming or why certain measures could not be computed. The votes in [P4] are threshold rules, not measurements, and I treat them as such. What I can say is that the price assumes Jarir deserves a higher multiple than United Electronics and a lower one than the rest of the reporting peers, and the data does not give us the rankings to test that assumption. The gaps are the story here.

data.headline: Dividends are regular, but the payout ratio is missing, so the yield lacks context.
data.text: I am answerable for what has been returned to owners. [P3] shows a steady dividend record: 0.20 SAR per share for Q2 2026, 0.21 SAR for Q1 2026, 0.26 SAR for Q4 2025, and a string of quarterly payments going back through 2024 [P1] [P3]. The amounts fluctuate quarter to quarter, which is normal, but they have not stopped. The last capital change was a 1:3 bonus issue on 2018-10-28, taking the capital from 900.0 million SAR to 1200.0 million SAR. [P3] That bonus issue means every per-share figure before that date was struck on a smaller share count, and comparing them directly to today's figures would mislead. The published dividend yield is 5.16%. [P1] Against the peers in [P5], that yield is above every one except United Electronics at 7.65%. So on yield alone, Jarir looks generous. But a yield without a payout ratio is a number with no discipline. The payout calculation that [P9] should provide, matching each dividend to the earnings window it was paid from, is not in this pack. I cannot tell you whether that 5.16% is a comfortable distribution from earnings or a stretch [P1]. A company paying out more than it earns can keep it up for a while, but not forever. The peer comparison on valuation cannot be settled by yield alone, and the piece that would let me judge the yield is missing. The dividend record says the company treats owners to a regular return; the missing payout ratio says I cannot tell you at what cost.

data.headline: Jarir's P/E is below most peers and its yield is high; the comparison supports the valuation.
data.text: I am answerable for the company against its sector. The peer list in [P5] gives us eight names in Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retail on TADAWUL. Five report a P/E. Jarir's P/E of 18.43x [P1] is below Aldrees at 26.07x, Al-Saif at 37.30x, Abo Moati at 33.62x, and SACO at 41.45x, and above only United Electronics at 10.43x. So on the most common valuation measure, Jarir trades at a discount to four of its five comparable peers. Its dividend yield of 5.16% [P1] is above every peer except United Electronics at 7.65%, and three peers report no yield at all. On both metrics, the peer comparison places Jarir on the cheaper side of the group. I must note what is absent: the sector percentiles for P/E, price-to-book, and dividend yield are all null in [P2]. The only percentiles that exist are for debt-to-equity at 89.7 and current ratio at 45.0, which speak to financial health, not valuation [P1] [P2]. So the ranking I am giving you is from the raw peer list, not from a computed percentile. On disclosures, the company announced a Kuwait showroom with a SAR 15 million investment on 2026-04-08, and a news item on 2026-07-15 reports the Chairman saying Gulf sales are up 29% with operations unaffected by shipping disruptions. [P6] That news item is a report, not a company filing, but it is the most recent signal we have. Taken together, the peer comparison shows Jarir's valuation is below most of the sector on P/E and above most on yield. The data supports the view that the valuation is not stretched relative to the listed Saudi retailers it is compared with.

data.headline: A ranking without verified returns is a comparison of prices, not businesses.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you place Jarir's P/E of 18.43x below four of five peers and call that support for the valuation [P1]. But a P/E is a price divided by an earnings figure, and I cannot verify the earnings for Jarir or for the peers you cite. Aldrees at 26.07x and United Electronics at 10.43x are numbers on a page with no return on capital attached to them. [P1][P5] The pack gives me an ROE of 67.25% and an ROA of 25.88% for Jarir, but neither figure carries a date, a denominator, or a sector percentile. [P2] If I do not know what capital those returns were earned on, I cannot say whether an 18.43x multiple is cheap or dear [P1]. A peer comparison built on unverified earnings is a comparison of prices, not of businesses. The question asks whether the peer group supports the valuation, and my answer is that the foundation the valuation rests on is not in the pack.
data.concedes: The peer list does show Jarir's P/E below four of the five peers that report one.

data.headline: A price that moves without earnings tells us nothing about value.
data.text: Marks, you say the price is assuming something, but with no quarterly record we cannot say what it is assuming. The one-year change of 24.95% from 13.87 SAR to 17.33 SAR and the day change of 8.18% on 2026-10-13 tell me the market is moving the price, but I cannot see what earnings did underneath it. [P1][P7] A P/E of 18.43x against a trailing EPS of 0.94 SAR is a snapshot. [P1] If earnings grew 30% last quarter, 18.43x might be cheap [P1]. If they shrank, it might be expensive. The peers in [P5] range from 10.43x to 41.45x, and Jarir sits in the middle, but a middle ranking without the trend is a ranking of photographs with no motion. The quarterly record that should be in [P9] is not here, and without it I cannot call a trend. The price is moving, the earnings are unseen, and the peer comparison cannot bridge that gap.
data.concedes: Without growth figures the P/E gap to peers is only a ranking.

data.headline: A yield without a balance sheet is an income claim I cannot test.
data.text: Alwaleed, you point to the 5.16% yield as a record of cash paid, and the dividend history in [P3] does show four consecutive quarterly payments. But a yield is an income claim, and I cannot check it against the cash or debt lines that would tell me whether it is sustainable. The balance sheet that should be in [P9] is not in this pack. I see a debt-to-equity of 0.0 ratio with a sector percentile of 89.7, which on its face is strong, but I cannot see the operands behind it. [P2] More telling is the peer list: United Electronics carries a yield of 7.65% and a P/E of 10.43x. [P5] The highest yield and the lowest P/E sit together, which suggests the market is pricing something into both. Without the balance sheet, I cannot build a scenario for what happens to that yield if earnings turn. The dividend is a fact, but the funding behind it is invisible.
data.concedes: Debt-to-equity of 0.0 ratio is a favourable reading on its face [P1].

data.headline: Below four of five peers is not evidence the price is reasonable.
data.text: Al-Rumayyan, you read Jarir's P/E of 18.43x below four of five peers as support for the valuation [P1]. But sitting below four peers in a sample of five that report a P/E is a thin reed. Three peers report no P/E at all, and the dates are mixed: Jarir's quote is 2026-10-13, while most peers are 2026-08-07 and Al-Saif is 2026-08-12. [P1][P5] On yield, Jarir's 5.16% is below United Electronics' 7.65%, so the ranking cuts both ways. [P5] More importantly, the sector percentiles for P/E and price-to-book are null in [P2]. No formal rank exists. The limitations and missing calculations that should be in [P9] are absent, so I cannot tell you what earnings the price is assuming or why certain measures could not be computed. The price is in the middle of a small, mixed-date sample. That is a description, not a conclusion about value.
data.concedes: Jarir sits inside the reported range, not at an extreme.

data.headline: Dividends paid are a fact, not an assumption about value.
data.text: Marks, you say the yield of 5.16% is only one side of the ranking and that the peer sample is thin [P1]. I accept both points. But the yield is not an assumption; it is a record of cash paid. The dividend history in [P3] shows four consecutive quarterly payments: 0.28 SAR for Q3 2025, 0.16 SAR for Q2 2025, 0.19 SAR for Q1 2025, and 0.23 SAR for Q4 2024, and the more recent quarters continue the pattern with 0.26 SAR, 0.21 SAR, and 0.20 SAR. [P3] These are amounts that left the company and went to owners. The peer list may be small and the dates may be mixed, but a dividend that has been paid quarter after quarter is a fact on the ground. The missing piece is the payout ratio, which [P9] should provide and does not. I cannot tell you whether that 5.16% is a comfortable distribution or a stretch [P1]. But the payment itself is not an assumption.
data.concedes: Without a matched payout I cannot show the dividend is covered by earnings.

data.headline: The peer list is the exchange's own classification, and Jarir sits mid-range.
data.text: Buffett, you are right that the returns behind the P/E are unverified. I cannot show you the earnings power that supports Jarir's 18.43x multiple or the peers' multiples, because the income statement is not in the pack [P1]. But the question is about the peer group, and the peer list in [P5] is the exchange's own classification of Consumer Discretionary Distribution & Retail companies on TADAWUL. On the figures that are available, Jarir's P/E of 18.43x sits below Aldrees at 26.07x, Al-Saif at 37.30x, Abo Moati at 33.62x, and SACO at 41.45x, and above United Electronics at 10.43x. [P1][P5] Its yield of 5.16% is above every peer except United Electronics. [P1][P5] I am not claiming the valuation is justified by verified returns; I am saying the peer comparison, on the metrics we have, places Jarir on the cheaper side of the group. That is what the data shows.
data.concedes: The missing P/E percentile means no formal rank exists, and three peers report no P/E.

data.text: The peer comparison supports a relative statement — Jarir's P/E of 18.43x sits below four of the five peers that report one — but it does not show the valuation is justified by earning power, because no return denominator is disclosed in P2 and the income statement that should be in P9 is absent. [P1][P2][P5]
data.would_change: A P9 income statement with a dated equity denominator and several years of earnings would let me judge whether the multiple is cheap or dear.

data.text: The peer P/Es place Jarir in the middle of the reported range, but without a quarterly record I cannot compare price movement to earnings movement. The news items describe store openings — a story — and not a trend I can count. [P5][P6]
data.would_change: At least four reported quarters, ideally with a prior-year comparison, would show which direction earnings are headed and whether the multiple fits.

data.text: The health percentiles rank Jarir high on leverage at 89.7 and mid-range on liquidity at 45.0, but they do not bear on the P/E comparison. [P2] Without a balance sheet I cannot build a scenario for how the machine would behave under strain.
data.would_change: A dated balance sheet showing cash, debt and payables would let me test whether the yield and the multiple can survive a turn in earnings.

data.text: The peer comparison is suggestive but thin — five usable P/Es on mismatched dates, three peers with no P/E at all, and no sector percentiles for valuation in P2. Confidence should stay below what that sample can bear. [P1][P2][P5]
data.would_change: Same-date peer P/Es, sector percentiles for valuation metrics, and P9 earnings would let me say what the price is actually assuming.

data.text: The dividend history is real and regular — four consecutive quarterly payments in P3 — and it supports the yield of 5.16% as a figure. [P1][P3] Whether earnings cover it cannot be shown here, because the payout ratio that P9 should provide is missing.
data.would_change: A P9 payout computed against a matched earnings window would tell me whether the 5.16% is a comfortable distribution or a stretch [P1].

data.text: Against the five peers with figures, Jarir's valuation reads as mid-range on P/E at 18.43x and high on yield at 5.16% [P1]. That is a placement in the exchange's own sector classification, not a judgment of value. [P1][P5]
data.would_change: Same-date peer data and sector percentiles for valuation metrics would turn a placement into a proper ranking.

data.headline: Peers place Jarir mid-range, but that placement cannot show the valuation is supported.
data.answer:
The peer table shows where Jarir sits, and the room agrees on that much. Among the five peers reporting a P/E, Jarir's 18.43 x is above United Electronics at 10.43 x and below Aldrees at 26.07 x, Abo Moati at 33.62 x, Al-Saif at 37.3 x and SACO at 41.45 x. [P1][P5] Jarir's yield of 5.16 % is below only United Electronics at 7.65 %. [P1][P5] Al-Rumayyan reads this as mid-range on P/E and high on yield.

The room also agrees on the limits. Three of the eight peers report no P/E or yield, and Jarir's quote is dated 2026-10-13 while most peer rows are dated 2026-08-07. [P1][P5] Jarir carries no sector percentile for P/E, price-to-book, return on equity or yield, so there is no formal rank. [P2] The P9 statements are not in the pack, so Buffett could not check the 67.25 % return on equity against a denominator, Lynch could count no quarters, and Dalio could read no dated balance sheet. [P2] Dalio notes debt-to-equity of 0.0 ratio, ranked at 89.7 in its class. [P2] Alwaleed confirms dividends of 0.2 SAR for Q2 2026, but no matched payout is available to show what earnings covered them. [P3]

On the question asked, the peer comparison shows relative placement only. It does not by itself show that the valuation is supported, because the earnings, growth and returns that would justify an 18.43 x multiple cannot be seen in this pack. [P1]
